entries.haystack: bridge-doctor diagnose, fix, and manage the iris bridge/daemon system — the local compute layer that executes hive tasks (som, code_generation, etc.). use when the bridge won't start, daemon shows "stopped", tasks aren't executing, port conflicts, key mismatches, or docker container collisions. pass an action as argument (e.g., "status", "diagnose", "fix", "restart", "sync-key"). --- name: bridge-doctor description: diagnose, fix, and manage the iris bridge/daemon system — the local compute layer that executes hive tasks (som, code_generation, etc.). use when the bridge won't start, daemon shows "stopped", tasks aren't executing, port conflicts, key mismatches, or docker container collisions. pass an action as argument (e.g., "status", "diagnose", "fix", "restart", "sync-key"). allowed-tools: - read - bash - grep - glob - edit - task --- # bridge doctor — local compute debugging skill diagnose and fix issues with the iris bridge + embedded daemon system. ## arguments `$arguments` — action to perform. examples: - `/bridge-doctor status` — quick health check of bridge, daemon, and node - `/bridge-doctor diagnose` — full diagnostic (port, keys, docker, config, daemon) - `/bridge-doctor fix` — auto-fix all safe issues (stop conflicting containers, sync keys) - `/bridge-doctor restart` — kill and restart bridge in local mode - `/bridge-doctor sync-key` — push current db key to ~/.iris/config.json via bridge api - `/bridge-doctor logs` — show recent bridge/daemon output - `/bridge-doctor tasks` — list pending/running tasks on this node - `/bridge-doctor port` — check what's on port 3200 --- ## architecture quick reference ### components | component | role | location | |-----------|------|----------| | **bridge** (`index.js`) | express server on port 3200. handles cli sessions (claude, ollama, opencode), file system access, messaging bots (telegram, discord, imessage) | `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/index.js` | | **embedded daemon** | authenticates with iris-api cloud, subscribes to pusher, executes dispatched tasks. runs inside the bridge process | `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/index.js` | | **schedule registry** | local cron scheduling via `node-cron`. persists to `schedules.json`, fires scripts, reports results to cloud with offline fallback | `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/schedule-registry.js` | | **config** | api keys, pusher config, pause state | `~/.iris/config.json` | | **doctor** | diagnostic script that checks all the above | `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/doctor.js` | ### startup flow ### key files - **bridge main**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/index.js` - **daemon class**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/index.js` - **cloud client**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/cloud-client.js` - **task executor**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/task-executor.js` - **pusher client**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/pusher-client.js` - **doctor script**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/doctor.js` - **config file**: `~/.iris/config.json` - **bridge .env**: `~/.iris/bridge/.env` ### npm commands ### common failure modes #### 1. "bridge already running — attaching as monitor" + daemon=stopped **root cause**: docker container `fl-coding-agent-bridge` is occupying port 3200. the bridge process can't bind, falls back to monitor mode against the docker container (which has no daemon). **diagnosis**: **fix**: `docker stop fl-coding-agent-bridge && npm run bridge:local` **auto-fix**: in iris_local=1 mode, index.js now auto-stops the docker container on eaddrinuse. #### 2. "http 401: invalid api key" on daemon startup **root cause**: key in `~/.iris/config.json` doesn't match any node in the iris-api database. usually happens when key was regenerated via ui but config file wasn't updated. **diagnosis**: **fix**: update `~/.iris/config.json` with the correct key from the db, or use ui "connect" modal → "sync to bridge". #### 3. daemon starts but tasks never execute **check**: is the node status `busy` with old tasks? are tasks stuck in `dispatched` status? #### 4. "no node_api_key found — bridge-only mode" **root cause**: no key in env var `node_api_key` and no `~/.iris/config.json` with `node_api_key` or `local_api_key`. **fix**: register a node via the hive ui, then either: - click "connect" → "sync to bridge" in the ui - or manually add key to `~/.iris/config.json` ### config file format - `node_api_key`: used when `iris_local` is not set (production mode) - `local_api_key`: used when `iris_local=1` (local development mode) - both connect to the same daemon code, just different api targets ### bridge api endpoints (for programmatic access) ### apple mail — send emails with attachments & cc the bridge can send emails via mail.app using applescript. supports file attachments and cc recipients. **parameters:** | field | type | required | description | |-------|------|----------|-------------| | `to_email` | string | yes | recipient email address | | `to_name` | string | no | recipient display name (defaults to email) | | `cc_email` | string or string[] | no | cc recipient(s) | | `subject` | string | yes | email subject line | | `body_text` | string | yes | plain-text email body | | `attachments` | string[] | no | array of absolute file paths to attach | **laravel (bridgeservice):** **requirements:** macos with mail.app configured. bridge must be running (`npm run bridge:local`). ### backend (iris-api) endpoints | endpoint | method | auth | purpose | |----------|--------|------|---------| | `/api/v6/nodes` | get | bearer | list user's nodes (now includes `api_key`) | | `/api/v6/nodes` | post | bearer | register new node (returns key once) | | `/api/v6/nodes/{id}/regenerate-key` | post | bearer | generate new key (invalidates old) | | `/api/v6/nodes/heartbeat` | post | x-node-key | daemon heartbeat (auth by node key) | | `/api/v6/nodes/tasks` | get/post | bearer | list/create tasks | ### frontend component - **hivenoderegistry**: `fl-elon-web-ui/components/hive/hivenoderegistry.vue` - connect modal shows key directly from node data (`api_key` field) - "sync to bridge" button pushes key to local bridge via `post /api/config/key` - "regenerate key" auto-syncs to bridge after generating - **vuex store**: `fl-elon-web-ui/store/nodes.js` --- ## action implementations ### status run `npm run bridge:doctor` and summarize the output. if bridge is healthy, confirm. if issues, explain each one. ### diagnose full investigation: 1. `lsof -i :3200` — who owns the port? 2. `curl — is bridge responding? 3. `cat ~/.iris/config.json` — are keys present? 4. `docker ps --filter "publish=3200"` — docker conflict? 5. check iris-api db for node + key match 6. check daemon logs for auth errors ### fix run `npm run bridge:doctor -- --fix` for automated fixes. for key mismatches, query the db and update config. ### restart ### sync-key 1. query iris-api for the node's current `api_key` 2. push to bridge via `post 3. verify with `get ### logs ### tasks

entries.name: capture-sops-and-process-maps
entries.describe: Capture SOPs as screen recordings instead of written docs, turn them into process maps, and separate out the rules that aren't procedures at all.
entries.haystack: sop-screen-recording-capture capture sops as screen recordings instead of written docs, turn them into process maps, and separate out the rules that aren't procedures at all. --- name: capture-sops-and-process-maps description: capture sops as screen recordings instead of written docs, turn them into process maps, and separate out the rules that aren't procedures at all. version: 2 on-error: stop --- # capture sops and process maps capture a process by recording your screen while you do it, turn that into a formal process map — and catch the parts that are actually rules, not procedures, before they get miscaptured as steps. > written from two experience art / x-art team calls: the sop-capture decision on > 2026-08-24 (bloq #570, board #182224) and the rules-gap discussion on 2026-08-21 > (board #181754/#181753). read every step before running it. ## why this exists — two capture problems, not one this team hit two distinct problems while building their "company brain," and conflating them is the failure mode this playbook exists to prevent: 1. **written sops are slow and drift from reality.** the fix: record the screen while doing the work, narrate the reasoning out loud, and let an agent turn that into the formal document — instead of someone writing it up after the fact from memory. 2. **not everything that feels like an sop is a procedure.** some of what people were trying to capture had no steps, no owner running it weekly, no maturity level — it was a **rule**: a scope (where it applies), a direction (do / never), and a reason someone will otherwise argue with. filing a rule as if it were a process step loses the part that actually matters. ## the worked example that makes the distinction concrete a company description existed in two versions, ~140 words each. one mentioned a specific brand touchstone; the other didn't. - version a (with the touchstone) → fine for journalists, fine for sales and clients - version a → **never** website-facing or public-facing that's not a process — there's no sequence of steps. it's a rule: **scope** (which channel), **direction** (use it / never use it here), **reason** (context journalists and sales conversations have that a cold website visitor doesn't). a second example from the same session: a coined phrase the team wants press to use but would never put on their own website, because nobody searches a phrase they invented — same shape, different rule. **where rules like this go:** not as loose bullet points beside the main content, but as their own linked pools — e.g. a "press language" skill linking out to approved pr keywords and the pr copy folder, separate from a "marketing language" skill with its own (different, sometimes contradictory) rules. rather than writing independent rules scattered across documents, group each audience/context into its own skill, and have each skill link to its proper pool of source data. that cross-referencing structure is the point — it's what keeps rule a ("always" for sales) from silently contradicting rule b ("never" for the public site) when they're read out of context. **rule of thumb for when to split:** keep a topic in one document until it gets too big; fork a section into its own skill only when it becomes a real, distinct business component that needs its own context — not preemptively. ## the capture pipeline itself manually-written sops are slow to produce and drift from what people actually do. the team's decision: the screen recording (with narration) is the source document. a written version is an *output* generated from it afterward, not a separate authoring step someone has to remember to do. a validated real-world signal this works: one team member ran a similar context-extraction pass over their own ai chat history and email, looking for codified rules rather than routine processes — and it surfaced roughly **47 distinct rule/inconsistency findings** (small corrections made repeatedly, like avoiding overuse of a specific word) that had never been written down anywhere as an explicit rule. the value wasn't in the prose responses — it was specifically in the corrections: the small moments where a person had to fix an ai's output for a domain-specific reason. that correction *is* the rule, and it's usually invisible until someone goes looking for it. ## steps ### step:step-1 record the process walkthrough ### step:step-2 transcribe the recording ### step:step-3 separate rules from procedure before drafting the map ### step:step-4 draft the process map from what's left ### step:step-5 file rules into their own linked pool, not beside the steps ### step:step-6 human review before either output is trusted ### step:step-7 file the finished artifacts in the company brain --- ## why these steps are instructions, not commands this was authored from two live meeting discussions, not a single recorded walkthrough of one process. each step is an instruction a person or agent carries out and can check first — not a black-box automation. promote a step to `mode: shell` yourself once you know the exact command for your own transcription/ingest tooling.

entries.describe: Create branded Instagram carousel announcements from daily diary entries and ship notes. Three template types — Feature (code-heavy, editorial), Event (clean, infographic-style), and iMessage mockups. Renders 9 slides at 1080x1440 (3:4 Instagram native). Pass a topic, template type, or feature list as argument (e.g., "may update", "event song wars 3", "imessage + pulse + hive", "ugc rewards for creators").
entries.haystack: carousel-announce create branded instagram carousel announcements from daily diary entries and ship notes. three template types — feature (code-heavy, editorial), event (clean, infographic-style), and imessage mockups. renders 9 slides at 1080x1440 (3:4 instagram native). pass a topic, template type, or feature list as argument (e.g., "may update", "event song wars 3", "imessage + pulse + hive", "ugc rewards for creators"). --- name: carousel-announce description: create branded instagram carousel announcements from daily diary entries and ship notes. three template types — feature (code-heavy, editorial), event (clean, infographic-style), and imessage mockups. renders 9 slides at 1080x1440 (3:4 instagram native). pass a topic, template type, or feature list as argument (e.g., "may update", "event song wars 3", "imessage + pulse + hive", "ugc rewards for creators"). allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - agent --- # carousel announce — branded instagram carousels create polished instagram carousels for feature announcements, event promos, and product marketing. three template types, two primary brands, all at 1080x1440. ## arguments `$arguments` — topic, template type, or feature list. examples: - `/carousel-announce atlas core data backbone` — product/platform carousel - `/carousel-announce may 16th update` — feature announcement carousel - `/carousel-announce event song wars 3 dallas` — event promo carousel - `/carousel-announce ugc rewards for creators` — product feature carousel - `/carousel-announce imessage + pulse + hive` — multi-feature carousel - `/carousel-announce last 7 days` — auto-scan diary for recent highlights - `/carousel-announce imessage-demo talent pipeline` — imessage mockup slides ## brand identity (use these) two primary brands with full design token kits in the api: ### iris (brand #8) — technology/saas - **accent:** emerald `#34d399` (irish spring green) - **handle:** @heyiris.io — ⚠️ the `heyiris` x account is currently **disabled** (`iris x accounts`); only @freelabelnet is connected. posting iris content from freelabel is a brand decision, not a fallback. ask before doing it. - **logo:** ` (white cube + iris wordmark on transparent) - **tagline:** "ai business operations system" - **voice:** confident, technical but approachable, direct, no fluff - **use for:** product features, cli tools, platform capabilities, saas announcements, atlas, agents, workflows - **design tokens:** `iris brands dt get iris` ### freelabel (brand #9) — creator/music community - **accent:** bold red `#ff192c` - **handle:** @freelabelnet - **logo:** ` (red fl square icon) - **full logo:** ` - **tagline:** "the leaders in online showcasing" - **voice:** bold, street-smart, high energy, community-first - **use for:** events, creator-facing, talent pipeline, music, booking, community - **design tokens:** `iris brands dt get freelabel` ### brand selection guide | topic | brand | why | |-------|-------|-----| | atlas, agents, workflows, cli, api | `heyiris` | technical product | | affiliate program, pricing, onboarding | `heyiris` | saas feature | | model proxy, branded ai, integrations | `heyiris` | infrastructure | | events, showcases, concerts | `freelabel` | community/music | | artist profiles, booking, talent | `freelabel` | creator economy | | ugc, discovery, content rewards | `freelabel` | creator monetization | | omnichannel messaging, outreach | `heyiris` | platform capability | ## template types ### 1. feature announcement (default) **best for:** ship notes, product launches, technical features, cli tools, platform capabilities **style:** editorial variant, code snippets, cli examples, stats from real data **slide layout:** | slide | content | notes | |-------|---------|-------| | 0 | cover | `*italic accent*` headline, subtitle, author | | 1 | feature 1 | serif italic title, body, optional code block | | 2 | feature 2 | big number overlay, title, body, optional code | | 3 | code/image showcase | full code block or architecture diagram (ascii art works great) | | 4 | stats grid | 2x2 cards with real numbers | | 5 | feature 3 | pull-quote style with code | | 6 | feature 4 | bordered card with code | | 7 | checklist | actionable commands to try | | 8 | cta | headline + install command | **content rules:** - 4 tips = 4 features. if 5+, put one on slide 3 (code snippet) - tips with `code` should use real cli commands from the diary - stats should use real numbers where possible - checklist = actionable commands users can run right now - headlines support `*italic accent*` markers for the green/purple accent text - always customer-facing — no internal client names, no lead ids - ascii art diagrams in `codesnippet` look great on slide 3 (see atlas core example) - keep code blocks readable — 12-20 lines max, use comments for context **proven headline patterns:** - "your data. *one system.*" (atlas core) - "onboard clients. *zero friction.*" (atlas onboarding) - "your ai. *your brand.*" (model proxy) - "earn recurring *commissions.*" (affiliate) - "one message. *every channel.*" (omnichannel) - pattern: `[bold statement]. *[accent payoff].*` ### 2. event announcement **best for:** live events, showcases, concerts, tournaments, meetups **style:** editorial variant but no code blocks — clean text, infographic feel **brand:** usually `freelabel` (red) for events **slide layout:** | slide | content | notes | |-------|---------|-------| | 0 | cover | event name (big), city + date + venue + time, hosted by | | 1 | the format | what kind of event, how it works | | 2 | the lineup | artists, performers, speakers (names + handles) | | 3 | key takeaway | fallback slide — reuses headline (no code/image needed) | | 4 | stats grid | artists, judges, past event views, ticket price | | 5 | social proof | "last time we did this..." — past event results | | 6 | how to get in | apply, buy tickets, dm to perform | | 7 | event details | date, venue, doors, price, stream info — checklist format | | 8 | cta | "city. date. be there." — short, punchy | **content rules:** - no code blocks — leave `code` field empty on all tips - no technical jargon — speak to artists, fans, attendees - stats should highlight past success (views, attendance, tickets sold) - checklist = event logistics (date, venue, doors, price, stream) - lineup can include "tba" slots + "dm to perform" call-to-action - use real event data from `.iris/events/` json files ### 3. imessage mockup **best for:** showing conversational ux, demonstrating @heyiris commands, talent booking flows **style:** iphone imessage ui with blue/gray bubbles **rules:** - `from: "user"` = blue bubble, `from: "iris"` = gray bubble - `timestamp` only on first message (centered divider) - `highlight` = bold white on blue, accent color on gray - 4-5 messages max per mockup ## ⚠️ verify the render. it used to lie. **`iris remotion carousel` shipped a version that rendered the composition's demo content and reported success.** the shell wrapper passed props as an inline string (`--props "$json"`); remotion could not parse it, fell back to placeholder copy, and every slide read *"5 ways to grow your brand on social media"* under `done. 9 slides saved`. it also resolved a relative `-o` against the remotion package rather than your cwd, printing that same success line over an **empty directory**. both fixed in cli **v1.3.198** — props now go via a file per slide, paths are absolute, and the slide count is read from disk. two habits outlive the fix, because the failure mode here is a wrong post, not an error: 1. **open `slide-0.png` and read it before uploading anything.** if it mentions growing your brand on social media, the props did not bind. a green run is not evidence. 2. **count the files:** `ls <outdir>/*.png | wc -l` must be 9. the cost of skipping this is not a broken build — it is generic marketing filler posted under the brand, with every command reporting success. ## pipeline (all templates) ### step 1: research - **how-to recipe:** if the subject is already a published recipe, stop and use the `howto-social` playbook instead — it maps the recipe deterministically and cannot say something the recipe does not. this playbook writes copy; that one transcribes it. check `iris how-to list` first. - **feature:** scan `daily-diary/` for shipped features, extract code + stats - **event:** read `.iris/events/` json + `daily-diary/` for event data + past results - **brand kit:** check `iris brands dt get <brand>` for design tokens and voice/tone - use agent (subagent_type: explore) for broad scans ### step 2: craft props - create props object in `remotion/src/root.tsx` - follow the template for your type (feature vs event) - customer-facing copy — no internal names, no lead ids - use the brand's voice and tone from the design tokens ### step 3: register in root.tsx **important**: always 1080x1440 (3:4). never 1080x1080. ### step 4: render ### step 5: open in finder ## previous carousels (reference — all shipped) ### iris brand (heyiris) | props variable | topic | key stats | |---------------|-------|-----------| | `atlascoreplatformprops` | atlas core — unified data backbone (doc + spreadsheet + db + ai memory) | 4-in-1, 100% encrypted, rest, rag | | `irisosmayupdateprops` | may 16th update (5 features) | pulse, imessage, hive, inbox, som | | `omnichannelprops` | omnichannel messaging (6 channels) | email, dm, sms, imessage, discord, slack | | `genesispagebuilderprops` | page builder (compose + diff + rollback) | 60+ components, ai compose | | `atlasonboardingprops` | client onboarding (zero-auth flows) | 34% conversion, 11 steps, 0 auth | | `brandedaiprops` | model proxy (white-label ai) | 6 models, branded, no api keys | | `affiliateprops` | affiliate program (recurring commissions) | 15-30%, $14.85/mo, stripe connect | ### freelabel brand | props variable | topic | key stats | |---------------|-------|-----------| | `ugcrewardsprops` | ugc for creators (get paid per view) | $0.002-0.05/view, auto-payout | | `ugcbrandprops` | ugc for brands (pay per view not per post) | performance pricing, no upfront | | `talentpipelineprops` | cold dm to booked artist pipeline | 5 steps, auto-outreach | ### events | props variable | topic | key stats | |---------------|-------|-----------| | `eventannouncementprops` | song wars live 2 (dallas, may 29) | 8 artists, 5 judges, live stream | ### imessage mockups - `imessagedemo1-3` — pipeline, inbox replies, morning pulse (heyiris) - `talentmsg1-3` — artist scrape, reply catch, lineup status (freelabel) ## carousel content strategy ### what makes a good carousel post 1. **slide 0 (cover)** hooks with a bold statement — the `*italic accent*` pattern works every time 2. **slides 1-2** establish the problem or show the feature with real code 3. **slide 3** is the "wow" slide — architecture diagram, full code block, or key visual 4. **slide 4** (stats) gives social proof with hard numbers 5. **slides 5-6** go deeper on specific capabilities 6. **slide 7** (checklist) makes it actionable — "try this right now" 7. **slide 8** (cta) drives to install/signup with one line ### post categories that work | category | example topics | brand | |----------|---------------|-------| | **platform feature** | atlas, genesis, pulse, omnichannel | heyiris | | **product launch** | affiliate program, model proxy, billing | heyiris | | **how it works** | cli walkthrough, agent setup, page building | heyiris | | **client showcase** | "how x uses iris" (anonymized) | heyiris | | **event promo** | song wars, showcases, meetups | freelabel | | **creator tools** | ugc rewards, profile builder, booking | freelabel | | **talent pipeline** | outreach automation, dm sequences | freelabel | | **comparison** | "iris vs [competitor]" — show cli power | heyiris | ### posting cadence - **iris (@heyiris.io):** 2-3 carousels/week — feature ships, platform updates, how-tos - **freelabel (@freelabelnet):** 1-2 carousels/week — events, creator tools, talent stories ## key files | file | purpose | |------|---------| | `remotion/src/carousel/carouselslide.tsx` | main component + schema | | `remotion/src/carousel/editorialcarouselslide.tsx` | editorial variant | | `remotion/src/carousel/imessagemockup.tsx` | imessage mockup | | `remotion/src/carousel/eventcarouselslide.tsx` | event variant | | `remotion/src/brands.ts` | brand configs (6 brands) | | `remotion/src/root.tsx` | all carousel props + composition registry | | `daily-diary/` | feature announcement source material | | `.iris/events/` | event data (venues, lineups, dates) | | `.iris/opportunities/` | linked opportunities (skills, deadlines) | | `brands/iris-tokens.json` | iris brand kit (emerald, inter, technical voice) | | `brands/freelabel-tokens.json` | freelabel brand kit (red, montserrat, street-smart voice) | ## output conventions - feature carousels: `remotion/carousel-{feature-slug}/` - event carousels: `remotion/carousel-{event-name}/` - imessage mockups: `remotion/carousel-{topic}/imessage/` - always open finder after rendering - always show the user 2-3 rendered slides for review before finishing

entries.name: client-host-doctor
entries.describe: Diagnose and recover a down IRIS-managed client host (Azure VM + Tailscale secure-access stack) — and audit for the silent billing lapses that cause most of these outages. Use when a client says "the server is down", when RDP/tunnel access fails, or as a periodic paid-through check. Pass an action (e.g. "diagnose", "recover", "verify", "audit-billing", "run").
entries.haystack: client-host-doctor diagnose and recover a down iris-managed client host (azure vm + tailscale secure-access stack) — and audit for the silent billing lapses that cause most of these outages. use when a client says "the server is down", when rdp/tunnel access fails, or as a periodic paid-through check. pass an action (e.g. "diagnose", "recover", "verify", "audit-billing", "run"). --- name: client-host-doctor description: diagnose and recover a down iris-managed client host (azure vm + tailscale secure-access stack) — and audit for the silent billing lapses that cause most of these outages. use when a client says "the server is down", when rdp/tunnel access fails, or as a periodic paid-through check. pass an action (e.g. "diagnose", "recover", "verify", "audit-billing", "run"). allowed-tools: - read - bash - grep - glob - edit --- # client host doctor — managed client infrastructure diagnose, recover, and verify a client-facing host on the azure vm + tailscale stack. built from the **2026-08-05 `qb-host-vanguard` outage** (vanguard healthcare / bloq #531), where two independent billing lapses took down a client's quickbooks server for ~4 days and neither was detected by us — the client reported it. ## arguments `$arguments` — action to perform: - `/client-host-doctor diagnose` — full triage: is it billing, power, network, or auth? - `/client-host-doctor recover` — execute the recovery sequence in the safe order - `/client-host-doctor verify` — prove both access paths actually work - `/client-host-doctor audit-billing` — **run this proactively**; catches lapses before clients do - `/client-host-doctor run "<cmd>"` — run a command on the host without credentials --- ## the single most important lesson > **when a client says "the server is down", check billing first — not networking.** ops instinct says ping, firewall, dns, service state. on managed client infra the most common root cause is that **something stopped being paid for**. both halves of the aug 5 outage were billing: | layer | what happened | surfaced as | |---|---|---| | azure | free-trial credit exhausted | vm auto-stopped, subscription read-only | | tailscale | trial ended | host silently **logged out** of the tailnet | neither looked like a billing problem from the symptom. both were. ## the two lies this stack tells you **lie #1 — "the subscription is enabled" (it isn't writable yet).** after upgrading to pay-as-you-go the metadata flips to `enabled` immediately, but arm write operations keep failing with `readonlydisabledsubscription` for minutes afterward. don't conclude the upgrade failed. retry on a loop. **lie #2 — "the tailscale service is running" (the node is logged out).** this one cost the most time. `get-service tailscale` reported `running / automatic` while the node was completely off the tailnet, because the expired trial had **logged the node out**, not stopped the service. **a running tailscale service tells you nothing about whether the node is logged in. always check `tailscale status` for `logged out.`** the tell from the client side: `tailscale status` on your own machine shows the peer with `tx` climbing and **`rx 0`** — you transmit, nothing ever comes back — and the peer drifts `active → idle`. that pattern means *logged out*, not *unreachable*. --- ## run commands on the host with no credentials the highest-leverage technique here. `az vm run-command` executes powershell as system via the azure guest agent, authorized by **azure rbac** — no rdp session, no host password, no ssh key, no `expect` wrapper. this supersedes the older approach (an `expect` wrapper over ssh with password auth, plus `powershell -encodedcommand` base64 to survive nested quoting). it works even when the host is off the tunnel — which is exactly when you need it most. escaping note: inside a bash double-quoted `--scripts`, escape powershell `$` as `\$`. > gap: `iris hive host` still has no `run` verb (bug #179098). until it lands, use `az vm > run-command` directly. `iris hive host` only exposes setup / add-user / grant / lockdown. --- ## action: diagnose work down the stack. stop at the first thing that's wrong. ### 1. billing / subscription state — check this first | reading | meaning | |---|---| | `state: enabled`, `quotaid: payasyougo_*`, `spendinglimit: off` | healthy | | `state: warned` | **grace period — resources get deleted at the end of it.** act today | | `state: disabled` | already read-only; nothing can start until billing is fixed | | `quotaid: freetrial_*` | a ticking clock. migrate before a client depends on it | | `spendinglimit: on` | this is what auto-stops vms when credit runs out | on a free trial you **cannot** just remove the spending limit — removing it *is* the upgrade to pay-as-you-go. one action, both problems. ### 2. vm power state `provisioningstate/failed/**vmstoppedtowarnsubscription**` is unambiguous: azure stopped it for billing. the timestamp is when azure *formalized* it, **not** when service was actually lost — see "dating the outage" below. ### 3. network reachability ⚠️ if `allocation: dynamic`, a stop/start **reassigns the public ip** and every saved client rdp shortcut breaks. check this before telling anyone "reconnect the same way." (on `qb-host-vanguard` it's `static`, so the ip survived.) ### 4. tailscale — service state vs login state if that prints `logged out.` → the node needs re-auth, not a restart. go to recover step 2. also check the tailnet itself hasn't lapsed (admin console → settings → billing). tailscale bills **per user, not per device** — several machines under one account = one seat. ### 5. dating the outage — do not trust the azure stop timestamp azure's `vmstoppedtowarnsubscription` time is when it *recorded* the stop. real service loss is usually earlier. two independent signals date it properly: on aug 5 the azure stamp said 19:15 utc **aug 5**, but the last backup was **aug 1 20:53z** and tailscale last-seen was **aug 1 19:01 cdt**. actual downtime ≈ **4 days**, not hours. know the real number before a client asks — even if you choose not to volunteer it. ### 6. backups — check before declaring a data emergency **`deleteoption: delete` on the os disk says nothing about whether backups exist.** on aug 5 that flag triggered a false "data is at risk" call that had to be retracted — a recovery services vault was present the whole time with restore points ~4×/day. check the vault before escalating to the client. caveat that survives: the vault usually lives **inside the same subscription**, so it protects against vm/disk loss but **not** against the subscription being purged. --- ## action: recover **order matters — step 5 will cut off the client if done early.** 1. **fix billing.** azure portal → subscriptions → *upgrade* (free trial → pay-as-you-go, attach card). tailscale admin → billing → choose a plan. sign in as the account that *owns* the subscription — often a personal account, not the work one. 2. **start the vm**, retrying through the read-only lag: 3. **re-auth tailscale** if the host reported `logged out.`: if the node identity is still valid this re-authenticates against the new plan with **no auth key needed**. only generate an auth key (admin → settings → keys → `--authkey=`) if this fails. 4. **verify both paths** — see the verify action. do not skip to step 5 on partial success. 5. **only after the client is confirmed on the tunnel**, lock down public rdp: running this while the client is still pointed at the public ip **cuts their access again**, turning one outage into two. 6. **notify the client**, then log to the bloq and the lead. --- ## action: verify every one of these must pass. partial success is a false all-clear. **pass criteria:** `backendstate: running` · `self.online: true` · ping returns `pong` and **upgrades off the derp relay to a direct peer address** (proves real p2p, not just relayed control plane) · both `nc` succeed · `termservice: running` · the client's actual app service is running · disk not full. a `pong` that stays on `derp(...)` forever means relay-only — degraded, worth investigating. --- ## action: audit-billing **run this proactively.** it is the whole point of the playbook. both aug 5 lapses were forecast in writing over a month earlier and still nobody watched the clock. for every managed client host: 1. subscription `state` — anything other than `enabled` is an incident forming 2. `quotaid` — any `freetrial_*` under a client dependency is a dated bomb 3. `spendinglimit` — `on` means "will auto-stop when credit runs out" 4. backup `lastbackuptime` — **stale backups are a leading indicator**; on aug 5 they went stale 4 days before anyone noticed the outage 5. tailscale plan status and seat count 6. **who pays?** client infra on a personal card is its own risk — it lapses when personal billing lapses, and it isn't recoverable by the client if you're unavailable anything found here goes to the owning bloq and the attached leads' pulse. > open product gap — bug **#179094**: iris provisions and tracks these hosts but models them > as connectivity only, with no notion of who pays, burn rate, or funding expiry. wanted: > alert on `state != enabled`, on trial quota with a projected exhaustion date, and on stale > `lastbackuptime`, surfaced on the pulse of leads attached to the bloq. --- ## action: run no credentials required — rbac only. see the technique section above. --- ## client communication restore service **before** messaging. then be specific about cause and about what stops it recurring — vagueness invites follow-up questions. template that worked: > hi <name> — quick update: the <system> is back online and fully operational. the issue was > on our end, with the cloud subscription hosting it. that's now moved onto a permanent paid > plan so it won't happen again. nothing was lost — the backups are intact and <app> is > running normally. <user> can reconnect whenever they're ready. sorry for the disruption. notes: name the cause (preempts "what happened?"); "permanent paid plan" is the line that actually reassures; confirm data integrity explicitly — it's their first unspoken worry. whether to state duration is the account owner's call, but **know the real number** (see "dating the outage") before you write anything. --- ## logging log to the owning **bloq** (running incident record) and to the **lead notes** of every affected contact — they surface on `iris leads pulse`, so the next person to touch the relationship sees the outage without digging. post a correction as its own entry when an earlier call turns out wrong (e.g. the false "no backups" alarm), rather than quietly editing. the correction is often the reusable lesson. ⚠️ `add-item` takes **two positionals** (`<bloq-id> <list-id>`) and the list id must be **numeric** — there is no `--list` flag, and `--title` alone fails with a confusing yargs error (bug #179097). `iris bloqs items <id>` shows `list_name` but not `list_id`. --- ## where the host-specific details live **deliberately not in this file.** this playbook is generated into `.claude/skills/<name>/skill.md`, which is **committed to the repo** — while `.iris/playbooks/` is gitignored. anything written here ends up in version control. per-host specifics — addresses, resource groups, account names, and especially **known-open weaknesses** — belong in the owning bloq, which is access-controlled. a file that pairs a public ip with "rdp is internet-facing and the admin password is weak" is an attack map, and for a healthcare client it is exactly the kind of thing that must not sit in a git history. for a given engagement, read the bloq for: resource group / vm name, public and tailnet addresses, backup vault, tailnet and plan, vm size and monthly cost, and the current open-risk list. - vanguard / quickbooks secure host → **bloq #531** (vpn iris hive); attached leads carry the incident history in their notes. **never** put host passwords, auth keys, public ips paired with weaknesses, or unresolved vulnerabilities in this playbook, the generated skill, the repo, or a public bloq item.

entries.name: compliance-review
entries.describe: Find the compliance gap before an auditor does, not the other way around. Figures out which regimes actually apply — HIPAA, SOC 2, SOC 1, FDA where relevant — before checking anything, separates what's actually enforceable today from what's only proposed, and points to the exact file and line instead of a vague sense that something's probably fine. Pass the scope as argument.
entries.haystack: compliance-review find the compliance gap before an auditor does, not the other way around. figures out which regimes actually apply — hipaa, soc 2, soc 1, fda where relevant — before checking anything, separates what's actually enforceable today from what's only proposed, and points to the exact file and line instead of a vague sense that something's probably fine. pass the scope as argument. --- name: compliance-review description: find the compliance gap before an auditor does, not the other way around. figures out which regimes actually apply — hipaa, soc 2, soc 1, fda where relevant — before checking anything, separates what's actually enforceable today from what's only proposed, and points to the exact file and line instead of a vague sense that something's probably fine. pass the scope as argument. allowed-tools: - read - grep - glob - bash - agent - task --- # compliance review — regulatory audit of actual code audit a code path against the compliance regimes that **actually bind it**, and report findings a person could hand to an auditor: each one anchored to a file, a line, and the specific rule it implicates. ## arguments `$arguments` — the scope to audit. a path, a service, a route group, a feature, or a regime. - `/compliance-review the case-file upload path` - `/compliance-review every route that can reach phi` - `/compliance-review the model proxy and the agent tool layer` - `/compliance-review the payout ledger and stripe billing` (soc 1 territory) - `/compliance-review --regime hipaa <service>` --- ## step 0 — determine which regimes bind. do this first. a compliance report that audits a regime which does not apply is noise, and noise is how the findings that *do* matter get ignored. establish scope before checking anything, and **state the determination in the report**. | regime | binds when | how to decide | |---|---|---| | **hipaa** | the code can store, transmit, or process ephi, or is a business associate of a covered entity | decide **per-path, not per-repo** — a healthcare or phi-bearing product line can bind while the rest of the platform does not. | | **soc 2** | you assert security/availability/confidentiality controls to customers | **yes** — it is a customer trust commitment, not a law | | **soc 1** | your software affects a **customer's financial reporting** | **only** for billing, credit ledger, payouts, invoicing, revenue recognition | | **fda** | the product is a medical device, samd, or a "cyber device"; or keeps records a predicate rule requires | **no by default — you must prove it applies** | ### the fda gate do not emit fda findings unless one of these is true. if none are, write one line saying fda was assessed and does not apply, and move on. 1. **21 cfr part 11** — applies only to electronic records/signatures kept to satisfy a *predicate rule* (an fda regulation requiring the record). clinical, manufacturing, or submission records. **ordinary healthcare-admin records are not part 11 records.** injury chronologies, demand packages and case files are legal/claims artifacts, not fda predicate records. 2. **21 cfr part 820 (qmsr)** — device manufacturers. as of **2 feb 2026** part 820 incorporates **iso 13485:2016** by reference and is called the qmsr; the old qsr language is gone. only relevant if a device is being made. 3. **fd&c act §524b** — "cyber devices": software + internet connectivity + plausible vulnerability, in a *premarket submission*. requires a cybersecurity plan, patchable design, and a **machine-readable sbom (cyclonedx or spdx)**. a submission can be refused outright for an inadequate sbom. if the answer is "this is a healthcare-adjacent saas, not a device maker", say so plainly. that is the correct finding, and it is far more useful than fabricated part 11 gaps. --- ## step 1 — the evidence contract this is the part that makes the report worth anything. **a check that could not run is not a check that passed.** every item lands in exactly one of four states, and the third is never silently merged into the second: - **pass** — verified in code, with file:line. - **fail** — verified absent or wrong, with file:line. - **not verified** — could not be established, *with the reason* (no access, needs a prod env var, needs a policy document, requires an org answer). - **n/a** — the regime does not bind this path (say which gate excluded it). a compliance report whose unverifiable items quietly read as green is worse than no report, because someone will rely on it. if you did not read the code, do not score the control. **separate what is enforceable from what is proposed.** two buckets, always: - **required today** — the hipaa security rule as it currently stands (45 cfr §164.308/310/312/314/316), where "addressable" means *implement or document why not* — it does **not** mean optional. - **proposed / prepare** — the **hipaa security rule nprm published 6 jan 2025** would make encryption at rest and in transit, mfa, network segmentation, asset inventories, and annual business-associate certification **mandatory** by removing the addressable/required distinction. **it is not final.** the comment period closed 7 mar 2025; omb's unified agenda (rin 0945-aa22) targets **july 2027**, pushed back from spring 2026. if finalised, there would be 240 days to comply (60 to effective + 180 more). flagging a proposed requirement as a present-day violation is the same error as reporting a source that was never searched as a source that found nothing. label the bucket. --- ## regime a — hipaa audit against the **security rule technical safeguards (§164.312)** first, because those are the ones that live in code. | § | control | what to actually check | |---|---|---| | §164.312(a)(1) | **access control** | unique user identification; is every phi read scoped to an authenticated, authorised subject? emergency access; automatic logoff; encryption/decryption. | | §164.312(b) | **audit controls** | is there a record of *who read which phi record, when*? read access, not just writes. is it append-only and outside the reach of the app's own delete paths? | | §164.312(c)(1) | **integrity** | can ephi be altered or destroyed without detection? | | §164.312(d) | **person or entity authentication** | is the identity claim actually proven, or inferred from something spoofable? | | §164.312(e)(1) | **transmission security** | tls everywhere phi moves — including service-to-service and to third-party apis. | then §164.308 administrative safeguards **that have a code footprint**: workforce access management (termination → token revocation), information-system activity review (is anyone reading the audit log?), and **§164.308(b) business associate contracts** — which in code means: *can a phi context reach a vendor you have no baa with?* also check **§164.502(b) minimum necessary** — does the query pull the whole record where a single field would do? ### adjacent confidentiality regimes phi is rarely the only sensitive class in one codebase. if the same paths also carry **legal-confidential** material (privileged communications, work product, claims files), **financial** records, or **educational** records under ferpa, note that a hipaa-clean path can still breach a different duty — and that legal privilege has no "addressable" tier. name the class per path: `phi`, `legal-confidential`, `financial`, `pii`, `public`. a single mixed store that cannot tell you which class a row belongs to is itself the finding. ### the de-identification question if the system claims data is de-identified, verify which method: **safe harbor** (§164.514(b)(2), all 18 identifier categories removed) or **expert determination** (§164.514(b)(1)). "we stripped the name" is neither. safe harbor includes dates more precise than year, zip beyond the first three digits under population thresholds, device identifiers, and full-face photos. --- ## regime b — soc 2 soc 2 is an attestation against the aicpa **trust services criteria**, examined under ssae 18. **security (the common criteria, cc1–cc9) is the only mandatory category**; availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy are included only if the organisation scoped them in. check which categories the report actually covers before auditing against all five. the code-visible criteria: - **cc6 — logical and physical access.** provisioning, de-provisioning, least privilege, credential management, encryption. this is where most code findings land. - **cc7 — system operations.** can you *detect* a problem? monitoring, alerting, incident identification. a control nobody would notice failing is a finding. - **cc8 — change management.** are changes authorised, tested, and traceable? migrations, deploys, feature flags. - **cc5 / cc9 — control activities and risk mitigation**, including vendor risk. - **processing integrity (pi1)** — if scoped: is processing complete, valid, accurate, timely? this is the criterion that catches "the job silently dropped 40% of rows". - **confidentiality (c1)** — retention and disposal, not just access. for a **type ii** report the question is not "does the control exist" but **"did it operate for the whole period"** — so a control added last week does not satisfy a twelve-month window. note the gap rather than marking it green. --- ## regime c — soc 1 only audit this if the code affects a **customer's financial reporting**. soc 1 (ssae 18 **at-c 320**) tests *control objectives* the organisation defines, not a fixed criteria list — so the audit is: are the stated objectives met, and are they the right objectives? for this platform that means the money paths, and nothing else: - billing and subscription state, usage metering, invoice generation - the credit balance / `credittransaction` ledger, and any second ledger that has not been unified with it - payouts, bounties, gig/clip settlement - stripe connect flows and charge-mode configuration the recurring soc 1 finding shape in code is **a ledger that can drift**: two sources of truth for a balance, a write that is not idempotent, a retry that can double-pay, a total computed at read time from rows that can be deleted. check completeness and accuracy of the *record*, and whether an unauthorised or duplicate transaction would be detectable after the fact. --- ## regime d — fda (only past the step 0 gate) **21 cfr part 11 (§11.10)** — for records that satisfy a predicate rule: - **(e) audit trail** — computer-generated, automatic, time-stamped, tamper-evident, capturing user identity, action, timestamp, and **old vs new values**. no user, *including an administrator*, may alter an entry. retained as long as the record itself and available for inspection. - **(a) validation** — the system is validated for accuracy, reliability, consistent intended performance, and **the ability to discern invalid or altered records**. - **(d) access limited to authorised individuals**; **(g)** authority checks; **(k)** controls over documentation. - subpart c — electronic signature components, uniqueness, and non-transferability. **qmsr (21 cfr 820, effective 2 feb 2026)** — iso 13485:2016 incorporated by reference plus fda supplemental requirements in subparts a and b. software design controls, dhf/dhr equivalents. note: fda does **not** require iso 13485 certification, and holding one does not exempt from inspection. **§524b** — cybersecurity plan, patchable-by-design, and a machine-readable **sbom in cyclonedx or spdx** covering commercial, open-source and off-the-shelf components, plus a plan for monitoring their known vulnerabilities. --- ## failure patterns that survive a checklist check these explicitly. every one has been true in a real system, and none is visible to a checklist that greps for the word "encrypt". 1. **a phi gate wired to only some routes.** a codebase can ship real phi-rejection middleware — regexes for ssn/mrn/icd-10/dea/npi, returning 422 on any request carrying phi — and register it on only a subset of routes, missing precisely the ones that carry clinical data into an agent loop. **verify the route list; the middleware's existence is not coverage.** when a stated "we never process phi" posture and the product's actual behaviour contradict each other in code, that contradiction is itself the top finding — resolve it deliberately rather than leaving a policy the product violates. 2. **safety that depends on an env var being set in prod.** phi storage separation is frequently correct *only if* a records-disk variable is actually set, where the fallback default is local disk and the generic "cloud" disk is a **public** bucket. a default that fails open is a finding even when the deployed value happens to be right — check the default and the deployed value, and report them as two separate lines. 3. **no baa-aware model routing.** `modelproxycontroller` centralises provider keys server-side (good) but a phi context can reach whichever provider the agent picked. **openai is not baa-covered here; google vertex is (ai studio is not); tailscale is not.** the check is: *from a phi context, is there any reachable provider without a baa?* also check whether de-identification happens before the model call at all. 4. **classification axes collapsed into one.** atlas treats `contains_phi`, `is_gated` and `is_sensitive` as **three independent axes**. merging any two leaves phi publicly readable. verify they are still independent and that inheritance only ever *restricts*, never relaxes. 5. **enforcement shipped before a write surface existed.** a control can be real, deployed, and decorative — guarding a path nothing uses yet. ask what actually exercises the control today. 6. **a "shipped" fix that was never deployed.** this repo has a documented case of a phi blind-index fix recorded as shipped and never released. **confirm the running commit**, do not infer it from a merge. `scripts/deployed.sh <service>` reads `railway_git_commit_sha`. never grep for a symbol to confirm a deploy — it reports success whenever the symbol already existed. 7. **field-level stripping as the only defence.** `appdataservice` strips fields tagged `visibility: private|phi` from dashboard payloads (default-deny, good). check whether any path bypasses that serializer — a raw query, an export, a webhook, an agent tool. 8. **audit logs for writes but not reads.** hipaa §164.312(b) is about *access*. a log that only records mutations cannot answer "who looked at this patient's file". --- ## output format lead with the scope determination, then the findings. one table, most severe first. **severity** reflects exposure, not effort: critical = phi or funds reachable by an unauthorised party, or a record an auditor would call falsified. high = a required control absent. medium = present but incomplete. low = hygiene. then: ### required today numbered, each with the remediation and the file it belongs in. ### proposed — prepare, not yet enforceable the 2025 nprm items, clearly labelled as not currently required. ### not verified every item, with what specifically is needed to close it. **this section must never be empty for a real audit** — if it is, you have almost certainly marked something green that you did not check. ### questions only a human can answer baa status, scoped tsc categories, whether a soc 1 objective exists at all, whether anyone reads the audit log. --- ## research protocol before writing anything: 1. **read the routes.** middleware existence proves nothing; the route registration is the evidence. list the routes that reach the data and which middleware each carries. 2. **trace one record end to end** — request → controller → service → storage → any third party. compliance failures live at the seams, not in the middle of files. 3. **check the default, not just the deployed value.** a config that is safe only when an env var is set is a finding. 4. **confirm what is running.** for anything reported as already fixed, verify the deployed commit rather than the merge. 5. **read the existing compliance material before re-deriving it.** most teams already have a gap analysis, a compliance status doc, or a security ledger. find it first. note that such material is often deliberately gitignored because it contains phi or client detail under no baa — **read it for grounding, and never copy its contents, client names, or bucket names into a committed or published artifact.** this playbook is one such artifact. 6. **never paste phi, secrets, or client-identifying data into the report.** cite file:line instead. the report itself is a disclosure surface. do not speculate about code you have not read. if a control cannot be located, that is not verified, not fail — and not pass. --- ## what this is not this produces an engineering assessment of code against published requirements. it is **not** a legal opinion, not a hipaa risk analysis under §164.308(a)(1)(ii)(a) (which is an organisational exercise covering people and physical safeguards), and not a soc report — only a licensed cpa firm can issue one. say so in the output when someone might mistake it for any of those.

entries.name: content-growth-strategy
entries.describe: Every marketing channel eventually stops working — the founders who survive that are the ones who knew why it worked in the first place. A field-tested framework for finding a growth channel, telling real signal from noise while you scale, and designing your company so the good decisions happen automatically instead of by heroics.
entries.haystack: content-growth-strategy every marketing channel eventually stops working — the founders who survive that are the ones who knew why it worked in the first place. a field-tested framework for finding a growth channel, telling real signal from noise while you scale, and designing your company so the good decisions happen automatically instead of by heroics. --- name: content-growth-strategy description: every marketing channel eventually stops working — the founders who survive that are the ones who knew why it worked in the first place. a field-tested framework for finding a growth channel, telling real signal from noise while you scale, and designing your company so the good decisions happen automatically instead of by heroics. version: 1 industries: - marketing - growth - content-strategy - agency args: business: type: string required: false description: what you're growing — a product, an agency, a channel you're currently betting on — in a sentence. allowed-tools: - read - write --- # content & growth strategy **source:** this is a distillation of hiten shah's thinking — founder of crazy egg and kissmetrics, and an early architect of content-led marketing — from a public interview (youtu.be/qua3pzrlo4a). the frameworks below are his; this playbook generalizes and organizes them so you can run them against your own business. where a claim is his opinion rather than a provable fact, treat it as an experienced operator's view worth weighing, not a settled result. ## arguments `$arguments` — what you're growing: a product, a service, or the channel you're currently betting on. --- ## 1. spend discipline depends on where the money came from money you raised and money you made are not interchangeable, even when the number is the same. raised money lets you spend ahead of revenue — someone else is betting the business will grow into the spend. money you made yourself, you cannot spend ahead of revenue, because there's nothing behind it if it doesn't work. that difference shapes *early*-stage decisions specifically — how fast you spend, how much runway you protect, how much you can afford to be wrong. it stops mattering once the business is generating real revenue and has to manage a real balance sheet either way. if you're deciding whether to raise or self-fund, don't ask "which is better" — ask **"how far can i get on what i already have, because the further you get before you take outside money, the more the business is still fully yours to decide."** ## 2. content is king — context only informs it the claim isn't that data and audience research don't matter. it's that they're not the thing that reaches anyone. content — anything meant to be read, watched, or heard, coming from a person, a brand, or a business — is what makes actual contact with an audience. research and analysis inform what you make; they are not, themselves, the thing anyone experiences. the practical test: if you're spending more time gathering context than producing the content that context is supposed to inform, you've inverted the priority. **work backwards from the last mile** — the actual post, page, or message a person sees — and ask what informs it, not the other way around. ## 3. channels are secrets — and the tactic is half of it people who understand a channel rarely tell you the whole thing, and a channel by itself is usually not the secret — **the channel plus the specific tactic** is. knowing "content marketing works" tells you nothing; knowing exactly how a specific company used a specific channel with a specific tactic, at a specific moment, tells you something you can actually test. this has a sharper edge than "try lots of channels." **every channel eventually decays** — it gets discovered, copied, and commoditized. the skill that matters isn't finding a channel, it's building the muscle to notice decay early and go find the next one before you're stuck. and when something does work, **you have to know why it worked, in detail** — because if you got lucky and don't understand the mechanism, you can't repeat it once it stops working or once the person who made it work leaves. getting lucky without understanding why is the same as not having found anything at all. ## 4. data-informed, not data-driven "data-driven" implies the data makes the call. in practice, data tells you what happened, not always what you should do next — especially when you have real conviction about something the data can't yet see (a new channel, a new product angle, timing nobody has measured yet). **be informed by data. don't outsource the decision to it.** the failure mode on one side is ignoring data that's telling you something isn't working; the failure mode on the other side is refusing to try anything the data can't already justify. both are avoiding a real decision. ## 5. design the environment, not just the culture culture is what people say a company is like. **environment is the actual structure and process that determines what happens** — and it's the stronger lever, because you can shape it deliberately while culture mostly just accumulates. the concrete example: one team built its core engineering discipline — plan thoroughly before writing code, get it reviewed, revise — directly into hiring. a candidate's take-home wasn't a coding test; it was a two-page plan, scored, discussed with the hiring manager, revised, and scored again. candidates experienced the actual environment they'd be working in *before* they were hired into it, not a values conversation about it. **apply this by asking**: what is the one process or structural decision that, if you got it right, would make good outcomes the default instead of something you have to personally enforce every time? build that into how people join and work, not into a values statement. ## 6. the reality check some of this is just uncertainty tolerance, and it's worth saying plainly rather than dressing it up: most decisions in a growing business will feel like they cost something real, most early wins won't feel like wins, and the plan you're most confident in will get blown up more than once. that isn't a sign you're doing it wrong — **founders who last aren't braver, they've just stopped waiting for clarity that was never coming.** if you need constant reassurance before you act, or you need everyone to agree with you before you make a call, that's worth knowing about yourself before you're relying on it under real pressure. --- ## how to actually use this pick the section that's live for you right now — usually it's #3 (a channel that's decaying and you don't know what's next) or #5 (you're scaling past the point where you can personally enforce quality). don't try to apply all six at once; this is a set of lenses, not a checklist to clear in order. if you're working with an iris onboarding specialist or agent on this, hand them the business description from `$arguments` and section 3 or 5 specifically — those are the two with the clearest next action (audit your current channel's decay stage, or design one process into your hiring/onboarding).

entries.name: create-profile
entries.describe: Create profiles and composable landing pages for real-world clients. Handles the full pipeline — profile creation, products, services, articles, and a matching landing page. Pass a client name, use case, or "help" as argument.
entries.haystack: create-profile create profiles and composable landing pages for real-world clients. handles the full pipeline — profile creation, products, services, articles, and a matching landing page. pass a client name, use case, or "help" as argument. --- name: create-profile description: create profiles and composable landing pages for real-world clients. handles the full pipeline — profile creation, products, services, articles, and a matching landing page. pass a client name, use case, or "help" as argument. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- # create profile — client profiles & composable pages create complete client profiles with products, services, articles, videos, and optional composable landing pages. based on real-world use cases and client requests. ## arguments `$arguments` — client name, use case type, or action. examples: - `/create-profile "ash moore" storefront` — create a product storefront profile - `/create-profile "jane doe" artist` — create an artist/creative profile - `/create-profile "abc detailing" services` — create a services-only profile - `/create-profile "company name" event-vendor` — vendor selling at events - `/create-profile help` — show available profile types and options - `/create-profile list` — list all existing profile seeders ## profile types | type | description | creates | |------|-------------|---------| | `artist` | creative / performer / talent | profile + services + articles + videos | | `storefront` | product seller / e-commerce | profile + products + landing page | | `services` | service provider / contractor | profile + services | | `event-vendor` | pop-up vendor / event seller | profile + products + landing page | | `brand` | brand / company presence | profile + products + services + articles + landing page | | `custom` | mix and match (interactive) | user chooses what to include | ## steps ### 1. gather client information ask the user for the following (skip what's already provided in arguments): **required:** - client name (display name) - profile slug (url-friendly, e.g., `moore-life`) - profile type (from table above) - brief bio/description **optional (ask based on type):** - products (name, description, price, tags) - services (name, description, tags) - social handles (instagram, tiktok, twitter, youtube) - contact info (email, phone) - photo url - website url - owner user id (default: 193) - whether to create a landing page at `/p/{slug}` ### 2. create the profile seeder create a new artisan command at: **critical patterns to follow** (from `seedbrookerizzutoprofile.php`): **command signature pattern:** **required imports:** ### 3. create products (if applicable) product fields: ### 4. create services (if applicable) service fields: ### 4b. create links (if applicable) links are stored as json on the profile record itself (not a separate table): ### 4c. create events (if applicable) ### 4d. create funding packages (if applicable) recurring membership/support tiers (fan funding — direct support for the profile owner): ### 4e. create programs / communities (if applicable) programs are standalone community/membership entities with their own pricing tiers. unlike funding packages (direct support), programs are full communities with enrollment, content access, and stripe billing. **funding packages vs programs:** - **funding packages** (`fanfundingpackage`) — simple recurring support tiers tied to a profile (like patreon). table: `users_profiles_funding_packages`. - **programs** (`program` + `programpackage`) — full communities with enrollment, content access, stripe billing, email lists, and workflows. table: `programs` + `program_packages`. ### 5. create landing page (if applicable) for storefronts and brands, also create a composable page seeder at: **available component types** (from componentrenderer.vue — only use these): | component | use for | |-----------|---------| | `hero` | page header with title, subtitle, cta buttons, background gradient | | `skillsgrid` | feature grid with icons and descriptions | | `gettingstartedsteps` | numbered steps / how-it-works | | `comparisoncards` | side-by-side cards with bullet points | | `textblock` | markdown text content | | `portfoliogrid` | grid of items with title + description | | `buttoncta` | standalone call-to-action button | | `codeblock` | code snippet display | | `callout` | highlighted callout box | | `sitenavigation` | top navigation bar | | `statscounter` | animated stat counters | | `featuregrid` | feature cards with icons | | `benefitssection` | benefits with descriptions | | `videoblock` | embedded video | | `featureiconsgrid` | icon-based feature grid | | `communitycta` | cta with community focus | | `sitefooter` | page footer | | `agentexamples` | example interactions | | `quoteblock` | testimonial / quote | | `accordionfeatures` | expandable feature list | **landing page pattern:** **page json structure:** ### 6. run the seeder after creating the command file, run it: ### 7. verify ## reference implementations - **artist profile**: `fl-api/app/console/commands/seedbrookerizzutoprofile.php` - **landing page**: `fl-api/app/console/commands/seedreachrlandingpage.php` - **generic creator**: `fl-api/app/console/commands/createprofilecommand.php` (json template based) - **page components**: `fl-elon-web-ui/components/profile/builder/componentrenderer.vue` ## common pitfalls 1. **`profile_id` must use `$profile->pk`** (integer auto-increment), not `$profile->id` (string slug). this is the #1 source of bugs. 2. **commands are auto-discovered** — just place the file in `app/console/commands/` and it works. no kernel registration needed. 3. **always clear profile caches** after creation (both by pk and id slug). 4. **`reference_no` on products** — may need to be generated if the column is not null. check if `referenceidgenerator::generateproductreferenceno()` is needed. 5. **existing records** — always check for existing profile/products before creating. use `--force` flag pattern. 6. **landing page ctas** — for sub-brand saas pages, use ` for profile storefronts, link to `/@{slug}`. 7. **font awesome icons** — use `fas fa-{icon}` format in component props (e.g., `fas fa-shopping-bag`). ## example: event vendor (product storefront) this is a common real-world use case — someone selling products at events who needs a profile page and a landing page. **profile:** `/@moore-life` — shows products for purchase **landing:** `/p/moore-life` — marketing page driving traffic to the profile products would include inventory with prices, descriptions, and tags. the landing page would use hero + skillsgrid (product highlights) + buttoncta (link to profile).

entries.name: creative-value-migration
entries.describe: The bid form that's charged agencies for 70 years breaks the moment AI makes execution nearly free — hours times rate hits zero even though the client still owes you real money. A framework for finding where the value actually went, with a historical precedent (Xerox did this exact transition once already) for how to reprice around it.
entries.haystack: creative-value-migration the bid form that's charged agencies for 70 years breaks the moment ai makes execution nearly free — hours times rate hits zero even though the client still owes you real money. a framework for finding where the value actually went, with a historical precedent (xerox did this exact transition once already) for how to reprice around it. --- name: creative-value-migration description: the bid form that's charged agencies for 70 years breaks the moment ai makes execution nearly free — hours times rate hits zero even though the client still owes you real money. a framework for finding where the value actually went, with a historical precedent (xerox did this exact transition once already) for how to reprice around it. version: 1 industries: - marketing - agency - production args: business: type: string required: false description: what you sell — editing, design, production, a specific creative service — in a sentence. allowed-tools: - read - write --- # where creative value goes when execution is free **source:** this distills a conversation between two creative-industry operators — one a longtime broadcast/motion designer and agency owner identified as steve — recorded publicly (youtu.be/wkgi7uz--2e). the five-beats framework and the historical parallels below are theirs; this organizes them into something you can apply to your own pricing. ## arguments `$arguments` — what you actually sell: editing, design, production, a specific creative service. the framework applies to any of them; the specifics change. --- ## 1. the problem, stated plainly the traditional agency bid form is rows and columns: time × rate × days = what you owe me. it's worked for a century because execution always took real time, and clients understood the language well enough to argue about it. ai collapses the time variable toward zero for a growing share of execution work — and **zero times any rate is still zero.** the bid form doesn't break loudly; it just quietly stops justifying the number you need to charge, even though the value you deliver hasn't gone to zero at all. ## 2. five beats of every technology disruption in a creative field this has happened before — repeatedly — and it has a shape: 1. **a technology democratizes access.** four-color printing, desktop publishing, cheap video — each time, a skill that used to require rare, expensive tools becomes available to far more people. 2. **democratized access produces a creative revolution.** more people making things is, on balance, genuinely good — it moves culture forward, and most people's careers were built on riding one of these waves. 3. **more supply becomes a glut**, and **value migrates toward whatever stays scarce.** the thing that got democratized (the tool, the technique) stops being the value — because everyone has it now. 4. **incumbent organizations defend yesterday's monetization**, not because they're wrong about the technology, but because they're structurally rewarded for protecting this quarter's revenue model. this is the opening: whoever is willing to actually reprice around the new reality moves before the organizations that can't afford to. 5. **access to the tool is not the advantage.** everyone having the same ai model available to them doesn't make them equally good with it — "my mom doesn't take better photos on her iphone than she did with anything else." the tool being democratized is exactly why it stops being what you charge for. **apply this now:** name which beat your specific service is in. if you're still charging for something that's fully in beat 3 (commoditized, glut, no longer scarce), that's the line item that needs to change first — not your whole business model. ## 3. what actually stays scarce: the decision, not the output copyright law is a useful, literal test here: ai-generated work isn't copyrightable because copyright protects a *human's creative decisions*, not an output by itself. that legal fact points at the real answer to "what are we still being paid for": **the decisions — what to make, for whom, and why — not the execution of making it.** the concrete example worth remembering: a piece of key art for a major film franchise, described by someone who's done the work as genuinely not great artwork on its own terms — but it was exactly right for the specific job it had to do (reach a specific audience segment the studio needed without giving away plot details the core fanbase already knew). **the value wasn't in execution quality. it was in the decision about what the piece needed to accomplish, made by someone who understood the actual objective.** that decision-making is not what ai automates, even as it automates more and more of the execution around it. ## 4. there's real precedent for repricing around collapsed execution time — xerox already did it when photocopying arrived, it didn't just speed up an existing task — it collapsed the time variable in a workflow that used to require real materials and real labor. xerox didn't try to keep billing by time-and-materials for something that no longer had meaningful time or materials in it. **they repriced by the actual unit of value delivered — per page** — because that was the thing that still scaled with what the customer got, even after execution time dropped to nearly nothing. this is the pattern to copy: when a technology shift removes the variable your price used to be built on (hours, in most creative work), **find the unit that still scales with the value the client actually receives**, and price against that instead. it might be per-deliverable, per result, per unit of reach or conversion the work produces — the specific unit depends on your business (see `price-your-business`, step 4, for the general method of finding your real variable cost/value driver). ## 5. the client conversation this actually requires the hard part isn't the pricing math — it's that your client has spent decades reading your old bid form fluently, and the new one requires a shared language you don't have yet. two moves that help: - **don't wait for a fee-free pitch to prove your value, then bill hourly on the win.** if execution now costs you a fraction of what it used to, you're in a much stronger position to ask for a stake in the outcome instead — you can afford to invest more upfront in exchange for performance-based upside, because the work itself costs you less to produce. - **agree on the metric before you start**, not after. if value is now tied to performance (conversions, retention, reach) instead of hours worked, the client needs to agree on what's being measured before the work happens — otherwise you're back to arguing about hours after the fact, on a bid form that no longer holds up. --- ## how to use this start with section 1 — write down, honestly, which of your current billable line items are already at or near zero execution time. those are the ones that need a new pricing unit now, not eventually. everything else in this playbook is about finding that unit and having the conversation that gets a client to agree to it.

entries.name: delete-everything-keep-graph
entries.describe: Explain to a client, in five minutes, why an AI system works the way it does instead of the way normal software does. Andrej Karpathy's framework for the three eras of programming — instructions, trained weights, and now plain English — plus the one architectural bet that replaced years of complexity with a single idea and hasn't been beaten since. The fastest way to make someone stop treating an AI product like a website with extra steps.
