entries.haystack: delete-everything-keep-graph explain to a client, in five minutes, why an ai system works the way it does instead of the way normal software does. andrej karpathy's framework for the three eras of programming — instructions, trained weights, and now plain english — plus the one architectural bet that replaced years of complexity with a single idea and hasn't been beaten since. the fastest way to make someone stop treating an ai product like a website with extra steps. --- name: delete-everything-keep-graph description: explain to a client, in five minutes, why an ai system works the way it does instead of the way normal software does. andrej karpathy's framework for the three eras of programming — instructions, trained weights, and now plain english — plus the one architectural bet that replaced years of complexity with a single idea and hasn't been beaten since. the fastest way to make someone stop treating an ai product like a website with extra steps. version: 1 industries: - marketing - agency - education args: audience: type: string required: false description: who you're explaining this to — a client, a new hire, an investor — in a sentence. allowed-tools: - read - write --- # "delete everything, keep graph" — andrej karpathy **source:** this distills a public stanford lecture by andrej karpathy (ex-openai, ex-tesla autopilot, back at openai) — youtu.be/xdbpcm4ygye, titled *"delete everything, keep graph."* the three-era programming framework and the architecture history below are his; this organizes them for the specific job of explaining ai to someone who isn't already an engineer. ## arguments `$arguments` — who you're explaining this to (a client, a new hire, an investor), so the examples can be pitched at the right level. --- ## 0. the move that produced everything you're using today: deletion, not addition before the architecture behind modern ai existed, the field's approach to machine translation was a large, carefully engineered system — a bidirectional recurrent network, a separate encoder and decoder, and a small attention component bolted on to help them communicate. it worked, but it was complicated, and the complexity was assumed to be necessary. then a 2017 paper asked a different question: what if the small attention piece is the part that's actually doing the work, and everything else is scaffolding you could remove? they deleted the recurrent network entirely and kept only attention. the paper's own conclusion, almost word for word: **delete everything, keep attention.** attention lets every element in a sequence directly communicate with every other element — you can picture it as a graph, where each token is a node passing messages to the others — which is where the video's title comes from. what makes this worth knowing, independent of the engineering: **that 2017 architecture, largely unchanged, is still what runs gpt-scale models today.** years of people trying to improve on it have mostly failed to find something that sticks. the lesson generalizes past ai: the breakthrough wasn't adding more machinery, it was correctly identifying which one piece of the existing machinery actually mattered and deleting the rest. --- ## 1. software 1.0 — you write the instructions this is programming as it's existed for 70 years: a person writes exact instructions, and the computer follows them precisely. it's gotten us everything from spreadsheets to operating systems. it has one hard limit — **some problems can't be reduced to explicit instructions at all.** nobody can write a step-by-step rule for "recognize a cat in a photo" — a cat can appear in too many forms for any rule to cover. same problem with self-driving, or playing chess well enough to beat a grandmaster. software 1.0 hits a wall wherever the rule itself can't be written down, no matter how skilled the programmer is. ## 2. software 2.0 — you curate the data, the training run writes the program instead of writing the rule, you collect examples of correct behavior, and a training process turns that data into the actual program — a set of neural network weights nobody wrote by hand and nobody can read directly. **you don't program the behavior, you program the process that produces the behavior**: gather data, train, deploy, watch where it fails, collect more data on exactly those failures, retrain. this is how modern computer vision, speech recognition, and game-playing systems actually work — nobody hand-wrote the rules for any of them. this is also where the graph from section 0 lives: the trained "program" is that attention graph's weights, not code you can read. the catch, for anyone evaluating one of these systems: the "program" isn't inspectable the way code is. you can't read the weights and know what it will do on a case you haven't tested. you can only test it, watch it fail, and feed those failures back in. ## 3. software 3.0 — you write the prompt, in english this is the new one, and it's the one your client is actually buying when they buy an ai product. a large language model is not a program that does one thing — it's closer to a **general-purpose computer that gets reconfigured at runtime by whatever you type into it.** the instructions are just english, and the "program" is the prompt. this sounds like a small difference from software 2.0. it isn't. it means: - **anyone can write a program now**, in the sense that anyone who can describe what they want in plain language can get a working result — no data collection, no training run, no code. - **the exact wording of the instruction is the whole ballgame.** ask a model a multi-step math question directly and it may just guess. ask it to work the problem out step by step and accuracy on the same question can jump from under 20% to over 80% — same model, same question, different instruction. this is not a minor tuning knob; it's the difference between a system that looks broken and one that works. - **a model will give you the average answer unless you tell it not to.** it was trained on a huge mix of writing at every level of care and expertise, so a generic question gets a generic (average-quality) answer back. asking it to answer as an expert, or specifying exactly the persona and standard you want, is not a gimmick — it's pointing the model at a narrower, better slice of what it learned. - **you can describe an entire system in english and have it behave like one runs.** karpathy's talk walks through prompts that turn a language model into a working linux terminal simulation, a smart-home controller that takes plain-english requests and returns valid commands, and even an app's entire backend — no code, just a description of what the backend should do with each kind of request. none of that is a special trick; it's the same mechanism as any other prompt, pushed further. ## what this means for explaining an ai product to someone new to it the single most useful sentence from this talk: **"the hottest new programming language is english."** if someone is confused about why an ai system feels different from software they've used before — why it needs a well-written instruction instead of just a button to click, why the same request can get a better or worse result depending on how it's phrased — this is the whole answer. it isn't a worse version of a normal app. it's a different kind of computer, and the prompt is the program. one more line worth keeping in your pocket for skeptical clients: **prompting is also how you program humans.** if you want a person to do something, you tell them, in language, what you want — with all the same sensitivity to phrasing, context, and framing that a good prompt needs. the fact that the same skill now also programs software isn't a coincidence to explain away; it's the actual reason non-engineers can be extremely good at this. --- ## how to use this in a real conversation don't walk through all three eras with every client — most only need to understand #3, and only need #1/#2 as contrast if they ask "why does this need such a specific prompt, can't it just figure out what i mean?" the answer is: it's doing exactly what it was told, in the language it was told it in — the same way a very capable new hire will do exactly what you actually said, not what you meant, until you get specific. section 0 is the one to reach for when someone asks "why should i trust this technology to be stable" — the honest answer is that the core mechanism has already survived years of people trying to replace it.

entries.name: demo-video
entries.describe: Record demo walkthrough videos for a lead's Genesis pages using Playwright. Finds all pages matching the lead's company/slug, records a smooth scrolling walkthrough of each, converts to MP4, and opens in Finder for drag-and-drop sharing via iMessage/email. Pass a lead ID or company slug as argument (e.g., "15743", "vanguard", "dent-society").
entries.haystack: demo-video record demo walkthrough videos for a lead's genesis pages using playwright. finds all pages matching the lead's company/slug, records a smooth scrolling walkthrough of each, converts to mp4, and opens in finder for drag-and-drop sharing via imessage/email. pass a lead id or company slug as argument (e.g., "15743", "vanguard", "dent-society"). --- name: demo-video description: record demo walkthrough videos for a lead's genesis pages using playwright. finds all pages matching the lead's company/slug, records a smooth scrolling walkthrough of each, converts to mp4, and opens in finder for drag-and-drop sharing via imessage/email. pass a lead id or company slug as argument (e.g., "15743", "vanguard", "dent-society"). allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash --- # demo video — lead walkthrough recorder record polished demo videos of a lead's live genesis pages. outputs mp4 files ready to share via imessage, email, or slack. ## arguments `$arguments` — lead id (numeric) or company/page slug prefix. examples: - `/demo-video 15743` — look up lead, find matching pages, record all - `/demo-video vanguard` — record all vanguard-* pages - `/demo-video dent-society` — record all dent-society-* pages - `/demo-video pathways` — record all pathways-* pages ## how it works ### step 1: resolve pages if a lead id is given: 1. run `iris leads get <id>` to get company name 2. slugify the company name 3. run `iris pages list` and filter by slug prefix if a slug prefix is given: 1. run `iris pages list` and filter directly ### step 2: generate playwright test create a temporary playwright spec at `tests/e2e/_demo-video-temp.spec.ts` that: - uses `video: { mode: 'on', size: { width: 1440, height: 900 } }` - sets `slowmo: 600` for smooth, watchable scrolling - visits each page, waits for render, scrolls through content - takes full-page screenshots at key points ### step 3: run & convert ### step 4: deliver 1. copy mp4s to `test-results/demo-videos/<slug>/` with readable names 2. open folder in finder: `open test-results/demo-videos/<slug>/` 3. if lead id was provided, add a note: `iris leads note <id> "demo videos generated: <list>"` ## video settings - resolution: 1440x900 (16:10 widescreen) - format: mp4 (h.264) — universal compatibility - slowmo: 600ms between actions (smooth, not rushed) - scroll: smooth behavior, 500px increments - pause: 2-3 seconds on each page hero, 1.5s between scrolls ## key patterns - always check `ffmpeg` is available before converting - use `test.settimeout(5 * 60 * 1000)` for long walkthroughs - clean up temp spec file after recording - if a page has a dashboard layout (type: "dashboard"), note it may require auth - custom domains (vanguardhcs.com etc) should be included if they resolve to matching pages ## output structure

entries.name: deploy-test-loop
entries.describe: Deploy-Test-Loop — deploy, E2E test against production, fix, re-deploy in one tight loop
entries.haystack: deploy-test-loop deploy-test-loop — deploy, e2e test against production, fix, re-deploy in one tight loop --- name: deploy-test-loop description: deploy-test-loop — deploy, e2e test against production, fix, re-deploy in one tight loop --- # deploy-test-loop: production e2e validation cycle deploy code, test against production endpoints, find bugs in real conditions, fix, and re-deploy — all in one tight loop. this flattens the iterative cycle by catching mass-assignment gaps, enum mismatches, and schema issues that only surface against real data. ## when to use - after implementing a feature that touches api endpoints + frontend - when shipping backend logic that creates/updates db records - any change involving model $fillable, validation rules, or new db columns ## the loop (5 phases) ### phase 1: pre-deploy validation (local) before committing, run targeted checks against the local docker environment: ### phase 2: commit & push - commit backend (fl-api) and frontend (fl-elon-web-ui) separately - push both to `master` to trigger railway auto-deploys - fl-api deploys from `master` branch (not `main`) - run `npm run fix-file` on any edited vue files before committing ### phase 3: production smoke test while deploy rolls out, test existing production data: ### phase 4: fix & re-push when bugs are found (they will be): - fix immediately — small targeted commits - push again to `master` - each fix is its own commit with clear message common bugs caught in this phase: - **$fillable missing fields** — model::create() silently drops them - **validation enum gaps** — existing prod data uses values not in your `in:` rule - **migration not run** — columns don't exist on target db - **auth context** — service tokens don't resolve $request->user() - **submodule drift** — api and frontend on different branches ### phase 5: production e2e verification once deploy lands: ## optimization insights ### what we learned works well - **tinker-first testing**: create records via tinker before touching any http endpoint. catches $fillable and schema issues immediately. - **query prod data before writing validation**: check what enum values already exist in production before adding `in:` validation rules. - **parallel push**: push fl-api and fl-elon-web-ui simultaneously — they deploy independently. - **python one-liners for json inspection**: `curl | python3 -c "import json,sys; ..."` is faster than jq for selective field checks. ### what could be improved - **pre-commit $fillable linter**: auto-check that any field used in ::create() exists in $fillable. would have caught the biggest bug instantly. - **production data snapshot**: before writing validation rules, always run a quick query against prod to see what values exist. we found `ugc_views` only after pushing. - **migration dry-run**: test migrations against a local db clone before pushing. the bounty_content_submissions table not existing locally caused a cascade failure. - **auth-aware test harness**: the service token (fl_raichu_api_token) doesn't resolve to a user for $request->user(). need a separate test user token for authenticated endpoint testing. ## key commands reference ## file checklist (before committing) - [ ] new db columns exist in migration and are listed in model $fillable - [ ] validation `in:` rules include all values that exist in production - [ ] `topublicarray()` or equivalent includes new fields in api response - [ ] frontend computed properties handle null/undefined for new fields - [ ] eslint fix run on all edited vue files

entries.name: desktop-ingest-documents
entries.describe: Get your own documents — SOPs, research, transcripts, spreadsheets — into IRIS from the desktop app, without a terminal, so agents can use them later instead of only in the message you pasted them into. Covers the file types the paperclip silently refuses, where documents should actually land, and how to prove the ingest worked rather than assume it.
entries.haystack: desktop-ingest-documents get your own documents — sops, research, transcripts, spreadsheets — into iris from the desktop app, without a terminal, so agents can use them later instead of only in the message you pasted them into. covers the file types the paperclip silently refuses, where documents should actually land, and how to prove the ingest worked rather than assume it. --- name: desktop-ingest-documents description: get your own documents — sops, research, transcripts, spreadsheets — into iris from the desktop app, without a terminal, so agents can use them later instead of only in the message you pasted them into. covers the file types the paperclip silently refuses, where documents should actually land, and how to prove the ingest worked rather than assume it. version: 1 industries: - onboarding - operations - healthcare - legal args: bloq: type: number required: false description: the atlas board the documents should land in. find yours with `iris atlas list`. leave empty to be walked through picking one. file: type: string required: false description: full path to the document to ingest. on windows, the full path including the drive, e.g. c:\users\you\downloads\sop.docx on-error: ask timeout: 900 --- # ingesting documents from the iris desktop app for anyone who has a document on their computer and wants iris to actually *know* it — not just read it once in a message and forget it. **you do not need a terminal.** the assistant inside the app can run every command here for you. say what you want in plain english; the commands below are what it will run. related: **`getting-started-with-iris`** is the broader first-day path (connect tools, ingest, publish a playbook). this playbook is the narrow desktop-specific slice of the ingest step, and it exists because the desktop app has a trap the terminal does not. --- ## step:trap the paperclip will silently refuse your document **read this first — it is the single most likely reason to think the app is broken.** the attach button and drag-and-drop in the message box accept **images and pdf only**: accepted_image_types = ["image/png","image/jpeg","image/gif","image/webp"] accepted_file_types = [...accepted_image_types, "application/pdf"] a `.docx`, `.md`, `.txt`, `.csv` or `.xlsx` is rejected by a bare `return` — **no error, no message, nothing appears.** the file simply does not show up. that is a bug (item:182421 / it-182421), not something you are doing wrong. two things follow, and the second matters more: 1. do not drag documents into the message box. use `step:ingest` below. 2. **even for accepted types, an attachment is not stored.** it is base64'd into that one message as an image part for the model to look at, and it is gone afterwards. attaching is *showing*, not *saving*. if you want iris to still have the document tomorrow — which is the whole point of "based on everything you've been given before today" — it has to be ingested, not attached. --- ## step:where decide where it should land, before you send it an ingest without a destination is a file you will not find again. pick the board that is the subject's home, not a scratch board. iris atlas list ask the assistant: *"which board should a surgery sop go in?"* if there is already a library for this kind of document — a sop library, a case board, a client board — use it. documents that live with their siblings get found by search; documents in a personal scratch board do not. **prove you picked a real one:** iris bloqs get <bloq> you should see its name and lists. `bloq not found` means either a wrong id or a board you are not a member of — both are worth resolving before you ingest, not after. --- ## step:path put the file somewhere with a name you can say out loud the assistant reads files by path. save the document to your **downloads** folder and use the full path. on windows that looks like: c:\users\<your name>\downloads\surgery-sop.docx not `~/downloads`, not `/tmp` — the assistant has been known to guess unix paths on windows and waste turns discovering they do not exist. give it the whole thing. --- ## step:ingest ingest it say it in plain english: > ingest c:\users\kristen montero\downloads\surgery-sop.docx into bloq 517 which runs: iris bloqs ingest <bloq> <file> this handles the formats the paperclip will not: **csv and excel become datasets, md/txt/docx become documents, html becomes an artifact.** the document becomes an item on the board — a thing with an id that other items can reference and that agents can retrieve later. **if you want the original file kept as an attachment too** (the actual .docx, not just its parsed text): iris bloqs files upload <bloq> <file> that one is read-back verified — it re-reads the stored bytes rather than trusting the upload reported success. --- ## step:verify prove it landed — do not assume this is the step people skip, and it is the one that makes the ingest real. an ingest that reports success and imports nothing looks exactly like one that worked. iris bloqs get <bloq> the new item should be there. then search for something you *know* is inside the document — a heading, a name, a phrase you remember: iris pulse check "<a phrase from inside the document>" if the phrase does not come back, the ingest did not finish or did not run. nothing found is a result, not a hiccup — say so rather than moving on. --- ## step:use now it is context, not a paste once ingested, the document is available to agents on that board without re-uploading. this is what makes the follow-up question possible at all: > based on everything you have been given before today, read this sop and tell me what i missed if you had attached the file instead, that question has nothing to read. for the review-and-curate loop on top of this — red flags as individually addressable items you can accept, reject, or mark "needs adding to" — see **item:182420 / it-182420**. --- ## what is still broken, so you know what to expect - the paperclip silently refuses documents (item:182421 / it-182421). widening the accepted types alone is **not** the fix: attachments become image parts, so a .docx would be base64'd into a prompt as an "image". the real fix is routing documents to ingest, with a visible error in the meantime. - attachments do not land anywhere durable — attach-to-bloq does not exist yet. - on windows the assistant may guess unix paths (`/tmp`, `/`) before finding your home directory. give full paths and it behaves. refs: item:182421 / it-182421 · item:182420 / it-182420 · epic item:182419 / it-182419 · playbook `getting-started-with-iris`

entries.name: discover-publish
entries.describe: Publish content across all brands (Beatbox, Discover, HeyIRIS, EMC Radio, Capital Collective, FreeLabel) via CopyCat AI pipeline. Upload to Instagram/TikTok/X, create instrumentals, download audio. Create profiles, sync Instagram feeds, and manage how content displays on profile pages. Pass an action as argument (e.g., "publish", "dry-run", "brands", "status", "logs", "create-profile", "sync-instagram").
entries.haystack: discover-publish publish content across all brands (beatbox, discover, heyiris, emc radio, capital collective, freelabel) via copycat ai pipeline. upload to instagram/tiktok/x, create instrumentals, download audio. create profiles, sync instagram feeds, and manage how content displays on profile pages. pass an action as argument (e.g., "publish", "dry-run", "brands", "status", "logs", "create-profile", "sync-instagram"). --- name: discover-publish description: publish content across all brands (beatbox, discover, heyiris, emc radio, capital collective, freelabel) via copycat ai pipeline. upload to instagram/tiktok/x, create instrumentals, download audio. create profiles, sync instagram feeds, and manage how content displays on profile pages. pass an action as argument (e.g., "publish", "dry-run", "brands", "status", "logs", "create-profile", "sync-instagram"). allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- # discover publish — multi-brand content publishing pipeline publish content from youtube across multiple brand identities to social media (instagram, tiktok, x) via the copycat ai engine. create and manage profiles, sync instagram feeds from residential ips, and control how content appears on profile pages. each brand has its own ai caption style, social accounts, and uploadpost routing. ## arguments `$arguments` — action and parameters. examples: - `/discover-publish publish <youtube_url>` — publish via beatbox pipeline (default brand) - `/discover-publish publish <youtube_url> --brand=discover` — publish as the discover page - `/discover-publish publish <youtube_url> --brand=heyiris` — publish as heyiris - `/discover-publish dry-run <youtube_url>` — test caption generation only (no social posts) - `/discover-publish dry-run <youtube_url> --brand=emc_radio` — test emc radio caption - `/discover-publish brands` — list all configured brands and their social accounts - `/discover-publish status` — check recent uploads and uploadpost results - `/discover-publish logs` — tail the dedicated `discover-uploads.log` - `/discover-publish submit` — handle a producer beat submission (beatbox only) - `/discover-publish clip <youtube_url> --brand=discover` — cut clip + publish (no instrumental) - `/discover-publish create-profile <slug> [--type=storefront]` — create a new profile (delegates to `/create-profile`) - `/discover-publish sync-instagram [slug]` — sync instagram feed for a profile (or `--auto` for all discover profiles) - `/discover-publish sync-instagram --auto` — auto-discover and batch-sync all profiles with instagram handles --- ## available brands | brand | caption style | instagram | tiktok | x | config | |-------|--------------|-----------|--------|---|--------| | `beatbox` | ap news wire, factual, `[#beatbox]` tag | `@thebeatbox__` | (not configured) | (not configured) | full pipeline: clip + audio + instrumental + discord | | `discover` | energetic, viral hooks, emojis | `@thediscoverpage_` | `@thediscoverpage_` | `@thediscoverpage_` | clip + social (fallback brand) | | `heyiris` | minimal tech journalism | `@heyiris.io` | `@heyiris.io` | `@heyiris.io` | clip + social | | `emc_radio` | underground electronic, boiler room style | `@thebeatbox__` (temp) | (not configured) | — | clip + social | | `capital_collective` | financial analysis, authoritative | `@capital.collective` | — | `@capital.collective` | clip + social | | `freelabel` | general music community | `@freelabelnet` | `@freelabelnet` | `@freelabelnet` | clip + social | **brand configs**: `fl-api/config/brandcaptions.php` (ai prompts, style, hashtags) **uploadpost routing**: `fl-api/config/uploadpost.php` (social account mapping per brand + platform) --- ## direct social publishing (photos, text, videos) for publishing **static images, text posts, or pre-made videos** (not youtube clips), use the `iris social` cli command: **how it works:** 1. local files are auto-uploaded to do spaces (cloud storage) first 2. calls `post /api/v1/social-media/publish` on fl-api 3. fl-api routes to uploadpostservice which handles multi-platform publishing 4. supports all brands: `@freelabelnet`, `@thediscoverpage_`, `@heyiris.io`, `@thebeatbox__`, `@capital.collective` **key files:** - cli command: `sdk/php/src/console/commands/socialcommand.php` - api endpoint: `fl-api/app/http/controllers/api/socialmediapublishercontroller.php` - uploadpost service: `fl-api/app/services/marketing/uploadpostservice.php` - config: `fl-api/config/uploadpost.php` **requires:** `upload_post_api_key` set in fl-api environment. currently only available via local docker (not yet on railway production). --- ## pipeline overview (youtube clips) ### beatbox pipeline (full — `beatbox_publish`) ### other brands pipeline (copycat direct — `trigger_video_clipper`) ### two services involved | service | role | key file | |---------|------|----------| | **iris-api** | orchestrator — `beatboxshowcaseintegrationservice` for beatbox; `copycataiintegrationservice` for all brands | `fl-iris-api/app/services/integrations/` | | **fl-api** | worker — `processvideoclip` job (ffmpeg, uploadpost, captions), `brandcaptionservice` | `fl-api/app/jobs/processvideoclip.php` | --- ## trigger methods ### 1. iris cli (recommended) ### 2. iris sdk (php) ### 3. rest api (curl) ### 4. php script (direct service) ### 5. agent chat (natural language) chat with any agent that has `beatbox-showcase` or `copycat-ai` integration: ### 6. producer submission (cli) --- ## parameters reference ### `beatbox_publish` (beatbox full pipeline) | parameter | type | required | default | description | |-----------|------|----------|---------|-------------| | `youtube_url` | string | yes | — | youtube video url | | `start` | string | no | `0:10` | clip start time | | `duration` | string | no | `90s` | clip duration | | `caption_prompt` | string | no | — | custom ai prompt for caption | | `platforms` | array | no | `['instagram']` | social platforms | | `dry_run` | bool | no | `false` | caption only, skip social + db | | `dry_run_download` | bool | no | `false` | also download audio in dry run | ### `trigger_video_clipper` (copycat — any brand) | parameter | type | required | default | description | |-----------|------|----------|---------|-------------| | `youtube_url` | string | yes | — | youtube video url | | `brand` | string | no | `discover` | brand identity for caption + routing | | `start` | string | no | `0:10` | clip start time | | `duration` | string | no | `90s` | clip duration | | `publish_to_social` | bool | no | `true` | publish to social media | | `social_platforms` | array | no | `['instagram','tiktok','x']` | platforms to publish to | | `text` | string | no | — | manual caption (overrides ai generation) | | `apply_lut` | bool | no | `true` | apply color grading lut | | `social_media_type` | string | no | `reels` | post type: `reels`, `post`, `story` | | `keep_local` | bool | no | varies | keep video on local storage vs gcs | ### `handle_submission` (beatbox producer submission) | parameter | type | required | description | |-----------|------|----------|-------------| | `producer_name` | string | yes | producer/artist name | | `email` | string | yes | producer email | | `instagram_handle` | string | yes | instagram handle | | `youtube_url` | string | yes | youtube url | | `beat_title` | string | yes | beat title | | `genre` | string | yes | genre (trap, drill, lo-fi, etc.) | | `bpm` | number | no | beats per minute | | `notes` | string | no | additional notes | --- ## brand configuration ### caption ai settings defined in `fl-api/config/brandcaptions.php`: | brand | model | temp | style | |-------|-------|------|-------| | `beatbox` | gpt-4o-mini (+ grok fallback) | 0.8 | ap news wire, `[#beatbox]` tag | | `heyiris` | gpt-4o-mini | 0.5 | minimal tech journalism | | `emc_radio` | gpt-4o-mini | 0.4 | underground label (boiler room/ra) | | `capital_collective` | gpt-4o-mini | 0.7 | financial analysis, `[#capitalcollective]` | | `discover` | gpt-4o-mini | 1.0 | energetic viral hooks, emojis | **note**: beatbox caption gen in iris-api uses xai grok directly (switched from openai after quota). fl-api brandcaptionservice has openai auto-fallback to grok. ### uploadpost profile routing defined in `fl-api/config/uploadpost.php`: | profile | platforms | used by | |---------|-----------|---------| | `@thebeatbox__` | instagram only | beatbox, emc_radio (temp) | | `@thediscoverpage_` | instagram, tiktok, threads, x | discover, copycat (default) | | `@freelabelnet` | instagram, tiktok, x | freelabel | | `@heyiris.io` | instagram, tiktok, x | heyiris | | `@capital.collective` | instagram, x, linkedin | capital_collective | ### beatbox environment config (hardcoded) | config | local | production | |--------|-------|------------| | profile id | `2318981` | `2318981` | | bloq id | `33` | `224` | | program id | `8` | `44` | | profile slug | `beatbox` | `beatbox` | --- ## monitoring & debugging ### dedicated log channel both fl-api and iris-api write to `discover_uploads` channel: ### check uploadpost status ### check recent instrumentals ### quick health check ### common failure points | issue | symptom | fix | |-------|---------|-----| | openai quota exceeded | caption gen fails | uses grok fallback (iris-api) or auto-fallback (fl-api) | | yt-dlp warning in title | corrupt filenames | fixed — 13 skip patterns in youtubedownloader | | playlist url | downloads multiple videos | fixed — `sanitizeyoutubeurl()` strips params | | audio "nonexistent.mp3" | bpm analysis fails | fixed — robust `converturltopath()` | | uploadpost stuck pending | upload never completes | check uploadpost status endpoint | | platform skipped | only instagram publishes | expected for brands with limited ig profiles | | brand not found | falls back to `discover` | check `config/brandcaptions.php` brand key | --- ## key files ### iris-api (orchestrator) | file | purpose | |------|---------| | `app/services/integrations/beatboxshowcase/beatboxshowcaseintegrationservice.php` | beatbox full pipeline — publish, submit, caption, discord | | `app/services/integrations/copycatai/copycataiintegrationservice.php` | copycat ai — 19 functions incl. `trigger_video_clipper`, `download_youtube_audio` | | `config/integrations/beatbox-showcase.yml` | beatbox yaml config | | `config/logging.php` | `discover_uploads` channel | ### fl-api (worker) | file | purpose | |------|---------| | `app/jobs/processvideoclip.php` | queue job — ffmpeg, brand analysis, uploadpost social publish | | `app/services/marketing/brandcaptionservice.php` | per-brand ai caption generation | | `app/services/marketing/uploadpostservice.php` | uploadpost api — publishes to instagram/tiktok/x | | `app/services/youtubedownloader.php` | yt-dlp wrapper — download, title extraction | | `app/models/instrumental.php` | instrumental model (beatbox_published, bpm, etc.) | | `config/brandcaptions.php` | brand ai settings (prompts, style, hashtags, model config) | | `config/uploadpost.php` | uploadpost profiles and brand → account routing | | `config/logging.php` | `discover_uploads` channel | ### sdk / cli | file | purpose | |------|---------| | `sdk/php/src/console/commands/toolscommand.php` | cli `beatbox-publish`, `beatbox-submit`, `clip-cut`, `youtube-audio` | | `sdk/php/src/resources/integrations/integrationsresource.php` | sdk `$iris->integrations->execute()` | --- ## steps (skill implementation) ### 1. parse the argument | argument | action | |----------|--------| | `publish <url> [--brand=x]` | publish via appropriate pipeline | | `dry-run <url> [--brand=x]` | test caption generation only | | `dry-run-download <url>` | test caption + download audio (beatbox only) | | `brands` | list all configured brands with accounts | | `status` | check recent uploads in logs + uploadpost status | | `logs` | tail the discover-uploads.log | | `submit` | guide through beatbox producer submission | | `clip <url> --brand=x` | copycat clip cut + social publish (no instrumental) | | `create-profile <slug> [--type=x]` | create a new profile (delegates to `/create-profile` skill) | | `sync-instagram [slug]` | sync instagram feed for specific profile | | `sync-instagram --auto` | auto-discover + batch sync all profiles with ig handles | | `debug <url>` | run diagnostics on a url | | (empty) | show usage help | ### 2. for `publish` — determine which pipeline - if `--brand=beatbox` or no brand specified for beats → use **beatbox full pipeline** via iris-cli: - if `--brand=discover|heyiris|emc_radio|capital_collective|freelabel` → use **copycat clip cut**: ### 3. for `brands` list brands from `config/brandcaptions.php` and `config/uploadpost.php`, showing: - brand name, enabled status - social accounts per platform - caption style summary ### 4. for `status` / `logs` ### 5. for `submit` ### 6. for `create-profile` delegate to the `/create-profile` skill. if quick setup is needed: for full profile creation (products, services, landing page), invoke `/create-profile "<name>" <type>`. ### 7. for `sync-instagram` after sync completes, verify the feed is cached: --- ## production access --- ## profile creation profiles are the foundation — content published via this pipeline needs a profile to live on. use the `/create-profile` skill for full profile creation, or create profiles directly via the iris cli. ### quick profile creation (cli) ### full profile creation (seeder) for new profiles with products/services/landing pages, use the `/create-profile` skill which creates an artisan seeder command. key patterns: ### profile → content display chain when a profile is created, published content appears at these urls: | what | url | served by | |------|-----|-----------| | profile page | ` | fl-elon-web-ui | | landing page | ` | iris-api | | social feed api | ` | fl-api | | discover page listing | ` | fl-elon-web-ui | **critical fields for a profile to appear on discover:** - `photo` — required for pool 1 (recently active profiles) - `instagram` — triggers instagram feed display + social feed sync - `updated_at` within last 30 days — ensures pool 1 priority - `spotify_id` / `youtube_channel_id` — for pool 2/3 if no recent activity --- ## instagram social feed sync instagram blocks api requests from cloud ips (digitalocean). the hive daemon runs on a residential ip (local mac) and fetches instagram data, then seeds it to production via the `seedsocialfeed` endpoint. ### how it works ### manual sync (single profile) ### auto-discover batch sync (all discover profiles) auto-discover logic: 1. queries `get /api/v1/profile?limit=n&sortby=best_match` (same algorithm as discover page) 2. filters to profiles with instagram handles 3. skips handles shared by multiple profiles (placeholder/junk data like `@paynow`) 4. deduplicates by handle (case-insensitive) 5. syncs sequentially with configurable delay (default 2s) to avoid ig rate limits ### via hive task (scheduled or on-demand) the daemon supports `social_feed_sync` as a task type. when prompt is empty, defaults to `--auto`. ### seed endpoint (fl-api) ### key files (instagram sync) | file | purpose | |------|---------| | `coding-agent-bridge/scripts/social-feed-sync.js` | zero-dependency node.js script — fetches ig, seeds to fl-api | | `coding-agent-bridge/daemon/task-executor.js` | `social_feed_sync` case — routes hive tasks to sync script | | `fl-api/app/services/socialmediafeedservice.php` | instagram fetch + persistent cache fallback | | `fl-api/app/http/controllers/profilecontroller.php` | `seedsocialfeed()` + `getsocialfeed()` endpoints | | `fl-api/routes/api/freelabel-routes.php` | route: `post /v1/profile/{id}/social-feed` | --- ## how content displays on profile pages ### profile page components the profile page (`/@{slug}`) renders a configurable set of components via `profilepagerenderer.vue`. the social feed is one of these components. | component | what it shows | visibility condition | |-----------|--------------|---------------------| | `profile-social-feed` | instagram grid (3-col) + stats + tiktok follow button | profile has `instagram` or `tiktok` field set | | `profile-hero` | name, bio, photo, cta buttons | always | | `profile-products` | product cards with prices | profile has products | | `profile-services` | service listings | profile has services | | `profile-articles` | blog/article cards | profile has articles | | `profile-videos` | video embeds | profile has videos | ### instagram feed display (profilesocialfeed.vue) **location**: `fl-elon-web-ui/components/profile/profilesocialfeed.vue` **what it renders:** - stats bar: posts count, followers, following (formatted k/m) - 3-column grid of up to 9 recent posts - hover overlay with likes/comments count - video indicator badge on video posts - lazy-loaded images with broken-image fallback - loading skeleton while fetching **data flow:** **visibility logic** (profilepagerenderer.vue line ~281): a profile must have `instagram` or `tiktok` set in the database for the social feed component to render. ### instagram image proxy instagram cdn urls expire and block hotlinking. all instagram image urls are rewritten through a server-side proxy: **route**: `get /api/v1/profile/ig-proxy` (public, no auth, `throttle:public-content` rate limit) **controller**: `profilecontroller::proxyinstagramimage()` ### discover page algorithm the discover page at `/discover` lists profiles using a 3-pool priority system: | pool | priority | criteria | sort | |------|----------|----------|------| | pool 1 | highest | updated in last 30 days + has photo or services | `updated_at desc` | | pool 2 | medium | has analytics data (spotify/youtube/twitter/instagram followers > 0) | `spotify_followers desc` | | pool 3 | lowest | has social ids (spotify/youtube/twitter/instagram) but no analytics | `updated_at desc` | profiles are merged, deduplicated by pk, and served from the `buildcuratedprofilescache()` method in profilecontroller. the discover page frontend uses `sortby=best_match` which triggers this 3-pool algorithm. **to ensure a profile appears on the discover page:** 1. set a profile photo (`photo` field) 2. set an instagram handle (`instagram` field) — this also enables social feed 3. update the profile within the last 30 days (touch `updated_at`) 4. clear the cache: profiles are cached for 5 minutes (`fallback_profiles_*` keys) ### caching layers | cache key | ttl | written by | read by | |-----------|-----|------------|---------| | `social_feed:instagram:{username}` | 1 hour | `seedsocialfeed()` or `socialmediafeedservice` | `getsocialfeed()` | | `social_feed:instagram:persistent:{username}` | 30 days | `seedsocialfeed()` or `socialmediafeedservice` | fallback when live fetch fails | | `profile_show_{md5(id)}` | 10 min | `profilecontroller::show()` | profile page load | | `fallback_profiles_{sort}_{limit}` | 5 min | `getfallbackprofiles()` | discover page | | `curated_profiles_{sort}` | 30 min | `buildcuratedprofilescache()` | discover page (main) | --- ## known issues & recent fixes 1. **beatbox caption gen uses xai grok** — switched from openai after quota. uses neuronai `baseagent::make()` with `grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning` 2. **fl-api brandcaptionservice has grok auto-fallback** — `openaiservice::createchatcompletion()` catches 429 and falls back 3. **only instagram active for beatbox** — tiktok/x need uploadpost profiles 4. **emc radio temporarily uses `@thebeatbox__`** — until `@emc_radio` ig account is created 5. **yt-dlp title extraction** — 13 skip patterns filter out warning/github lines 6. **youtube url sanitization** — strips `list`, `start_radio`, `index`, `si` params 7. **audio path conversion** — `converturltopath()` handles do spaces, gcs, local, absolute paths 8. **dual logging** — all operations log to both main channel and `discover_uploads` 9. **partial success model** — beatbox pipeline continues even if steps fail; discord notifies on failure ## adding a new brand 1. add brand config to `fl-api/config/brandcaptions.php` (ai prompt, style, hashtags) 2. add uploadpost profile to `fl-api/config/uploadpost.php` (social accounts) 3. add brand routing in `uploadpost.php` `defaults` section 4. create the instagram/tiktok account on uploadpost dashboard 5. test with dry run: `php bin/iris tools clip-cut --url="..." --brand="new_brand" --dry-run` ## adding a new profile to discover + social feed 1. **create profile** via `/create-profile` skill or iris cli 2. **set instagram handle**: `php bin/iris profile set <slug> instagram "<handle>" --force` 3. **set profile photo**: `php bin/iris profile set <slug> photo "<url>" --force` (or let sync auto-populate from ig) 4. **sync instagram**: `node scripts/social-feed-sync.js <slug>` (from `coding-agent-bridge/`) 5. **verify on discover**: visit ` — profile should appear in pool 1 6. **verify feed**: visit ` — instagram grid should render ### currently synced profiles (as of march 2026) | profile | instagram | followers | posts | status | |---------|-----------|-----------|-------|--------| | moore-life | @remedyelixirbar | 29 | 1 | active | | billy-otto | @billyotto | 21,646 | 9 | active | | zoe | @migos | 12,652,523 | 9 | active | ### data quality issues | profile | handle | issue | |---------|--------|-------| | jayyrose, blocboyjb, devantekershaw | @paynow | same placeholder handle on 3 profiles — auto-filtered by batch sync | | creativegs | @keepitcut3ent | instagram account doesn't exist (404) | | 1k15grzzatscjygj4byiez | @luhtyler_ | spotify id used as profile slug — profile lookup resolves wrong profile |

entries.name: document-crossref
entries.describe: Ingest documents from a cloud folder — PDFs, scans, spreadsheets — extract them into typed records, then cross-reference those records against a source of truth and report every discrepancy. Built for invoice-vs-PO reconciliation and the same shape of check anywhere else — what a document CLAIMS versus what you AUTHORISED. Fails loudly and exits non-zero when they disagree, because a checker that cannot fail is not a checker.
entries.haystack: document-crossref ingest documents from a cloud folder — pdfs, scans, spreadsheets — extract them into typed records, then cross-reference those records against a source of truth and report every discrepancy. built for invoice-vs-po reconciliation and the same shape of check anywhere else — what a document claims versus what you authorised. fails loudly and exits non-zero when they disagree, because a checker that cannot fail is not a checker. --- name: document-crossref description: "ingest documents from a cloud folder — pdfs, scans, spreadsheets — extract them into typed records, then cross-reference those records against a source of truth and report every discrepancy. built for invoice-vs-po reconciliation and the same shape of check anywhere else — what a document claims versus what you authorised. fails loudly and exits non-zero when they disagree, because a checker that cannot fail is not a checker." version: 2 args: source: type: string required: false default: google_drive description: "bulk-ingestable source: dropbox | google_drive | s3 | google-cloud-storage | onedrive | microsoft. anything else is read-only and cannot be walked." path: type: string required: true description: folder to ingest. google drive takes a folder id (not a path); dropbox takes a path; s3/gcs take a prefix. bloq: type: number required: true description: bloq id the documents land in. schema: type: string required: true description: atlas dataset slug the typed records go into. create it first with `iris atlas:datasets schemas create`. reference: type: string required: true description: path to a json file of reference records — the source of truth (pos, approvals, a contract register). either a list, or an object keyed by the join value. key: type: string required: false default: po_reference description: field used to join an extracted record to its reference record. assert: type: string required: false default: "total=approved_total" description: "comma-separated extracted=reference field pairs to compare, e.g. total=approved_total,vendor=vendor" tolerance: type: string required: false default: "0.005" description: absolute tolerance for numeric comparisons. money should not be compared with ==. phi: type: string required: false default: "no" description: "yes = these documents may contain phi or other regulated personal data. turns off content echoing in the report so extracted values never land in a log, a terminal transcript, or a ci artifact — only pass/fail and field names." images: type: string required: false default: "yes" description: "yes (default) = read scans and photographs with vision ocr. no = skip them, and the job reports how many it skipped. most documents worth cross-referencing are scans; this is on by default for that reason." model: type: string required: false default: gpt-4.1-nano description: "nano model for field extraction (the ocr model is chosen separately by the vision chain). allowed: gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-nano, gpt-5-nano — anything else is silently downgraded to gpt-4o-mini. avoid gpt-5-nano here unless you have raised the token budget: it is a reasoning model and will spend its whole allowance thinking and return nothing." on-error: stop timeout: 900 --- # document cross-reference takes a folder of documents and answers one question: **does what this document claims match what we authorised?** the pipeline is ingest → extract → compare, and each stage is verified before the next runs. that ordering is not decoration. every stage of this pipeline has, at some point, reported success while doing nothing: a lookup that matched no integration, a listing that read the wrong key and found no files, a download that wrote base64 text to disk, a re-sync that duplicated every record. the checks below exist because each of those once passed silently. ## what it needs first - the source connected: `iris integrations list-connected` (and `iris data-sources survey` to see what is actually bulk-importable — most sources are read-only). - a dataset schema for the fields you want extracted: `iris atlas:datasets schemas create --name "…" --slug <slug> --fields fields.json` where fields.json is `{"fields":[{"key":"total","type":"number","label":"total"}, …]}`. - a reference json file — the authorised side of the comparison. ## steps ### step:preflight confirm the source can actually be walked ### step:ingest ingest the folder into typed records ### step:verify-ingest wait for it, and refuse to continue on a partial ### step:crossref compare every extracted record to its reference ### step:cleanup remove the scratch files ## known failure modes, and what each means | symptom | cause | |---|---| | `no active '<type>' integration found` | the source key is not the integration type — `google_drive` resolves to `google-drive`, `s3` to `aws-s3` | | `no files found in specified path` | drive takes a folder **id**, not a path | | job stuck at `processing` | the extraction model's provider is out of credit and the fallback chain could not reach one either | | `n image file(s) skipped` | run with `images=yes` | | `unmatched` | the document cites a reference that does not exist — treat as a finding, not noise | ## which models can actually read a scan measured 2026-08-30 by handing each the same rendered image and asking it to transcribe. not copied from a capability table — several models that "support vision" on paper returned a 404. | model | reads an image | note | |---|---|---| | `gpt-4o-mini` | yes | the default ocr model | | `gpt-4.1-nano` | yes | transcribed correctly | | `grok-4.3` | yes | 0.98 confidence on a rotated, noised invoice; also described a red paid stamp | | `gpt-5-nano` | accepts the image, **answers nothing** | a reasoning model — spent its entire 256-token budget on reasoning and returned empty with `finish_reason: length`. give it a much larger budget or it scores zero while looking like it cannot see | | `glm-5.2` / `kimi-k3` / `minimax-m3` | **no** | openrouter: `no endpoints found that support image input` | the extraction model and the ocr model are different choices. ocr is decided by the vision chain (openai → openrouter → xai); `model=` here only sets the nano model that turns ocr'd text into typed fields. benchmark them on your own documents rather than trusting this table: `iris playbook run ocr-benchmark`. ## regulated documents set `phi=yes` for anything clinical, legal or otherwise identifying — case files, affidavits, claims, medical records. it stops the report echoing extracted values. without it a cross-reference prints `document=… reference=…` for every field, which is how a patient name, a date of birth or a claim number ends up in a terminal scrollback, a ci log and a screenshot of a terminal. with it you get the field names and pass/fail, which is all a reconciliation actually needs. it does **not** make the pipeline compliant. the documents still travel to a vision provider, and that is a decision about your agreements, not a flag.

entries.name: editorial-ad
entries.describe: Take an ad from a one-line idea to a published post — check which accounts you can actually post from, turn the idea into a brief, render or attach creative, write a caption sized to the platform, stop at a real human gate, then publish. Renderer-agnostic; bring your own image or wire any render command. Publishing is always a second, deliberate run. Pass the idea as argument (e.g., "our scheduling tool now handles reschedules automatically").
entries.haystack: editorial-ad take an ad from a one-line idea to a published post — check which accounts you can actually post from, turn the idea into a brief, render or attach creative, write a caption sized to the platform, stop at a real human gate, then publish. renderer-agnostic; bring your own image or wire any render command. publishing is always a second, deliberate run. pass the idea as argument (e.g., "our scheduling tool now handles reschedules automatically"). --- name: editorial-ad description: take an ad from a one-line idea to a published post — check which accounts you can actually post from, turn the idea into a brief, render or attach creative, write a caption sized to the platform, stop at a real human gate, then publish. renderer-agnostic; bring your own image or wire any render command. publishing is always a second, deliberate run. pass the idea as argument (e.g., "our scheduling tool now handles reschedules automatically"). version: 2 args: topic: type: string required: true description: what the ad is about — the offer, launch or angle in one line brand: type: string required: false default: default description: brand slug to post as. must be one you have connected. platforms: type: string required: false default: x description: comma-separated platforms. only ones actually connected are attempted. layout: type: string required: false default: auto description: >- which editorial layout to ask your renderer for. `auto` lets the brief pick using the rubric below. layouts are arguments, not skins — see "choosing a layout". image: type: string required: false description: >- url of creative you already have. given this, the render step is skipped entirely. this is the zero-setup path — the playbook is useful before you own a renderer. render_cmd: type: string required: false description: >- shell template that renders the creative and prints a path. receives {{layout}}, {{headline}}, {{subhead}}, {{items}}, {{out}}. left empty and with no `image`, the run still completes and the gate reports creative as missing. model: type: string required: false default: iris/glm-5.3-flash description: copy model. small models are correct here — this is short-form, constrained writing. action: type: string required: false default: review enum: [review, publish] description: review = assemble and stop at the gate (default). publish = go live, after the gate. confirm: - "publish*" on-error: stop --- # editorial ad — idea to published post, with a gate you cannot skip most "post an ad" automations fail in the same three ways: they produce creative for an account you cannot actually post from, they let a model publish on the first ask, and they pick a layout because it looks nice rather than because the copy needs it. this is the shape that avoids all three. it is deliberately **renderer-agnostic** — the value is the order of operations and the gate, not any one image tool. ## what this does and does not do makes **organic, ad-shaped posts**: a graphic plus a caption, published to an account you own. it does **not** buy placement — no ads-manager api is involved, so "boost this" stays a human action in the platform's own ui. ## why it stops before publishing `action` defaults to `review` and the gate is a real `mode: human` pause, not a printed warning. an ad is the rare post where the caption, the image and the account must all be right *at the same time*, and any model that is able to publish will publish on the first ask. assemble, show, stop. publishing is a second decision you make on purpose. ## choosing a layout — the part worth stealing layout should follow **what the copy is doing**, not what looks good in a picker. a useful starting rubric, which maps onto whatever your renderer supports: | the copy is… | layout | why | |----------------------------------|---------------|-----| | announcing something | **masthead** | a dateline and a band read as news | | listing n capabilities | **index** | numbering makes a list scannable and finite | | one line that is the product | **quote** | give the sentence the whole canvas | | comparing specs or tiers | **ledger** | label → value rows on hairlines | | one number that carries it | **stat** | the figure is the hero | two rules that matter more than the table: 0. **read the brand kit before choosing anything.** `/p/iris-brand-kit` and `/p/freelabel-brand-kit` already define the marks, the inks and what each layout is for, and twenty-five slide components are already built under `remotion/src/carousel/`. on 2026-09-01 a brief was written for three campaigns that invented hero objects and palettes from scratch; every one of them already existed, named, with a rule attached. **the work is choosing a form, not designing one.** 0a. **for paid social, the 110px rule decides before taste does.** the freelabel kit says of flyer: *"the only layout that survives the profile grid — at 110px a document is grey mush and this reads clean."* an ad is seen at that size. a document-dense layout is therefore disqualified for paid regardless of how good it looks full-size — measured, not theorised: the press campaign ran split sheet, run sheet and patch list as ads and returned **8,348 impressions and 2 clicks, $6.29 per click**. render at full size, then look at it at 110px before approving. if it is mush, fall back to flyer and carry the argument as three lines. 1. **never invent the number.** a `stat` layout given a figure that is not in the source copy renders beautifully and says nothing. that is decoration wearing the costume of evidence. 2. **do not let the subhead restate the headline** — especially with `index`, where the list below already enumerates. saying the same thing three times in one frame reads as a malfunction, not as emphasis. a diagram of the list you are already reading is decoration. keeping a layout because it is *available*, rather than because it is better at something, turns a design system into a skin picker. ## steps ### step:check-accounts which accounts can this brand actually post from ### step:brief turn the idea into an ad brief ### step:creative render or attach the creative ### step:caption write the post caption ### step:review approve before anything goes public ### step:publish publish the ad ## adapting this to your stack two integration points, both optional: - **`render_cmd`** — any shell command that writes an image and exits 0. it receives `{{layout}} {{headline}} {{subhead}} {{items}} {{out}}`. a remotion still, an imagemagick script, a call to your own service, a figma export — all fine. - **`image`** — skip rendering entirely and hand it a url. start here; wire a renderer later. with neither, the run still produces a brief and a caption and stops at the gate. that is a useful thing on its own, and it means the playbook is worth installing before you have anything else set up.

entries.name: electron
entries.describe: Automate Electron desktop apps (VS Code, Slack, Discord, Figma, Notion, Spotify, etc.) using agent-browser via Chrome DevTools Protocol. Use when the user needs to interact with an Electron app, automate a desktop app, connect to a running app, control a native app, or test an Electron application. Triggers include "automate Slack app", "control VS Code", "interact with Discord app", "test this Electron app", "connect to desktop app", or any task requiring automation of a native Electron application.
entries.haystack: electron automate electron desktop apps (vs code, slack, discord, figma, notion, spotify, etc.) using agent-browser via chrome devtools protocol. use when the user needs to interact with an electron app, automate a desktop app, connect to a running app, control a native app, or test an electron application. triggers include "automate slack app", "control vs code", "interact with discord app", "test this electron app", "connect to desktop app", or any task requiring automation of a native electron application. --- name: electron description: automate electron desktop apps (vs code, slack, discord, figma, notion, spotify, etc.) using agent-browser via chrome devtools protocol. use when the user needs to interact with an electron app, automate a desktop app, connect to a running app, control a native app, or test an electron application. triggers include "automate slack app", "control vs code", "interact with discord app", "test this electron app", "connect to desktop app", or any task requiring automation of a native electron application. allowed-tools: bash(agent-browser:*), bash(npx agent-browser:*) --- # electron app automation automate any electron desktop app using agent-browser. electron apps are built on chromium and expose a chrome devtools protocol (cdp) port that agent-browser can connect to, enabling the same snapshot-interact workflow used for web pages. ## core workflow 1. **launch** the electron app with remote debugging enabled 2. **connect** agent-browser to the cdp port 3. **snapshot** to discover interactive elements 4. **interact** using element refs 5. **re-snapshot** after navigation or state changes ## launching electron apps with cdp every electron app supports the `--remote-debugging-port` flag since it's built into chromium. ### macos ### linux ### windows **important:** if the app is already running, quit it first, then relaunch with the flag. the `--remote-debugging-port` flag must be present at launch time. ## connecting after `connect`, all subsequent commands target the connected app without needing `--cdp`. ## tab management electron apps often have multiple windows or webviews. use tab commands to list and switch between them: ## common patterns ### inspect and navigate an app ### take screenshots of desktop apps ### extract data from a desktop app ### fill forms in desktop apps ### run multiple apps simultaneously use named sessions to control multiple electron apps at the same time: ## color scheme playwright overrides the color scheme to `light` by default when connecting via cdp. to preserve dark mode: or set it globally: ## troubleshooting ### "connection refused" or "cannot connect" - make sure the app was launched with `--remote-debugging-port=nnnn` - if the app was already running, quit and relaunch with the flag - check that the port isn't in use by another process: `lsof -i :9222` ### app launches but connect fails - wait a few seconds after launch before connecting (`sleep 3`) - some apps take time to initialize their webview ### elements not appearing in snapshot - the app may use multiple webviews. use `agent-browser tab` to list targets and switch to the right one - use `agent-browser snapshot -i -c` to include cursor-interactive elements (divs with onclick handlers) ### cannot type in input fields - try `agent-browser keyboard type "text"` to type at the current focus without a selector - some electron apps use custom input components; use `agent-browser keyboard inserttext "text"` to bypass key events ## supported apps any app built on electron works, including: - **communication:** slack, discord, microsoft teams, signal, telegram desktop - **development:** vs code, github desktop, postman, insomnia - **design:** figma, notion, obsidian - **media:** spotify, tidal - **productivity:** todoist, linear, 1password if an app is built with electron, it supports `--remote-debugging-port` and can be automated with agent-browser.

entries.name: find-your-channel
entries.describe: Every marketing channel eventually stops working — the founders who survive that are the ones who knew why it worked in the first place. A field-tested framework for finding a growth channel, telling real signal from noise while you scale, and designing your company so the good decisions happen automatically instead of by heroics.
entries.haystack: find-your-channel every marketing channel eventually stops working — the founders who survive that are the ones who knew why it worked in the first place. a field-tested framework for finding a growth channel, telling real signal from noise while you scale, and designing your company so the good decisions happen automatically instead of by heroics. --- name: find-your-channel description: every marketing channel eventually stops working — the founders who survive that are the ones who knew why it worked in the first place. a field-tested framework for finding a growth channel, telling real signal from noise while you scale, and designing your company so the good decisions happen automatically instead of by heroics. version: 1 args: business: type: string required: false description: what you're growing — a product, an agency, a channel you're currently betting on — in a sentence. allowed-tools: - read - write --- # find your channel **source:** this is a distillation of hiten shah's thinking — founder of crazy egg and kissmetrics, and an early architect of content-led marketing — from a public interview (youtu.be/qua3pzrlo4a). the frameworks below are his; this playbook generalizes and organizes them so you can run them against your own business. where a claim is his opinion rather than a provable fact, treat it as an experienced operator's view worth weighing, not a settled result. ## arguments `$arguments` — what you're growing: a product, a service, or the channel you're currently betting on. --- ## 1. spend discipline depends on where the money came from money you raised and money you made are not interchangeable, even when the number is the same. raised money lets you spend ahead of revenue — someone else is betting the business will grow into the spend. money you made yourself, you cannot spend ahead of revenue, because there's nothing behind it if it doesn't work. that difference shapes *early*-stage decisions specifically — how fast you spend, how much runway you protect, how much you can afford to be wrong. it stops mattering once the business is generating real revenue and has to manage a real balance sheet either way. if you're deciding whether to raise or self-fund, don't ask "which is better" — ask **"how far can i get on what i already have, because the further you get before you take outside money, the more the business is still fully yours to decide."** ## 2. content is king — context only informs it the claim isn't that data and audience research don't matter. it's that they're not the thing that reaches anyone. content — anything meant to be read, watched, or heard, coming from a person, a brand, or a business — is what makes actual contact with an audience. research and analysis inform what you make; they are not, themselves, the thing anyone experiences. the practical test: if you're spending more time gathering context than producing the content that context is supposed to inform, you've inverted the priority. **work backwards from the last mile** — the actual post, page, or message a person sees — and ask what informs it, not the other way around. ## 3. channels are secrets — and the tactic is half of it people who understand a channel rarely tell you the whole thing, and a channel by itself is usually not the secret — **the channel plus the specific tactic** is. knowing "content marketing works" tells you nothing; knowing exactly how a specific company used a specific channel with a specific tactic, at a specific moment, tells you something you can actually test. this has a sharper edge than "try lots of channels." **every channel eventually decays** — it gets discovered, copied, and commoditized. the skill that matters isn't finding a channel, it's building the muscle to notice decay early and go find the next one before you're stuck. and when something does work, **you have to know why it worked, in detail** — because if you got lucky and don't understand the mechanism, you can't repeat it once it stops working or once the person who made it work leaves. getting lucky without understanding why is the same as not having found anything at all. ## 4. data-informed, not data-driven "data-driven" implies the data makes the call. in practice, data tells you what happened, not always what you should do next — especially when you have real conviction about something the data can't yet see (a new channel, a new product angle, timing nobody has measured yet). **be informed by data. don't outsource the decision to it.** the failure mode on one side is ignoring data that's telling you something isn't working; the failure mode on the other side is refusing to try anything the data can't already justify. both are avoiding a real decision. ## 5. design the environment, not just the culture culture is what people say a company is like. **environment is the actual structure and process that determines what happens** — and it's the stronger lever, because you can shape it deliberately while culture mostly just accumulates. the concrete example: one team built its core engineering discipline — plan thoroughly before writing code, get it reviewed, revise — directly into hiring. a candidate's take-home wasn't a coding test; it was a two-page plan, scored, discussed with the hiring manager, revised, and scored again. candidates experienced the actual environment they'd be working in *before* they were hired into it, not a values conversation about it. **apply this by asking**: what is the one process or structural decision that, if you got it right, would make good outcomes the default instead of something you have to personally enforce every time? build that into how people join and work, not into a values statement. ## 6. the reality check some of this is just uncertainty tolerance, and it's worth saying plainly rather than dressing it up: most decisions in a growing business will feel like they cost something real, most early wins won't feel like wins, and the plan you're most confident in will get blown up more than once. that isn't a sign you're doing it wrong — **founders who last aren't braver, they've just stopped waiting for clarity that was never coming.** if you need constant reassurance before you act, or you need everyone to agree with you before you make a call, that's worth knowing about yourself before you're relying on it under real pressure. --- ## how to actually use this pick the section that's live for you right now — usually it's #3 (a channel that's decaying and you don't know what's next) or #5 (you're scaling past the point where you can personally enforce quality). don't try to apply all six at once; this is a set of lenses, not a checklist to clear in order. if you're working with an iris onboarding specialist or agent on this, hand them the business description from `$arguments` and section 3 or 5 specifically — those are the two with the clearest next action (audit your current channel's decay stage, or design one process into your hiring/onboarding).

entries.name: fix-light-mode
entries.describe: Fix hardcoded dark-mode Tailwind classes in Vue components so they render correctly in light mode. Pass a file path or component name as argument.
entries.haystack: fix-light-mode fix hardcoded dark-mode tailwind classes in vue components so they render correctly in light mode. pass a file path or component name as argument. --- name: fix-light-mode description: fix hardcoded dark-mode tailwind classes in vue components so they render correctly in light mode. pass a file path or component name as argument. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash --- # fix light mode — elon web ui component fix a vue component so it properly supports light mode by replacing hardcoded dark tailwind classes with dynamic `islightmode` ternaries. ## arguments `$arguments` — path to a vue file or component name to fix. if a component name is given, search `fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui/components/` for it. ## reference read the full guide at: `fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui/docs/light_mode_fix_guide.md` ## steps ### 1. read the target file read the full contents of the component specified in `$arguments`. if only a name is given, use glob to find it under `fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui/components/`. ### 2. audit for hardcoded dark classes look for these patterns in the template section: - `bg-gray-800`, `bg-gray-900`, `bg-gray-700` — dark backgrounds - `text-white`, `text-gray-100`, `text-gray-300` — light text that won't show on white - `border-gray-700`, `border-gray-600` — dark borders - `hover:bg-gray-700`, `hover:bg-gray-600` — dark hover states - `bg-gradient-to-br from-gray-800 to-gray-900` — dark gradients - `placeholder-gray-500` on dark bg check if these are already inside `:class` ternaries using `islightmode`. if they are, skip them. only fix hardcoded (non-conditional) dark classes. ### 3. check for existing `islightmode` look in the `computed` section of the script block. **if it exists and uses `domainnavigationservice.ispathwaysdomain()`** — replace it with the themeservice pattern: **if it exists and already uses themeservice** — leave it as-is. **if it doesn't exist** — add it to the `computed` block. **if the component uses `effectivelightmode` (like agentgallery)** — fix the fallback detection to use themeservice instead of `ispathwaysdomain()`. ### 4. replace hardcoded classes with ternaries use these mappings: | dark class | light equivalent | |---|---| | `bg-gray-800` | `bg-white` | | `bg-gray-900` | `bg-gray-50` | | `bg-gray-700` | `bg-gray-100` | | `bg-gradient-to-br from-gray-800 to-gray-900` | `bg-white border border-gray-200` | | `bg-gradient-to-br from-gray-900 via-gray-800 to-gray-900` | `bg-gradient-to-br from-indigo-50 to-purple-50` | | `text-white` | `text-gray-900` | | `text-gray-100` | `text-gray-900` | | `text-gray-300` | `text-gray-600` | | `text-gray-400` | `text-gray-500` | | `border-gray-700` | `border-gray-200` | | `border-gray-600` | `border-gray-300` | | `hover:bg-gray-700` | `hover:bg-gray-100` | | `hover:bg-gray-600` | `hover:bg-gray-200` | | `hover:text-gray-300` | `hover:text-gray-700` | | `bg-blue-600 bg-opacity-30` | `bg-blue-100` | | `bg-red-900 bg-opacity-30` | `bg-red-100` | **template pattern — static to dynamic:** before: after (split static/dynamic): keep non-theme classes (flex, padding, margin, width, etc.) in the static `class` attribute. move only theme-dependent classes into `:class`. ### 5. remove unused imports if you replaced `domainnavigationservice.ispathwaysdomain()` usage and nothing else in the file uses it, remove: ### 6. run eslint fix after all edits, run: ### 7. verify re-read the file briefly to confirm: - no duplicate `islightmode` computed properties - no unused imports - all previously hardcoded dark classes now have light alternatives - eslint passes clean ## important notes - **never use `this.$toast`** — use the messagesutility mixin from `utils/mixins/messages.js` - **use `$api` not `$axios`** for authenticated api calls - **nuxt 2 / vue 2 only** — use options api, not composition api - if a child component needs light mode awareness, prefer passing `:is-light-mode="islightmode"` as a prop - some components may have too many elements to ternary — consider `:global(.theme-light)` css overrides instead (see `workspacetoolslist.vue` for an example)

entries.name: freelabel-ads
entries.describe: Take an ad from an idea to a published post — brief, branded creative, caption, a human approval gate, then publish to the brand's own connected accounts. Stops at the gate by default; publishing is a separate, deliberate act. Creative comes from the existing campaign-image tools, publishing from the ownership-enforced social layer.
entries.haystack: freelabel-ads take an ad from an idea to a published post — brief, branded creative, caption, a human approval gate, then publish to the brand's own connected accounts. stops at the gate by default; publishing is a separate, deliberate act. creative comes from the existing campaign-image tools, publishing from the ownership-enforced social layer. --- name: freelabel-ads description: take an ad from an idea to a published post — brief, branded creative, caption, a human approval gate, then publish to the brand's own connected accounts. stops at the gate by default; publishing is a separate, deliberate act. creative comes from the existing campaign-image tools, publishing from the ownership-enforced social layer. version: 2 args: topic: type: string required: true description: what the ad is about — the offer, launch or angle in one line brand: type: string required: false default: freelabel description: brand slug to run the ad as. must be one you have connected (see step check-accounts). platforms: type: string required: false default: x description: comma-separated platforms, e.g. "x,instagram". only ones connected for the brand will go. variant: type: string required: false default: masthead enum: [masthead, index, quote, ledger, stat] description: >- editorial layout. these are arguments, not skins — pick by what the copy does. masthead = an announcement (default) · index = a list of n capabilities · quote = the line is the product · ledger = a spec comparison · stat = one real number carries it (never invent the figure). story: type: string required: false default: "no" enum: ["no", "yes"] description: render 1080x1920 (stories/reels) instead of 1080x1080 agent: type: number required: false default: 474 description: agent that writes the brief, creative and caption. 474 = marketing content creator. not 420 (patty refuses non-legal prompts). model: type: string required: false default: iris/glm-5.3-flash description: routing model. gpt-4.1-nano is too weak to reach niche tools reliably; nano/mini only per house rules. action: type: string required: false default: review enum: [review, publish] description: review = stop at the approval gate (default). publish = go live after the gate. on-error: stop timeout: 900 --- # freelabel — ad from idea to published post chains three things that already exist and had never been connected: the campaign-image tools that render branded creative, the agent that writes copy, and the ownership-enforced publishing layer. ## what this can and cannot do it makes **organic ad-shaped posts** — a branded graphic plus a caption, published to an account you own. it does **not** buy placement. there is no x ads or meta marketing connection in the stack, so "boost this" remains a human action in the platform's own ui. measurement is lopsided and worth knowing before you plan around it: upload-post reports analytics for **instagram, tiktok, linkedin and facebook — not x**. an x campaign is publish-and-look, not publish-and-measure, until x's own api is wired. ## why it stops before publishing `action` defaults to `review`, and the gate is a real `mode: human` pause rather than a printed warning. an ad is the one kind of post where the caption, the image and the account must all be right at once, and a model that can publish will publish on the first ask — that is exactly what happened the first time the agent tool was tested. so the run assembles everything, shows it, and stops. `--action=publish` is a second, deliberate decision. ## steps ### step:check-accounts which accounts can this brand actually run ads from ### step:brief turn the topic into an ad brief ### step:creative render the branded graphic and host it ### step:caption write
