**someone reads the diary** (unread autonomy is spend, not leverage). go `passive` for a week first. the diary tells you what it *would* have done, at no risk. ### step:kill emergency stop only when an agent is actively doing damage — looping, burning tokens, or acting on wrong data. - `iris monitor kill <id>` — disables heartbeat **and** pauses every job the agent owns blunt and wide: it stops the agent's entire scheduled surface, not just the runaway job, and reversing it means re-enabling the mode and un-pausing each schedule by hand. prefer the narrow fix when you have one — `iris schedules toggle <id>` for the one offending schedule, or `iris agents update <id> --heartbeat-mode passive` to keep it observing while you diagnose. `kill` is for when you do not yet know which of six schedules is the problem and the meter is running. ### step:cadence set the cadence, then confirm it beats

entries.name: iris-hive
entries.describe: Run AI work across the machines you already own instead of paying for compute you don't need, and actually know when a node goes quiet instead of finding out days later. Checks reachability, dispatches tasks, and tells you which transport rail will get through. Pass an action as argument.
entries.haystack: iris-hive run ai work across the machines you already own instead of paying for compute you don't need, and actually know when a node goes quiet instead of finding out days later. checks reachability, dispatches tasks, and tells you which transport rail will get through. pass an action as argument. --- name: iris-hive description: run ai work across the machines you already own instead of paying for compute you don't need, and actually know when a node goes quiet instead of finding out days later. checks reachability, dispatches tasks, and tells you which transport rail will get through. pass an action as argument. version: 2 allowed-tools: - read - bash - grep - glob - edit - agent - webfetch --- # iris hive — compute mesh management manage multi-node hive compute mesh. dispatch tasks across machines, send notifications, debug daemon issues, and run health checks. ## use cases concrete scenarios, mapped to the actions below. | i want to… | run | note | |---|---|---| | kick off a build/job on my other machine, keep working here | `iris playbook run iris-hive dispatch --node <id> --prompt "npm run build"` | serial only — don't fan out to two nodes at once | | know the instant a remote job finishes | `iris playbook run iris-hive ping --node <id>` | `message` type — the one reliable, no-subprocess path | | sanity-check the whole mesh before relying on it | `iris playbook run iris-hive status` | every node + this machine's daemon, one call | | a node won't take tasks / looks stuck | `iris playbook run iris-hive debug --node <id>`, then `doctor` | `debug` = one node's detail; `doctor` = whole-daemon diagnostic | | move a file, a db dump, or a directory between machines | **don't** dispatch it — see rail picker below | rail 1 can't carry bytes faithfully; use tailscale (`scp`/`rsync`) instead | | prove the mesh survived a deploy, not just "looks fine" | `iris playbook run iris-hive test` | the real cross-network playwright e2e suite | | figure out which network path will actually work right now | `iris playbook run iris-hive rails --node <hostname-or-ip>` | probes cloud / lan / tailnet live instead of assuming | ## quick reference ## rail picker — which transport to use full measured writeup: (2026-08-23). hive can reach another machine three different ways. they are not interchangeable — pick the rail from what you're moving, not from what the command is called. | rail | reach | carries | status | |---|---|---|---| | **1 · cloud** (`iris hive dispatch`, `iris hive ping`) | any network, crosses nat, no open ports | task control only — pty pane scrape, not real stdout | native, but serial only (parallelism is 1 regardless of what the node advertises) | | **2 · lan mesh** (mdns `_iris-hive._tcp`, daemon `:3200`) | same lan, in theory | nothing today | native but unreachable — daemon binds `127.0.0.1` while the advert names a routable host (`daemon/index.js:1624`, `#182079`) | | **3 · tailscale** (`ssh`/`scp`/`rsync`/`rdp` over the 100.x tailnet ip) | any network | any protocol, byte-exact | works, but it's borrowed — not hive's own transport | **rules that follow from the measurements:** - never parallelise hive dispatch — fan-out loses every task but one. - never trust hive dispatch output byte-for-byte — it's a tmux pane scrape (merged stdout/stderr, ansi escapes, the wrapper's own command line included), not real stdout. use it for exit-shaped questions and short status; for anything structured, write to a file on the node and carry the file over tailscale (rail 3). - verify any file moved over tailscale with a digest on both ends — sizes can match when contents don't. - treat an empty `ssh` read as unknown, not empty, if the path is inside a tcc-protected app container — `sshd` is denied those paths and returns empty rather than denied. re-read through the daemon (rail 1, gui-session ambient authority) before concluding a directory is empty. ### step:rails check which rails are actually reachable ## executable steps (v2) ### step:status hive mesh status ### step:ping send notification to node ### step:dispatch dispatch shell command to node ### step:test run e2e hive mesh tests ### step:doctor diagnose hive issues ### step:debug-node debug a specific node ## arguments `` — action to perform: - `/iris-hive status` — show all nodes + local daemon health - `/iris-hive ping --node <id>` — send macos notification to a remote node - `/iris-hive dispatch --node <id> --prompt <msg>` — dispatch a message task - `/iris-hive test` — run e2e hive mesh playwright tests (6 tests) - `/iris-hive doctor` — full diagnostic: daemon, cloud, config, errors, shell, nodes - `/iris-hive debug --node <id>` — deep dive on a specific node: hardware, tasks, heartbeat - `/iris-hive rails --node <hostname-or-tailnet-ip>` — which transport rail is actually reachable right now (cloud / lan mesh / tailscale) — see "rail picker" above ## task types reference | type | what it does | subprocess? | reliable? | |------|-------------|-------------|-----------| | `message` | macos notification + console log | no — inline osascript | yes — use this for notifications | | `shell` | `sh -c <prompt>` | yes — spawns shell | pending iris-api deploy | | `notification` | `osascript` with title/subtitle config | yes — spawns osascript | pending iris-api deploy | | `hive_script` | node.js script execution | yes — spawns node | broken — routes through bash via `runruntimeprocess` | | `custom_playwright` | playwright test execution | yes — spawns npx playwright | works but heavy | | `som_batch` | som outreach campaigns | yes — spawns som-all.js | works | | `discover` | content discovery scraper | yes — spawns playwright | works | **key insight**: `message` type (task-executor.js line 548) is a short-circuit that runs before the runtime/subprocess check. it's the most reliable path for simple tasks. ## targeting a specific node put `node_id` at the **top level** of the task payload. not inside `config.target_node` (that doesn't work). ## common issues | symptom | cause | fix | |---------|-------|-----| | daemon says "running" but node is offline | auth failed silently — check `~/.iris/status.json` | `iris daemon restart` or reinstall | | `iris update` crashes with bun shell error | desktop app update template syntax | fixed in v1.3.65+ (try-catch wrapped) | | tasks fail with exit code 2 | `.bashrc` has broken docker init | `sed -i.bak '/docker\/init-bash.sh/d' ~/.bashrc` | | `hive_script` tasks run as bash | `runruntimeprocess` bypasses switch | use `message` type instead | | node stuck in `busy` for days | `nodes:detect-stale` scheduler not running | manual: restart node or wait for scheduler fix | | `iris update` downgrades | force-pushed tag corrupted github latest | delete rogue release: `gh release delete <tag>` | | customer can't run `iris` after install | macos quarantine | `curl -fssl \| bash` | ## e2e test

entries.name: iris-hive-start
entries.describe: Turn a second machine you already own into compute you can actually use — from nothing, in one sitting. Find it, authorise it, prove the transport really carries bytes, and get one real command to run on it. The nothing→working path; `iris-hive` is the playbook for after this one.
entries.haystack: iris-hive-start turn a second machine you already own into compute you can actually use — from nothing, in one sitting. find it, authorise it, prove the transport really carries bytes, and get one real command to run on it. the nothing→working path; `iris-hive` is the playbook for after this one. --- name: iris-hive-start description: turn a second machine you already own into compute you can actually use — from nothing, in one sitting. find it, authorise it, prove the transport really carries bytes, and get one real command to run on it. the nothing→working path; `iris-hive` is the playbook for after this one. version: 2 args: node: type: string required: true description: the node's name as it will appear in `iris hive nodes list` — defaults to that machine's hostname when you enroll it target: type: string required: false description: user@ip of the machine — only needed if you are enrolling it over ssh from here instead of running `iris hive connect` on it command: type: string required: false description: the first real command to run on it — defaults to `uname -a && df -h /` on-error: continue timeout: 600 --- # iris hive — from nothing to a working node **what it is:** a way to run work on machines **you already own** — the laptop in the other room, the box at the office — from wherever you are, without opening a port or paying for a vm. **what it is not:** - **not a cluster scheduler.** no fan-out. dispatch is **serial per node** — one task in flight, regardless of the `2/3` concurrency the node advertises. parallelising loses tasks. - **not remote access to machines you do not control.** every path needs a credential you already have: your iris login on the box, or ssh key auth you already installed. - **not a file transfer.** `iris hive run` returns a **tmux pane scrape**, not real stdout. bytes move on a different rail — see the last step. ## the state everyone misreads: registered ≠ online ≠ usable registered ──daemon starts──> online ──selftest passes──> usable (a row in (heartbeat (the transport actually your account) seconds ago) carries output) `iris hive nodes list` shows **online**. online means a heartbeat arrived. it says nothing about whether a dispatched task runs, runs *there*, or returns anything readable. that gap is why `iris hive selftest` exists, and its own source says why: *"#182004 sat broken while the node reported online, 147 tasks completed, heartbeat 5s."* **`online` is where most people stop, and it is one step short of the thing they wanted.** ## two directions, and one prerequisite hive connect run it on the machine. needs egress only. no ssh, no vpn, no ports. hive enroll <t> run it from here. needs a routable address + ssh key auth. `connect` works behind nat, cgnat, corporate wifi and on a laptop that changes networks; `enroll` cannot onboard a machine you cannot already reach. **prefer `connect`.** the prerequisite either way: **you are logged in** (`iris auth whoami`) and the target logs in **as the same account**. nodes belong to an account, not a person or a network — one registered under a second login is invisible here, and looks identical to one that failed to register. ## steps ### step:account whose hive is this, and what is already in it ### step:find find the machine — and know what finding proves skip this entirely if you can go type on the machine — `connect` needs no address at all. - `iris hive scan` — arp sweep of your lan; `--vendor apple|dell|raspberry` to filter. - `iris hive probe <ip>` — ports, ssh banner, vendor, os for one host. - `iris hive ssh <ip> [user]` — does key auth already work? tries common users. - `iris hive discover <user@ip>` — is iris installed there, current, already registered? `scan`, `probe` and `ssh` are local and read-only — no api calls at all. **`scan` shows every device on the network, including ones that are not yours** — a printer, a hue bridge, someone else's phone. that list is a network fact, not a permission, and `iris hive ssh` answering "yes" only means *you already had a key on that box*. hive never creates one for you. `discover` is the one worth running before enrolling: it says whether the machine is already a node, sitting on a *different* user id, or running an iris older than yours. ### step:add authorise it — this installs and runs software on that machine **this is the irreversible step.** everything before it reads; this one puts a long-lived daemon on a computer and hands it a credential. **preferred — three commands, typed on the target machine itself:** 1. `curl -fssl | bash` — only if iris isn't there yet. 2. `iris auth login` — the same account as step:account. 3. `iris hive connect --name ${{args.node}}` — registers, saves the key, starts the daemon, and waits until the node actually reports online rather than trusting that a process launched. **or from here, over ssh** — `iris hive enroll <user@ip>` (the `target` arg), with `--dry-run` first to read what it will do. `--auto-key`, on by default, runs `ssh-copy-id` if key auth is missing — which means this path can prompt for the remote password once. check before you run either: - **same account?** `iris auth whoami` on both machines. - **do you accept a persistent daemon here?** it starts at boot, dials out continuously, and will execute shell commands you send it. on a shared or client machine that is a decision. - **already a node?** `iris hive discover <user@ip>`. re-registering is usually safe — `connect` fingerprints the hardware (macos `ioplatformuuid`, linux `machine-id`) and reclaims the existing row rather than minting a duplicate. - **do not reach for `--force` casually.** it rotates the node key, leaving the old row in your account unable to authenticate from that machine — a ghost. **there is no `iris hive nodes remove`**: that command group has only `list` and `show`, so the cli's own advice to "remove it with `iris hive nodes`" names something that does not exist. cleaning up a ghost node is a support problem, not a command. ### step:online confirm it registered and is reporting in ### step:prove prove the transport carries bytes — the step people skip ### step:first get one real result ### step:bytes what `connect` did not give you `connect` buys exactly one rail: **outbound cloud dispatch**. enough to run commands, not enough for three things you will want within a week: - **moving bytes** — `iris hive fs push/pull` runs over **tailscale + ssh**, sha256-verified at both ends. there is no byte-faithful path on the cloud rail. - **`iris hive doctor <node>`** on the *remote* machine is an ssh probe and needs the same. local `iris hive doctor` needs neither. - **a service port** on that machine — tailscale. hive has no port-forward. set it up when you need it: `iris hive vpn check` → `install` → `up` → `status`, then `iris hive vpn enroll <tailnet-ip>` to register a node over the tunnel instead of a lan address. **do not wait for the lan rail.** hive advertises over mdns on `:3200`, but the daemon binds `127.0.0.1` while the advert names a routable host — unreachable by design accident (`daemon/index.js:1624`, #182079). same-lan is not a shortcut around tailscale today. **you are done when** the node reads `online`, `selftest` passes its first two assertions, and one real command of yours returned a result you believe. from there, `iris-hive` is the operator playbook for the day-to-day: `iris playbook run iris-hive status|dispatch|debug|rails`.

entries.name: iris-integrations
entries.describe: Stop guessing why an integration silently stopped working. Connect a service once, see what's actually live versus quietly broken, and fix an auth failure without digging through logs to find which of 40-plus connections is the culprit. Pass an action as argument.
entries.haystack: iris-integrations stop guessing why an integration silently stopped working. connect a service once, see what's actually live versus quietly broken, and fix an auth failure without digging through logs to find which of 40-plus connections is the culprit. pass an action as argument. --- name: iris-integrations description: stop guessing why an integration silently stopped working. connect a service once, see what's actually live versus quietly broken, and fix an auth failure without digging through logs to find which of 40-plus connections is the culprit. pass an action as argument. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- # iris integrations — ai engine integration manager manage the 40+ integrations available in the iris ai engine. connect oauth services, configure api keys, execute integration functions, test connectivity, and debug authentication issues — all via the `iris` cli. ## arguments `$arguments` — action and parameters. examples: - `/iris-integrations list` — show all available integrations + connection status - `/iris-integrations status` — show connected integrations with health - `/iris-integrations connect gmail` — start oauth flow for gmail - `/iris-integrations connect google-drive` — connect google drive - `/iris-integrations setup mercury --api-key "key"` — configure api-key-based integration - `/iris-integrations exec gmail read_emails maxresults=5` — execute an integration function - `/iris-integrations exec google-drive search_files query="proposal"` — search google drive - `/iris-integrations exec mercury list_accounts` — list mercury bank accounts - `/iris-integrations functions gmail` — list available functions for an integration - `/iris-integrations test gmail` — test connectivity for a specific integration - `/iris-integrations debug` — diagnose integration auth issues --- ## integration registry ### oauth-based integrations (require `iris connect`) | | microsoft email | | `google-drive` / `googledrive` | search_files, export_file, read_doc | file storage & docs | | `google-docs` / `googledocs` | read_doc, search_docs | document access | |
