<-> iris-api)**: --- ## steps — action dispatch | argument | action | |----------|--------| | `list` | run `iris integrations list-integrations` and format output | | `status` | run `iris list-connected`, show health per integration | | `connect <type>` | run `iris connect <type>`, walk user through oauth flow | | `setup <type>` | run `iris integrations setup <type>` with api key flags | | `exec <type> <fn>` | run `iris integrations exec <type> <function> [params]` | | `functions <type>` | list available functions for a specific integration type | | `test <type>` | execute a minimal function call to verify connectivity | | `test all` | loop through connected integrations, test each one | | `debug` | check logs, env vars, token expiry, cross-service auth | | `add <type>` | guide through adding a new integration service class | ### when listing integrations 1. run `iris integrations list-integrations` 2. cross-reference with connected status if available 3. group by category (oauth, api-key, platform-internal) 4. show which ones are connected vs available ### when connecting an oauth integration 1. run `iris connect <type>` — this generates an oauth url 2. tell the user to complete the browser auth flow 3. verify connection: `iris integrations exec <type> <simple_function>` 4. report success or troubleshoot ### when executing a function 1. validate the integration type exists in the registry 2. run `iris integrations exec <type> <function> [key=value ...]` 3. parse and display the json response 4. if error, check: (a) is integration connected? (b) are params correct? (c) is token expired? ### when debugging 1. check `iris list-connected` for connection status 2. check iris-api logs: `tail -f storage/logs/laravel.log | grep integration` 3. verify env vars in production: ssh + `php artisan tinker` 4. test with minimal function call 5. if oauth issue, re-connect: `iris connect <type>` 6. if cross-service issue, check `fl_raichu_api_token` ### when adding a new integration 1. create service class in `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/app/services/integrations/<name>integrationservice.php` 2. register in `integrationregistry.php` (both iris-api and fl-api if needed) 3. add routes in `routes/api.php` if custom endpoints needed 4. add oauth config to `config/services.php` if oauth-based 5. create migration for any custom tables 6. add to this skill's registry table above 7. test: `iris integrations exec <new-type> <function>` --- ## notes - **test emails always go to alex@freelabel.net** — never send test emails to real clients - **ai models**: when testing integrations that use ai (intent routing, servis-ai analysis), only use gpt-5-nano, gpt-4.1-nano, or gpt-4o-mini - **iris-api vs fl-api**: both have integration registries. iris-api is the primary for cli execution. fl-api has its own for backend workflows - **composio**: some integrations were originally built on composio but migrated to native. if composio is mentioned in code, prefer the native implementation - **rate limits**: google apis have per-user quotas. mercury has strict rate limits. buffer has posting limits per plan - **credential storage**: all credentials encrypted at rest in the `integrations` table. never log or expose raw tokens

entries.name: iris-khalo
entries.describe: Produce a finished design artefact from the IRIS Khalo component system — pick an existing layout instead of inventing one, render it, and catch the four defects that have shipped from this system before. Every check here is one that reached a live page or a paid ad.
entries.haystack: iris-khalo produce a finished design artefact from the iris khalo component system — pick an existing layout instead of inventing one, render it, and catch the four defects that have shipped from this system before. every check here is one that reached a live page or a paid ad. --- name: iris-khalo description: produce a finished design artefact from the iris khalo component system — pick an existing layout instead of inventing one, render it, and catch the four defects that have shipped from this system before. every check here is one that reached a live page or a paid ad. version: 2 args: subject: type: string required: true description: what the artefact is about, in a sentence — the claim it has to carry composition: type: string required: false description: component id to render (e.g. flyerslide). omit to be walked through choosing one. preset: type: string required: false description: path to a props json under remotion/presets/ on-error: continue timeout: 900 --- # iris khalo **ai-augmented design, not image generation.** khalo does not invent a picture from a prompt. it pours a subject into a layout that already exists, in a brand ink that already exists, and returns an artefact you can verify. thirty-one components sit under `remotion/src/carousel/`; two brand kits already name the inks, the type roles and what each layout is for. **so the job is choosing, not designing.** a brief written on 2026-09-01 invented hero objects and palettes for three campaigns without opening either kit. all of it already existed, named, with a rule attached. ## the four defects this system has actually shipped not hypotheticals. all four happened, all four rendered *cleanly* while being wrong. 1. **components carry copy from the subject they were born for.** five found in one day: `pingslide` printed **"■ you did nothing"** on an iris install ad; `apprenticeshipslide` printed **"no tuition"** and, on the red flip bar, **"you stop paying → you start getting paid"** on a $49/mo subscription — a false claim about money in the ad's most prominent element; `indexslide` hardcoded the corner wordmark to **iris** and the badge to the iris cube on a freelabel creative. **grep the component for string literals before you trust the render.** 2. **a layout that overflows argues against its own headline.** `indexslide` at 12 entries showed eight, under a headline reading twelve products. it rendered perfectly. nothing catches this but looking at the output. 3. **a document layout is grey mush at 110px, which is where an ad is first seen.** measured: press/document creatives ran **8,348 impressions for 2 clicks at $1.29 cpc**, against **$0.0043** for a poster-format ad on the same account the same week. two of four line items produced zero clicks across 3,432 impressions. 4. **flyer lines collide when adjacent lines are similar in width.** `flyerslide` sets every line at a fixed 162px with `nowrap` and `lineheight: 0.86`, so lines always overlap by design — and in light mode the offset plate uses `multiply`, printing heavy. `keep / 100% / ownership` steps short→medium→long and reads as layering. `already / earning? / keep 100%` is three long lines and reads as mush. **it is not a character limit** — an earlier version of this file said six characters and that was wrong; `ownership` is nine and reads fine. ## choosing the form from the brand kits, and it is a mapping, not a preference: announcing something -> masthead a dateline and a band read as news listing n capabilities -> index numbering makes a list finite one line that is the product -> flyer give the sentence the whole canvas comparing tiers or specs -> ledger label -> value rows on hairlines one number that carries it -> stat the figure is the hero a threshold someone crosses -> apprentice a rule, with the ink reversing across it what runs while you are away -> night sheet the industry's own paperwork for absence one move, n destinations -> patch list a patch bay is a handover who keeps what -> settlement the middle column is the argument **if the form does not carry the argument, the copy is doing work the layout should do.** two angles changed form mid-build on 2026-09-01 for exactly this reason and both got better. ## steps ### step:inventory what already exists ### step:literals does the component carry copy from another subject? ### step:render render it full size ### step:thumbnail the 110px test — the size it is actually first seen at ### step:verify look at the render before believing it open both files and answer three questions. this step is a human on purpose: every defect in this playbook's list rendered without an error. - **does any text appear that you did not put in the props?** that is defect 1. - **is every row, entry or line you passed actually visible?** a list that silently drops items argues against its own headline. that is defect 2. - **at 110px, is the argument still there?** if it is texture, change the form, not the copy. that is defect 3. ### step:publish upload, and verify the url that ended up in the document ### step:card if this artefact becomes a link card, the page is not the card only if the artefact is an `og:image` for something a link card will render. **fixing the page does not fix the card.** x caches cards keyed on the page's **canonical**, so appending `?utm_source=…` does not bust it — verified on 2026-09-02, two different urls returned a byte-identical stale card, still showing copy that had been removed from the page hours earlier. re-scrape each destination at ` then create the ad post. the log lines are the confirmation: `page fetched successfully` / `n metatags were found` / `card loaded successfully`. the preview pane is gone — the re-scrape still happens. ### step:record put the artefact where the next person will find it an artefact nobody can find gets rebuilt. write the preset path, the composition, the cdn url and — most usefully — **why this form** into wherever the work lives: the brief page, the epic, or the `ad-campaigns` dataset if it is a paid creative. "ruled out, and here is how" is worth more than the artefact.

entries.name: iris-lexicon
entries.describe: Run a legal matter end to end through Lexicon's five doors — intake, conflicts, engagement, chronology, demand — in the order a matter actually moves, with the one gate nothing in the tooling enforces called out where it belongs.
entries.haystack: iris-lexicon run a legal matter end to end through lexicon's five doors — intake, conflicts, engagement, chronology, demand — in the order a matter actually moves, with the one gate nothing in the tooling enforces called out where it belongs. --- name: iris-lexicon description: run a legal matter end to end through lexicon's five doors — intake, conflicts, engagement, chronology, demand — in the order a matter actually moves, with the one gate nothing in the tooling enforces called out where it belongs. version: 2 args: enquiry: type: string required: false description: raw enquiry text — call notes, web form, pasted email. the front door of the lifecycle. party: type: string required: false description: prospective client and/or adverse party name to sweep for conflicts lead: type: string required: false description: lead / matter id, once the matter exists. engagement, chronology and demand all need it. bloq: type: string required: false description: matter bloq id — where artefacts get filed on-error: continue timeout: 600 --- # iris lexicon **what it is:** the front door onto five legal playbooks that already existed — `legal-matter-intake`, `legal-conflict-check`, `legal-engagement-letter`, `legal-matter-chronology`, `legal-demand-letter` — given a name a firm can type. `iris lexicon demand 123` and `iris playbook run legal-demand-letter 123` are the same rails. **what it is not: a matter management system.** no tables, no routes, no service class. it stores nothing — not which matters are open, which conflicts are cleared, which letters went out — and it has no send command. **what it is not: a lawyer.** every artefact below is a **draft for a qualified person to review**: the sweep surfaces conflict candidates and does not clear a conflict, the letter is a drafting aid rather than approved terms, the demand says `attorney review required` and means it. **this is not a sixth implementation.** it is the order of operations — what the five playbooks cannot know, because none knows what ran before it. ## the order a matter moves — and the gate nothing enforces enquiry ──intake──> matter record ──conflicts──> clearance ──engagement──> engaged ▲ │ an attorney, not a command │ demand <──readiness── chronology <─────────────────────┘ - **conflicts must precede the engagement letter.** `legal-matter-intake` says so in prose; its brief ends `next: run legal-conflict-check on the conflict_names before engaging.` - **nothing enforces it.** verified: `legal-engagement-letter` contains no reference to a conflict check — no gate, no precondition — and neither does the demand or the chronology. `iris lexicon engagement 123` runs happily on a matter never swept. the order is a discipline this playbook carries; it is not a rail. - **chronology before demand is a dependency, not etiquette.** the demand's readiness step reads the log the chronology assembles; off an empty log, `ready with gaps` means *we could not look*. ## the state everyone misreads **there is no matter state.** the lead's crm status is the only durable field and its taxonomy is a sales one — `new, prospected, qualified, proposal, in negotiation, active, won, lost`. none means *conflicts cleared* or *engaged*, and nothing in lexicon writes it. "has this been swept?" is answerable only from the bloq, or from a person. - **`--bloq` without `--list` silently does not file.** all five playbooks print `no --list given; printing instead of filing` and exit 0 — a successful-looking run that wrote nothing. get the list id from `iris bloqs get <bloq>`. - **intake and everything after it speak different languages.** `intake` takes an enquiry *string*; the other four take a numeric *lead id*. the bridge is `--open yes` → `iris leads create`, called **without `--json`**, so the new id is printed in prose and read off the output by eye. - **args are positional, in declaration order** (`enquiry party lead bloq`) — enter mid-lifecycle by passing empty strings for the earlier ones: `iris playbook run iris-lexicon "" "jane roe" 29092 570`. an empty optional interpolates to an empty string, so every step tests and skips rather than run on nothing. ## steps ### step:intake prove the doors open, then structure the enquiry read `dates_that_bite` first, and the `basis` on each. `computed` means the model derived it from a stated incident date — **a prompt to check a limitation period, not an authority.** ### step:open open the matter record creating the lead is the first thing here that writes. - `iris lexicon intake "<enquiry>" --practice <area> --open yes` — extracts, then creates - `iris leads get <id>` — confirm what landed; `iris bloqs get <bloq>` — get the list id **the lead is created from the extracted client name alone.** a misread name gives a matter under the wrong person — and the sweep that follows then searches for the wrong person. ### step:conflicts sweep — and sweep wider than the playbook does the second command is the point of this step. `legal-conflict-check` closes with `coverage note: cross-matter item search is not available via cli` — **that note is stale.** `iris leads search` sweeps *"crm records + mentions across your bloq projects"*, reaching matters that playbook never opens. but when nothing matches every word it silently falls back to `n partial crm match(es)` tagged `evidence: crm-partial` — searching "zzqx party" returns ten of them, one being an address containing "party". **partial hits are noise, not candidates.** covered by neither sweep: paper files, a previous firm, an untyped entity name. ### step:engage clearance first — then the engagement letter **a clean sweep is not a clearance.** it says nothing surfaced in the sources searched — a statement about the search, not the conflict. an attorney reviews the candidate sheet and signs off; until that has happened, nothing below this line runs. no command enforces it, which is why the gate lives inside the step it gates. file the clearance yourself (`iris bloqs add-item <bloq> <list> --title "conflicts cleared — <party>"`). then, and only then, draft the client-facing instrument: - `iris lexicon engagement <lead> --fee "contingency 33.3% pre-suit, 40% post-filing"` - `iris lexicon engagement <lead> --mode review --letter "<paste an existing letter>"` - add `--bloq <id> --list <id>` to file rather than print **it will not propose a fee** — without `--fee` it writes `[to confirm: fee arrangement]`. **it will not include jurisdiction-specific disclosures**, ending with a `jurisdiction check` list instead: written-fee-agreement, contingency and independent-counsel rules are checked by nothing here. every `[to confirm: ...]` is a fact the record lacked — resolve them all first. `--mode review` is the underused half: party mismatch, scope, signature blocks, fee ambiguity — the defects that surface at resolution. ### step:chronology assemble what the firm actually did read the channel breakdown *first*. a chronology built from four logged messages is four rows long and reads like a quiet matter — when what happened is nobody ran `iris atlas:comms ingest`. **a thin log and a quiet matter are indistinguishable in the output.** `--rate <n>` adds time and value from logged comms, not timekeeping — stamped `estimate only`, never bill it. ### step:demand draft the demand the most consequential document here — the only one whose failure mode is sending it early. - `iris lexicon demand <lead> --demand "185000 — specials 62k, 3x" --recipient "<carrier>"` - `iris lexicon demand <lead>` — drafts with the figure left open read the readiness verdict before the letter. **`not ready` stamps `draft only — the readiness check did not pass. do not send.` at the top and still produces a letter** — producing one is not permission to send it. **the number is the attorney's:** without `--demand` it writes `[attorney to set: demand amount and basis]` and proposes nothing, not even a range. **it cites no statute or case law by design.** ### step:close what survived, and what did not

entries.name: iris-memory
entries.describe: Give your agents a memory that survives between conversations instead of starting over every session. Store what matters, ask for it back in plain language later, and see how a lead, task, or invoice connects to everything else around it. Pass an action and arguments.
entries.haystack: iris-memory give your agents a memory that survives between conversations instead of starting over every session. store what matters, ask for it back in plain language later, and see how a lead, task, or invoice connects to everything else around it. pass an action and arguments. --- name: iris-memory description: give your agents a memory that survives between conversations instead of starting over every session. store what matters, ask for it back in plain language later, and see how a lead, task, or invoice connects to everything else around it. pass an action and arguments. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- # iris agent memory — unified memory management store, search, and manage persistent agent memory through the iris cli. the memory namespace provides both **unstructured working memory** (facts, insights, context, documents) and **structured crm entity access** (leads, tasks, invoices, outreach steps) through a single unified interface. ## arguments `$arguments` — action and parameters. examples: - `/iris-memory store 11 "client prefers morning meetings"` — store a fact - `/iris-memory store 11 document "contract: john doe hired as dj..."` — store a document - `/iris-memory search 11 "meeting preferences"` — search memories - `/iris-memory list 11` — list all memories for agent - `/iris-memory entities 11` — list leads in agent's workspace - `/iris-memory entities 11 tasks` — list tasks across all leads - `/iris-memory graph 11` — full entity relationship map - `/iris-memory delete <uuid>` — delete a memory --- ## important: always use production api **all memory and diary commands must hit the production iris-api**, not local docker containers. the local environment often lacks agent data and will return "agent not found" errors. **production base url**: ` (railway production url — replaces old do endpoint) ### primary method: direct curl to production ### fallback method: sdk cli (for local debugging only) the sdk `.env` at `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/.env` has `iris_env=production`, but agent resolution can still fail if the agent id doesn't exist as a `bloqagent` in the production fl_api db. when using the diary endpoint, prefer `bloq_id=217` over `agent_id=11`. ### agent/bloq id reference | agent | bloq | name | |-------|------|------| | 11 | 217 | iris platform growth - q1 2026 | | 407 | (default) | production general agent | for diary entries, always use `bloq_id` (more reliable than `agent_id`). --- ## memory types | type | purpose | dedup | |------|---------|-------| | `fact` | learned information ("client budget is $50k") | yes | | `insight` | discovered patterns ("open rates peak tuesdays") | yes | | `context` | project/workflow status ("phase 3 of 5 complete") | yes | | `preference` | user preferences ("prefers formal tone") | yes | | `relationship` | info about other agents | yes | | `document` | contracts, agreements, reference docs | **no** (dedup skipped) | **dedup behavior:** for all types except `document`, the system checks the first 200 chars for >80% similarity via `similar_text()`. if a match is found, the existing memory is updated instead of creating a duplicate. documents skip this entirely because contracts with the same event/date prefix would incorrectly merge. --- ## commands reference ### store memory ### search memory ### list memories ### delete memory ### entity memory (structured crm proxy) these commands resolve the **agent -> bloq -> leads** chain automatically. --- ## architecture ### three-tier memory ### url routing the sdk routes memory requests to **iris-api** (`heyiris.io`), not fl-api: - memory endpoints: ` - routing rule in `sdk/php/src/http/client.php:buildurl()` matches `/v6/memory` - entity endpoints query fl_api db via iris-api's `fl_api` database connection ### key files | file | purpose | |------|---------| | `fl-iris-api/app/http/controllers/api/agentmemorycontroller.php` | rest api (crud + entities + graph) | | `fl-iris-api/app/neuron/tools/agentmemorytool.php` | agent tool path (used by ai agents during workflows) | | `fl-iris-api/app/models/agentsurfacememory.php` | memory model (uuid, soft-delete, chromadb embeddings) | | `fl-iris-api/app/models/flapi/lead.php` | lead model with tasks/invoices/outreach relationships | | `fl-iris-api/app/models/flapi/leadtask.php` | task model for entity proxy | | `fl-iris-api/app/models/flapi/customrequest.php` | invoice/deal model for entity proxy | | `fl-iris-api/app/models/flapi/leadoutreachstep.php` | outreach step model for entity proxy | | `fl-iris-api/routes/api.php` | routes under `v6/memory` prefix | | `sdk/php/src/resources/memory/memoryresource.php` | sdk resource class (cli auto-proxy) | | `sdk/php/src/http/client.php` | url routing (`/v6/memory` -> irisurl) | ### entity chain resolution --- ## daily diary the diary provides a **unified timeline** that merges two data sources: 1. **diary entries** (bloqitems) — structured markdown entries from heartbeats and manual cli input 2. **heartbeat memories** (agentsurfacememory) — auto-stored summaries from the heartbeat system diary lives at the **bloq level** — each bloq has a "daily diary" list. agents resolve to their bloq automatically. ### diary commands ### diary architecture --- ## common workflows ### daily standup ### store contracts ### sales agent context load --- ## troubleshooting ### "the selected memory type is invalid" the `memory_type` enum in the database doesn't include the type you're trying to use. run the migration: ### 404 on memory endpoints the sdk might be routing to fl-api instead of iris-api. check `sdk/php/src/http/client.php:buildurl()` — memory endpoints must contain `/v6/memory` to route to `irisurl` (heyiris.io). ### documents getting merged/overwritten the dedup check in `agentmemorycontroller.php` and `agentmemorytool.php` must skip `type=document`. look for: ### "agent has no associated bloq" on entities the agent doesn't have a `bloq_id` set. entities require the agent -> bloq -> leads chain. check: --- ## steps ### 1. parse the argument | argument pattern | action | |-----------------|--------| | `store <agent_id> "<content>"` | store as fact (default) | | `store <agent_id> <type> "<content>"` | store with specific type | | `search <agent_id> "<query>"` | search memories | | `list <agent_id>` | list memories (optionally with filters) | | `delete <uuid>` | delete a memory | | `entities <agent_id>` | list leads | | `entities <agent_id> <type>` | list tasks/invoices/outreach | | `graph <agent_id>` | full relationship graph | ### 2. run the command via production api always use direct curl to the production iris-api do url: for diary entries, use `bloq_id=217` instead of `agent_id=11` (more reliable). only fall back to the sdk cli (`cd fl-docker-dev/sdk/php && php bin/iris ...`) when explicitly debugging local development. ### 3. display results format the json response for readability. for `graph` responses, consider displaying the tree structure visually.

entries.name: iris-pulse
entries.describe: Score health for a subject that has a row and for work that does not — read your own account readiness, one account's deal health, or sweep the trail a topic left across commits, diary, files, agent sessions and mail. Then arm an alert so the score comes to you instead of you going to it.
entries.haystack: iris-pulse score health for a subject that has a row and for work that does not — read your own account readiness, one account's deal health, or sweep the trail a topic left across commits, diary, files, agent sessions and mail. then arm an alert so the score comes to you instead of you going to it. --- name: iris-pulse description: score health for a subject that has a row and for work that does not — read your own account readiness, one account's deal health, or sweep the trail a topic left across commits, diary, files, agent sessions and mail. then arm an alert so the score comes to you instead of you going to it. version: 2 args: keyword: type: string required: false description: topic to sweep — e.g. "creator os". work with no lead row, no owner, no id, only a trail. lead: type: string required: false description: lead id, name or email, to score one account instead of yourself days: type: string required: false description: sweep window in days (default 30). momentum compares it against the equally-long window before it. on-error: continue timeout: 300 --- # iris pulse **what it is:** a scoring engine with its own subjects, history and alarms. `scoperegistry` declares seven subjects — `lead`, `user`, `heartbeat_lead`, `heartbeat_user`, `creator`, `project`, `topic` — each scored across ~20 signals (setup, agent liveness, comms, billing, integrations, outreach, tasks, content, knowledge, meetings, response time, referrals, deliverables, opportunities). `pulse:tick` snapshots those scores into `readiness_runs`, `pulse_alert_rules` fire against consecutive snapshots, `readiness_remediation_tasks` hold what to do about it. **what it is not: a view over your crm.** that is the obvious guess and it is wrong. three scopes — `creator`, `project`, `topic` — score subjects that **have no crm row at all**. that is the point of `pulse check`: *"creator os" has no id, no owner and no record — only a trail*, across commits, diary, agent transcripts, files, messages and mail. pulse walks that trail and files the result as a scored entity in the **signal corpus** (`signal_entities`, `signal_observations`, `signal_entity_vectors`), so the second time you ask there is history to diff instead of a fresh grep. leads cannot represent that subject, so this cannot be a view over them. ## three subjects, one word iris pulse → you how healthy is my own account? iris leads pulse <id> → one account how healthy is this deal? iris pulse --admin → every client agency scorecard (other people's data) iris pulse check "<kw>" → a trail is this thread warm enough to continue? **confusing these is the most common pulse mistake.** a bad number on the wrong subject sends you to fix the wrong thing. ## the state everyone misreads **a low signal usually means "not measured," not "unhealthy."** setup scoring 10/100 because `iris init` never ran looks identical to setup scoring 10/100 because setup is broken. the score cannot distinguish *we looked and it is bad* from *we could not look*. confirm the input exists before acting on a red — otherwise you are optimising a measurement gap. three more, each of which has cost someone an afternoon: - **`--for n` counts `pulse:tick` snapshots, not your cli runs.** the tick is `everytwohours()`, so `--for 3` is roughly six hours of sustained badness. (the comment above it still says "every 15 min" — stale. trust the code.) - **momentum `null` is not "flat."** null means no prior observation to diff against. a first sweep is always null. - **the corpus scheduler is off unless `corpus_scheduler_enabled` is set.** `corpus:tick` and `corpus:sweep` spend quota and send discord, so a deploy is deliberately not allowed to start them. if nobody enabled it, corpus scores are as fresh as the last manual sweep. ## steps ### step:score read your own account first ### step:read decide which reds are real sort each red into one of two piles. this is the whole judgement call and no command makes it for you. - **not measured.** setup is low because `iris init` never ran; knowledge base is low because nothing was ingested. the fix is to supply the input, not to fix the thing being scored. - **measured and bad.** comms is low and there genuinely has been no inbound in weeks. only the second pile is a problem. chasing the first is how a health score becomes busywork. the cli points at the worst signal under "next step" — a suggestion, not a verdict. the worst score is frequently the least-measured one rather than the most broken one. ### step:lead score one account a **different scope** (`lead`) with different signals than `iris pulse` (`user`) — deal health, payment gates and comms recency, not your own setup. a lead can be failing while your account is healthy, and vice versa. it also accepts `--hydrate`, which **generates and sends a follow-up** when the payment gate is unpaid and the throttle window has passed. do not add that flag to explore. it contacts a real person. ### step:trail sweep a topic without filing it `--no-push` is the honest first run: it sweeps and prints but files nothing, so you can see whether the keyword matches the thing you meant before it becomes a permanent corpus entity. sources are `git, diary, files, claude_code, opencode, imessage, email, gmail, bloq` — narrow with `--sources` when a run is slow or noisy. a source reporting *unavailable* is not a zero; it means that channel could not be read (not signed in, bridge down) — the "not measured" trap again. ### step:file file it in the signal corpus **`iris pulse check` pushes by default.** dropping `--no-push` permanently writes a scored entity plus one observation per source into the signal corpus. that is what you want once the keyword is right — it gives the *next* sweep something to diff against — but it is a write, so do it deliberately: iris pulse check "<keyword>" --days <n> **do not add `--include-context` casually.** it uploads the actual text of messages, mail and agent sessions, off by default precisely because those carry credentials and client data. there is no un-uploading them. pick the keyword like a name, not a search: it becomes the entity's identity, and a vague one ("app") produces an entity that matches everything and means nothing. ### step:alerts see what is already armed read the existing rules before adding one. two rules on the same signal at nearby thresholds means every dip pages you twice, which is how a team learns to ignore the channel. ### step:arm arm a new alert adding a rule is arming something that will **message real people on a schedule**, so this is a decision, not an exploration: iris pulse alerts add -s <signal> --below <n> --for <n> -c discord|imessage|log - **`-s`** takes the underlying signal key — `comms_freshness`, `deal_health`, `config`, `requirements`, `liveness` — not the pretty label in the score output. - **`--for`** is consecutive snapshots at two hours each. `--for 1` fires on a single bad tick, which for a noisy signal means it fires constantly. - **`-c log`** arms the rule without notifying anyone. use it to watch a threshold for a day and learn how often it would have fired before you point it at discord. remove with `iris pulse alerts remove <id>` — also irreversible, and the rule's history goes with it. ### step:agency the agency view `iris pulse --admin` switches subject entirely: diary digest, lead scorecard and ungated leads **across your clients**. it filters with `--status` (default `won,active,in negotiation,negotiating`) and `-b/--bloq`. **this is other tenants' data.** run it when you have a reason to look at client health, not to explore what the command prints. `--notify` additionally sends the summary to you over imessage. if a client scores badly, go back to `step:read` and sort their reds into *not measured* and *measured and bad* first. most agency-view alarm is the former.

entries.name: iris-reachr
entries.describe: Turn "we should follow up with these people" into a sequence that survives the week — audit the offer you are carrying, build an outreach strategy once, apply it to a lead, work the steps through the comms router so every touch lands in the ledger, and issue the licence when someone says yes. Reachr owns the whole arc — what you sell, how it reaches people, and what a yes produces.
entries.haystack: iris-reachr turn "we should follow up with these people" into a sequence that survives the week — audit the offer you are carrying, build an outreach strategy once, apply it to a lead, work the steps through the comms router so every touch lands in the ledger, and issue the licence when someone says yes. reachr owns the whole arc — what you sell, how it reaches people, and what a yes produces. --- name: iris-reachr description: 'turn "we should follow up with these people" into a sequence that survives the week — audit the offer you are carrying, build an outreach strategy once, apply it to a lead, work the steps through the comms router so every touch lands in the ledger, and issue the licence when someone says yes. reachr owns the whole arc — what you sell, how it reaches people, and what a yes produces.' version: 2 args: bloq: type: string required: true description: board (bloq) id the strategy lives on — strategies belong to a board, not to you lead: type: string required: false description: lead id to apply a strategy to, once one exists strategy: type: string required: false description: strategy id, if you already know which one on-error: continue timeout: 300 --- # iris reachr **what it is:** the revenue chain. reachr's end state is a **collected payment** you can trace back through fulfilment → licence → payment → package → opportunity → buyer → organization. if you cannot walk that chain, a relationship is missing. offers what you are selling iris reachr offers audit strategies how it reaches somebody iris reachr list / apply <- the steps below send the touch actually going out iris outreach-send send licence what a yes produces iris reachr licence issue **the crm models relationships, not contacts.** a person belongs to several organizations, may influence one deal while somebody else pays, may refer, may administer a licence. an organization has locations, brands, subscriptions, licences and several live opportunities. every connection is stored with a **role** — buyer · decision maker · champion · billing contact · user · referral source · partner · licence administrator. five atlas datasets hold this: reachr-organization the account reachr-relationship person <-> org <-> opportunity, with a role reachr-opportunity one primary package, expected value, next action, owner reachr-payment the closing event, linked to everything around it reachr-fulfilment what was delivered, checkpoints, renewal, churn risk, expansion **the four questions.** for every active relationship the system must answer: what is the highest-value outcome available · what package fits it · what evidence or action moves it forward · who owns the next action. **no package, no next action, no owner, or no expected value means it is not a deal — it is an unqualified contact**, and it does not belong in a forecast. **the progression.** captured → qualified → scoped → package selected → checkout sent → payment pending → paid → activated → fulfilled → retained → expanded → referred. the point is not more stages; it is that every stage creates a **measurable position relative to payment**. **rank by expected collected revenue, not activity.** package value × likelihood × urgency × relationship strength × decision-maker access, decayed by time since the last real touch — and **subtract** for no next step, no identified buyer, no package selected, stale follow-up. the output is one answer to "what do i do today": move the highest-value, most-likely-to-pay opportunity one step closer to checkout. **payment does not end it.** payment creates entitlement, entitlement defines access, and access belongs to a person *or an organization*. on payment: assign the package, issue the licence, start fulfilment, schedule checkpoints, watch renewal, surface expansion. a *strategy* is a sequence of steps — what to say, in what order, how long to wait. you write it once, apply it to any lead, and reachr tracks where each person is in it. **the middle part is only as good as the first.** a sequence carries an offer; if the offer has no stack, no price anchor and no guarantee, more follow-ups will not fix it — they will just reach more people with the same reason to say no. that is why this playbook starts by auditing the offer rather than by writing copy. **what it is not: a single send button — yet.** `outreach-send send`, `vary` and `personalize` report **"not yet available"**. that is a **missing wire, not a missing capability**: this platform sends every day, through paths that already log to the comms ledger. iris mail send <to> email, via the comms router — lands in the log iris imessage send <handle> sms/imessage, logged to the comms ledger those two are the only commands that call the router (`routersend` in comms-send.ts). `iris som` is campaign machinery against /api/v1/som/campaigns — it has its own server-side ledger, but it is not the same code path and should not be reached for when you mean "send this one person their next step". **and the missing wire is 40 lines, not a feature.** the server door is already built: `post /api/v1/atlas/comms/send` (`routes/api.php:2789`) carries the comment *"every non-php surface (cli `reachr send`, agent tools, dashboard) sends through here so the ledger write cannot be skipped"*. `commsrouter` enforces caps and suppression, writes `lead_comms`, and `outreachprogress::oncommlogged()` **completes the step automatically** from `step_id`. the cli's `sendcmd` is a stub that says *"not implemented on the server"* — which is no longer true. **so the loop is real, it is just not one command.** reachr says who is owed what; you send through `mail`, `imessage` or a som campaign; the comms ledger records it; you mark the step complete. the gap between "reachr told me to send this" and "the send happened" is currently a human, and closing it is wiring `outreach-send send` to the router that `mail` and `imessage` already use — not building a sender. **know which one you are in.** som is for *campaigns* — many leads, one script, with a ledger and retry. reachr is for *sequences* — one lead, several steps, over time. using som for a sequence gives you no memory of where each person is; using reachr for a campaign means sending by hand a hundred times. ## the shape offer what the sequence is carrying │ iris reachr offers audit ▼ strategy (lives on a board, reusable) step 1 ─┐ step 2 │ apply to a lead step 3 ─┘ │ ▼ lead's own step list ── you send it ──> mark complete ──> yes ──> licence └─ cannot contact ─> mark invalid iris reachr licence issue **a strategy belongs to a board, not to a person.** that is why every command takes a `<bloq-id>` — and it is what makes the strategy reusable instead of something one person keeps in their notes. ## what lands in the ledger, and what silently does not **send through reachr, or log it after. never neither.** a touch that is not on the lead record did not happen, as far as anyone else is concerned — no follow-up fires, no one covering for you knows it went out, and "we never heard from you" becomes unarguable. the trap is inverted, which is why it keeps catching people: **the flags that make a message more deliberate are the ones that drop it out of the record.** a specific sender identity, a cc, an attachment — each one silently switches to a direct bridge send. it prints `not logged to comms` and exits 0, so nothing looks wrong. sending from a client address, the most careful thing you can do, is exactly what loses the trace. tracked as **#183515**. same for anything sent by hand — gmail in a browser, mail.app, a phone. it is not in the ledger until you put it there. ### log a touch that went out any other way `--channel` takes any of the ten real channels — `gmail · imessage · apple_mail · whatsapp · instagram · linkedin · sms · phone · in_person · other`. the help used to list four of them and validate none, so people concluded email could not be logged and skipped it. fixed in **#183514**; if your cli still shows four, upgrade. then confirm it actually landed — the write succeeding is not the same as the row being there: ### do not reach for `comms ingest` to backfill `ingest` sweeps a channel and attaches what it finds. its lead matching has been wrong in production: `--channel all` on a client lead once pulled **22 messages from an unrelated private conversation** onto that client's record, because phone matching used a substring comparison. fixed in **#183513**, but the lesson survives the fix — **ingest writes to a named client record without asking.** prefer `comms log` for one known touch. if you do ingest, name one channel, never `all`, and read `comms list` immediately after. if something wrong does land: it refuses to run unnarrowed, shows you what matches, and asks before deleting. ## before you start you need a **board id** and, to get past planning, at least one **lead id** on it. if you have neither, this is the wrong playbook — you need leads first. ## steps ### step:offer what are you actually asking them to buy ### step:existing what strategies already exist on this board ### step:design write the strategy as a file, not as a thought strategies are created from json: - `iris reachr create <bloq-id> --from-json <file>` write the file first, and keep the sequence honest: - **every step is something a human will actually do.** reachr does not send, so a step that says "automated nurture email" is a step that will never complete. - **spacing is the product.** the difference between a sequence that works and one that annoys is almost entirely the gaps between steps. - **name what the step is for**, not what channel it uses. "ask if the pilot answered their question" survives; "email 2" does not. start from an existing strategy — `iris reachr show <bloq-id> <id>` prints one with its steps, and editing a real one beats inventing a schema. ### step:create create it ### step:apply apply it to one real lead ### step:work work the steps ### step:review does the sequence actually work after a full pass through a strategy on several leads, look at it as a whole: - **which step do people stop at?** that step is wrong, not the people. - **which steps get marked invalid most?** usually a channel problem, not a message problem. - **did anyone reply before the sequence finished?** then the later steps are noise and the sequence is too long. update the strategy — `iris reachr update <bloq-id> <id> --from-json` — rather than writing a new one. a board with nine near-identical strategies is how this product stops being useful. `iris som` gives the campaign-level view across everything, and `iris outreach-campaign` manages campaigns rather than individual sequences. ## when someone says yes the sequence ends in an entitlement, not a reply. that is the third part of the arc and it lives under the same product: iris reachr licence issue --email=them@example.com --tier=pro --seats=3 # give them the key; they run: iris licence claim <key> iris reachr licence me # what they are entitled to now `issue`, `list` and `revoke` are operator actions and answer **404** to anyone else — a licence endpoint that confirms it exists to the wrong caller is an invitation. so "not found" there means "you are not an operator", not "the key is wrong".

entries.name: lead-health-sweep
entries.describe: Sweep all active leads, identify the weakest pulse scores, generate AI follow-up recommendations, and optionally send outreach. Run daily or on-demand to keep deals from going cold.
entries.haystack: lead-health-sweep sweep all active leads, identify the weakest pulse scores, generate ai follow-up recommendations, and optionally send outreach. run daily or on-demand to keep deals from going cold. --- name: lead-health-sweep description: sweep all active leads, identify the weakest pulse scores, generate ai follow-up recommendations, and optionally send outreach. run daily or on-demand to keep deals from going cold. version: 2 args: action: type: string required: false default: report enum: [report, draft, send] description: report = show findings, draft = generate follow-ups, send = dispatch outreach threshold: type: number required: false default: 50 description: pulse score threshold — leads below this are flagged limit: type: number required: false default: 10 description: max leads to process on-error: continue timeout: 120 --- # lead health sweep automated deal health maintenance. finds leads with low pulse scores, analyzes why they're stalling, and generates (or sends) follow-up actions. ## steps ### step:fetch-and-filter fetch leads and filter by pulse score ### step:report generate report you are a crm health analyst. here are leads with low pulse scores (below the threshold): ${{steps.fetch-and-filter.output}} for each lead, provide: 1. why the score is likely low (based on the data: no recent notes, no payment gate, stale contact) 2. a specific recommended action (follow-up email topic, meeting request, content to share) 3. priority level (urgent / important / monitor) format as a clean summary table. be concise — one line per lead. ### step:draft-followups draft follow-up messages based on the lead analysis: ${{steps.report.output}} draft a brief, personalized follow-up message for each lead. the tone should be professional but warm — not salesy. reference something specific about their business. each message should be 2-3 sentences max. format as json array: [{"lead_id": 123, "lead_name": "...", "subject": "...", "message": "..."}] ### step:send-outreach send follow-up messages ### step:summary final summary

entries.name: legal-conflict-check
entries.describe: Sweep the firm's own records — leads, profiles, and a matter board — for a prospective party, and assemble a candidate sheet for an attorney to clear. Surfaces candidates; it does NOT clear the conflict.
entries.haystack: legal-conflict-check sweep the firm's own records — leads, profiles, and a matter board — for a prospective party, and assemble a candidate sheet for an attorney to clear. surfaces candidates; it does not clear the conflict. --- name: legal-conflict-check description: sweep the firm's own records — leads, profiles, and a matter board — for a prospective party, and assemble a candidate sheet for an attorney to clear. surfaces candidates; it does not clear the conflict. category: legal version: 2 args: party: type: string required: true description: prospective client or adverse party name to search for also: type: string required: false description: comma-separated additional names to sweep (spouse, employer, carrier, related entities) bloq: type: number required: false description: matter bloq to also scan, and to file the sheet against list: type: number required: false description: list id within that bloq to file the sheet into on-error: continue timeout: 180 --- # legal — conflict check sweeps the firm's own records for a prospective party and assembles a candidate sheet. **read this before using it.** there is no conflicts database behind this playbook, and iris has no cross-matter item search — so this covers leads, profiles, and one named matter board, and nothing else. a clean result means *"nothing surfaced in these sources"*, which is **not** the same as *"no conflict exists"*. **an attorney clears the conflict.** this only makes sure they are looking at what the firm can see. ## steps ### step:sweep sweep firm records for the party ### step:assess assemble the candidate sheet you are assisting a law firm's conflicts review. below is raw output from a search across the firm's records for one or more party names. produce a conflicts review sheet: 1. **candidate hits** — every record that plausibly refers to a searched party. for each: what record it is, which name matched, and why it might matter (current client, former client, adverse party, related entity, shared counsel). 2. **match confidence** — exact / probable / weak-name-collision. be strict: a common surname alone is a weak collision, not a hit. 3. **not covered** — restate the coverage gap from the sweep output, plus anything the search could not resolve (entities sharing a name, records with empty party fields). rules: - if nothing surfaced, say so plainly and state that this is not a clearance. - do **not** state a conclusion about whether the firm may take the matter. that is the attorney's determination. - end with this exact line: `clearance required: an attorney must review and sign off before engagement.` ### step:file file the sheet against the matter

entries.name: legal-demand-letter
entries.describe: Check a matter is ready to demand, then draft the demand from the record — liability, damages, and the number, argued rather than guessed.
entries.haystack: legal-demand-letter check a matter is ready to demand, then draft the demand from the record — liability, damages, and the number, argued rather than guessed. --- name: legal-demand-letter description: check a matter is ready to demand, then draft the demand from the record — liability, damages, and the number, argued rather than guessed. category: legal version: 2 args: lead: type: number required: true description: lead / matter id demand: type: string required: false description: demand amount and its basis, as decided by the attorney (e.g. "185000 — specials 62k, 3x multiplier") recipient: type: string required: false description: who the demand is addressed to (carrier, adjuster, opposing counsel) bloq: type: number required: false list: type: number required: false on-error: continue timeout: 240 --- # legal — demand letter readiness check first, then the draft. the readiness step exists because the expensive failure is not a weak letter — it is a demand sent before the evidence supports it. **the number is the attorney's.** this playbook will not invent one; if `--demand` is absent it drafts with the figure left open. ## steps ### step:record pull the matter record and communications ### step:readiness check the matter is ready to demand assess whether this matter is ready for a demand. report: 1. **present** — what the record establishes: parties, liability facts, damages evidence, the authority to act (engagement, releases, authorisations). 2. **missing** — what a demand normally rests on that is absent here. be specific. 3. **verdict** — one of `ready`, `ready with gaps`, or `not ready`, with the reason in a single sentence. do not soften a `not ready`. a demand sent early is harder to recover from than a demand sent late. ### step:draft draft the demand draft a demand letter from the record and the readiness assessment. readiness: record: addressed to: `${{args.recipient}}` demand figure and basis, set by the attorney: `${{args.demand}}` structure: introduction and representation; liability, argued from the facts in the record; damages, itemised from what the record supports; the demand and its basis; a response deadline left as `[to confirm: response deadline]`; and a closing. rules that override everything above: - **every factual assertion must trace to the record.** no invented treatment, expense, witness, or date. where the letter needs a fact the record lacks, write `[to confirm: ...]` in place of it. - if `${{args.demand}}` is empty, write `[attorney to set: demand amount and basis]` and do not propose a figure — not even a range. - do not cite statutes or case law. you have not verified any, and an unverified citation in a demand is worse than none. - if readiness was `not ready`, put this line at the very top: `draft only — the readiness check did not pass. do not send.` end with: `attorney review required before sending.` ### step:file file the draft

entries.name: legal-engagement-letter
entries.describe: Draft an engagement letter from the matter record, and check an existing one for the defects that surface at resolution — missing signature, wrong scope, party mismatch.
entries.haystack: legal-engagement-letter draft an engagement letter from the matter record, and check an existing one for the defects that surface at resolution — missing signature, wrong scope, party mismatch. --- name: legal-engagement-letter description: draft an engagement letter from the matter record, and check an existing one for the defects that surface at resolution — missing signature, wrong scope, party mismatch. category: legal version: 2 args: lead: type: number required: true description: lead / matter id mode: type: string required: false default: draft enum: [draft, review] description: draft = produce a letter; review = check a letter you paste in letter: type: string required: false description: existing letter text (required when mode=review) fee: type: string required: false description: fee arrangement in plain words (e.g. "contingency 33.3% pre-suit, 40% post-filing") bloq: type: number required: false list: type: number required: false on-error: continue timeout: 180 --- # legal — engagement letter draft or review the instrument that lets you act. a defective engagement is not discovered when it is signed — it is discovered at resolution, when it is far too late. this is a drafting and checking aid: **an attorney approves the letter and its fee terms**, and the fee arrangement must comply with your jurisdiction's rules, which this does not check. ## steps ### step:matter pull the matter record ### step:draft draft the engagement letter draft an engagement letter from this matter record. fee arrangement as instructed by the attorney: `${{args.fee}}` include, in order: parties and the client being engaged; scope of representation and what is expressly excluded; the fee arrangement exactly as given; costs and how they are advanced and recovered; client responsibilities; termination by either side; and a signature block for every party who must sign. rules: - mark every fact you did not find in the record as `[to confirm: ...]`. **do not invent names, dates, fee terms, or scope.** - if the fee arrangement was not supplied, write `[to confirm: fee arrangement]` rather than proposing one. - do not include jurisdiction-specific required disclosures — you do not know the jurisdiction's rules. instead end with a checklist headed `jurisdiction check — confirm before sending:` listing the categories of disclosure that commonly apply (fee-agreement writing requirements, contingency-fee disclosures, right to independent counsel, arbitration clause rules). ### step:review review an existing engagement letter check this engagement letter against the matter record for defects. matter record: letter: report, as a defect list ordered by severity: 1. **party mismatch** — anyone named in the letter who is not in the record, or a client in the record not engaged by the letter. 2. **scope problems** — representation broader or narrower than the matter, or scope that cannot be determined from the text. 3. **signature and execution** — missing blocks, unsigned parties, absent dates. 4. **fee and costs** — terms that are absent, internally inconsistent, or ambiguous about when a percentage changes. 5. **consistency with posture** — anything contradicting the matter's stage or parties. for each defect: what it is, where it appears, and what it costs if it goes unfixed. if a category is clean, say so in one line. quote the letter only where needed to locate a defect. end with: `attorney review required — this is a drafting aid, not an approval.` ### step:file file the output

entries.name: legal-matter-chronology
entries.describe: Assemble every logged communication on a matter into a dated chronology with a work summary — the thing you reach for when a client disputes what was done.
entries.haystack: legal-matter-chronology assemble every logged communication on a matter into a dated chronology with a work summary — the thing you reach for when a client disputes what was done. --- name: legal-matter-chronology description: assemble every logged communication on a matter into a dated chronology with a work summary — the thing you reach for when a client disputes what was done. category: legal version: 2 args: lead: type: number required: true description: lead / matter id rate: type: number required: false description: hourly rate — if given, the work summary carries estimated time and value bloq: type: number required: false description: bloq to file the chronology against list: type: number required: false description: list id within that bloq on-error: continue timeout: 240 --- # legal — matter chronology pulls the unified communications log and the matter notes, and assembles a dated chronology of what the firm actually did. this is the use case that pays for itself: reconstructing a matter history by hand is hours of work, and it is what you need when a client asks what they are paying for. **estimates are estimates.** any time or value figure below is derived from logged communications, not from a timekeeping system. it is a starting point for a bill review, never a substitute for one. ## steps ### step:gather gather the record ### step:chronology assemble the chronology you are assembling a matter chronology for a law firm. below is the raw record: matter details, the unified communications log, a channel breakdown, and matter notes. produce: **1. chronology** — a dated table, oldest first: | date | channel | who | what happened | work performed | |---|---|---|---|---| one row per discrete event. `work performed` describes the firm's activity in plain professional language ("reviewed and responded to carrier's coverage position"), not a restatement of the message. **2. work summary** — grouped by activity type (client communication, third-party correspondence, document review, negotiation), with a count of events per group. **3. gaps** — periods with no logged activity longer than 30 days, and anything in the record that is ambiguous or undated. rules: - **every row must trace to something in the record above.** never infer an event that is not logged. if the record is thin, the chronology is short — say so. - undated entries go in a separate "undated" section, not guessed into the timeline. ### step:value add estimated time and value given this chronology and an hourly rate of `${{args.rate}}`: add an estimated-time column to the work summary and a total. use conservative, defensible increments for the activity types shown. open with this exact line, and do not soften it: `estimate only — derived from logged communications, not from timekeeping records. verify against time entries before billing.` ### step:file file the chronology

entries.name: legal-matter-intake
entries.describe: Turn a free-text enquiry (call note, web form, email) into a structured matter intake — parties, posture, dates that bite, and a routing recommendation — then open it as a lead.
entries.haystack: legal-matter-intake turn a free-text enquiry (call note, web form, email) into a structured matter intake — parties, posture, dates that bite, and a routing recommendation — then open it as a lead. --- name: legal-matter-intake description: turn a free-text enquiry (call note, web form, email) into a structured matter intake — parties, posture, dates that bite, and a routing recommendation — then open it as a lead. category: legal version: 2 args: enquiry: type: string required: true description: raw enquiry text — call notes, form submission, or pasted email practice: type: string required: false default: general description: practice area hint (personal-injury, employment, immigration, general) open: type: string required: false default: "no" enum: ["no", "yes"] description: yes = create the lead record; no = extract and print only on-error: continue timeout: 120 --- # legal — matter intake structured capture from an unstructured enquiry. extracts the fields a matter record needs, flags what is missing, and recommends where it should go. **this does not qualify or engage anyone.** whether a licensed attorney must speak to a prospective client before engagement is a rule of your jurisdiction, not a setting here. run `legal-conflict-check` before any engagement. ## steps ### step:extract extract the matter fields you are a legal intake specialist. convert this enquiry into a structured intake record. practice area hint: `${{args.practice}}` enquiry: return json only, no prose: rules: - use `""` for anything not stated. **never invent a fact, a date, or a party.** - `dates_that_bite`: any limitation or deadline exposure. mark `basis` honestly — if you derived it from a stated incident date, that is `computed`, and computed dates are a prompt to check, never an authority to rely on. - `conflict_names`: every human or entity named anywhere, for the conflict sweep. - `missing`: the fields an intake person must go back and ask for. ### step:brief write the intake brief turn this structured intake into a short brief an attorney can read in thirty seconds. format: - **matter** — one sentence. - **parties** — client, adverse, counsel/carrier if known. - **clock** — each date that bites, with its basis marked. if any are `computed`, say so. - **missing** — what intake still has to collect. - **route to** — recommendation and urgency, with the reason. end with: `next: run legal-conflict-check on the conflict_names before engaging.` ### step:open open the lead record

entries.name: licensing
entries.describe: Put a client on IRIS with a licence key instead of a discount code — issue it, send it, confirm they can actually use it, and price it while the deal is still being negotiated. Covers the whole path from "we agreed to work together" to "they are working", including the checks that catch a client seeing an empty workspace before they do.
entries.haystack: licensing put a client on iris with a licence key instead of a discount code — issue it, send it, confirm they can actually use it, and price it while the deal is still being negotiated. covers the whole path from "we agreed to work together" to "they are working", including the checks that catch a client seeing an empty workspace before they do. --- name: licensing description: put a client on iris with a licence key instead of a discount code — issue it, send it, confirm they can actually use it, and price it while the deal is still being negotiated. covers the whole path from "we agreed to work together" to "they are working", including the checks that catch a client seeing an empty workspace before they do. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- # licensing — from "we agreed" to "they are working" every command below runs against production via `railway ssh -s fl-api -- php artisan ...`. each one has worked examples in `--help`; this playbook is the order, which `--help` cannot show. ## the shape of the thing a licence **exists before anyone owns it** — that is what makes it sendable. claiming sets the owner and the first seat. seats are rows rather than a counter, so you can always see *which* people. nothing is deleted: released seats and removed products stay for the audit trail. three commercial states are **derived, never stored**: there is no `--state` flag. a stored state would be a copy that can disagree with the fields it came from, and the disagreement is silent. see `/p/epic-licence-pricing`. ## steps ### 1 · issue the licence `--trial-days` ends the **free part**. `--days` sets an expiry, which ends **access**. they are different and you almost always want the first — otherwise a 45-day trial is implemented by threatening to switch someone off on day 46. seats should match their headcount, not their first user. a key that runs out on person four is a support conversation you scheduled for yourself. ### 2 · provision the workspace before sending anything this is the step that gets skipped, and it is the one a client notices. signing up creates a user and nothing else. without a workspace row they sign in perfectly and see an **empty product**, which reads as broken rather than unfinished. check the bloq name before you use its id. if it says *"not client-visible"*, it means it. ### 3 · confirm their workspace actually answers the rag suite proves the *pipeline* works against its own fixtures. this proves **their** workspace answers from **their** material — a different question, and the only one they care about. retrieval and generation are reported separately: a generic answer is either "nothing retrieved" or "plenty retrieved and ignored", and one number cannot tell those apart. do not send the email until every query retrieves something. ### 4 · send the key client onboarding and partner copy are **different commands on purpose**. sending client onboarding to the partner who set the deal up explains their own product back to them. never print a multi-seat key on a public page. a promo code with a use cap can live in public; a licence key **is** the access, and the first n strangers to find it take the seats. ### 5 · price it while they use it price is a **sum over products × seats**, never a number typed on the licence. `--price` is per seat per month in **cents**. `--agreed` records what was actually settled, which may be less than the quote — both are kept, so "why is this $600 when the products say $750" is answerable next year. agreeing a price during a trial does **not** end the trial. that is the point: you negotiate while they are using it. ### 6 · answer "is this person licensed?" one call covers both levels — their own licence, or a seat on someone else's team licence. it exits non-zero when they are not, so it drops straight into a script. ## traps - **credits are not licences.** `--credits` touches the marketplace balance. it does **not** change what a desktop client may spend — that is a dollar cap in `fl-iris-api`. granting credits to fix "they cannot use the app" changes nothing at all. - **a licence key typed into the sign-in window works.** it is recognised by shape (`iris-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx`) in the same field that takes promo codes. if someone reports it rejected, check the shape before checking the licence. - **`license:manage list` shows revoked keys too.** revoking keeps seats and history — that is deliberate, and it means the list is not a list of live licences. - **releasing a seat removes access immediately**, and the row stays. "who had access in march" is a question that gets asked. ## related - `/p/epic-licence-pricing` — why the state enum was deleted, and what is still knowingly wrong - `/p/epic-billing-unification` — why credits and desktop spend are two different meters

entries.name: live-meeting-to-build-pipeline
entries.describe: Turn a live client meeting into a shared Atlas item, an open-questions list, a scoped epic, landed data and a shipped UI — then onboard, collect feedback, and run it again.
entries.haystack: live-meeting-to-build-pipeline turn a live client meeting into a shared atlas item, an open-questions list, a scoped epic, landed data and a shipped ui — then onboard, collect feedback, and run it again. --- name: live-meeting-to-build-pipeline description: turn a live client meeting into a shared atlas item, an open-questions list, a scoped epic, landed data and a shipped ui — then onboard, collect feedback, and run it again. version: 2 on-error: stop --- # live meeting → build pipeline capture a live team/client meeting as it happens, synthesize it into a single living atlas item the room can watch update in real time, surface the open questions instead of burying them, turn decisions into a scoped epic with child tickets, and carry that through to shipped sops, landed data, a genesis ui, and any automation the meeting called for. it is a loop, not a line. the last step onboards the people who will use what shipped and collects their feedback — which is a live meeting, which is step one again. the second lap captures better than the first, because people critique a real thing far more precisely than they describe a hypothetical one. ## steps ### step:step-1 capture the transcript as it lands, in segments ### step:step-2 ingest each segment into the relevant crm lead(s) ### step:step-3 create one living atlas item for this meeting, not one per segment ### step:step-4 track every document, template, and example someone offers to send ### step:step-5 structure the atlas item so open questions come first ### step:step-6 share the atlas item — private by default, gated before public ### step:step-7 add a ui design deliverable before the epic gets finalized ### step:step-8 convert decisions into an epic with child tickets ### step:step-9 fold human sops + agent skills into the playbook ### step:step-10 land the client's data — triage, schema, transport, read-back ### step:step-11 ship the genesis ui, scored against the design audit ### step:step-12 onboard, train, and collect feedback — which restarts this playbook --- ## why these steps are instructions, not commands several of these were drafted from a live working session, not a single clean recorded walkthrough. each step is an instruction a person or agent carries out and can verify — not a black-box automation. promote a step to `mode: shell` once you know the exact command for your own atlas/bloq/lead tooling; this playbook deliberately stays tool-agnostic on flag names since those are known to drift (see the linked platform bug reports for two real examples hit while building this).

entries.name: local-devops
entries.describe: Manage the local Docker development environment — start/stop services, switch profiles (minimal/workers/n8n/full), check status, view logs, reset containers, run migrations. Use when Docker isn't starting, services are down, you need workers, want to add n8n, or need to troubleshoot the local stack. Pass an action as argument (e.g., \"status\", \"up\", \"up workers\", \"up n8n\", \"down\", \"logs api\", \"reset iris-api\", \"diagnose\").
