migrations. use when docker isn't starting, services are down, you need workers, want to add n8n, or need to troubleshoot the local stack. pass an action as argument (e.g., \"status\", \"up\", \"up workers\", \"up n8n\", \"down\", \"logs api\", \"reset iris-api\", \"diagnose\"). --- name: local-devops description: "manage the local docker development environment — start/stop services, switch profiles (minimal/workers/n8n/full), check status, view logs, reset containers, run migrations. use when docker isn't starting, services are down, you need workers, want to add n8n, or need to troubleshoot the local stack. pass an action as argument (e.g., \"status\", \"up\", \"up workers\", \"up n8n\", \"down\", \"logs api\", \"reset iris-api\", \"diagnose\")." allowed-tools: - read - bash - grep - glob - edit - askuserquestion --- # local devops — docker development environment manager manage the freelabel docker compose development stack with profile-based service tiers. ## arguments `$arguments` — action to perform. examples: - `/local-devops status` — show running containers, ports, health, resource usage - `/local-devops up` — start minimal dev stack (7 services) - `/local-devops up workers` — start with queue workers + scheduler + iris-worker - `/local-devops up n8n` — start with n8n workflow automation stack - `/local-devops up full` — start everything (20 services) - `/local-devops down` — stop all services - `/local-devops restart [service]` — restart one or all services - `/local-devops logs <service>` — tail logs for a service (api, iris-api, elon-frontend, etc.) - `/local-devops reset <service>` — rebuild and restart a single container - `/local-devops diagnose` — full diagnostic (docker running, ports, disk, health, envs) - `/local-devops mysql` — open mysql console - `/local-devops tinker` — open laravel tinker in fl-api - `/local-devops migrate` — run migrations on fl-api - `/local-devops shell <service>` — shell into a container --- ## architecture the docker compose stack uses **profiles** to control which services start: ### default (7 services) — `docker compose up -d` | service | container | port | purpose | |---------|-----------|------|---------| | database | fl-database | 3306 | mysql 8 | | redis | fl-redis | 6379 | cache, sessions, queues | | api | fl-api | 9000 (fpm) | laravel backend | | api-nginx | fl-api-nginx | 8000 | nginx → api reverse proxy | | api-worker | fl-api-worker | — | queue worker (default, agent-jobs, workflows, background, video-processing) | | iris-api | fl-iris-api | 7201 | iris api (v6 workflows, pages, agents) | | elon-frontend | fl-elon-frontend | 9300 | nuxt 2 frontend | ### `--profile workers` (adds 3 services) | service | container | purpose | |---------|-----------|---------| | api-scheduler | fl-api-scheduler | laravel scheduler (runs every minute — heavy cpu) | | fl-api-workflows-worker | fl-api-workflows-worker | dedicated workflow queue worker | | iris-worker | fl-iris-worker | iris api queue worker | ### `--profile n8n` (adds 3 services) | service | container | port | purpose | |---------|-----------|------|---------| | postgres-n8n | fl-n8n-postgres | 5433 | postgresql for n8n | | n8n | fl-n8n | 5678 | n8n workflow automation ui | | n8n-worker | fl-n8n-worker | — | n8n queue worker | ### `--profile full` (adds everything above + extras) additional: typesense, langraph-api, elizabeth, coding-agent-bridge, proxy (80/443) ### `--profile hive` (specialized) | service | container | purpose | |---------|-----------|---------| | hive-daemon | fl-hive-daemon | local hive compute node | ### `--profile hive-test` (specialized) | service | container | purpose | |---------|-----------|---------| | hive-node-alpha | fl-hive-node-alpha | test hive node a | | hive-node-beta | fl-hive-node-beta | test hive node b | ## key directories ## common operations ### starting services ### checking status ### viewing logs ### running commands inside containers ### rebuilding ### common issues | symptom | cause | fix | |---------|-------|-----| | "cannot connect to docker daemon" | orbstack/docker not running | open orbstack app or `open -a orbstack` | | port 3306 in use | mysql already running on host | `brew services stop mysql` or change port in compose | | port 9300 in use | another nuxt instance | `lsof -ti:9300 \| xargs kill` | | api container exits | missing .env or composer deps | `docker compose exec api composer install` | | iris-api crashes | missing chromium / memory | check dockerfile.dev has chromium, increase docker memory | | elon-frontend slow | node_modules volume stale | `docker compose down -v elon_node_modules && docker compose up -d elon-frontend` | | "table not found" | migrations not run | `docker compose exec api php artisan migrate` | | queue jobs not processing | api-worker not started | it's in default profile now — check `docker compose ps` | | elon 401s on every fl-api call | dead `fl_raichu_api_token` (reseed wiped the user/token the jwt points to) | `./fix-elon-token.sh` (see below) | | elon 401→**500** after reseed | corrupted/incomplete db schema (missing tables) | `docker compose exec api php artisan migrate --force` then `./fix-elon-token.sh` | | `.env` change ignored after `restart` | `restart` reuses existing env; env_file only read at **create** | `docker compose up -d --no-build --force-recreate <service>` (not restart, not rebuild) | ### environment files - `fl-api/.env` — laravel backend config (db, redis, api keys) - `fl-iris-api/.env` — iris api config (same pattern) - `fl-elon-web-ui/.env` — frontend config (api urls, pusher) > **⚠️ editing a `.env` does not take effect on `docker compose restart`.** `restart` reuses the > container's *existing* environment — `env_file` is only read when a container is **created**. to > pick up a new `.env` value you must **recreate** the container: > `docker compose up -d --no-build --force-recreate <service>`. you almost never need an image > **rebuild** for env changes (nuxt dev / laravel read env at runtime). restart = stale, > recreate = fresh, rebuild = unnecessary. ### elon → fl-api 401 / 500 (the `fl_raichu_api_token` nuance) elon (`fl-elon-frontend`) authenticates **every** fl-api call with `bearer $fl_raichu_api_token` (set in `fl-elon-web-ui/.env`). that token is a passport jwt tied to a specific user + an `oauth_access_tokens` row. a `migrate:fresh`/reseed wipes them → passport rejects the token → the whole frontend 401s ("auth broken"). **one-command fix:** it mints a fresh token (`php artisan elon:mint-token --quiet-token`), writes it into `fl-elon-web-ui/.env` (backup first), `--force-recreate`s the elon container, and curl-verifies `/api/v1/profile`. **manual equivalent:** use `elon:mint-token` (real passport `->accesstoken` jwt) — not `api:generate-token`, which makes a sanctum random string elon can't authenticate with. **if a fresh token still 401s, or flips to 500 — the local db schema is incomplete.** symptom: `select count(*) from users` errors / table missing, or 500 like `table 'fl_api.jobs' doesn't exist`. diagnose + repair: fl-api migrations are guarded (`schema::hastable`/`hascolumn`) so re-running skips existing objects and creates only what's missing. gotchas: pure **data-backfill** migrations (no `schema::` ops) can stall/fail when run out-of-order (they boot eloquent models) — their data is usually already in the seed, so mark them run: `insert into migrations (migration,batch) values ('<name>',<maxbatch+1>)`. alters on big tables (`user_profiles` ≈ 518k rows) take ~20s each — run `migrate` in the background, it's not stuck. > **test against a real authed route — not `/api/v1/user` (that 404s).** use `/api/v1/profile` or > `/api/v1/user/onboarding-status`: 401 = dead token, 500 = token ok but schema broken, 200 = good. ### service urls | service | url | |---------|-----| | frontend | | | api | | | iris api | | | n8n (if started) | | | mysql | localhost:3306 (fl_user/secret) | | redis | localhost:6379 | ## diagnostic checklist when running `/local-devops diagnose`: 1. **docker daemon running?** — `docker info` should work 2. **disk space?** — `docker system df` (docker can eat 50gb+) 3. **all containers healthy?** — `docker compose ps` 4. **ports free?** — check 3306, 6379, 7201, 8000, 9300 5. **env files exist?** — fl-api/.env, fl-iris-api/.env, fl-elon-web-ui/.env 6. **mysql accepting connections?** — `docker compose exec database mysqladmin ping` 7. **redis accepting connections?** — `docker compose exec redis redis-cli ping` 8. **api responding?** — `curl -s 9. **frontend responding?** — `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" 10. **volume mounts working?** — check file changes reflect in container

test chain logic only | | `architecture` | print architecture diagram | | `gaps` | analyze gaps and risks | | `logs [target]` | tail logs | | `sessions` | check browser session health | | `n8n` | n8n workflow status | | (empty) | show usage help | ### 2. for `run` ### 3. for `status` check all pipeline components in parallel: report as a dashboard: ### 4. for `debug` systematic diagnosis: ### 5. for `debug chain` focused chain diagnosis: ### 6. for `test` run pipeline tests: ### 7. for `test chain` ### 8. for `architecture` print the architecture diagram from this skill file (the one above under "pipeline architecture"). additionally, trace the n8n workflow: ### 9. for `gaps` analyze and report gaps: **check for these known risks:** 1. **n8n som nodes disabled** — som outreach is fully delegated to daemon chain. if daemon isn't running, no outreach happens after buffer publish. check: is daemon running? 2. **no error workflow in n8n** — n8n workflow has no `errorworkflow` configured. failed executions are silent. check: add error workflow or webhook notification. 3. **single continueonfail node** — only twitter dm som has it. other node failures can break the pipeline. check: which nodes should have error tolerance? 4. **no retry on n8n nodes** — no retry settings configured. transient api failures cause permanent loss. check: add retry to http request nodes. 5. **session expiry monitoring** — no automated check for youtube/instagram session age. sessions expire silently. check: add session age to health dashboard. 6. **buffer queue not auto-cleared** — clear buffer queue node is disabled. old posts accumulate. check: is this intentional? 7. **rendering depends on localhost:3200** — render carousel and render opportunity ads call `localhost:3200/tasks`. only works when daemon is running locally. check: is this blocking? 8. **no dedup on buffer posts** — same video scraped twice = duplicate buffer posts. check: does n8n or fl-api dedup? 9. **enrichment cooldown is per-lead, not per-run** — 7-day cooldown. if a lead was attempted but failed, it's locked out for 7 days. check: should failed enrichments reset cooldown? 10. **newsletter schedule runs independently** — daily newsletter schedule (weekdays 9am) runs whether or not discover pipeline ran. they're decoupled. check: should newsletter wait for fresh content? ### 10. for `logs` ### 11. for `sessions` ### 12. for `n8n` --- ## scheduled jobs (production) the pipeline runs automatically via fl-api's heartbeat scheduler (`bloq_scheduled_jobs` table): | job # | frequency | type | what it does | |-------|-----------|------|-------------| | #759 | daily | discover | yt feed scrape → n8n → chain to som_batch | | #760 | hourly | som_batch | outreach (15 leads, enrich, warmup) | ### how scheduling works **critical bug (apr 19 fix):** the old path went through `dispatchhivetask → /api/v6/nodes/tools/execute` which read the `hiveleadgendiscovery` yaml config and overrode `task_type` from `discover` to `leadgen`. the daemon then ran `npm run leadgen:execute` (doesn't exist) and the chain never fired. fix: `dispatchdirecttask()` bypasses the tool yaml entirely for chainable types. ### viewing scheduled jobs ### viewing logs ### manual test of scheduled dispatch --- ## debugging playbook ### "pipeline ran but som:all never fired" 1. was it run via daemon? (`discover` task type) — chain only fires from daemon 2. was it dispatched via `/api/v6/nodes/tasks` (correct) or `/api/v6/nodes/tools/execute` (broken)? - check fl-api logs: `grep "direct task dispatch\|dispatching hive task via tool" storage/logs/laravel.log` - "direct task dispatch" = correct path, "via tool" = wrong path (yaml overrides type) 3. check task-executor.js has `chainabletypes` including `discover` 4. check the discover task didn't have `chain_outreach: false` in config 5. check daemon logs for `chain dispatch failed` or `chaining: discover complete` 6. check `cloud.submittask` endpoint is reachable (iris-api) ### "youtube scrape works but n8n doesn't process" 1. is n8n running? `curl localhost:5678` 2. is the workflow active? check via n8n mcp 3. did the chat message actually get sent? check `test-results/screenshots/n8n-chat-sent.png` 4. check n8n execution history for errors 5. was n8n_email/n8n_password set in .env? ### "buffer posts not appearing" 1. check n8n execution — did add to buffer v2 node succeed? 2. check fl-api buffer endpoint is reachable from n8n 3. check fl-api has valid buffer api credentials 4. check buffer queue: `curl raichu.heyiris.io/api/v1/buffer/manage-content` ### "som outreach sending but no dms" 1. check instagram session for the campaign account 2. check the campaign's board has eligible leads 3. check enrichment status — are leads enriched? 4. check som-config.js has correct boardid/strategy 5. run `npm run som:courses -- dry=1 limit=1` to test without sending ### "everything times out" 1. `discover` has 1-hour timeout (task-executor.js line 1936) 2. youtube spec has 15-minute playwright timeout 3. n8n workflow has no timeout (unlimited) 4. check if the daemon timeout is killing the process 5. even on timeout, chainable tasks resolve — check if chain fires --- ## testing strategy ### unit tests (chain logic) ### integration tests ### monitoring tests

entries.name: meal-plan-day
entries.describe: Generate TODAY's meals — different recipes every single day, never repeating what was cooked in the last two weeks — from what is already stocked, with a same-day shopping list under a hard dollar cap. Reads live Stockpile Levels and the last 14 days of plans from MAYO — Life Atlas (#544) and writes today's plan back into it. Runs daily.
entries.haystack: meal-plan-day generate today's meals — different recipes every single day, never repeating what was cooked in the last two weeks — from what is already stocked, with a same-day shopping list under a hard dollar cap. reads live stockpile levels and the last 14 days of plans from mayo — life atlas (#544) and writes today's plan back into it. runs daily. --- name: meal-plan-day description: generate today's meals — different recipes every single day, never repeating what was cooked in the last two weeks — from what is already stocked, with a same-day shopping list under a hard dollar cap. reads live stockpile levels and the last 14 days of plans from mayo — life atlas (#544) and writes today's plan back into it. runs daily. version: 2 args: action: type: string required: false default: report enum: [report, write] description: report = show the plan only, write = also save it as an item in the bloq budget_max: type: number required: false default: 25 description: ceiling for a trickle stop today (usd). daily is snacks + frozen top-ups only — bulk goes on a themed run, never here. provisional number; alex has not set one. lookback: type: number required: false default: 14 description: how many recent daily plans to read for the no-repeat rule model: type: string required: false default: iris/glm-5.3-flash description: ai model for planning (nano models only per house rules) agent: type: number required: false default: 704 description: iris agent id for the planning chat. 704 is the agent attached to the life atlas bloq itself. do not use 420 — that is patty, the pathways legal case-management agent, whose persona refuses cooking prompts outright ("i cannot assist with personal cooking plans"). on-error: continue timeout: 240 --- # meal plan — daily (mayo life atlas #544) generates **today's** cooking: different recipes every day, built from what is already in the freezer and pantry, with a same-day shopping list under a **hard $40 ceiling**. ## the one thing that makes this work: the no-repeat rule a nano model given the same pantry every morning will happily produce the same three meals every morning. so variety is **not** left to the model. step `read-history` pulls the dish names from the last 14 days of plans and hands them over as an explicit ban list. every plan ends with a machine-readable `recipes:` line for exactly this purpose — that line is the memory, and removing it silently breaks variety. ## 💵 where the daily job sits in the budget (corrected aug 20) the real model is **themed bulk runs capped at ~$150, roughly monthly** — not a weekly allowance. see **shopping schedule, budget & cadence #162938**. the daily job owns **only the trickle lane**: snacks, frozen top-ups, and whatever is thin. it must **never** put a bulk item in today's basket. when it sees a category running low it routes that item to the correct themed run — 🥩 meats · 🥬 veggies+fruits · 🍝 pastas+breads · 🧁 baking+other — so the next big trip stays themed and stays under $150. that routing is the point. trickling deliberately is what keeps the next re-up small, instead of going dry and being forced into a $160 emergency run. the $25 default is **provisional** — alex gave a per-run number, not a per-day one. it is a ceiling, not a target, and most days should still be $0. ## steps ### step:read-atlas read stockpile + templates from the bloq ### step:read-history read recent plans so nothing repeats ### step:plan-day draft today's recipes ### step:write-plan save today's plan into the bloq ### step:summary done

entries.name: n8n-sync
entries.describe: Get your n8n automations under version control instead of trusting a UI with no undo. Pull a workflow down to a file you can actually read and review, see exactly what changed before anything live is touched, then push it back with confidence.
entries.haystack: n8n-sync get your n8n automations under version control instead of trusting a ui with no undo. pull a workflow down to a file you can actually read and review, see exactly what changed before anything live is touched, then push it back with confidence. --- name: n8n-sync description: get your n8n automations under version control instead of trusting a ui with no undo. pull a workflow down to a file you can actually read and review, see exactly what changed before anything live is touched, then push it back with confidence. --- # n8n workflow sync manage n8n workflows with pull/push/diff commands, mirroring the /pages pattern. ## commands ### n8n:list — list all workflows ### n8n:pull {id} — pull workflow json to local file ### n8n:push {id} — push local json to n8n instance ### n8n:diff {id} — compare local file vs live n8n instance ### n8n:activate {id} — turn workflow on ### n8n:deactivate {id} — turn workflow off ### n8n:versions {id} — view version history ## key workflow ids | id | name | status | |----|------|--------| | ieiqivpwcmmeyjvr | youtube upload analysis fixed | active (production) | ## local file mapping - `fl-docker-dev/n8n/workflows/marketing-workflow.json` — canonical version-controlled copy of `ieiqivpwcmmeyjvr` ## docker import behavior - `fl-docker-dev/n8n/init-n8n.sh` imports workflows on **first run only** (checks if workflows exist in db) - `.disabled` suffix prevents auto-import - strategy: keep `marketing-workflow.json` as the canonical copy - `n8n:pull` overwrites this file; `n8n:push` reads from it - on fresh `docker-compose up`, init script imports the .json file, seeding the instance ## n8n mcp tools reference - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_list_workflows` — list workflows - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_get_workflow` — get workflow (modes: full, details, structure, minimal) - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_create_workflow` — create new workflow - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_update_full_workflow` — full workflow update - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_update_partial_workflow` — partial update (name, active, etc.) - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_delete_workflow` — delete workflow - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_workflow_versions` — version history - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_validate_workflow` — validate workflow - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_test_workflow` — test workflow execution - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_health_check` — health check - `mcp__n8n-mcp__n8n_executions` — execution history ## som outreach bridge (n8n → hive) after buffer publishing, the workflow triggers hive som outreach via iris-api: **endpoint**: `post **auth**: bearer token (platform jwt) **payload template**: **active campaigns**: - instagram: type=som, prompt=courses, boardid=38, strategy="ai course | v3", igaccount=heyiris.io - linkedin: type=linkedin, prompt=dm-outreach (built) - twitter: type=twitter, prompt=dm-outreach (phase 3 — needs spec)

entries.name: ocr-benchmark
entries.describe: Benchmark vision models on YOUR scanned documents. Reads the same images with each model, scores every extracted field against ground truth you supply, and reports accuracy and latency side by side. Model choice for OCR is measurable — a leaderboard built on someone else's documents does not tell you which model reads your invoices.
entries.haystack: ocr-benchmark benchmark vision models on your scanned documents. reads the same images with each model, scores every extracted field against ground truth you supply, and reports accuracy and latency side by side. model choice for ocr is measurable — a leaderboard built on someone else's documents does not tell you which model reads your invoices. --- name: ocr-benchmark description: "benchmark vision models on your scanned documents. reads the same images with each model, scores every extracted field against ground truth you supply, and reports accuracy and latency side by side. model choice for ocr is measurable — a leaderboard built on someone else's documents does not tell you which model reads your invoices." version: 2 args: path: type: string required: true description: folder of scanned images to benchmark. google drive takes a folder id, not a path. bloq: type: number required: true description: bloq the runs land in. each model writes into its own list so results stay separable. schema: type: string required: true description: atlas dataset slug holding the fields to extract and score. expect: type: string required: true description: "path to ground-truth json — a list of records, or an object keyed by the id field. what the documents actually say, typed by hand once." models: type: string required: false default: "gpt-4o-mini,gpt-4.1-nano,gpt-5-nano" description: "comma-separated models to compare. extraction allows gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-nano, gpt-5-nano; anything else is silently downgraded to gpt-4o-mini, which would make two rows identical and look like a tie." key: type: string required: false default: invoice_number description: field identifying a document, used to line an extracted record up with its ground truth. source: type: string required: false default: google_drive description: "bulk-ingestable source: dropbox | google_drive | s3 | google-cloud-storage | onedrive | microsoft." on-error: stop timeout: 1800 --- # ocr model benchmark runs one folder of scans through several models and scores them against what the documents actually say. **why measure rather than read a benchmark.** published scores are built on public datasets — clean receipts, standard forms, english. your documents are a supplier's fax-quality pdf, a photograph taken at an angle, a form with a stamp over the total. the only ranking that predicts anything is one produced on your own paper. **what ground truth costs.** you type it once, for a handful of documents. there is no way around that: without it, "the models agree" is indistinguishable from "the models are wrong the same way", and consensus between two models that both misread a 7 as a 1 reads as high confidence. ## steps ### step:preflight check the inputs before spending vision calls ### step:run ingest the same folder once per model ### step:score score each model against ground truth ### step:cleanup remove scratch files ## reading the result - **accuracy before speed.** a model that is twice as fast and misreads one total in fifty has cost you more than it saved. - **a missing record counts against the model.** scoring only what a model returned rewards it for skipping documents it found hard. - **agreement is not correctness.** two models misreading the same smudged 7 agree perfectly. that is what the ground-truth file is for.

entries.name: page-seo-audit
entries.describe: Check that a page's title and social metadata are actually SERVED, not just set in the browser. Every check here is one that shipped broken on a page carrying paid traffic — a link card previewing the wrong product, a signup page inheriting the platform's boilerplate. Run it before pointing an ad, a DM or a campaign at any URL.
entries.haystack: page-seo-audit check that a page's title and social metadata are actually served, not just set in the browser. every check here is one that shipped broken on a page carrying paid traffic — a link card previewing the wrong product, a signup page inheriting the platform's boilerplate. run it before pointing an ad, a dm or a campaign at any url. --- name: page-seo-audit description: check that a page's title and social metadata are actually served, not just set in the browser. every check here is one that shipped broken on a page carrying paid traffic — a link card previewing the wrong product, a signup page inheriting the platform's boilerplate. run it before pointing an ad, a dm or a campaign at any url. version: 2 args: url: type: string required: true description: full url to audit, including any query string the ad will actually use on-error: continue timeout: 90 --- # page seo audit **the one idea:** a crawler and a link card read the html the server sent. **they never run your javascript.** so anything set client-side — `document.title`, a vue `<head>`, a react helmet — is invisible to precisely the audience this metadata exists for. everything below fetches the page with `curl` for that reason. opening it in a browser tab is how both of this file's founding bugs looked fine. ## what this exists to prevent both of these were live, on pages with money pointed at them, on 2026-09-01: - a bug-bounty ad previewed as **"open bounty — iris bounty os"**. the page set the right title with `document.title`, so the browser tab was correct and every x link card was not. - `/downloads` — the destination of every `/register`, `/signup` and get started link — previewed as **"iris - business operations system | ai agents, crm, workflows & more"**, the platform default, because the route never passed a `pageseo` prop. neither was visible from a browser. both were obvious in one `curl`. ## steps ### step:title is there a server-rendered `<title>`? ### step:og do the open graph tags exist, and are they this page's? ### step:generic is the metadata just the platform boilerplate? ### step:match does og:title agree with what the page renders? ### step:canonical canonical and robots ### step:image does og:image actually resolve to an image? ### step:verdict score it

entries.name: pages
entries.describe: Manage composable page builder pages via the IRIS CLI (Genesis). Commands work as both `pages` and `genesis`. List, view, create, update (atomic dot-notation), pull/push/sync JSON, diff local vs remote, publish, version history, rollback. Pass an action and slug as arguments.
entries.haystack: pages manage composable page builder pages via the iris cli (genesis). commands work as both `pages` and `genesis`. list, view, create, update (atomic dot-notation), pull/push/sync json, diff local vs remote, publish, version history, rollback. pass an action and slug as arguments. --- name: pages description: manage composable page builder pages via the iris cli (genesis). commands work as both `pages` and `genesis`. list, view, create, update (atomic dot-notation), pull/push/sync json, diff local vs remote, publish, version history, rollback. pass an action and slug as arguments. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- # pages (genesis) — composable page management via rest api manage composable landing pages and dashboards using the iris cli. the `pages` command is aliased as `genesis` — both work interchangeably. all operations are http rest calls — no ssh, no tty, no `doctl apps console`, no seeders. ## arguments `$arguments` — action and target. examples: - `/pages list` — list all pages (default: production) - `/pages list local` — list local pages - `/pages view genesis` — view full page json - `/pages get genesis "components.0.props.title"` — read a specific value (dot notation) - `/pages set genesis "theme.mode" "light"` — atomic update (dot notation) - `/pages set genesis "components.0.props.title" "new hero"` — update component prop - `/pages pull genesis` — download page json locally - `/pages push genesis` — upload local json to api - `/pages diff genesis` — compare local file vs remote - `/pages sync genesis` — pull remote, diff, push local changes - `/pages publish genesis` — publish page - `/pages unpublish genesis` — back to draft - `/pages create my-page "my landing page"` — create new page - `/pages components genesis` — list all components with indices - `/pages versions genesis` — view version history - `/pages rollback genesis 3` — rollback to version 3 - `/pages duplicate genesis --new-slug=genesis-v2` — duplicate page ## cli location **configuration:** `.env` in `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/` — credentials already configured. ## environment switching use `--env` to target local or production without editing `.env`: default environment is set by `iris_env` in the sdk `.env` file. ## steps ### 1. parse the action from `$arguments` | action | what to do | |--------|-----------| | `list [env]` | run `php bin/iris pages --env={env}` | | `view <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages view {slug} --json` | | `get <slug> "<path>"` | run `php bin/iris pages get {slug} "{path}"` | | `set <slug> "<path>" "<value>"` | run `php bin/iris pages set {slug} "{path}" "{value}"` | | `pull <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages pull {slug}` | | `push <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages push {slug}` | | `diff <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages diff {slug}` | | `sync <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages sync {slug}` | | `publish <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages publish {slug}` | | `unpublish <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages unpublish {slug}` | | `create <slug> "<title>"` | run `php bin/iris pages create --slug={slug} --title="{title}"` | | `components <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages components {slug}` | | `versions <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages versions {slug}` | | `rollback <slug> <version>` | run `php bin/iris pages rollback {slug} --page-version={version}` | | `duplicate <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages duplicate {slug} --new-slug={new}` | | `delete <slug>` | run `php bin/iris pages delete {slug}` | ### 2. determine environment if the user specifies "local" or "production" anywhere in the arguments, pass `--env=local` or `--env=production`. if not specified, use production (the default in the sdk `.env`). ### 3. run the cli command always run from the sdk directory: ### 4. show results display the cli output to the user. for json output, parse and summarize key information. ## dot notation reference the `set` and `get` commands use dot notation to navigate the page json structure: ### common update patterns ## pull/push workflow for larger edits, use the pull/push workflow: local files are stored in `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/pages/{slug}.json`. ## available pages (sub-brands) | slug | type | description | |------|------|-------------| | `genesis` | landing | ai-powered creative builder | | `acre` | landing | ai real estate platform | | `atlas` | landing/dashboard | ai chief of staff | | `beatbox-submit` | landing | beat submission platform | | `geekgang` | landing | community/education | | `freelabel-landing` | landing | freelabel landing page | | `iris-landing` | landing | iris landing page | | `pathways` | landing | healthcare portal landing | | `pathways-attorney` | dashboard | attorney dashboard | | `pathways-provider` | dashboard | provider dashboard | | `pathways-patient` | dashboard | patient dashboard | ## cta url convention all sub-brand saas pages should use absolute urls for ctas: **not** relative `/pricing` (pages are served from `heyiris.io`, relative urls resolve to wrong domain). supported sources: `reachr, copycat, vault, heartbeat, atlas, genesis, acre, hive, echo, lexicon` ## shared partials (`$partial` references) pages can reference shared component partials instead of inlining props. one partial drives many pages — edit once, all consuming pages update instantly. no page push needed. ### how it works instead of inlining a full sitenavigation config on every page: the `$partial` key tells fl-api's `pagecontroller::resolvepartials()` to: 1. look up `vanguard-nav` in the `page_partials` table 2. merge the partial's props into the component (partial = defaults, page `props` = overrides) 3. strip `$partial` from the response — vue renderer receives clean json **override contract**: page-level props override partial defaults via `array_replace_recursive($partialprops, $pageprops)`. pass an empty `props: {}` for full partial control, or set specific keys to override individual values per page. ### cli commands ### current partials in production | partial slug | component | used by | |---|---|---| | `vanguard-nav` | sitenavigation | 6 vanguard pages | | `vanguard-footer` | sitefooter | 6 vanguard pages | | `dent-society-nav` | sitenavigation | 5 dent society pages | | `dent-society-footer` | sitefooter | 5 dent society pages | ### adding a partial to a new page 1. create partial: `iris partials create --slug brand-nav --component-type sitenavigation` 2. set props: `iris partials set brand-nav "props.logo.imageurl" " 3. in page json, replace the inlined component with: `{ "type": "sitenavigation", "id": "nav", "$partial": "brand-nav", "props": {} }` 4. push the page: `iris pages push <slug>` ### local file format partials live in `./partials/{slug}.json` (sibling of `./pages/`): ### any component type works not just navs and footers — share a `servicemenu`, `testimonialssection`, `announcementbanner`, or any component that repeats across a brand's pages. ## important notes - **all operations are rest api calls** — no ssh, no tty, no `doctl apps console` - **credentials in** `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/.env` — already configured for production - **atomic updates create versions** — you can always rollback - **`set` auto-detects value types** — json objects, numbers, booleans parsed automatically - **`getbyslug` includes drafts** by default in cli mode - **the old `/seed-pages` and `/pathways-pages` skills are deprecated** — use `/pages` instead genesis page builder composable page publish a page web page site

entries.name: pathways-intake-review
entries.describe: Take an intake case from "documents collected" to "assigned to a navigator" — evidence checked on the machine that holds the records, risk and workload computed, and a physician approving both the case and the assignment on one screen.
entries.haystack: pathways-intake-review take an intake case from "documents collected" to "assigned to a navigator" — evidence checked on the machine that holds the records, risk and workload computed, and a physician approving both the case and the assignment on one screen. --- name: pathways-intake-review description: take an intake case from "documents collected" to "assigned to a navigator" — evidence checked on the machine that holds the records, risk and workload computed, and a physician approving both the case and the assignment on one screen. version: 2 args: case_id: type: string required: true case_root: type: string required: true # no default on purpose. a default here would bake one tenant's folder layout into a # playbook meant to run for any of them, and a wrong-but-plausible path returns "no # documents found" — a false finding about someone's medical file rather than an error. node: type: string required: true # required, not defaulted. naming the machine is the decision: this step reads records # that must not leave the node entitled to them, so guessing which node is not a # convenience, it is a phi boundary. on-error: stop timeout: 300 --- # pathways intake review from the intake conversation of 2026-08-25. intake collects the file; a physician approves or rejects it; on approval it leaves intake for coordinating care and is assigned to a navigator. **multi-tenant by construction:** `case_root`, `case_id` and `node` are all required arguments. nothing about one client's folder layout or machine names is baked in, so the same playbook runs for any tenant whose records live on a node they control. **the reason this is a hive playbook and not a cloud workflow:** step 1 reads the case folder, which is phi. it runs on the node entitled to those records and returns a derived checklist — present/absent, counts, how recent. the documents never leave that machine. ## steps ### step:evidence check the case file is complete ### step:risk summarise the records and set a risk tier ### step:navigator suggest a navigator, with reasoning ### step:approve physician approves the case and the assignment

entries.haystack: pathways-pages create, update, and maintain pathways dashboard pages rendered by iris-api. pass an action and target as arguments. --- name: pathways-pages description: create, update, and maintain pathways dashboard pages rendered by iris-api. pass an action and target as arguments. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- # pathways pages — deprecated > **deprecated**: use `/pages` instead. the `/pages` skill uses rest api calls (no ssh, no tty, no seeders). > examples: `/pages set pathways-attorney "layout.navitems.0.label" "home"`, `/pages components pathways-attorney` legacy skill for pathways dashboard pages. prefer the `/pages` skill for all new work. ## arguments `$arguments` — action and target. examples: - `/pathways-pages create pathways-attorney-cases "cases analytics"` — create a new page - `/pathways-pages update pathways-attorney` — read and update an existing page - `/pathways-pages add-component casetimeline` — add a new vue component to the registry - `/pathways-pages reseed` — re-run the seeder to apply changes - `/pathways-pages list` — list all pathways pages and available components ## architecture overview ### rendering pipeline ### key files | file | purpose | |------|---------| | `fl-docker-dev/fl-api/app/console/commands/seedpathwaysdashboardscommand.php` | defines page content as php arrays (json). the source of truth for page data. | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/resources/js/pages/publicpage/render.vue` | page renderer with `componentmap` — all components must be registered here. | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/resources/js/components/dashboard/dashboardlayout.vue` | sidebar + header layout wrapper for dashboard-type pages. | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/resources/js/components/pagebuilder/` | directory containing all available page builder vue components. | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/resources/js/components/dashboard/` | dashboard-specific components (dashboardprovider, dashboardlayout, statcard, kpigrid, promocodecard). | ### current pages | slug | type | layout | |------|------|--------| | `pathways` | landing | no sidebar (standard components) | | `pathways-attorney` | dashboard | dashboardlayout with sidebar nav | | `pathways-provider` | dashboard | no dashboardlayout (simple) | | `pathways-patient` | dashboard | no dashboardlayout (simple) | ### page json structure ### available dashboard nav icons these icons are mapped in `dashboardlayout.vue` iconmap: | key | lucide icon | |-----|-------------| | `chart-bar` | barchart3 | | `chart-pie` | chartpie | | `folder` | folder | | `document-text` | filetext | | `document-duplicate` | files | | `cpu-chip` | cpu | | `dashboard` | layoutdashboard | | `users` | users | | `settings` | settings | | `messages` | messagesquare | | `scale` | scale | to add a new icon: import from `lucide-vue-next` and add to `iconmap` in dashboardlayout.vue. ### available pagebuilder components common components for pathways pages: | component | use case | |-----------|----------| | `hero` | page header with title, subtitle, gradient | | `textblock` | markdown or plain text content | | `widgetstatsrow` | kpi cards row (value, change, icon, theme color) | | `quickactions` | action buttons grid (cards or buttons variant) | | `filtertabbar` | horizontal filter tabs with counts | | `casepipelineboard` | kanban board with columns and case cards | | `taskqueuelist` | ai task queue with status indicators | | `caseeconomics` | financial line-item breakdown | | `demandtracker` | settlement negotiation timeline | | `apexchart` | interactive chart (bar, line, area, donut) via apexcharts with preline pro card styling, multi-series, summary items, progress bars | | `datachart` | simple svg bar, line, or area chart (no library dependency) | | `datatable` | searchable/paginated table with typed columns | | `activityfeed` | timeline of events with timestamps | | `casecard` | individual case summary card with metrics | | `progresstracker` | step-by-step progress indicator | | `roleselector` | role selection cards (landing page) | | `widgetareachartcard` | area chart in a card wrapper | | `widgetchecklistcard` | checklist items in a card | | `section` | recursive grid layout wrapper | ## steps ### 1. parse the action from `$arguments` | action | what to do | |--------|-----------| | `create <slug> "<title>"` | create a new page | | `update <slug>` | read and modify an existing page | | `add-component <name>` | register a new vue component in the pipeline | | `reseed` | run the seeder to push changes | | `list` | show all pages and available components | ### 2. for `create` — add a new page 1. **read the seeder**: `fl-docker-dev/fl-api/app/console/commands/seedpathwaysdashboardscommand.php` 2. **add a `createpage()` call** in the `handle()` method following the existing pattern 3. **add a new content method** (e.g., `getcasesanalyticscontent()`) returning the page json array 4. **for dashboard pages with sidebar**: include `layout` with `type => 'dashboard'` and `navitems` 5. **always include** `'thememode' => 'light'` in component props (pathways uses light mode) 6. **use unique component ids** within the page — these become anchor targets 7. **if the new page should appear in sibling page navs**: update navitems in sibling pages too ### 3. for `update` — modify an existing page 1. **read the seeder** to find the relevant content method (e.g., `getattorneydashboardcontent()`) 2. **make the requested changes** to the php array 3. **if modifying navitems**: consider if sibling pages need matching updates ### 4. for `add-component` — register a new vue component three files need changes: 1. **create the vue component** in `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/resources/js/components/pagebuilder/<name>.vue` - use vue 3 composition api (`<script setup lang="ts">`) - accept props matching what the seeder will pass - support `thememode` prop for light/dark styling - use tailwind v4 classes 2. **register in render.vue** (`fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/resources/js/pages/publicpage/render.vue`): - add `defineasynccomponent` import at the top (follow existing pattern) - add to `componentmap` object 3. **use in seeder** — add the component to a page's `components` array ### 5. for `reseed` — apply changes run the seeder locally: for production (after code is deployed): ### 6. for `list` — show available resources 1. list current pages by reading `handle()` in the seeder 2. list available components by scanning `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/resources/js/components/pagebuilder/` ### 7. verify changes after reseeding: - visit the page at ` (or production url) - if iris-api fetches from fl-api via http, ensure both containers are running - check browser console for vue component resolution errors - if a component shows blank, verify it's registered in render.vue's `componentmap` ## important notes - **iris-api uses vue 3 + typescript + tailwind v4** — not the nuxt 2 elon frontend - **pathways pages use light mode** — always set `'thememode' => 'light'` and `'mode' => 'light'` in theme - **component types are case-sensitive** — `'type' => 'widgetstatsrow'` must match the key in `componentmap` - **page content is stored in gcs** via `$page->savejsontogcs()` — the seeder handles this automatically - **the seeder lives in fl-api**, but the rendering happens in iris-api — both services must be running - **use `--force` flag** to update existing pages, otherwise they'll be skipped - **never use gpt-3.5-turbo** — only gpt-5-nano, gpt-4.1-nano, or gpt-4o-mini - **run `vendor/bin/pint --dirty`** after editing php files in iris-api (laravel pint formatter)

entries.name: playbook-publish
entries.describe: Write and actually publish a playbook — the full path from an empty directory to a live public URL someone can install. Covers the sync-versus-publish trap that silently leaves work local, the three scopes, frontmatter that parses, and how to verify a publish really landed instead of trusting a green check. Also covers how-tos, whose publisher fails closed on one bad file. Pass an action as argument such as new, publish, verify, scopes, howto, or troubleshoot.
entries.haystack: playbook-publish write and actually publish a playbook — the full path from an empty directory to a live public url someone can install. covers the sync-versus-publish trap that silently leaves work local, the three scopes, frontmatter that parses, and how to verify a publish really landed instead of trusting a green check. also covers how-tos, whose publisher fails closed on one bad file. pass an action as argument such as new, publish, verify, scopes, howto, or troubleshoot. --- name: playbook-publish description: write and actually publish a playbook — the full path from an empty directory to a live public url someone can install. covers the sync-versus-publish trap that silently leaves work local, the three scopes, frontmatter that parses, and how to verify a publish really landed instead of trusting a green check. also covers how-tos, whose publisher fails closed on one bad file. pass an action as argument such as new, publish, verify, scopes, howto, or troubleshoot. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash --- # publishing a playbook a playbook is a runnable procedure. writing one is easy; **publishing one is where people stop early and think they are done.** this exists because of that. ## arguments `$arguments` — an action: - `/playbook-publish new <name>` — scaffold and write one - `/playbook-publish publish <name>` — get it live, with a url - `/playbook-publish verify <name>` — prove it published - `/playbook-publish scopes` — private vs project vs public - `/playbook-publish howto` — the how-to surface, which is separate - `/playbook-publish troubleshoot` — the known failures --- ## the trap — read this before anything else **`iris playbook sync` does not publish.** both print a green check. only one of them published anything. this is the whole reason for this playbook: a `✓` that answers a narrower question than the one you asked is indistinguishable from the one you wanted. `sync` is for making a playbook available to **your own** agent as a skill. `publish` is for making it exist for anybody else. if you want both — and you usually do — run both, or `sync --api`. --- ## 1. write it frontmatter is required: **frontmatter must be valid yaml, and the failure is unhelpful.** a `description:` containing double quotes breaks the parse, and `iris playbook sync` reports only: — with nothing after the colon. keep the description a plain unquoted scalar: no `"`, no `: ` inside it. em-dashes, commas, parentheses and apostrophes are all fine. **the description is the product.** it is what the skill list shows, what an agent reads to decide whether to invoke, and what the marketplace card displays. say what it does and when to reach for it, not what it is. **lead with the value, not the mechanism — write it for a human, not a spec.** the most common way a description fails is not being wrong, it's reading like documentation instead of a reason to care: that is a feature list and a call signature. nobody scanning a marketplace card decides to install something because it "queries structured crm entities" — they decide because it solves a problem they recognize. same playbook, written for the person instead of the api: same information, reordered around **why it matters before how it works**. before you publish, check the description against this: - **does it open with the outcome or the mechanism?** "launch a campaign without x risk" beats "manage x — does a, b, c." if the first six words are a verb + a feature, not a benefit, rewrite the opening. - **would you say it out loud to a person, not paste it into a config file?** "checks your funding, confirms no one else is already spending" reads like a sentence. "funding preflight, armed-spend check, create-paused" reads like a changelog. say it the first way. - **does it name the fear or friction this removes?** a runaway bill, a bottleneck person who never wrote anything down, a follow-up that gets forgotten — the sentence should make the reader feel the problem before they see the fix. - **is it free of internal vocabulary?** `bounty_type`, `preview_mode`, argument flags, table names — none of that means anything to someone deciding whether this playbook is for them. save the mechanism for the body of the playbook, not the sentence that sells it. - **could you delete "pass an action as argument such as x, y, z" and lose nothing?** that clause describes the cli, not the value. it is fine as a trailing note if the actions aren't obvious, but it should never be the sentence doing the selling. this is not cosmetic. the description is the only thing most readers ever see — the marketplace card, the skill-list one-liner, the thing an agent reads to decide whether to invoke you at all. a correct playbook with a mechanism-first description undersells itself every single time it's shown. ### steps, and the two ways they silently do nothing a v2 playbook's steps are `### step:<id> <title>`, then a fence populates neither the body nor the code, so the step validates as "ai step has no prompt body." tag it yaml mode: playbook playbook: capture-sops-and-process-maps args: <positional, mapped onto the child's declared args in order> bash iris playbook items add <name> --label "intake sop" --bloq-item <atlas-item-id> iris playbook items add <name> --label "score a case" --skill <id> iris playbook roles add <name> --title "intake coordinator" bash iris playbook test <name> # syntax + schema bash iris playbook publish <name> --scope public scope public access free url marketplace playbook-<uid>-<name> (pending_review) ✓ published <name> as public cannot publish to the marketplace: bloq <id> is inside a phi boundary (contains_phi). bash # the page exists and carries the body (not a null playbook prop) curl -s | grep -c data-page # it is in the live registry the library page reads curl -s | python3 -c " import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin) rows=d.get('data') or d.get('playbooks') or [] print('listed:', '<name>' in [r.get('name') for r in rows], '| total:', len(rows))" bash $editor iris-code/scaffold/how-to/<slug>.md iris how-to publish --dir iris-code/scaffold/how-to --dry-run iris how-to publish --dir iris-code/scaffold/how-to ``` three things that will catch you: - **`category` must come from a fixed list.** an unknown one is rejected: getting started · agents & automation · pages & design · data & atlas · crm & sales · content & media · infrastructure · finance · bounty & community. - **it fails closed across the whole batch.** one bad file publishes *nothing* — "1 recipe(s) have invalid front-matter — nothing published." good design; surprising the first time. - **the cli reads how-tos from its compiled binary, not your source directory.** so a new recipe will not appear in `iris how-to view` until the cli is rebuilt, even though `publish --dir` reads the directory and works fine. do not conclude the file is broken. - **local-only recipes never publish.** `~/.iris/how-to` ones are flagged on every publish; move one into the repo with `iris how-to promote <name>`. --- ## troubleshoot | symptom | cause | | --- | --- | | published but not in the library | you ran `sync`, not `publish` | | `failed to parse frontmatter` with nothing after it | double quotes or `: ` in `description` | | page 200s but looks empty | non-public scope — null playbook prop; parse `data-page` | | marketplace card missing | `pending_review`; the url and `install` already work | | new how-to not in `iris how-to view` | cli reads its compiled binary; `publish --dir` still works | | how-to publish did nothing | one file has a bad category — it fails closed for the batch | --- ## the shape of the mistake every failure above is the same one: **a command succeeded at something narrower than what was asked, and said so in a way that reads as done.** `sync` syncs. `test` tests a different schema than `sync` parses. a 200 means a page rendered, not that it has content. a green batch means nothing was invalid, not that anything published. check the thing you actually wanted, not the thing the command reported.

entries.name: playwright-tests
entries.describe: Build, run, debug, and maintain Playwright E2E tests for the Freelabel platform. Pass an action (create, run, debug, fix) and optional target as arguments.
entries.haystack: playwright-tests build, run, debug, and maintain playwright e2e tests for the freelabel platform. pass an action (create, run, debug, fix) and optional target as arguments. --- name: playwright-tests description: build, run, debug, and maintain playwright e2e tests for the freelabel platform. pass an action (create, run, debug, fix) and optional target as arguments. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- # playwright e2e tests — build, run & maintain create, run, debug, and fix playwright end-to-end tests for the freelabel nuxt 2 frontend. ## arguments `$arguments` — what to do. examples: - `/playwright-tests create signup` — create a new test for the signup flow - `/playwright-tests create "page builder drag and drop"` — create a test from a description - `/playwright-tests run signup` — run a specific test file - `/playwright-tests run all` — run the full e2e suite - `/playwright-tests debug signup` — run headed with debug output - `/playwright-tests fix signup` — diagnose and fix failing tests - `/playwright-tests list` — list all existing test files - `/playwright-tests coverage` — show what flows have/lack test coverage ## project configuration ### key paths | file | purpose | |------|---------| | `/users/alexmayo/sites/freelabel/playwright.config.ts` | global config (timeouts, projects, reporters) | | `/users/alexmayo/sites/freelabel/tests/e2e/` | all test spec files | | `/users/alexmayo/sites/freelabel/tests/e2e/helpers/` | shared helpers (auth, page objects, providers) | | `/users/alexmayo/sites/freelabel/test-results/screenshots/` | test screenshots | | `/users/alexmayo/sites/freelabel/playwright-report/` | html report output | ### config summary ### environment variables ### run commands ## test file template every new test must follow this exact structure: ## critical patterns ### 1. nav_opts — always use for page navigation nuxt 2 ssr is slow. never use bare `page.goto()`: ### 2. authentication — inject via localstorage for tests that need a logged-in user: or use the helper class: ### 3. test isolation — clear auth between tests **critical**: localstorage persists between tests. if any test sets auth data, subsequent tests may redirect unexpectedly. use `addinitscript` to clear before page js runs: **why `addinitscript` instead of `page.evaluate`?** because `page.evaluate` runs after page js loads — the nuxt `beforecreate` hook may have already read localstorage and triggered a redirect before your cleanup runs. ### 4. api response mocking mock external apis to prevent real account creation / payments: ### 5. request payload capture monitor outgoing api calls without blocking: ### 6. api error detection capture 4xx/5xx responses during test execution: ## locator strategies (preferred order) use the most stable selector available: ## screenshot conventions **naming**: `{feature}-{step-number}-{description}.png` always `mkdir -p test-results/screenshots` before running tests. ## known gotchas ### nuxt 2 ssr load times - pages take 3-8 seconds to hydrate after navigation - always add `await page.waitfortimeout(3000)` after `page.goto()` - use `waituntil: 'domcontentloaded'` not `'networkidle'` (networkidle waits for websocket/pusher) ### nuxtlink same-component navigation bug nuxt 2 intercepts same-origin `<a>` clicks and routes through vue router. **vue router silently fails** for same-component dynamic route param changes (e.g., `/login/register` -> `/login/signin` both map to `_method.vue`). **workaround**: verify the `href` is correct, then use `page.goto()`: ### localstorage domain scoping must navigate to the app domain before setting localstorage: ### form submit without .prevent if testing forms, verify `@submit.prevent` is present. without it, native form post fires alongside the vue handler, causing page reload. ### vue 2 prop defaults vs null in vue 2, passing `null` to a prop overrides its default. use `undefined` to respect defaults: ## existing helpers reference ### authhelper (`tests/e2e/helpers/auth-helper.ts`) ### leadspage (`tests/e2e/helpers/leads-page.ts`) ### testhelpers (`tests/e2e/helpers/leads-page.ts`) ### progressmanager (`tests/e2e/helpers/progress-manager.ts`) crash recovery for long-running scraper tests. saves progress to disk, resumes if `resume=1`. ## existing test coverage | area | test file | auth required | |------|-----------|---------------| | signup/register | `signup.spec.ts` | no | | pricing checkout | `pricing-checkout.spec.ts` | no | | profile checkout | `profile-checkout.spec.ts` | no | | booking wizard | `dent-society-booking.spec.ts` | no | | profile features | `profile-features.spec.ts` | yes | | page builder | `page-builder.spec.ts` | yes | | bloq chat | `bloq-chat.spec.ts` | yes | | command bar | `command-bar.spec.ts` | yes | | lead outreach | `leads-outreach-workflow.spec.ts` | yes | | batch leads | `batch-process-5-leads.spec.ts` | yes | | quick start | `quick-start.spec.ts` | yes | | social sessions | `save-{platform}-session.spec.ts` | yes | | scrapers | `{platform}-scraper.spec.ts` | yes | | lead gen | `leadgen-scrape.spec.ts` | yes | **missing coverage** (no tests yet): - login/signin flow - logout - password reset - onboarding wizard - dashboard home - agent creation/configuration - workflow builder - settings pages - billing/subscription management - marketplace ## steps ### 1. parse arguments determine the action from `$arguments`: - **create [name/description]**: generate a new test file - **run [file or "all"]**: execute tests - **debug [file]**: run headed with verbose output - **fix [file]**: read failures, diagnose, and fix - **list**: show all test files with descriptions - **coverage**: audit what's tested vs not ### 2. for "create" — build a new test 1. **identify the target flow**: read the relevant vue pages/components to understand: - route url and page component file - form fields, validation rules, api endpoints - success/error states and redirects - required auth state (logged in or guest) 2. **read existing tests** for similar patterns — reuse auth, locator, and assertion strategies 3. **write the test file** at `tests/e2e/{name}.spec.ts` following the template above 4. **include these test cases at minimum**: - page loads with correct elements visible - form validation (if applicable) - successful happy-path flow (with api mocking if needed) - error state handling - edge cases (pre-filled params, redirects, etc.) 5. **verify the test discovers correctly**: 6. **run the test** and fix any failures: 7. **check screenshots** in `test-results/screenshots/` for visual verification ### 3. for "run" — execute tests report the pass/fail count and any error summaries. ### 4. for "debug" — diagnose failures 1. run the test with `--headed` to see the browser 2. check failure screenshots in `test-results/` 3. read the error context files (`error-context.md`) generated by playwright 4. check browser console logs captured by the `consolelogs` array 5. verify api responses if routes are being intercepted ### 5. for "fix" — repair broken tests 1. run the test to reproduce the failure 2. read the failure screenshot 3. read the relevant vue component to check if selectors changed 4. common fixes: - **element not found**: check if class/id/text changed in the component - **timeout**: increase `waitfortimeout` or use `waitfor({ state: 'visible' })` - **auth redirect**: add `addinitscript` to clear stale localstorage - **api mock mismatch**: check if the endpoint url changed - **flaky timing**: add explicit waits after actions ## important notes - **always run from project root**: `/users/alexmayo/sites/freelabel` - **never create real accounts** in tests — always mock the registration api - **never call real payment apis** — mock stripe checkout responses - **screenshots are cheap** — take them at every major step for debugging - **console logs are your friend** — use `console.log()` liberally with step markers - **test isolation matters** — clear localstorage in `beforeeach` if any test sets auth - **eslint vue files** after editing: `npm run fix-file <path>` in `fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui/`

entries.name: price-your-business
entries.describe: Find out if your price actually pays your bills, instead of guessing and hoping. A step-by-step pricing audit — built from a real internal pricing model, stripped of the company-specific numbers — that catches the mistakes that sink a product, a service, or an agency before a client ever asks about a discount. Pass what you're pricing as argument.
entries.haystack: price-your-business find out if your price actually pays your bills, instead of guessing and hoping. a step-by-step pricing audit — built from a real internal pricing model, stripped of the company-specific numbers — that catches the mistakes that sink a product, a service, or an agency before a client ever asks about a discount. pass what you're pricing as argument. --- name: price-your-business description: find out if your price actually pays your bills, instead of guessing and hoping. a step-by-step pricing audit — built from a real internal pricing model, stripped of the company-specific numbers — that catches the mistakes that sink a product, a service, or an agency before a client ever asks about a discount. pass what you're pricing as argument. version: 1 args: business: type: string required: true description: what you're pricing, in a sentence — a product, a service, or an agency engagement, and roughly how it's sold today (or how you're planning to sell it). allowed-tools: - read - write - bash --- # price your business most prices are not wrong by a little. they are wrong by a factor — and the way you find that out is not a competitor spreadsheet, it is real arithmetic done in the open, with your own numbers, in front of the people the price actually has to work for. this playbook is that arithmetic. it is generalized from a real pricing audit run on an actual business, with every company-specific number stripped out — what survives is the method, not the figures. run it against **your own** numbers. if a step doesn't apply to what you sell, say so and move to the next one; do not force a fit. ## arguments `$arguments` — what you are pricing, in a sentence: a product, a service, or an agency engagement, and how it is sold today (or how you plan to sell it). --- ## before anything else: are you pricing one business, or two? a product (self-serve, software, something a customer configures themselves) and a service (you or your team doing the work) have **opposite cost structures**. a product's cost barely moves as you add customers. a service's cost moves in a straight line with headcount — every new client is another chunk of somebody's calendar. if what you sell is actually both — software plus a person who sets it up, or a subscription plus a dedicated contact — **you are pricing two businesses with one number**, and that number will be wrong for both of them. a price cheap enough to read as software, with a human attached, does not compute for the buyer: they can't tell if they bought a tool or hired a person, and neither economics survives being priced like the other one. **do this now:** if you sell both, split them. give the product its own price and the service its own price, priced by two different methods (below). everything past this point assumes you know which one you are pricing at any given moment — if you're not sure, that uncertainty is the finding, not a detail to smooth over. --- ## 1. the load test before any spreadsheet, ask the person who actually does the work — you, a contractor, an employee — one question: **does this price, at the volume you're actually running today, pay your real bills?** if the honest answer is *"this isn't going to pay my bills, i still need another gig,"* that is not a negotiation and it is not a morale problem. **it is the pricing model failing a load test with one real person on it.** no amount of confidence in the underlying math survives that sentence being true. fix the model before you fix the mood. this is the cheapest diagnostic in this whole playbook and the most skipped. if nobody delivering the work has said this to you, ask directly — don't wait for it to come out sideways in a resignation. --- ## 2. know what you actually pay — and how sure you are list every real cost your price has to cover. for each line, tag it with a confidence level: | confidence | means | | --- | --- | | **measured** | you have a number from an actual invoice, statement, or system of record | | **estimated** | you're inferring it from something adjacent (a rate card, a rough average) | | **unknown** | you genuinely don't know, and haven't looked | the failure mode this catches: a pricing model quietly built on "unknown" lines that got treated as "fine" by default, because nobody wrote down that they were guesses. **the lines that move when your business grows are usually the ones marked unknown** — storage, compute, anything that scales with customers or data — while the lines everyone worries about (a monthly subscription, a tool license) are already small and already known. **do this now:** write the list. where a number is a guess, say so in the same sentence as the number, not in a footnote you'll forget to write. a cost audit that hides its own uncertainty is worse than no audit — it just moves the surprise later. one more thing worth checking here: if you have a dashboard or report that claims to show your cost and it reads suspiciously clean — a flat number, a zero, something that never moves — check whether that instrument can actually see the cost, or whether it's reading a source that was never wired up to see it in the first place. a tool reporting "$0" is not the same fact as "this costs nothing." --- ## 3. pricing a service: backwards from capacity do not price a service against competitors. price it backwards from what the role actually costs and how many clients that role can genuinely hold — in that order. 1. **what does this role need to earn to be worth doing full-time?** use a real market number for the skill, not a wish. 2. **how many clients can one person actually serve well?** not "how many could they technically be assigned" — how many before quality, responsiveness, or the relationship itself starts to break down. be honest about what the job actually requires (real context, real attention), not the optimistic version. 3. **cost per client = (1) ÷ (2).** this is the floor, not the price — it's what the client already costs you before a cent of margin. 4. **price per client = cost per client ÷ your target margin.** if you want the role to keep 60% of what a client pays, cost-per-client is 40% of the price, not the whole thing. the output is a number with a *reason* behind it — not "what feels defensible" and not "what the market seems to charge for something adjacent." a price with no derivation is a price you can't defend the first time someone pushes back on it. **watch for this specific trap:** a price that looks reasonable divided across "how many clients could theoretically fit on a calendar" instead of "how many clients this role can actually serve well." that's how a role ends up profitable on paper and broke in practice — see step 1. --- ## 4. pricing a product: backwards from the real cost driver find the **one thing that actually varies** with usage — not a proxy for it. if your real variable cost is compute, storage, api calls, or raw materials, meter and price against *that*, not against a stand-in unit (seats, "credits," a flat per-user rate) that can quietly decouple from what it's supposed to represent. why this matters: if you price by a proxy unit and the true cost-per-unit changes underneath you — a vendor raises rates, a supplier's price shifts, a process gets more expensive — your margin moves and nothing you priced against told you it was about to happen. price against the real driver and the same event just changes how fast a customer burns through what they bought; your margin per unit doesn't move at all. **never gate your cheapest tier on capability to make it look smaller.** withholding quality from a low tier doesn't make it cheaper, it makes it worse at the job — and a customer who was disappointed by the product does not upgrade out of that disappointment, they leave. gate on volume or budget, not on whether the thing works properly. --- ## 5. the one-page proforma for one real, representative customer, write out: | line | type | | --- | --- | | revenue | what they actually pay you | | direct cost | the cost that exists only because this specific customer exists (labor, compute, materials) | | allocated cost | your share of costs that exist regardless of this one customer (hosting, tools, your own time) | | contribution margin | revenue minus direct minus allocated | do this for one real name, not a hypothetical average customer — averages hide the case that's actually losing money. **leave a line blank rather than guess at it**, and say what would need to be true to fill it in. a proforma that's honestly half-finished is more useful than one that's confidently wrong — the blank lines are your actual to-do list, not a cosmetic gap. if you don't currently attribute cost per customer at all, that is itself the finding: it usually means the business *looks* profitable because the cost that would say otherwise has never been assigned to anyone. --- ## 6. stress test the price you don't need to worry equally about every cost line — usually only one or two things can actually break a price. find them and bound them with numbers, not general anxiety. the two classic ones: - **fixed cost failing to dilute.** usually it doesn't — fixed costs divided across a growing customer count shrink to nothing per customer fairly fast. do the division at your current count and at 10x; if it's already small, stop worrying about this one and say so explicitly, so you don't keep re-litigating it. - **variable cost growing faster than revenue.** this is the one that actually sinks prices. work out how much usage headroom your price buys at your cheapest cost option and at your most expensive one — the gap between those two numbers is usually enormous, and it tells you that your margin is sensitive to a choice you're making (which vendor, which tier, which process), not to how much business you're doing. whichever one is real for your business, that's the thing to monitor. the other one, once you've done the math, you can stop worrying about — and say so, so it doesn't quietly come back as a vague fear later. --- ## 7. check the market — but normalize the unit first a price only means something next to a comparable price if they're expressed in the **same unit**. "$99 a month" next to "$45 per seat per month" tells you nothing until you know how many seats your $99 covers. convert your price into the unit the market actually uses (per seat, per hour, per project, per outcome) before deciding whether you're expensive, cheap, or fine. this single step routinely reveals two opposite mistakes in the same pricing model: one product priced far below what the category supports (leaving real money on the table, often in the category where buyers are least price-sensitive and most used to paying more), and another priced aggressively below a single-purpose competitor once normalized — which can be a deliberate, defensible land grab, but only if it's a decision and not an accident nobody checked. --- ## 8. sell a ladder, not a single price a single price point gives a buyer nothing to grow into and nothing to compare against — it's a yes/no decision. a ladder (three tiers, a few named products, a clear "more of this costs more") gives the buyer an anchor, a reason the middle option looks reasonable, and a path to spend more with you later without a renegotiation. if everything you sell is currently one price, that's usually leaving both a cheaper entry point and a larger deal on the table at the same time. --- ## 9. can a customer actually buy it? all of the above is theoretical until someone can reach a checkout. walk your own buying path end to end, as a stranger would: does every price you've decided on actually have a working link to pay for it? does the page describing it list anything you've stopped offering — a feature, an integration, a service you quietly retired? an outdated claim on a live pricing page isn't a copywriting issue, it's a live promise you can't keep, sitting in front of paying customers. **do this now, literally:** try to buy your own thing, on every tier, today. the gap between the price you decided on and the price a customer can actually act on is where a correct pricing model quietly fails in production. --- ## 10. outcome-based pricing is the right destination — in the wrong order, right now charging for the result instead of the work (a resolved case, a completed piece, a shipped deliverable) aligns your price with what the customer actually values, and it is usually where a mature pricing model should end up. it cannot be the first move. guaranteeing a price for an outcome requires knowing what that outcome costs you to deliver — and if you just found, in step 2, that you don't reliably know your own cost per customer, you are not ready to underwrite a result whose true cost you can't see. that's the same failure that produces a broken price in the first place, now with a contract attached to it. get real cost visibility first (steps 2 and 5); outcome pricing is the reward for having done that work, not a shortcut around it. --- ## the shape of the mistake every failure this playbook catches is the same one, wearing a different outfit: **a number got treated as known when it was actually assumed, or as fixed when it was actually growing.** a dashboard reading "$0" got trusted instead of checked. a price got compared to a competitor without converting to the same unit. a proforma got filled in with an average instead of left honestly blank. a pricing page kept advertising something that was quietly cancelled months ago. none of these are arithmetic errors — the math is usually fine once you do it. they are all the same kind of mistake: **deciding before measuring.** measure first, in the open, and let the price follow from what you actually find.
