description: search keyword for trace action confirm: - "redeploy*" on-error: continue timeout: 120 allowed-tools: - read - bash - grep - glob - edit - agent - webfetch --- # production deploy — railway production management manage the freelabel production deployment on railway (primary production platform, fully migrated from digitalocean april 12, 2026). > **see also**: `/deploy-test-loop` — the tight deploy-test-fix cycle for validating new features against production. use it when shipping code that touches api endpoints, db records, or model $fillable. catches mass-assignment gaps, enum mismatches, and schema issues that only surface against real data. ## executable steps (v2) ### step:health-api fl-api health check ### step:health-iris iris-api health check ### step:health-frontend frontend health check ### step:health-typesense typesense health check ### step:health-pages pages smoke test ### step:health-report status summary ### step:errors-api fl-api error extraction ### step:errors-iris iris-api error extraction ### step:errors-frontend frontend error extraction ### step:errors-report error summary ### step:logs-tail tail service logs ### step:trace-search trace keyword across services ### step:queue-check queue health check ### step:benchmark-all benchmark all endpoints ### step:product-doors product front door check ### step:redeploy-service trigger redeploy ## arguments `$arguments` — action to perform. examples: ### deployment & infrastructure - `/production-deploy status` — health check all services - `/production-deploy restart <service>` — restart a service - `/production-deploy health` — test all endpoints and db connectivity - `/production-deploy domains` — check custom domain status and ssl - `/production-deploy env <service>` — list env vars for a service - `/production-deploy env-diff <service>` — compare do vs railway env vars - `/production-deploy env-sync <key> <service>` — sync a specific env var from do to railway - `/production-deploy redeploy <service>` — trigger a redeploy - `/production-deploy deploy-service <name> <image>` — deploy a new docker image service - `/production-deploy benchmark` — compare response times across all services - `/production-deploy migrate` — run artisan migrate on fl-api via railway mysql proxy ### client readiness gate (ship checklist) - `/production-deploy client-ready <feature>` — run the full 21-gate client readiness checklist before shipping a feature - `/production-deploy client-ready` — run the checklist for the most recent commit/changes on the current branch ### log debugging (primary debug workflow) - `/production-deploy logs <service>` — tail live logs for a service (fl-api, fl-iris-api, fl-elon-web-ui, typesense, redis, mysql) - `/production-deploy logs-all` — tail all services in parallel (opens multiple streams, summarizes output) - `/production-deploy errors [service]` — extract only error/critical/exception lines. if no service specified, checks all. - `/production-deploy trace <keyword>` — search a keyword (workflow id, user id, error string) across all service logs - `/production-deploy queue-debug` — check queue health: failed jobs, stuck workers, queue sizes, recent failures - `/production-deploy laravel-log <service>` — read the laravel storage/logs/laravel.log inside the container (fl-api or fl-iris-api) - `/production-deploy recent-errors [minutes]` — show errors from last n minutes (default: 30) across all services --- ## client readiness gate (22-gate ship checklist) before shipping any feature to production, run `/production-deploy client-ready <feature>` to execute all 21 gates below. a feature is not client-ready until every gate passes. the goal is to ensure nothing ships that feels "admin-only" or "developer-internal" — everything a client touches must be polished, documented, and tested. the checklist runs in two halves. **gates 1-18 are release**: does it work, is it safe, did it ship. **gates 19-22 are post-release**: is it a reusable genesis component, is the happy path runnable as a playbook, is anyone being taught, and — when the release introduces a product — does that product have a front door. the second half was added 2026-08-21 because features were passing the first half and reaching nobody — surfacing in the ui was the slowest step in the pipeline, and training had no gate, no channel, and no owner at all. **critical principle: "client-ready" means a client can use this without us.** if they need us to run it, explain it, set it up, or interpret the output — it's not client-ready. it's operator tooling. operator tooling is fine to ship, but it fails gate 1 and must be labeled as such. ### gate 1: client-facing angle audit (the hard one) **question: can a client use this feature without our help? would they even know it exists?** this is the gate that catches "we built a great engine but there's no steering wheel." be brutally honest. #### step 1: the client walkthrough test (mandatory) pretend you are a client who just ran `iris update`. walk through these questions in order. stop at the first fail — that's your gap. | # | question | pass criteria | fail means | |---|----------|---------------|------------| | 1 | **can the client discover this feature exists?** | it shows up in `iris help`, `iris <area> --help`, or a ui they already use. they don't need to be told about it. | no client surface — it's admin tooling. fail. | | 2 | **can they invoke it with a single command or click?** | `iris inbox scan` or a button in the ui. not `board_id=38 npx playwright test som/whatsapp-inbox-check.spec.ts --headed` | requires dev tooling (env vars, npx, playwright, raw scripts). fail. | | 3 | **do they need to know our internal concepts?** | they never see `bloq_id`, `board`, `spec`, `provider`, `api_base`, `token`. they see "your leads", "your inbox", "3 new replies". | internal concepts leak into the client experience. fail. | | 4 | **is the output client-friendly?** | clean summary: "found 3 replies: john smith, sarah k, mike d". not raw console.log with lead ids and http status codes. | output is developer diagnostics. fail. | | 5 | **can they handle errors themselves?** | "your whatsapp session expired — run `iris inbox connect whatsapp` to reconnect". not `session expired: default — re-scan qr code`. | errors require developer knowledge to resolve. fail. | | 6 | **does it work without our config?** | uses their `~/.iris/config.json` for auth, board, account. not hardcoded tokens or env var fallbacks they'd need to know about. | requires manual env var setup. fail. | **scoring:** - **6/6 pass** → gate 1 pass (truly client-ready) - **4-5/6 pass** → gate 1 warn (almost there — list gaps, can ship with follow-up ticket) - **0-3/6 pass** → gate 1 fail (operator tooling — must build client surface or label as admin-only) #### step 1.5: surface exposure check (mandatory) every feature must be evaluated against all surfaces below. not every feature needs all of them, but you must explicitly mark each as done, planned, or n/a **with justification**. "we'll add it later" is planned and needs a ticket, not a shrug. this was a four-surface check until 2026-08-21, when shipping p4 (forkable exports) passed it with cli + api + agents and still reached nobody who reads docs: there was no how-to, and `/p/docs` never mentioned it. a feature that exists in the binary and nowhere a human looks is the same failure this whole checklist exists to catch — so **mcp, tui, how-to and /docs are now surfaces, not afterthoughts.** | # | surface | done / planned / n/a | how to verify | |---|---------|---------------------|---------------| | 1 | **cli** — is there an `iris <command>` that exposes this? | check: `iris help 2>/dev/null \| grep -i "<feature>"` and `iris <command> --help` | if no cli command exists, file a ticket for one. operator-only features still need cli. | | 2 | **ui (genesis)** — is there a **reusable genesis component** that surfaces this? | check: `ls fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/resources/js/components/pagebuilder/ \| grep -i "<feature>"` — then confirm it renders on a real page, not just that the file exists. | **genesis is the ui surface. elon is legacy — do not build new surfaces there.** a new ui built in `fl-elon-web-ui` is a surface we are committed to deleting. depth check is gate 19. | | 3 | **api** — are the endpoints documented and accessible via authenticated rest calls? | check: `grep -n "<feature>" fl-docker-dev/fl-api/routes/api.php 2>/dev/null` and test with curl. | every feature that writes data must have an api surface. | | 4 | **ai agents (v6 engine)** — can an ai agent invoke this via tool calling? | check: `grep -ri "<feature>" fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/app/tools/ fl-docker-dev/fl-api/app/services/integrations/ 2>/dev/null \| head -5` | n/a for pure display features. required for any action an agent should automate (link sessions, tag leads, create content). | | 5 | **mcp** — can an external coding agent (claude code, cursor, opencode) reach it through the iris mcp gateway? | check: the command is in `packages/opencode/capabilities.json` (`entries[].name`), which is what mcp discovery and `iris find` read. then probe over json-rpc — do not infer from the file. | a cli command absent from the capability index is invisible to every agent, which is how the old hand-typed catalog decayed to 15 of 120. | | 6 | **tui** — is it reachable from the interactive terminal ui, or does it only exist as a flag on a subcommand? | check: run the tui and look for it; or confirm the command is discoverable via `iris find <keyword>`. | n/a for one-shot exports and scripts. required for anything a person does repeatedly while working. | | 7 | **`--help`** — does `iris <command> --help` explain what it does, its required args, and show an example? | check: `iris <command> --help` | a command whose help is just a usage line is a command only its author can use. | | 8 | **how-to** — is there a `how-to` recipe walking the happy path? | check: `iris how-to list \| grep -i "<feature>"` | 44 how-tos exist. a feature with none is one nobody can be onboarded onto without us. | | 9 | **/docs** — is it on the public docs page and, if developer-facing, on `/p/iris-developers`? | check: `curl -s and the developers page json for the command name. | docs are where people look before asking. absent here means every question comes to us. | | 10 | **site nav** — if this is a named product, is it in the heyiris nav? | the menu is defined once in `fl-iris-api/resources/js/components/landing/navbar.vue` and shared by every page via `irislandingnav`. **solutions** = named products, each pointing at its own `/p/<name>` page (atlas, heartbeat, playbooks, genesis, hive, vault, pulse, commons…). **resources** = docs and reading. **ecosystem** = integrations and ventures. **clients** = live client work. | **only products go in the nav; features go in /docs.** `agents export` is a feature of the cli and belongs on /p/docs and /p/iris-developers, not in solutions. but a product with no nav entry is one nobody browses to — navbar.vue's own comment records integrations having been "reachable from nowhere at all". | **rules:** - a feature shipping with 0 surfaces is not client-ready (it's a backend engine only). - **cli + `--help` + how-to + /docs is the floor for anything a person invokes.** p4 shipped with the first two and neither of the last two; that is how a released feature stays invisible. - **mcp is not optional for a cli command.** if it is not in the capability index, no coding agent can find it, and "agents can use iris" stops being true one command at a time. - **decide product vs feature before checking surface 10.** a product earns a nav entry and a `/p/<name>` page; a feature earns docs. putting a feature in the nav bloats the menu, and leaving a product out of it means the only people who find it are the ones we tell. - **a nav entry and its page ship together.** an entry pointing at a 404 is worse than no entry — audit with: `grep -oe 'href: "/p/[a-z0-9-]+"' navbar.vue` then curl each one. absence of a local `pages/*.json` proves nothing; pages created directly in production have no local copy and still resolve 200. - cli + api is the minimum for any data-writing feature. - ui is required for features clients interact with daily. - ai agent surface is required for any repeatable action an agent could automate (follow-ups, tagging, linking, scheduling). #### step 2: language & leak scan (automated) #### step 3: determine scope classification based on the walkthrough, classify the feature: | classification | criteria | action required | |---|---|---| | **client-ready** | passes 6/6 walkthrough. client can discover, use, and troubleshoot independently. | ship it. | | **client-adjacent** | backend/engine work that enables a future client feature. no client surface yet. | ship it, but file a follow-up ticket for the client surface (cli command, ui). label the daily diary as "phase 1 — engine only". | | **operator tooling** | only we can run it. requires dev setup, env vars, or internal knowledge. | ship it, but do not call it client-ready. label the daily diary as "admin tooling". plan the client wrapper. | **a feature classified as "operator tooling" is not a failure — it's honest.** the failure is calling it client-ready when it's not. ### gate 2: qa / test coverage **question: is this tested against production data, not just local mocks?** run these in order — stop at first failure: checklist: - [ ] unit tests pass (all green) - [ ] e2e spec exists and runs (even if dry-run) - [ ] production api endpoints the feature depends on return 200 - [ ] no new production errors after deploying - [ ] edge cases tested (empty data, expired sessions, rate limits) - [ ] if client-facing: test the client path (the `iris` command or ui), not just the engine ### gate 3: swot analysis (lightweight) **question: what could go wrong, and is the tradeoff worth it?** for every feature shipping to clients, do a 2-minute swot: | | positive | negative | |---|---|---| | **internal** | **strengths**: what does this do well? what's solid? | **weaknesses**: what's fragile? missing? hacky? | | **external** | **opportunities**: what does this unlock for clients? revenue? retention? | **threats**: what could break for clients? data loss? confusion? regression? | rules: - if any **threat** is "data loss" or "breaks existing workflow" — stop. fix before shipping. - if **weaknesses** include "no tests" — go back to gate 2. - if **opportunities** is empty — ask: why are we shipping this to clients? - **if "opportunities" says "clients can't use this yet"** — classify as client-adjacent or operator tooling in gate 1. not a blocker, but be honest. - document the swot in the daily diary entry for the feature. ### gate 4: iris cli discovery & documentation **question: can a client (or future-you) find and use this feature without asking?** checklist: - [ ] **client invocation exists**: there is an `iris <command>` that a client can run. not a raw `npx playwright` or `node script.js` invocation. - [ ] **`iris help` shows it**: the command appears in `iris help` or the relevant subcommand help. - [ ] **`--help` is useful**: running `iris <command> --help` shows what it does, required args, and an example. - [ ] **error messages guide the user**: if something goes wrong, the error tells them what to do next (not a stack trace). - [ ] **how-to exists**: a `how-tos/` entry or inline help that walks through the happy path. - [ ] **daily diary**: a `daily-diary/yyyy-mm-dd-<feature>.md` entry documenting what shipped. - [ ] **known limitations filed**: if the feature has gaps, they're in `iris bug list`. **if gate 1 classified this as "operator tooling"**: gate 4 still passes if there's a daily diary and the admin invocation is documented. but file a ticket for the client wrapper. ### gate 5: related bug reports (optional — nice to have) **question: are there known bugs that this feature interacts with?** - [ ] search `iris bug list` for the feature area - [ ] search github issues: `gh issue list --search "<feature keyword>" --repo freelabel/iris-opencode` - [ ] search daily diaries for past mentions: `grep -rl "<feature>" daily-diary/` - [ ] if related bugs exist: either fix them in this pr, or document them as known limitations in the daily diary ### gate 6: security audit **question: could this feature leak data, bypass auth, or be exploited?** checklist: - [ ] **no hardcoded secrets in client-visible code**: api tokens, webhook urls, and keys must come from env vars. hardcoded fallbacks are ok only in private repos / internal tooling that clients never access. - [ ] **auth boundary respected**: does the feature check authentication? are api calls using per-user tokens (not shared service tokens) where appropriate? - [ ] **input validation**: any user/external input sanitized before use? no raw string interpolation into sql, shell commands, or api urls. - [ ] **owasp top 10 scan**: check for injection (sql, command, xss), broken auth, sensitive data exposure, ssrf. - [ ] **rate limiting**: if the feature calls external apis or production endpoints in a loop, is there throttling? could a bad actor trigger excessive api calls? - [ ] **credential rotation**: if secrets are committed (even in private repos), are they rotatable? note any that need rotation. ### gate 7: portability & environment safety **question: will this work on a fresh machine, a hive node, or in ci — not just your laptop?** checklist: - [ ] **no absolute paths**: grep for `/users/`, `/home/`, or machine-specific paths. all paths must be relative or use env vars / `os.homedir()`. - [ ] **dependencies declared**: any new `import` or `require` references a package that's in `package.json`. no phantom deps. - [ ] **env var fallbacks documented**: every env var the feature uses has a sensible default or a clear error message when missing. - [ ] **cross-platform**: does it work on macos and linux? any `darwin`-only apis (`open`, `pbcopy`, macos paths)? - [ ] **offline resilience**: if production api is unreachable, does the feature fail gracefully (not crash)? - [ ] **hive compatibility**: if this runs on hive nodes, does it work with `browser_session_file` protocol? does it respect `headless=1`? ### gate 8: regression & smoke test **question: did we break anything that was already working?** new features don't matter if existing client workflows are broken. before every ship, run the 5 most common client workflows as a smoke test. #### the "big 5" client workflows (run every time) these are the workflows clients use daily. if any of these break, the deploy is blocked — no exceptions. checklist: - [ ] all 5 smoke tests return 200 (not 500, 502, 404) - [ ] response times are reasonable (< 5s for apis, < 10s for pages) - [ ] no new production errors appeared in the last 30 minutes - (heyiris.io/developers has feature reference) 19. run **gate 18** — marketing landing page (public page explaining + selling the feature) 20. run **gate 19** — genesis reusable component (registry entry, generated schema, no drift, renders) 21. run **gate 20** — how-to → playbook (happy path is runnable, skill synced) 22. run **gate 21** — training & enablement (email / social / portal, and a named owner) 23. run **gate 22** — product front door (only if this release adds or renames a product) 24. print a **pass / fail / warn** summary with action items **gates 19-22 are the post-release half.** gates 1-18 answer "did it ship and is it safe?" gates 19-22 answer "is it surfaced where people compose things, is the path runnable, and is anyone being taught?" a feature passing 1-18 and failing 19-21 is released and unused. output format: --- ## log debugging reference ### service names for `railway logs --service <name>` | service | name | has logs | log type | |---------|------|----------|----------| | fl-api | `fl-api` | yes | laravel + nginx + php-fpm | | iris-api | `fl-iris-api` | yes | php-fpm passthrough only | | frontend | `fl-elon-web-ui` | yes | node.js errors + stack traces | | typesense | `typesense` | yes | c++ raft/gc/search logs | | redis | **tbd** | no (`redis` not found) | — | | mysql | **tbd** | no (`mysql` not found) | — | ### log formats by service **fl-api** emits 3 interleaved streams: 1. **laravel app logs**: `[2026-05-06 14:50:10] production.info: bot throttled {"type":"legit-bot-api",...}` - format: `[yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss] environment.level: message {json_context}` - levels: `info`, `warning`, `error`, `critical` 2. **nginx access logs**: `100.64.0.4 - - [06/may/2026:14:50:10 +0000] "get /api/v1/path http/1.1" 200 691 ...` - includes response timing: `rt=0.359 uct="0.000" uht="0.358" urt="0.358"` - `rt` = total, `uht` = upstream header time (backend latency) 3. **php-fpm passthrough**: `127.0.0.1 - timestamp "method /index.php" status_code` - internal nginx→php, shows only status code — less useful for debugging **fl-iris-api** emits only php-fpm passthrough: - `127.0.0.1 - 06/may/2026:14:50:04 +0000 "get /index.php" 301` - no full urls, no request paths — just status codes (200, 301, 401) - for real debugging, must ssh in and `tail -f storage/logs/laravel.log` **fl-elon-web-ui** (nuxt/node): - -- chmod -r 775 /var/www/html/storage` make permanent by adding to dockerfile entrypoint. ### "could not resolve host: api-nginx" iris-api trying to call fl-api via docker internal hostname. set `fl_api_base_url= on iris-api. ### "cloudflare proxy detected" on custom domains railway needs dns-only (grey cloud in cloudflare). turn off orange cloud proxy. ### container crashes with "starting container" only oom kill — increase memory in settings > scale > replica limits. iris-api needs 4gb due to chromium. ### docker image service crashes with "resource temporarily unavailable" thread limit exceeded. reduce thread pool via env vars (e.g., `typesense_thread_pool_size=8`). railway containers have lower thread limits than bare metal. ### env vars set but not taking effect railway `freelabel.net` has an active domain mapping (`page_slug: freelabel`) in the db. the root redirect in `redirectfromrootdomain.php` must run before the domain mapping check, or the mapping intercepts it. verify with: `curl -si should return 302 → `web.freelabel.net/discover`. to revert to landing page: comment out the 4-line root redirect block. ### pricing page redirects to web.heyiris.io client-side redirect in `pages/pricing.vue` `mounted()`. the `appdomains` list must include the current hostname. fallback url was `web.heyiris.io`, changed to `web.freelabel.net` in commit `009aab3f`. ### auth "unauthenticated" errors check `fl_raichu_api_token` is the full ~900 char jwt, not truncated. ### health check shows "bloq_agent_job_executions" error table name was fixed in commit `4fbb667d` — actual table is `agent_job_executions`. if still failing, redeploy fl-api. ## legacy: digitalocean (sunsetting) do app platform is being sunset. these ids are kept for reference during transition: - **iris-api do app**: `68ad4e37-3502-4681-8f28-9c5725044dce` (components: fl-iris-api, fl-iris-worker) - **fl-api do app**: `de3441a0-eb76-401c-9191-67c634ee446a` (components: fl-api, fl-api-queue-worker) - **heyiris.io**: still served by do app `49a0c8c6-263e-4b03-ab17-19c19d760a55` via cloudflare (dns switch pending) ### do cli reference (for env var sync during transition) once `heyiris.io` dns is switched to railway, do can be fully decommissioned. ## iris cli release & update pipeline the iris cli (`iris` command) is distributed via the installer at `heyiris.io/install-code`. updates are pulled from the `main` branch of `freelabel/iris-opencode` on github. ### how `iris update` works 1. `latest()` in `packages/opencode/src/installation/index.ts` calls the **github releases api**: ` 2. reads `tag_name` (e.g., `v1.3.37`), strips the `v` prefix → compares against local `opencode_version` 3. `upgrade()` downloads the **compiled binary** from the release assets (e.g., `iris-darwin-arm64.zip`) 4. replaces the binary at `~/.iris/bin/iris` **it does not read `package.json` at update time.** the `package.json` version is baked into the binary at build time via `opencode_version` env var. ### release checklist (all 3 steps required) the release workflow (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) triggers on tag push (`v*`). it builds binaries on 5 platforms (macos arm64/x64, linux x64/arm64, windows x64) and creates a github release with all assets attached. ### what can go wrong | symptom | cause | fix | |---------|-------|-----| | `iris update` says "already on latest: 1.3.xx" | no github release exists for the new version | push a `v1.3.xx` tag to trigger the release workflow | | release exists but `iris update` downloads old binary | `package.json` version wasn't bumped before building | bump version, push, re-tag, re-release | | tag pushed but no release appears | ci workflow failed | check `gh run list` for failures | | `iris --version` shows `0.0.0-main-yyyymmdd` | running from source/dev build, not an installed release | run `iris update` to get the release binary | ### common pitfall: tag without release a git tag alone does not create a release. the tag must trigger the github actions workflow which builds binaries and creates the release. if the workflow is skipped or fails, no release exists and `iris update` won't see the new version. ### releasing: use `release.sh` (one command) the `release.sh` script in the iris-code repo root handles the entire pipeline: what it does automatically: 1. reads current version from `packages/opencode/package.json` 2. bumps to target version 3. commits + creates git tag `v1.x.x` 4. pushes commit + tag to `origin main` 5. watches ci release workflow (builds binaries on 5 platforms) 6. optionally syncs `dev` branch with `main` **safety checks built in**: must be on `main`, clean working tree, tag can't already exist, confirms before proceeding. ### manual release flow (if release.sh unavailable) ### key paths | item | location | |------|----------| | version source | `iris-code/packages/opencode/package.json` → `"version"` | | repo | `freelabel/iris-opencode` | | release branch | `main` (protected, prs from `dev`) | | dev branch | `dev` (default working branch) | | installer | `heyiris.io/install-code` | | binary | `~/.iris/bin/iris` | | update command | `iris update` | ### verifying a release

entries.name: project-management-setup
entries.describe: Get a team's Notion-based project management actually running — structure, roles, properties, and the cadence that keeps it honest.
entries.haystack: experience-art-project-management get a team's notion-based project management actually running — structure, roles, properties, and the cadence that keeps it honest. --- name: project-management-setup description: get a team's notion-based project management actually running — structure, roles, properties, and the cadence that keeps it honest. version: 2 on-error: stop --- # project management setup get a team's notion-based project management actually running: structure, roles, custom properties, and the review cadence that keeps "in notion" meaning something. > written from the experience art / x-art team standup, 2026-08-24 (five-part call — see > heyiris.io bloq #570, board cards #182221–#182225). generalize the names below to your own > team; the structure and reasoning are the reusable part. ## why this exists — the rule, verbatim the team's own words: **"if it's not in notion, it doesn't exist."** not a suggestion — a lead flatly stated he's never seen a project turn out well without active project management, and made getting organized the literal precondition for the next external-facing meeting (they held off inviting a technology partner to a call *specifically* because the team wasn't organized yet — walking in disorganized would have cost them credibility and negotiating leverage). the corollary that matters as much as the rule: **tell people why, not just what.** one member was explicit that the team shouldn't be handed new process for its own sake — "i don't want them to think we're just creating stuff for them to do... there's a reason behind it and who it's coming from." rolling this out without that context reads as busywork, not infrastructure. ## the two-document structure nearly every team that does this ends up with (at minimum) two notion pages, and conflating them is the most common early mistake: 1. **the plan** — the overall vision/architecture document: what you're building, why, in what phases, and the file/folder structure everything else hangs off of. read-and- reference, edited rarely, by leadership. 2. **the task board** — where actual work lives day to day. everyone's individual tasks, in priority order, with real statuses and properties (below). this is the one people touch constantly. keep these separate. the plan document drifts out of date fast if people also try to log day-to-day work in it — this team caught themselves mid-project having exactly that drift ("we haven't updated that plan based on recent conversations") and had to do a live reconciliation pass. ## status categories (the ones that actually earned their keep) - **doing** — active work, top of the board. - **stuck** — blocked on a dependency (see below). not "someone forgot" — a task with an unmet prerequisite belongs here structurally, not in doing. - **next up** — everything else, i.e. the real backlog. - **maybe later** — deliberately separate from next up. things worth recording but not worth pretending are near-term. without this bucket, low-priority ideas either get lost or clutter next up until nobody trusts it. ## two custom properties worth setting up before anyone starts filling in tasks - **dependency** (relational property) — links a task to the other task(s) that must complete first. if a task can't move forward until another finishes, it goes in stuck and gets tagged here, not left ambiguous in a comment. - **support staff** — a person tagged as helping execute a task without being its owner. distinct from ownership; use it to spread load without diffusing accountability for who actually delivers. setting these up *before* the team starts populating tasks avoids a second painful pass later where half the board has to be retrofitted. ## steps ### step:step-1 explain the why before the what ### step:step-2 stand up the two-document structure ### step:step-3 set up the status categories and custom properties ### step:step-4 confirm everyone has access and can find the workspace ### step:step-5 pull every task out of people's heads and onto the board ### step:step-6 put everything in priority order and mark dependencies ### step:step-7 assign an owner and, where useful, supporting staff to every task ### step:step-8 name interim and traveling-lead ownership explicitly ### step:step-9 set a recurring review cadence ### step:step-10 offer hands-on onboarding, don't just document it ### step:step-11 treat the plan document as living, not fixed --- ## a worked example, for calibration from the source call: a task existed on the board ("set up the apollo integration") with no description — nobody knew what it actually meant anymore. resolution, in order: 1. someone flagged the gap directly rather than guessing or ignoring it. 2. the task's origin and intent got re-explained (plug a third-party api into the shared data layer so internal tools can enrich records on demand). 3. an owner was assigned to execute (not the person who originally scoped it). 4. a supporting person was tagged via the support staff property (also not the scoper). 5. a concrete due date was set, tied to an already-scheduled working session. 6. the original scoper committed to handing over what they had — links, context, prior research — directly into the task. that's the whole loop this playbook is trying to produce, repeatably: gap noticed → intent clarified → owner assigned → support tagged → due date set → handoff happens in the task itself, not in someone's head or a side channel. ## why these steps are instructions, not commands several of these were drafted from a spoken walkthrough. transcription mishears domain terms, and a model filling in a command nobody actually said is how a procedure quietly acquires a step no one approved. each step here is an instruction a person or agent carries out and can verify, not a black-box automation. promote a step to `mode: shell` yourself once you know the exact command for your own notion/workspace setup — this playbook deliberately stays tool-agnostic on the mechanics.

entries.name: revenue-path-audit
entries.describe: Prove that a stranger can actually give you money, before you pay for traffic. Walks each revenue path from ad click to a real payment-provider session, checks the fee is taken and not merely recorded, and refuses to accept a zero until it can tell "nothing happened" from "nothing was configured". Every check here is one that shipped broken while every dashboard looked healthy.
entries.haystack: revenue-path-audit prove that a stranger can actually give you money, before you pay for traffic. walks each revenue path from ad click to a real payment-provider session, checks the fee is taken and not merely recorded, and refuses to accept a zero until it can tell "nothing happened" from "nothing was configured". every check here is one that shipped broken while every dashboard looked healthy. --- name: revenue-path-audit description: prove that a stranger can actually give you money, before you pay for traffic. walks each revenue path from ad click to a real payment-provider session, checks the fee is taken and not merely recorded, and refuses to accept a zero until it can tell "nothing happened" from "nothing was configured". every check here is one that shipped broken while every dashboard looked healthy. version: 2 args: path: type: string required: true description: the revenue path to audit, named as a click — e.g. "iris ad to downloads to subscription" destination: type: string required: false description: the exact url the ad points at, including query string on-error: continue timeout: 900 --- # revenue path audit **the one idea:** a revenue path is not code, it is a sequence of things a stranger does. every step of it can pass its own test while the sequence delivers nothing — and the money layer is worse than most, because **it balances**. reports agree with each other about a fee that was never taken. nothing errors. **run this before spending, and again whenever a path changes.** it takes under an hour and it has never once come back clean. ## what this exists to prevent three real outcomes, all with healthy dashboards: - **1,319 clicks, 0 conversions.** not a low rate — an *arithmetically impossible* one. every funded bounty gated on a program with `member_count: 0`, so the set of people permitted to convert was empty. cpc was **$0.0043**, the best in the account's history. - **an 8% platform fee that was 0%.** `config('stripe.seller_app_fee_percentage', 0.15)` returned **null**, because a default applies to a *missing* key and that key was present-but-null. then `ceil($amount * null) === 0`. every seller on the default path was transferred 100% of gross, while `platform_fee_cents`, `platform_earnings` and every sales report recorded the rake as taken. **the books balanced perfectly against a share that never moved.** - **a pricing page selling four tiers nobody could buy.** every "choose <tier>" button routed to a free onboarding flow whose own source says *"deliberately has no payment step."* the tier arrived as a query parameter that nothing consumed for billing. ## the philosophies, each paid for 1. **walk the path. do not read it.** reading the code proves a checkout *exists*. clicking the button proves a stranger reaches a payment session. only one of those is the question. 2. **before anything else, ask: how many people can complete this action today?** it is one query. if the answer is zero, no creative, budget, targeting or landing-page work can matter. 3. **a zero that means "not configured" reads everywhere as "nothing owed."** before drawing any conclusion from a zero, find the field that separates *not measured* from *measured as none*. if no such field exists, the number cannot support a conclusion in either direction. 4. **verify at the layer that decides, not the layer whose name matches.** a trial bug was hunted in `packagescontroller` for an hour. the pricing page never calls it — it posts to `/users/upgrade/checkout`, and *that* controller contained zero occurrences of the word "trial". 5. **test as a stranger, not as yourself.** a checkout opened as the account owner pre-fills the owner's email and can suppress a trial they already used. your own session is the one account whose behaviour is guaranteed unrepresentative. 6. **the ad platform cannot see past the click, and every metric it owns will look excellent.** cpc, ctr, impressions and pacing are all real and all about a click that could never become anything. **when ad metrics are strong and outcomes are zero, stop reading the ad platform.** 7. **state your hypothesis, then try to kill it.** "the trial is suppressed because i am an existing customer" was reasonable, confident, and wrong — $209.95 was $199 + a 5% + $1 service fee, an arithmetic identity no suppression story can produce. assuming it either way would have closed the investigation on the wrong answer. 8. **enumerate by what creates a charge, not by what you advertise.** an audit shaped like your campaign list finds the paths you already knew about. self-serve signup, an admin-issued invoice, a partner link and a renewal are all revenue paths with no ad behind them. 9. **recorded is not collected.** a fee written to your own tables is an accounting entry. find the line where the payment provider is told to take it — `application_fee_amount`, `transfer_data`, a destination charge. if that line does not exist, the money stayed with the seller. ## steps ### step:inventory what paths exist, and what does each one sell **enumerate by what creates a charge, not by what you are advertising.** an audit built from the ad list finds only the paths you already knew about. on 2026-09-02 that missed one entirely: platform signup auto-mints a lead and a $49 payable gate — *"payment gate created: $49 for 'iris platform - starter package'"* — with no ad pointing at it. it was the only path reliably producing payable links that day, and it was invisible to an audit that walked campaigns. ### step:eligible how many people can complete this action today **this is the cheapest step and the one that has saved the most money. do it before any other.** get a number for: *how many people are currently permitted to complete the money action?* - a purchase gated on membership → how many confirmed members exist? - a checkout gated on a plan or entitlement → how many accounts hold it? - an apply/submit flow → does the endpoint refuse anyone the ad can reach? zero is not rare and it is not obvious from any dashboard. the bounty campaign bought 354,060 impressions into an empty set, and the eligibility query took one minute to run *afterwards*. ### step:walk click it, all the way to the payment provider open the destination and **click what a stranger clicks.** not the api. not the code. the button. - stop when you reach the payment provider's own domain, and record what it says — the **amount**, the **interval**, and whether it matches what the page promised. - a discrepancy here is the finding. a page promising "$0 due today" against a session demanding the full amount is a broken promise at the last possible moment. - **do not complete the payment.** navigate away once you have the session. - if you are signed in, note it — see philosophy 5. re-check the amount for a new email before concluding anything about trials or discounts. **a path that does not reach a payment session is not monetised**, whatever the pricing page says. ### step:rate is the fee actually taken, or only written down ### step:fired has this ever actually happened ### step:attribute could you tell which ad produced a sale ### step:record write down what you ruled out log the audit where the next person will look — the findings board, the epic, the campaign registry. include, in this order: - **each path and its verdict**, with the evidence: the session id you reached, the amount shown - **what you ruled out and how.** this is the most valuable part and the part everyone skips. a disproved hypothesis stops the next person spending an hour on it. - **the numbers you could not get**, named as such. "not verified" is a finding. "assumed fine" is how the last one shipped. then decide the spend. **a path that cannot take money should not be receiving traffic** — pausing is one call and costs nothing but the pause.

entries.name: reverse-ui
entries.describe: Reverse-engineer a UI you've seen into a working, data-backed IRIS page. Build the interface first as a dead self-contained mockup, land it in the right Genesis lane, then plug the backend with the Genesis SDK. Use when you have screenshots of a competitor's product, a design you want to match, or an idea you can only describe visually. Pass a target as argument (e.g., "from-screenshots ~/Documents/shots", "land <slug>", "bind <slug>", "audit <slug>").
entries.haystack: reverse-ui reverse-engineer a ui you've seen into a working, data-backed iris page. build the interface first as a dead self-contained mockup, land it in the right genesis lane, then plug the backend with the genesis sdk. use when you have screenshots of a competitor's product, a design you want to match, or an idea you can only describe visually. pass a target as argument (e.g., "from-screenshots ~/documents/shots", "land <slug>", "bind <slug>", "audit <slug>"). --- name: reverse-ui description: reverse-engineer a ui you've seen into a working, data-backed iris page. build the interface first as a dead self-contained mockup, land it in the right genesis lane, then plug the backend with the genesis sdk. use when you have screenshots of a competitor's product, a design you want to match, or an idea you can only describe visually. pass a target as argument (e.g., "from-screenshots ~/documents/shots", "land <slug>", "bind <slug>", "audit <slug>"). allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - artifact - agent --- # reverse ui — interface first, backend last normal order builds the backend, then discovers the ui wants different data. this inverts it: **design the interface against real content until it is right, then plug the data in.** it works because the genesis sdk makes the plug-in step small — one script tag, no keys, no build step, and the authorization is already enforced server-side. the output is not a mockup. it is a published page that reads live, correctly-scoped data. ## arguments `$arguments` — action and target: - `from-screenshots <dir>` — read shots, extract structure, build the mockup - `from-url <url>` — same, from a live page - `from-idea "<description>"` — no reference, straight to design - `land <slug>` — take an approved mockup into a genesis lane - `bind <slug>` — wire the data - `audit <slug>` — score against the design standard + check the render --- ## the four stages | | stage | output | where it lives | |---|---|---|---| | 0 | **read the target** | a structure map — regions and what each one does | notes | | 1 | **build it dead** | self-contained html, real content, no data | artifact | | 2 | **land it** | a published genesis page | `pages/<slug>.json` | | 3 | **plug it in** | live, scoped data | genesis sdk | stage 1 is where the design work happens and it is the only stage worth iterating on. stages 2 and 3 are mechanical if stage 1 was honest about the content. --- ## stage 0 — read the target, not the pixels copying pixels produces a page that looks like someone else's product. copying *structure* produces one that works. for each region, write down what it **does**, not what it looks like: **the test:** could this structure carry a different subject unchanged? if yes you copied a template and it will not survive contact with real content. if no, you got the actual idea. then decide, explicitly, what you are **not** copying. brand marks, wordmarks, exact palettes and traced proportions are a different act from adopting information architecture, and only one of them is defensible. write the line down before you start. ## stage 1 — build it dead one self-contained html file. no framework, no build, no data. **rules that make stage 3 cheap later:** - **real content throughout.** never lorem, never `item 1 / item 2`. use actual records from the system you are going to bind — real collection names, real counts, real states. fake content hides the fact that a column is too narrow or a label is wrong, and you find out after wiring. - **every value that will come from the server gets a stable hook** — `data-bind="collections"`, `id="kpi-records"`. stage 3 becomes find-and-replace instead of a rewrite. - **semantic state in form, not just color** — a pill, a dot, a severity stripe. colour alone fails for a third of readers and washes out in a screenshot. - **mono + `tabular-nums` on every number.** counts, money, versions, timestamps. - load `artifact-design` before writing. it is mandatory and it calibrates treatment. publish it as an **artifact** for review. the loop is seconds — no deploy, no cache, no csp — and the reviewer clicks through it instead of imagining it. iterate here until approved. **do not skip to stage 2 with an unapproved mockup.** landing is cheap; re-landing is not. ## stage 2 — land it in the right lane two lanes, and the choice is decided by one question: **does it need bound data?** ### bespoke lane — `render_mode: "html"` your hand-authored html + css, one page. fast, total design control. **no dataset bindings** — a bespoke page has no `components[]`, so `pagedatasetcontroller` has nothing to resolve. it can still use every other part of the sdk. ### component lane — `components[]` register the component in `utils/componentresolver.js` (the single map) with a top-level `type` in its `schema.json`, or it is un-pushable. give it a `datasetslug` prop and it inherits the whole authz model for free: owner from the page, scope from the gate, phi default-deny, cross-tenant guard. ### bespoke + bindings — you can have both (verified 2026-08-21) an earlier version of this playbook said records force you into the component lane. **that is wrong.** `pagedatasetcontroller::findcomponent()` reads `json_content.components[]` and matches on `id`; it never checks `render_mode`. and the bespoke renderer never receives `components` at all — `publicpagecontroller` hands `public-html.blade.php` only `title, seometa, pagefavicon, html, css, head`. so the two never collide. a bespoke page can carry `components[]` as **pure binding declarations** — invisible to rendering, fully visible to the data controller: proven live: the page served raw html with zero spa markers, and `/api/v1/public/pages/<slug>/data/cases` moved from `component_not_found` (404) to `gate_required` (401) — binding found, dataset resolved, viewer scope demanded. **this got simpler on 2026-08-21 (sdr-10 / sdr-11).** an earlier version of this playbook said you must borrow `datatable` and hand-author its `columns`. **no longer true.** `datatable` now declares `datasetslug`, and the binding endpoint emits `datasetmeta.fields[]` — so the component derives its own columns from the schema. verified anonymously against `/p/sdr-binding-proof`, whose entire component is: the server-rendered payload came back with **6 rows injected, `columns` not authored**, and `datasetmeta.fields = [{key:name,label:"company",type:text}, …]` — headers derived from the schema's own labels, in the first paint, with no client fetch. parse the `data-page` attribute to check this; grepping the html gives a false negative because the payload is escaped. note the security shape while you are here: `datasetfieldmeta()` takes the hidden-key list as a **required** argument, so the same keys that strip `visibility=private|phi` values from the rows also strip their labels and types. emitting the labels would hand a client role the phi schema it was just denied. **one catch remains.** bound reads are **authed-first** — anonymous callers get `gate_required`; the public lane (`schema.public` + signed token) is not built. a public dashboard cannot show bound rows yet. **so choose the lane on rendering, not on data:** bespoke for full design control, component lane when you want genesis components rendered for you. both can bind. ### landing gotchas — each of these has cost a real page - **`json_content` must be an object, not a json string.** round-tripping it to a string fails with the misleading `the json content must be an array.` check the committed shape with `git show head:pages/<slug>.json` rather than guessing at the validator. - **`iris pages push` reads `./pages` from the cwd.** a persisted `cd` into fl-iris-api reads its stale shadow `pages/` and silently ships an old page over the live one. verify with `iris pages get`, never by grepping the served html. - **`iris pages create` is broken** (sitefooter.copyright) — clone with `iris pages duplicate`. - **customhtml has no isolation.** it injects via `v-html`, so namespace **every** selector (`.myapp h2`, never bare `h2`) or it leaks into the host page. - **theme rules invert between the two lanes — this cost a shipped page.** a **customhtml block inside a composable page** has real host chrome: switch on `html.dark`, never `prefers-color-scheme` (which would render dark inside a light page), and never paint its own `background` or it becomes a slab floating on the page ground. a **standalone `render_mode: html` page has no host — it is the document.** verified in the browser: `html`, `body` and the wrapper all compute to `rgba(0,0,0,0)`, and the only dark rules present are the page's own. so it **must** paint its own ground and **must** honour `prefers-color-scheme`, because nothing will ever set `html.dark` for it. keep the `[data-theme]` stamps as overrides for if a host toggle is added later. - **check the slug is free before you clone.** `iris pages duplicate --slug <x>` can report a validation error while `push` still writes to an existing page of that name — which silently replaces a live page. `iris pages get <slug>` first; if it returns anything, pick another slug. recovery is `git show head:pages/<slug>.json > pages/<slug>.json && iris pages push <slug> --publish`, which only works if the page was committed. - **no webfont cdns.** the genesis csp blocks them and it falls back to arial silently. build stacks from faces that ship on macos and windows, or inline a data uri. (artifacts may use google fonts; genesis pages may not.) ## stage 3 — plug the backend with the genesis sdk one script tag. **pin the version.** the unversioned `/js/iris-sdk.js` sits behind cloudflare at `max-age=14400`, so a change takes up to four hours to reach a browser — that is how a fix was found still serving the old body from a container demonstrably running the new one. **never inline the sdk**: `script-src` is `'self' 'unsafe-inline'` shipped *report-only*, and the stated intent is to enforce it and strip `'unsafe-inline'` via nonces. anything pasted inline stops running that day; `/js/` survives. ### why it needs no credential — and must never be given one the csp is `connect-src 'self'`. a page can only reach its own origin. that is the enabler, not the limit: the visitor's `atlas_session` cookie is **first-party** on that origin, so it rides along on its own, and every endpoint the sdk calls is a same-origin route already gated server-side. this is why `iris atlas:datasets api <slug>` is the wrong reach from a browser — it hands you a cross-origin url (blocked) *and* an operator bearer key (a leak). ### the surface `whoami()` returns `null` when signed out rather than throwing — a public page with no visitor is the normal case, not an error. ### reading bound rows **verified live 2026-08-21.** `pagedatasetcontroller` is deployed and routed: it is same-origin, so it works through the sdk **today**, with no sdk change: > **the `genesis-sdk` how-to is stale on this point.** it says "no atlas dataset reads — yet" > and tracks it as sdk-2. the controller and both routes exist and answer; a probe returns > `component_not_found` (a *semantic* 404 from inside the controller — route resolved, page and > owner resolved) rather than a routing 404. sdk-2 is a thin wrapper over a working route, not a > backend build. fix the how-to before someone else rebuilds what is already there. the binding is read **from the page**, never from the client, so a request cannot widen scope to a dataset the page is not bound to. **never build an `/atlas/datasets/{slug}` proxy** — the component lane addresses data by *binding id*, never by dataset slug, precisely so a visitor cannot pivot tenants by editing a url. a slug proxy throws that property away. ### errors every rejection is an `iriserror` with `status`, a flattened `fields` map, `isgate`, `isvalidation`. fl-api reports validation in two different shapes (`errors` and `validation_errors`); both are flattened so a page only learns one. ### what the sdk deliberately does not do **no authorization decisions.** it asks; the server answers. a permission check written in page javascript is decoration over a server rule — and if the rule is missing, the decoration is a hole. if you find yourself writing `if (user.role === 'admin')` in the page, the rule belongs on the server and is probably absent. ## stage 4 — verify, and mean it - **open it in a browser.** grepping strings out of the served html is not verification. point 10 of the design audit exists because this failed in production. - beware the instrument: a black screenshot with `document.visibilitystate === 'hidden'` is a backgrounded window, not a broken page. run a known-good control before calling anything broken. - score the 10-point audit at `/p/design-philosophy-and-page-audit`. **9–10 ship · 6–8 revise · 0–5 redesign.** check 01 is the predictor: *could this design move to a different subject unchanged?* if yes it is a template and local fixes will not rescue it. - check both themes at token level and confirm no horizontal overflow. - confirm the data is really scoped — sign out and reload. a gated region that still renders rows is a hole, not a feature. --- ## why this order works the reason the inversion is safe is that **authorization never lives in the ui.** you can design the whole interface against real-looking content without making a single security decision, because every decision is already made server-side and the page cannot override it. the worst case for a wrong mockup is a wrong-looking page, not a leak. that is also the limit. if a region needs a rule that does not exist server-side yet, stage 3 will not save you — write the rule first, then bind. ## related `iris how-to view genesis-sdk` · `iris how-to view bespoke` · `iris how-to view genesis-design-standard` · `/p/genesis-sdk-case-study` · `/p/iris-sdk-check`

entries.name: run-tests
entries.describe: Run the test suite, analyze failures, fix broken tests, and increase coverage. Pass a mode (eco/quick/standard/full) or specific area (frontend/cypress/billing) as argument.
entries.haystack: run-tests run the test suite, analyze failures, fix broken tests, and increase coverage. pass a mode (eco/quick/standard/full) or specific area (frontend/cypress/billing) as argument. --- name: run-tests description: run the test suite, analyze failures, fix broken tests, and increase coverage. pass a mode (eco/quick/standard/full) or specific area (frontend/cypress/billing) as argument. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- # run tests — freelabel ecosystem test maintenance run tests, diagnose failures, fix broken code, and increase test coverage across the freelabel platform. ## arguments `$arguments` — what to run. examples: - `/run-tests` — run eco mode (free, fast) and fix any failures - `/run-tests full` — run the full suite ($2-3 in ai costs) - `/run-tests quick` — run quick mode (~$0.02) - `/run-tests eco` — run eco mode only (unit tests, $0) - `/run-tests local` — run local ollama llm tests ($0, tests agent framework with local models) - `/run-tests eval` — run v6 ai quality evals only (~$0.10-0.30, real llm calls) - `/run-tests frontend` — run frontend jest + custom test runner - `/run-tests cypress` — run cypress prod-ready e2e tests - `/run-tests billing` — run only the billinglogictest - `/run-tests fix` — run eco, find all failures, fix them - `/run-tests coverage` — analyze what's untested, suggest new tests - `/run-tests health` — run health checks only ## platform architecture (v6 active) **v6 is the active system. v4 and v5 are deprecated.** | system | container | status | what it covers | |--------|-----------|--------|----------------| | **v6** | fl-iris-api | **active** | yaml-driven tool registry, react loop, multi-channel messaging | | **core** | fl-api | **active** | billing, stripe, rag, outreach (shared platform logic) | | v4 | fl-api | deprecated | legacy intent routing (opt-in only) | | v5 | fl-iris-api | deprecated | legacy neuron nodes (opt-in only) | ### v6 key components - **systemtoolsloader** — loads tools from `config/system-tools.yaml` - **v6toolregistry** — registers, validates, and health-checks tools - **reactloopservice** — react reasoning loop with tool summarization - **channeladapters** — discord, telegram, email, webhook messaging - **doomloopdetector** — prevents infinite react cycles ## testing strategy (10:1 unit-to-e2e ratio) follow a **layered pyramid** approach for maximum coverage with minimum cost: ### layer 1: pure unit tests (10x priority — instant, $0) - isolate **atomic composable functions** first - each utility, service method, or data transform gets its own focused test - runs in ~30ms per suite — zero browser, zero docker, zero ai calls - **backend**: phpunit in `tests/unit/` — pure logic, no db, no http - **frontend**: custom test runner in `fl-elon-web-ui/tests/unit/` — zero-dependency node.js - example: domainnavigationservice, billinglogic, link detection, credit balance math ### layer 2: feature/integration tests (moderate cost) - test service interactions with mocked dependencies - uses `databasetransactions` trait for db isolation - validates api endpoints with `actingas($user, 'api')` - **backend**: phpunit in `tests/feature/` — mocked services, real db ### layer 3: e2e smoke tests (1x priority — expensive, slow) - **one cypress smoke test per feature** — not comprehensive e2e - only validates critical user paths (login, search, signup) - runs in 2+ minutes per spec vs 30ms for unit tests - use sparingly — high cost, low incremental value over unit tests **principle**: if a unit test can catch the bug, don't write an e2e test for it. ## test modes the orchestrator at `fl-docker-dev/run-tests.sh` supports two arguments: ### mode (1st argument) | mode | cost | what runs | |------|------|-----------| | eco | $0 | pure unit tests (billinglogic, outreach, cloudfile rag, workflow progress, stripe, ollama routing) + v6 unit tests | | local | $0 | ollama routing unit tests + live ollama connectivity, model discovery, prompt, full pipeline | | quick | ~$0.02 | units + mocked feature tests + eval:v6 dry-run wiring check | | standard | ~$0.20 | above + real e2e with 5-10 ai calls + eval:v6 quick quality evals | | full | ~$2-3 | everything: 150-230 ai calls, all integrations, e2e workflows + eval:v6 full with regression | | eval | ~$0.10-0.30 | v6 ai quality evals only — workflow_engine + quality_loops + agent_eval (quick cases, real llm) | ### system selector (2nd argument) | system | what runs | |--------|-----------| | `v6` (default) | v6 tests + core business logic | | `core` | core business logic only (billing, stripe, rag, outreach) | | `v4` | legacy v4 intent routing tests (deprecated) | | `v5` | legacy v5 neuron node tests (deprecated) | | `legacy` | v4 + v5 together (deprecated) | | `all` | everything: v6 + v4 + v5 + core | ### usage examples ## steps ### 1. determine what to run parse `$arguments` to decide the scope: | argument | action | |----------|--------| | (empty) or `eco` | run eco mode backend tests (core + v6) | | `local` | run local ollama llm tests (routing + connectivity + pipeline) | | `quick` | run quick mode backend tests + eval:v6 dry-run | | `standard` | run standard mode backend tests + eval:v6 quick quality evals | | `full` | run full mode backend tests + eval:v6 full with regression compare | | `eval` | run v6 ai quality evals only (workflow_engine + quality_loops + agent_eval, quick cases) | | `frontend` | run frontend jest + custom test runner | | `cypress` | run cypress prod-ready tests | | `billing` | run billinglogictest only | | `health` | run health check only | | `fix` | run eco, analyze all failures, then fix them | | `coverage` | analyze coverage gaps and suggest new tests | | `all` | run eco backend + frontend + cypress | ### 2. run the appropriate tests **backend tests** (run from project root `/users/alexmayo/sites/freelabel`): **frontend tests** (run from project root): **cypress tests** (run from frontend directory, not in docker): important: use the `timeout` parameter on bash calls for test commands. backend eco/quick: 300000ms (5 min). standard: 600000ms (10 min). full: 600000ms. frontend: 120000ms. cypress: 300000ms. ### 3. parse the output look for these patterns in test output: **phpunit/pest (backend)**: - `tests: x, assertions: y` — total count - `pass` / `fail` — individual test result - `✓` / `✗` — pass/fail indicators - `failures!` — summary line if any failed - `ok (x tests, y assertions)` — all passed **custom frontend runner**: - `results: x/y passed` — summary - `all tests passed!` or `some tests failed` — overall status **cypress**: - `all specs passed!` or specific failure messages - `passing: x`, `failing: y` ### 4. on failure — diagnose and fix when tests fail: 1. **read the failure output carefully** — identify which test failed and the error message 2. **read the test file** to understand what it expects 3. **read the source code** being tested to find the bug 4. **determine root cause**: is the test wrong, or is the source code wrong? - if test expectations are outdated (e.g., price changed from $250 to $350), update the test - if source code has a bug, fix the source code - if a service is unreachable (docker not running, api down), report it — don't try to fix infrastructure 5. **make the fix** using edit tool 6. **re-run only the failing test** to verify the fix before running the full suite again 7. **run eslint fix** if you edited any vue files: `cd /users/alexmayo/sites/freelabel/fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui && npm run fix-file <path>` ### 5. coverage analysis (if `coverage` argument) when asked to analyze coverage, follow the **10:1 unit-to-e2e** principle: 1. **read `fl-docker-dev/run-tests.sh`** to understand what's already tested 2. **scan for untested areas** — prioritize unit-testable logic: - grepping for service classes in `fl-iris-api/app/services/v6/` that have no corresponding test - checking `fl-api/app/services/` for untested platform services - reviewing `fl-elon-web-ui/utils/` and composable functions without unit tests - checking `fl-elon-web-ui/components/` for components with complex logic but no tests 3. **prioritize by risk**: billing, payments, auth, and data integrity tests are highest priority 4. **prefer unit tests over e2e**: for every new feature, suggest 10 unit tests before 1 cypress test 5. **suggest specific test files to create** with descriptions of what each should test 6. **for v6 backend tests**: follow existing patterns in `fl-iris-api/tests/feature/`: - unit tests: `fl-iris-api/tests/unit/` — pure logic, no db - feature tests: `fl-iris-api/tests/feature/` — with db, use `databasetransactions` trait - v6-specific: `fl-iris-api/tests/feature/v6/` — react loop, channels, tool registry 7. **for core backend tests**: follow patterns in `fl-api/tests/unit/`: - unit tests: `fl-api/tests/unit/` — pure logic, no db - feature tests: `fl-api/tests/feature/` — with db, use `databasetransactions` trait - use `actingas($user, 'api')` for auth, never token headers 8. **for frontend tests**: follow the custom runner pattern (preferred over jest for new tests): - create in `fl-elon-web-ui/tests/unit/` or `tests/integration/` - use `const { testrunner, assert } = require('../../test-runner')` - export nothing, call `runner.run()` at the end - target: atomic composable functions, utility methods, data transforms 9. **for cypress tests**: only for critical smoke tests in `cypress/e2e/prod-ready/` - one smoke test per major feature, not comprehensive e2e coverage ## key test files reference ### v6 backend (fl-iris-api) — active system | test file | what it tests | |-----------|--------------| | `tests/feature/v6toolregistryhealthchecktest.php` | tool registry health checks, yaml integration | | `tests/feature/v6toolregistryyamldriventest.php` | yaml-driven tool execution (40+ tests) | | `tests/feature/v6/reactloopbroadcasttest.php` | react loop broadcast & tool summarization | | `tests/feature/v6/multichannelmessagingtest.php` | discord, telegram, email, webhook channel adapters | | `tests/feature/userscopedragsearchtest.php` | rag with v6 user scoping | | `tests/feature/businesscontextintegrationtest.php` | business context integration | | `tests/feature/ollamaprovidertest.php` | ollama provider switching, config, multi-agent (14 tests) | ### core business logic (fl-api) — platform-wide | test file | what it tests | |-----------|--------------| | `tests/unit/billinglogictest.php` | package pricing, billing status transitions, retry logic | | `tests/unit/outreachservicetest.php` | lead outreach service logic | | `tests/unit/cloudfileragtest.php` | cloudfile rag vector integration | | `tests/unit/workflowprogresstest.php` | workflow progress calculations | | `tests/unit/userupgradestripeservicetest.php` | stripe upgrade/downgrade logic | | `tests/unit/ollamaroutingtest.php` | aimodelrouter ollama pattern detection, config routing, nano bypass | ### artisan commands (fl-api) | command | what it tests | |---------|--------------| | `php artisan test:ollama` | full ollama pipeline: connectivity, discovery, prompt, routing | | `php artisan test:ollama --quick` | connection check + single prompt only | | `php artisan test:ollama --discover-models` | list available ollama models | | `php artisan test:ollama --model=llama3.2` | test specific model | | `php artisan test:ollama --json` | json output for ci/cd | ### frontend (fl-elon-web-ui) — custom test runner (preferred) | test file | what it tests | |-----------|--------------| | `tests/unit/linkdetection.test.js` | link detection and html generation | | `tests/unit/multistepprogressaccordions.test.js` | accordion ui state | | `tests/unit/multiagentchat.test.js` | multi-agent chat logic | | `tests/unit/communityinbox.test.js` | community messaging | | `tests/unit/leaddataintegrity.test.js` | lead data validation | | `tests/unit/paygcreditbalance.test.js` | payg credit tracking | | `tests/unit/billingservice.retrypayment.test.js` | payment retry logic | | `tests/unit/userbillingdashboard.billingstatus.test.js` | billing status detection | | `tests/unit/userbillingdashboard.handlebillingaction.test.js` | action routing | ### cypress (e2e smoke tests — use sparingly) | test file | what it tests | |-----------|--------------| | `cypress/e2e/prod-ready/discover-ui.cy.js` | discover page ui | | `cypress/e2e/prod-ready/elon-search-functionality.cy.js` | search feature | | `cypress/e2e/prod-ready/home-cta-signup-upgrade.cy.js` | signup/upgrade ctas | | `cypress/e2e/prod-ready/iris-dashboard-integrity.cy.js` | iris dashboard | ## important notes - **always start with eco mode** — it's free and catches logic regressions instantly - **v6 is the default system** — all modes run v6 + core unless you pass a system selector - **v4/v5 are deprecated** — only run with `legacy`, `v4`, `v5`, or `all` system selectors - **v6 tests run in fl-iris-api container** — check it's running: `docker compose ps | grep iris-api` - **core tests run in fl-api container** — check it's running: `docker compose ps | grep fl-api` - **prefer unit tests over e2e** — 10 unit tests for every 1 cypress test; unit tests run in ~30ms, cypress in 2+ minutes - **use local mode to test ollama** — `./run-tests.sh local` validates agent framework routing with local llms at $0 cost. requires ollama running (`ollama serve`). gracefully skips live tests if ollama is unavailable. - **optional ollama docker container** — start with `docker compose --profile local-ai up ollama`, then pull models: `docker compose exec ollama ollama pull llama3.2` - **never skip reading test output** — the error messages tell you exactly what's wrong - **ai model tests cost money** — only run standard/full when you need to validate ai integration - **never use gpt-3.5-turbo in tests** — only gpt-4.1-nano, gpt-5-nano, or gpt-4o-mini - **use `$api` not `$axios`** for authenticated api calls in any test that hits the backend - **never use `this.$toast`** — use messagesutility mixin from `utils/mixins/messages.js` - **run eslint after editing vue files** — `npm run fix-file <path>` - **for billing tests**: the billinglogictest validates package pricing math — if prices change in the codebase, update the test assertions to match

entries.name: run-the-graph-pass
entries.describe: Run the three seams over the knowledge graph — discover what is not linked, audit what is, and ask the questions only a human can settle. Proposes edges from concrete evidence, caps the review queue, applies nothing until a person says so, and verifies every write by reading it back. Written after a real pass that moved a 156-node graph from 88% isolated to 79%.
entries.haystack: run-the-graph-pass run the three seams over the knowledge graph — discover what is not linked, audit what is, and ask the questions only a human can settle. proposes edges from concrete evidence, caps the review queue, applies nothing until a person says so, and verifies every write by reading it back. written after a real pass that moved a 156-node graph from 88% isolated to 79%. --- name: run-the-graph-pass description: run the three seams over the knowledge graph — discover what is not linked, audit what is, and ask the questions only a human can settle. proposes edges from concrete evidence, caps the review queue, applies nothing until a person says so, and verifies every write by reading it back. written after a real pass that moved a 156-node graph from 88% isolated to 79%. version: 2 args: scope: type: string required: false default: all description: "all, or a bloq id to scope the pass to that node and its 1-hop neighbours." cap: type: number required: false default: 20 description: maximum proposals to emit in one run. the limit is review bandwidth, not compute. on-error: continue timeout: 900 --- # run the graph pass a graph nobody links is a graph nobody can traverse, and a link nobody checked is worse than no link. this runs the three seams in order, each feeding the next. **the rule the whole playbook exists to enforce: seam 1 proposes, a human disposes, and every applied edge is verified by reading it back.** ## steps ### step:measure census the graph, and check your instrument before you trust it ### step:seam1 discover what is not linked — propose, apply nothing ### step:review hand the proposals to a human ### step:apply apply what was accepted — then read it back ### step:seam2 audit the edges that already exist ### step:seam3 comprehend, then ask — and write canon ### step:diary record what the pass got wrong
