entries.name: seo-management
entries.describe: Diagnose, fix, and monitor SEO health across the Freelabel platform. Audit bot blocking, indexing issues, robots.txt, Core Web Vitals, meta tags, sitemaps, and Google Search Console problems. Pass an action as argument (e.g., "audit", "fix-403s", "check-robots", "check-meta", "check-vitals", "sitemap", "status").
entries.haystack: seo-management diagnose, fix, and monitor seo health across the freelabel platform. audit bot blocking, indexing issues, robots.txt, core web vitals, meta tags, sitemaps, and google search console problems. pass an action as argument (e.g., "audit", "fix-403s", "check-robots", "check-meta", "check-vitals", "sitemap", "status"). --- name: seo-management description: diagnose, fix, and monitor seo health across the freelabel platform. audit bot blocking, indexing issues, robots.txt, core web vitals, meta tags, sitemaps, and google search console problems. pass an action as argument (e.g., "audit", "fix-403s", "check-robots", "check-meta", "check-vitals", "sitemap", "status"). allowed-tools: - read - bash - grep - glob - edit - agent - webfetch - websearch --- # seo management — search engine optimization for freelabel manage seo health across the freelabel platform: fl-elon-web-ui (the.freelabel.net), fl-iris-api (freelabel.net), and marketing-sites-ui (web.freelabel.net). ## arguments `$arguments` — action to perform. examples: - `/seo-management audit` — full seo audit (bot blocking, meta tags, robots.txt, sitemap, redirects, lcp) - `/seo-management fix-403s` — find and fix bot-blocking causing 403 errors to googlebot - `/seo-management check-robots` — audit all robots.txt files across services - `/seo-management check-meta` — scan for noindex, nofollow, missing meta tags, bad canonicals - `/seo-management check-vitals` — audit core web vitals (lcp, cls, inp) blockers - `/seo-management check-redirects` — find broken redirect chains, wrong redirect targets - `/seo-management sitemap` — check sitemap configuration and coverage - `/seo-management status` — quick health check of seo-critical systems - `/seo-management add-bot <name>` — add a bot to the blocklist - `/seo-management remove-bot <name>` — remove a bot from the blocklist --- ## architecture — where seo lives ### bot blocking (single source of truth) - **middleware**: `fl-elon-web-ui/middleware/bot-blocker.js` - runs server-side on `/content/*` routes only - uses explicit blocklist approach (block only known bad bots, allow everything else) - never use broad regex like `/bot|crawl|spider/` — this catches legitimate crawlers - page-level asyncdata should not duplicate bot detection ### robots.txt (three locations) 1. **fl-elon-web-ui** (the.freelabel.net): `servermiddleware/robots.js` — dynamic, served by express middleware 2. **fl-iris-api** (freelabel.net): `public/robots.txt` — static file 3. **marketing-sites-ui** (web.freelabel.net): `public/robots.txt` — static file (if exists) **rules:** - googlebot, googlebot-image, googlebot-video, storebot-google, bingbot, applebot, duckduckbot → `allow: /` with no crawl-delay - ai scrapers (gptbot, ccbot, claudebot, bytespider) → `disallow: /` - seo scrapers (ahrefsbot, semrushbot, mj12bot, dotbot, blexbot) → `disallow: /` - all others → `allow: /` with `crawl-delay: 5` - always include: `sitemap: ### content url routing - `freelabel.net/content/*` → 301 redirect to `the.freelabel.net/content/*` (via iris-api redirectfromrootdomain middleware) - content pages are rendered by `fl-elon-web-ui` on `the.freelabel.net`, not `web.freelabel.net` - canonical urls should always be ` ### meta tags - artist pages: `fl-elon-web-ui/pages/content/spotify/artist/_id.vue` — head() method - track pages: `fl-elon-web-ui/pages/content/spotify/track/_id.vue` — head() method - album pages: `fl-elon-web-ui/pages/content/spotify/album/_id.vue` — head() method - **never** use `noindex` on content pages — creates chicken-and-egg problem (no index → no views → stays noindex) - always include: title, description, og:title, og:description, og:image, canonical, robots ### ssr performance (core web vitals / lcp) - **ssr cache**: `nuxt.config.js` render.bundlerenderer.cache — lru cache for rendered pages - current: 10k pages max, 1-hour ttl - must be large enough for crawler volume (328k+ indexed pages) - **api timeout**: asyncdata fetches should use 5s timeout (not 2s) — crawlers need complete html - **images**: hero images need `fetchpriority="high"` + width/height. below-fold images need `loading="lazy"` - **font awesome**: loaded from cdn, render-blocking — consider preload or self-hosting --- ## key files ### bot blocking - `fl-elon-web-ui/middleware/bot-blocker.js` — the bot blocker (only place bot decisions happen) ### robots.txt - `fl-elon-web-ui/servermiddleware/robots.js` — dynamic robots.txt for the.freelabel.net - `fl-iris-api/public/robots.txt` — static robots.txt for freelabel.net ### content pages (seo-critical templates) - `fl-elon-web-ui/pages/content/spotify/artist/_id.vue` — artist pages (~328k indexed) - `fl-elon-web-ui/pages/content/spotify/track/_id.vue` — track pages - `fl-elon-web-ui/pages/content/spotify/album/_id.vue` — album pages ### redirects - `fl-iris-api/app/http/middleware/redirectfromrootdomain.php` — freelabel.net → the.freelabel.net routing ### sitemap - `fl-elon-web-ui/servermiddleware/sitemap.js` — dynamic sitemap generation ### ssr config - `fl-elon-web-ui/nuxt.config.js` — ssr cache, server middleware, render config --- ## audit checklist when running `/seo-management audit`, check all of the following: ### 1. bot blocking audit ### 2. robots.txt audit ### 3. meta tags audit ### 4. redirect audit ### 5. core web vitals audit ### 6. sitemap audit --- ## blocked bots (current list) these bots are blocked in `middleware/bot-blocker.js`: | bot | reason | |-----|--------| | ahrefsbot | seo tool scraper | | semrushbot | seo tool scraper | | mj12bot | majestic seo scraper | | dotbot | moz seo scraper | | blexbot | webmeup scraper | | dataforseo | seo data scraper | | bytespider | tiktok aggressive scraper | | petalbot | huawei aggressive scraper | | gptbot | openai content scraper | | ccbot | common crawl (high volume) | | claudebot | anthropic content scraper | | scrapy | python scraping framework | | httrack | website copier | | webcopier | website copier | | offline explorer | website copier | ### adding a new bot to block 1. add the bot name (lowercase) to the `maliciousbots` array in `middleware/bot-blocker.js` 2. add a `user-agent: botname` + `disallow: /` entry to both robots.txt files 3. commit and deploy ### removing a bot from block 1. remove from `maliciousbots` array in `middleware/bot-blocker.js` 2. remove from both robots.txt files 3. commit and deploy --- ## critical rules 1. **never use broad bot-detection regex** — patterns like `/bot|crawl|spider/` catch googlebot, bingbot, etc. 2. **never add noindex to content pages** — creates chicken-and-egg (no index → no traffic → stays noindex) 3. **content urls always redirect to the.freelabel.net** — not web.freelabel.net 4. **googlebot must never have a crawl-delay** — they ignore it, but it signals you don't want crawling 5. **ssr timeout must be >= 5s** — crawlers need complete html, not a javascript skeleton 6. **ssr cache should be as large as memory allows** — 10k+ pages with 1hr+ ttl 7. **all images below the fold must have loading="lazy"** — prevents unnecessary bandwidth 8. **hero/lcp images must have fetchpriority="high" + width + height** — tells browser what to prioritize --- ## google search console quick reference after deploying seo fixes, monitor: - **coverage report**: 403 count should drop within 7-14 days - **request indexing**: manually request re-crawl of high-value urls - **core web vitals**: lcp should improve within 28 days (crux data cycle) - **sitemap**: submit at ` if not done test with googlebot Catches the silent failure where the resolver authorizes a publish and upload-post then drops it. Read-only by default; --action=fix reconciles.
entries.haystack: social-health health sweep for the social publishing layer — plan capacity, expired logins, and the drift between what config/uploadpost.php claims and what upload-post actually holds. catches the silent failure where the resolver authorizes a publish and upload-post then drops it. read-only by default; --action=fix reconciles. --- name: social-health description: health sweep for the social publishing layer — plan capacity, expired logins, and the drift between what config/uploadpost.php claims and what upload-post actually holds. catches the silent failure where the resolver authorizes a publish and upload-post then drops it. read-only by default; --action=fix reconciles. version: 2 args: action: type: string required: false default: report enum: [report, fix] description: report = show drift only, fix = also run social:connect --sync --all to reconcile user_id: type: number required: false default: 193 description: the account that owns the brands being checked service: type: string required: false default: fl-api description: railway service to run against on-error: continue timeout: 600 --- # social publishing health sweep three things go wrong in this layer and **all three look like success**. nothing throws, the resolver returns a profile, the publish call succeeds — and no post appears. 1. **plan capacity.** profiles are what upload-post bills and caps. run out and the next tenant brand cannot be connected at all. 2. **expired logins.** `reauth_required` makes upload-post silently drop every post to that account. this is how clips stopped reaching @thediscoverpage_ for days. 3. **config-vs-upstream drift.** `config/uploadpost.php` is aspirational. it has claimed profiles that do not exist (`@capital.collective`), profile names that are wrong (`@heyiris.io` is really `heyirisio`), and platforms nobody ever linked (tiktok, on every profile). each false row makes the resolver say *yes* to a publish that then goes nowhere. drift is the dangerous one, because it is the only failure with **no error anywhere** — not in our logs, not in upload-post's response. ## why this reads the vendor and the database separately the whole point is to compare two sources that are each individually plausible. reading only our `integrations` rows tells you what we *think* is connected. reading only upload-post tells you what *is* connected but not what we would route to it. the gap between them is the bug. ## steps ### step:capacity plan capacity — can we onboard another brand? ### step:connections what the database thinks this account can publish as ### step:expired expired logins that silently drop every post ### step:drift compare config's claims against what upload-post actually holds ### step:reconcile reconcile the database against upstream reality

entries.name: social-onboard-brand
entries.describe: Onboard a tenant brand onto the social publishing layer — check plan capacity, mint the branded connect link where they attach their OWN Instagram/TikTok/X, then sync what they linked into ownership rows and verify the resolver can route it. The connect step needs a human; this playbook is the two halves either side of it.
entries.haystack: social-onboard-brand onboard a tenant brand onto the social publishing layer — check plan capacity, mint the branded connect link where they attach their own instagram/tiktok/x, then sync what they linked into ownership rows and verify the resolver can route it. the connect step needs a human; this playbook is the two halves either side of it. --- name: social-onboard-brand description: onboard a tenant brand onto the social publishing layer — check plan capacity, mint the branded connect link where they attach their own instagram/tiktok/x, then sync what they linked into ownership rows and verify the resolver can route it. the connect step needs a human; this playbook is the two halves either side of it. version: 2 args: brand: type: string required: true description: brand slug to onboard (must already exist and be owned by user_id) stage: type: string required: false default: connect enum: [connect, finish] description: connect = mint the link and stop; finish = sync what they linked and verify user_id: type: number required: false default: 193 description: the account that owns the brand redirect: type: string required: false default: "" description: url to send the tenant back to after they finish linking logo: type: string required: false default: "" description: logo url to brand the linking page service: type: string required: false default: fl-api description: railway service to run against on-error: continue timeout: 600 --- # onboard a brand onto social publishing run this in **two passes** with a human in between. `--stage=connect` mints the link; the tenant opens it and attaches their own accounts; `--stage=finish` writes what they attached into ownership rows. ## why the second pass is not optional `socialaccountresolver` reads ownership from `integrations` rows. upload-post knows the tenant linked their instagram; **we do not**, until sync runs. skip `finish` and you get an account that publishes perfectly upstream and is invisible everywhere authorization is decided — connected to everyone except the code that decides who may post. ## capacity is a hard wall, not a warning profiles are the billed and capped unit: 2 on free, 5 on basic, 25 on professional, 75 on advanced, 225 on business. if the plan is full the connect step returns a 409 and there is no way around it except upgrading. check first so you find out before the tenant does. ## steps ### step:capacity is there room for another profile? ### step:connect mint the link the tenant opens ### step:sync pull what they actually linked into ownership rows ### step:verify prove the resolver can actually route a post

entries.name: som-outreach
entries.describe: Manage SOM outreach campaigns — view all campaigns at a glance, edit scripts, update strategies, manage leads, run batches, and monitor performance. Pass an action as argument (e.g., "overview", "edit creators", "update-script", "leads", "run", "status").
entries.haystack: som-outreach manage som outreach campaigns — view all campaigns at a glance, edit scripts, update strategies, manage leads, run batches, and monitor performance. pass an action as argument (e.g., "overview", "edit creators", "update-script", "leads", "run", "status"). --- name: som-outreach description: manage som outreach campaigns — view all campaigns at a glance, edit scripts, update strategies, manage leads, run batches, and monitor performance. pass an action as argument (e.g., "overview", "edit creators", "update-script", "leads", "run", "status"). allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- # som outreach — sales outreach machine campaign manager manage the som outreach campaigns that power automated instagram dm outreach. view strategies, edit scripts, manage leads, run batches, and monitor results — all from the cli. ## arguments `$arguments` — action and parameters. examples: - `/som-outreach overview` — show all campaigns at a glance - `/som-outreach overview -s` — with full script text - `/som-outreach edit creators` — edit creator outreach scripts inline - `/som-outreach update-script creators "new script text here"` — update step 1 script directly - `/som-outreach leads creators` — show lead stats for creators board - `/som-outreach run` — trigger a full som batch (all active campaigns) - `/som-outreach run creators` — run just creators campaign - `/som-outreach status` — check latest batch results - `/som-outreach strategies` — list all strategy templates across boards --- ## campaign registry the live registry is resolved by `tests/e2e/som-config.js` via **three-tier resolution**: (1) the disk cache `.som-campaigns-cache.json` next to the config (written by `npm run som:sync` from `/api/v1/som/campaigns`), else (2) the inline baked-in defaults. **the cache wins when present** — the bridge daemon copy (`fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/som/`) has its own cache, so the daemon and a local `tests/e2e/` run can resolve differently. when in doubt, read the cache file, not the inline table. `getresolutionsource()` tells you which one is live. current campaigns (from the live cache): | campaign | board | ig account | strategy | audience | |----------|-------|------------|----------|----------| | creators | 80 | @thediscoverpage_ | creator outreach \| v1 (id:18) | artists, creators, hip-hop culture | | courses | 38 | @heyiris.io | ai course \| v3 | ai builders, tech founders | | beatbox | 224 | @thebeatbox__ | dj outreach \| v2 | djs, producers, beatmakers | | mayo | 176 | @hourdemayo | mayo outreach \| v2 | — | | freelabelnet | 80 | @freelabelnet | creator outreach \| v1 | creators (freelabelnet-branded) | | venues | 292 | @freelabelnet | venue partnership \| v1 | cafes, venues, event spaces | | atxbeauty | 283 | @atxbeautylab.lisa | beauty & wellness outreach \| v1 | beauty/wellness | | gooddeals | 302 | (linkedin) | linkedin founder outreach \| v1 | founders | | saddlepass | 337 | (linkedin) | equestrian bdr \| v1 | equestrian | > **ffat live-event invite** (first friday art trail, @freelabelnet): strategy `artist outreach | > ffat v1` — the canonical record is **strategy 35 on board 355**, with a same-named copy (**id 47**) > on **board 80** so it can be sent to the creators audience. step-1 dm names the event + date > in-body; bump the date here when the event changes. board 355's leads are exhausted — send to > board 80. ### ⚠️ strategies are matched by name, scoped to the target board `batch-with-login.spec.ts` fetches `/bloqs/{board_id}/outreach-strategy-templates` and picks the template whose `.name === strategy_name`. a strategy template only exists on the board it was created on — running `strategy="x"` against a board that has no template named exactly `x` silently won't match. to reuse a script across boards (e.g. the ffat invite on creators board 80), **create a copy on that board**, don't just reference the original. ### force all sends from one instagram account (`ig=` override) to make every campaign in a batch send from a single account (e.g. consolidate to @freelabelnet): `som.js` aliases `ig=` → `ig_account`; `som-all.js` passes it through to every campaign. this is a **runtime override** — it does not change `som-config.js`. for a durable change, edit `igaccount` in both `som-config.js` inline defaults **and** the cache json (both the `tests/e2e/` and bridge copies), since the cache wins. the sending account needs a valid session file `instagram-auth-<account>.json` in `tests/e2e/` (the bridge copies are stubs) — stale sessions force a re-login. ## cli commands ### php cli (from `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/`) ### typescript cli (iris binary — works from anywhere) --- ## how outreach scripts work each campaign has a **strategy template** with **steps**. the som batch (`npm run som:all`) applies the strategy to each lead and executes step by step: ### script flow 1. **apply strategy** → creates steps on the lead (step 1: ig dm, step 2: follow-up, etc.) 2. **generate message** → uses the step's `instructions` as the base script 3. **ai variation** → the `ai_prompt` field tells the ai how to personalize per lead (reference their bio, genre, etc.) 4. **send dm** → opens their instagram profile, pastes the varied message, sends ### script fields - **`instructions`** — the base dm/email text. merge fields: `{first_name}`, `{name}`, `{company}`, `{email}`, `{instagram}` - **`ai_prompt`** — instructions for the ai to personalize the script per lead. should specify: what to reference from their profile, tone, length limit, what not to include (urls, income claims) - **`delay_hours`** — hours to wait before this step (0 = immediate, 48 = follow-up after 2 days) - **`type`** — channel: `instagram`, `email`, `sms`, `phone`, `linkedin` ### script best practices (from swot analysis) - **no urls in step 1** — triggers instagram spam filters. save links for step 3+ - **no income claims** — "$100k monthly" triggers skepticism and spam detection - **lead with monetization** — what they get paid for, not what your tech stack is - **single audience** — don't list "founders, creators, brands, entrepreneurs" — pick one per campaign - **soft cta** — "what are you working on?" or "want an invite?" — not "sign up now" - **under 4 sentences** — mobile dms are small. get to the point - **ai prompt does the heavy lifting** — the script is the template, the ai personalizes per lead --- ## managing campaigns (toggle on/off) campaigns are toggled via `som-config.js`. use the iris cli: the `active` flag in `som-config.js` controls which campaigns run during `som:all`. turning a campaign off means it won't be included in batch runs. changes take effect on the next `som:all` run. ### current campaign state (live cache, jun 2026) > the inline fallback in `som-config.js` differs from the cache (e.g. inline marks venues/atxbeauty > off and maps `freelabelnet` to board 355). the **cache is authoritative** — verify with > `getresolutionsource()` or by reading `.som-campaigns-cache.json`. --- ## strategy templates & ai prompts ### viewing strategies or via api: ### active strategies (referenced in som-config.js) | campaign | strategy name | board | steps | |----------|--------------|-------|-------| | courses | ai course \| v3 (id: 17) | 38 | 4 | | creators | creator outreach \| v1 (id: 18) | 80 | 4 | | beatbox | dj outreach \| v2 | 224 | varies | | mayo | mayo outreach \| v1 | 176 | varies | ### understanding `instructions` vs `ai_prompt` each strategy step has two text fields that control the dm: - **`instructions`** — the base message template. this is what gets sent if there's no ai variation. should be a complete, ready-to-send message. - **`ai_prompt`** — instructions for the ai to rewrite/personalize the message per lead. when present, the "vary it" button rewrites the entire message using this prompt. when `null`, "vary it" does minor word swaps on the original `instructions` instead. **when to use `ai_prompt`:** - you want the ai to reference the lead's bio, genre, niche, or recent posts - you want significantly different messages per lead (not just word swaps) - you're ok with the ai sometimes changing the tone or structure **when to leave `ai_prompt` null:** - you want consistent messaging across all leads - the script is already personalized enough with merge fields - you want "vary it" to only do minor word substitutions (synonym swaps, sentence reordering) **as of apr 21, 2026:** `ai_prompt` was cleared from all steps on ai course v3 and creator outreach v1 because the ai rewrites were too aggressive — changing tone, adding claims, losing the original voice. now "vary it" does lightweight variation on the original script. ### updating a strategy step **via iris cli (recommended):** the `edit` command shows the current script + ai_prompt, lets you pick what to edit (script, ai prompt, both, or title), and pushes the update to the api. **via sql (for bulk operations like clearing ai_prompt):** ### creating a new strategy version when you want to test a new approach without losing the old one: 1. duplicate the existing strategy in the ui or api 2. edit the copy's steps 3. update `som-config.js` to point to the new strategy name 4. the old strategy stays intact for rollback ### step completion after sending a dm, the outreach step should be marked as completed so the lead doesn't get the same message again on the next run. two mechanisms: 1. **api-based** (reliable): `put /leads/{id}/outreach-steps/{stepid}` with `{is_completed: true}` 2. **ui-based** (fragile fallback): click the checkbox in the heyiris step card the batch script (`batch-with-login.spec.ts`) uses api-based completion after each dm send. --- ## updating scripts via api (direct) when the cli isn't available, update scripts directly via the api: **important:** the put endpoint **replaces all steps**. always send the complete step list, not just the one you're changing. fetch current steps first, modify the one you need, then send them all back. --- ## running som batches ### automated (via hive daemon) the daemon auto-chains: youtube feed import → som batch. runs on schedule. ### manual ### lead generation --- ## monitoring & troubleshooting ### check campaign health ### common issues - **"all leads already have outreach"** — board is exhausted, scrape fresh leads - **"no instagram handle — skipping"** — venue/business leads without ig. run enrichment or add ig-native leads - **"lead map api timed out"** — 4 parallel campaigns overwhelm the api. stagger helps but isn't perfect - **"no open instagram btn"** — lead doesn't have an ig handle in the system. the outreach step renders but can't open ig - **"no send message in menu"** — private account or ig blocked dms. marked as failed, moves to next lead - **422 on task completion** — output too large. fixed by truncating to 50kb ### key files - `tests/e2e/som.js` — campaign registry (board ids, strategies, ig accounts) - `tests/e2e/som-all.js` — batch orchestrator (enrichment, parallel campaigns, stagger) - `tests/e2e/batch-with-login.spec.ts` — playwright outreach spec (dm sending logic) - `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/src/console/commands/somoverviewcommand.php` — php som:overview - `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/src/console/commands/someditcommand.php` — php som:edit - `iris-code/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/platform-som.ts` — typescript iris som - `iris-code/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/platform-outreach.ts` — typescript iris outreach --- ## steps ### 1. parse the argument | argument | action | |----------|--------| | `overview` / (empty) | run `php bin/iris som` or `iris som` | | `overview -s` | run with full scripts flag | | `edit <campaign>` | run `php bin/iris som:edit <campaign>` or `iris som edit <campaign>` | | `update-script <campaign> "<text>"` | update step 1 script via api call | | `leads <campaign>` | show leads for that board | | `run` / `run <campaign>` | trigger som batch via npm | | `status` | check daemon logs for latest batch results | | `strategies` | list all strategies across all boards | ### 2. when editing scripts 1. always fetch the current strategy first to avoid overwriting other steps 2. show the current script to the user before editing 3. after updating, run `php bin/iris som -c <campaign>` to verify 4. remind user about best practices: no urls in step 1, lead with monetization, under 4 sentences ### 3. when running batches 1. check if the daemon is running (`npm run bridge`) 2. verify lead supply (`php bin/iris som` — check lead counts) 3. if leads are exhausted, suggest running leadgen first 4. monitor via daemon logs for errors --- ## running a campaign against an existing list (board not in som-config) added 2026-08-22, after running it end-to-end against board 529. the sections above cover discovery and script editing; this one covers the case where the leads already exist on a board that has **no campaign entry** in `tests/e2e/som-config.js`. you do not need to add a campaign. `som:custom` takes overrides: `board=` / `bloq=` → board_id · `ig=` → ig_account · `dry=1` → dry_run · aliases live at the top of `tests/e2e/som.js`. ### the order that matters **1. find the board's real strategy name — do not guess it.** `som:custom` defaults to `strategy: 'custom campaign'`, which exists on **no** board. run it without a `strategy=` override and the dry run reports `⚠ strategy script not found — using fallback`, then composes a generic *"hey @handle! noticed you're doing some interesting work…"*. that is the failure this playbook's "matched by name" warning describes, seen from the other side: it does not error, it silently substitutes filler. **if you see `strategy script:` in the dry-run output you have the real script; if you see `using fallback` you do not.** **2. dry run, and read the preflight funnel.** preflight runs **before** chromium launches and prints the whole funnel: a percentage over 100% (`"social media outreach": 15/4 (375%)`) means a second, generic step set was applied to some leads and is polluting the funnel — usually the default 5-step dm/sms/email/phone/proposal template. clear it before running, or the counts lie. **3. confirm the message a human will actually receive.** the dry run truncates to ~50 chars. read the whole thing with `iris outreach-strategy show <board> <id>` — the text is in the step's `instructions` field, and the variation rules are in `ai_prompt`. **4. real sample of 2–3 before the batch.** drop `dry=1`, keep `limit=2`. **5. then the batch**, respecting the cap the run prints: `daily dm cap (@acct): 0/40 sent today`. ### what the dry run will not tell you - **`⚠ ai variation failed — using raw script`** means every recipient gets a byte-identical dm. the `ai_prompt` exists precisely to prevent that. two identical dms is a sample; 278 is a pattern instagram recognises, and the account is worth more than the list. **never run a batch while this warning is showing.** root-caused and fixed 2026-08-22 — worth knowing because the symptom is three layers from the cause. the spec calls `post /api/v1/ai/generate-personalized-message`; that controller asks for `gpt-4o-mini` (with a comment saying nano is too weak to paraphrase); and `openaiservice::generateresponseclean()` read `instructions` and `max_tokens` out of `$options` and **never read `model`**, hardcoding `callgrokdirect()`. so the chosen model was discarded, every call went to xai, xai was out of credit and 403'd, and the batch silently degraded to one identical message for everybody. fixed in `35b6863d` + `5bc9fa7b` (fl-api). to check it directly, without burning a 3-minute browser run: run it twice against different handles. **different text = working. identical, or `success:false` = do not batch.** - **session age is printed but not enforced** — `session age: 73d` still passed. meanwhile `ig preflight check failed: page.goto: target page… has been closed` appeared and the runner logged `continuing anyway`. a dry run that reports `fail: 1` on browser teardown is the harness, not the lead. - **the list is not the strategy.** board 529 is *live stream guests* and its strategy invites people to be featured — but 104 of the leads on it typed the single word "site" on one giveaway post. check `custom_fields.comment` and `source_post_url` before assuming intent: ### verified run, 2026-08-22 | | | |---|---| | command | `npm run som:custom -- board=529 ig=thediscoverpage_ "strategy=guest feature \| v1" limit=2 dry=1` | | preflight | 278 never contacted · 308 pending across 3 steps | | wrong strategy | `fail: 1`, fallback filler message | | correct strategy | `would send: 2 · skip: 0 · fail: 0`, real script loaded | | runtime | ~3.4-3.6 min for 2 leads (chromium, api-direct engine) | | after the variation fix | two distinct openings — *"we're in the process of selecting…"* / *"we're excited to feature…"* — `fail: 0` | **chromium is flaky and it is not your code.** one run in three died on `page.goto: target page, context or browser has been closed` with no orphaned processes and 53% memory free; the identical command passed on retry. `session age: 73d` is printed but never enforced, and the inbox scan fails in most runs with `continuing to outreach`. retry once before diagnosing anything.

entries.name: stress-test
entries.describe: Break features on purpose — generate and run edge case batteries against CLI commands, API endpoints, and DB writes. Auto-discovers what changed, builds attack vectors (XSS, injection, boundary values, type confusion, auth bypass, race conditions), runs them against production, reports pass/fail, and cleans up test artifacts. Use after shipping a feature or before a client-ready check. Pass a feature name, CLI command, or API endpoint as argument (e.g., "iris content", "/api/v1/my/profiles", "upload flow").
entries.haystack: stress-test break features on purpose — generate and run edge case batteries against cli commands, api endpoints, and db writes. auto-discovers what changed, builds attack vectors (xss, injection, boundary values, type confusion, auth bypass, race conditions), runs them against production, reports pass/fail, and cleans up test artifacts. use after shipping a feature or before a client-ready check. pass a feature name, cli command, or api endpoint as argument (e.g., "iris content", "/api/v1/my/profiles", "upload flow"). --- name: stress-test description: break features on purpose — generate and run edge case batteries against cli commands, api endpoints, and db writes. auto-discovers what changed, builds attack vectors (xss, injection, boundary values, type confusion, auth bypass, race conditions), runs them against production, reports pass/fail, and cleans up test artifacts. use after shipping a feature or before a client-ready check. pass a feature name, cli command, or api endpoint as argument (e.g., "iris content", "/api/v1/my/profiles", "upload flow"). allowed-tools: - read - bash - grep - glob - edit - write - agent --- # stress test — break it before clients do generate and execute edge case batteries against cli commands, api endpoints, and database writes. the goal is to find bugs through adversarial input, boundary conditions, and unexpected usage patterns — the same things real users will do accidentally. ## arguments `$arguments` — what to test. examples: - `/stress-test iris content` — test all `iris content` subcommands - `/stress-test /api/v1/my/profiles` — test a specific api endpoint - `/stress-test upload flow` — test the upload workflow end-to-end - `/stress-test <feature>` — auto-discover commands and endpoints from recent commits ## how it works ### phase 1: discovery identify what to test by examining: 1. **recent commits** — `git log --oneline -5` + `git diff --name-only head~3` 2. **cli commands** — grep for `cmd({` patterns, extract command names and positional args 3. **api endpoints** — grep for `irisfetch`, `route::get/post`, extract url patterns 4. **db writes** — grep for `::create`, `->update`, `->delete`, `post /api`, `put /api`, `delete /api` ### phase 2: attack vector generation for each discovered target, generate test cases from these categories: #### category 1: input boundary testing | vector | what it tests | example | |--------|--------------|---------| | empty string | null/empty handling | `iris content get ""` | | zero | off-by-one, division | `--profile 0`, `--limit 0` | | negative numbers | unsigned assumptions | `iris content get -1` | | very large numbers | integer overflow | `iris content get 999999999999` | | max length strings | buffer/truncation | `--title "$(python3 -c "print('a'*10000)")"` | | unicode/emoji | encoding issues | `--search "日本語🔥"` | | null bytes | c-string termination | `--title $'\x00hidden'` | | whitespace only | trim failures | `--search " "` | | special url chars | encoding issues | `--search "a&b=c?d#e"` | #### category 2: security testing | vector | what it tests | example | |--------|--------------|---------| | xss in text fields | html injection | `--title '<script>alert(1)</script>'` | | sql injection | parameterized queries | `--search "'; drop table users;--"` | | path traversal | file access | `--profile "../../etc/passwd"` | | command injection | shell escaping | `--title "$(whoami)"`, `` --title "`id`" `` | | auth bypass | token handling | call endpoint without auth header | | idor | object ownership | access another user's content by id | | rate limiting | abuse prevention | 20 rapid sequential calls | #### category 3: type confusion | vector | what it tests | example | |--------|--------------|---------| | string where number expected | type coercion | `iris content get "abc"` | | number where string expected | type coercion | `--search 12345` | | boolean-ish strings | truthy/falsy | `--profile "false"`, `--profile "null"` | | array-like input | parser confusion | `--type "video,article"` | | json in string field | injection | `--title '{"key":"value"}'` | #### category 4: state & concurrency | vector | what it tests | example | |--------|--------------|---------| | duplicate create | idempotency | upload same url twice | | delete then access | ghost references | delete video, then `get` it | | modify then diff | consistency | push changes, immediately diff | | rapid sequential ops | race conditions | 5 uploads in parallel | | stale local file | sync conflicts | modify local json, api changes independently | #### category 5: ux flow testing | vector | what it tests | example | |--------|--------------|---------| | first-run experience | empty state | run command with no data | | ctrl+c mid-operation | cleanup | interrupt during upload | | --json piping | machine-readable output | `cmd --json 2>/dev/null \| python3 -c "import json,sys;json.load(sys.stdin)"` | | --help completeness | self-documentation | every subcommand has --help | | error message quality | user guidance | error says what to do next | | non-interactive mode | ci/cd compat | pipe input, no tty | #### category 6: user journey paths (the important one) this is the category that catches "it works in isolation but the workflow is broken." walk through the paths a real client takes — in order, with real data, checking that each step's output feeds correctly into the next. **how to build journey tests**: for each feature, map the 3-5 most common user workflows. each journey is a sequence of commands where the output of step n informs the input of step n+1. if any step fails or produces output that can't feed the next step, the journey fails. ##### journey templates **journey a: discovery → first use → daily use** **journey b: create → verify → modify → delete (full lifecycle)** **journey c: error recovery** **journey d: power user multi-step** **journey e: onboarding (brand new user)** ##### journey test execution pattern ##### persona-based journey matrix every feature must be tested from **5 personas**. each persona has different context, expectations, and failure modes: **persona 1: new user (day 1)** - just ran `iris init`, has auth but no content/profiles - expectation: guided experience, no jargon, clear next steps - common failures: empty state crashes, "no data" with no guidance, assumes config exists **persona 2: existing user (daily driver)** - has profiles, content, active workflows - expectation: fast, reliable, remembers context - common failures: slow queries on large datasets, stale cache, pagination breaks **persona 3: admin/operator (managing for clients)** - managing content across multiple profiles/brands - expectation: bulk operations, cross-profile access, --json for scripting - common failures: user scoping blocks admin access, no bulk operations, id confusion between profiles **persona 4: ci/automation (non-interactive)** - running in a script, cron job, or hive task - expectation: no prompts, predictable exit codes, parseable output - common failures: interactive prompts block execution, ansi codes in piped output, non-zero exit on success **persona 5: adversarial user (pentester/abuse)** - trying to break things, access other users' data, inject payloads - expectation: every input sanitized, auth enforced, no 500s - common failures: xss stored, idor, sql injection, command injection, path traversal ##### what makes a good journey test | good | bad | |------|-----| | tests a sequence of 3-5 related commands | tests isolated commands (that's category 1-5) | | output of step n feeds step n+1 | steps are independent | | uses real production data | uses mocked/fake data | | tests the path a client would take | tests the path a developer would take | | includes at least one error/recovery step | only tests the happy path | | verifies cleanup (no orphans) | leaves test data behind | ### phase 3: execution run each test case and collect results: ### phase 4: cleanup after all tests: 1. delete any test records created (videos, profiles, etc.) 2. restore any modified records (push original json back) 3. verify no test artifacts remain in production 4. report any artifacts that couldn't be cleaned ### phase 5: report output format: ## pre-built test suites ### cli command suite for any `iris <command>`: ### sensitive data leak detection when checking for leaked secrets in source code, use **precise patterns** that match actual credential variables — not display-only words like "tokens" (token counts) or "secret_count". **why this matters:** broad patterns like `console.log.*token` flag every line that displays token *counts* (e.g., `${tokens}` showing "12.5k tokens"), password *requirements* text, or secret *status* messages. these false positives erode trust in the test suite — teams start ignoring failures. use assignment/interpolation context to distinguish "logging a credential value" from "displaying a word that contains 'token'". ### api endpoint suite for any `get/post/put/delete /api/v1/<path>`: ### upload/write suite for any feature that creates db records: ## integration with production deploy the stress-test skill can be invoked from `/production-deploy client-ready` as part of gate 2: to invoke programmatically: ## severity levels | level | criteria | action | |-------|----------|--------| | **critical** | 500 error, data loss, auth bypass, command injection | block ship. fix immediately. | | **high** | xss stored, idor, rate limit bypass | fix before client-ready. | | **medium** | poor error message, missing validation, slow response (>5s) | fix in follow-up. ship with known issue. | | **low** | cosmetic (emoji in output, truncation off-by-one) | note it. fix when convenient. | ## quick start examples

entries.name: test-distributed-atomically
entries.describe: Test a feature that spans several machines WITHOUT using production as your debugger. Cut the system at its boundaries, test every part that is not genuinely remote with no network at all, reproduce the remote condition locally instead of borrowing the remote system, assert shape rather than success, and make distributed answers attributable rather than identical. Use when a change touches a queue, a daemon, a webhook, a device, a worker, or anything else where "just deploy and see" is the tempting move.
entries.haystack: test-distributed-atomically test a feature that spans several machines without using production as your debugger. cut the system at its boundaries, test every part that is not genuinely remote with no network at all, reproduce the remote condition locally instead of borrowing the remote system, assert shape rather than success, and make distributed answers attributable rather than identical. use when a change touches a queue, a daemon, a webhook, a device, a worker, or anything else where "just deploy and see" is the tempting move. --- name: test-distributed-atomically description: test a feature that spans several machines without using production as your debugger. cut the system at its boundaries, test every part that is not genuinely remote with no network at all, reproduce the remote condition locally instead of borrowing the remote system, assert shape rather than success, and make distributed answers attributable rather than identical. use when a change touches a queue, a daemon, a webhook, a device, a worker, or anything else where "just deploy and see" is the tempting move. version: 2 args: feature: type: string required: true description: what you are building or fixing, in one line. hosts: type: string required: false description: "the machines the request crosses, if you already know them. e.g. 'browser -> api -> queue -> worker -> db'" on-error: continue timeout: 1800 --- # test something distributed, atomically **the trap.** a feature spans five hosts. you cannot put that under a debugger, so you test it end to end, it fails, you guess, you deploy, you wait, you test again. each lap costs a build. three laps in you have learned almost nothing, because an end-to-end failure tells you *that* it broke, never *where*. **the claim.** most bugs in a distributed feature are not distributed bugs. they are ordinary bugs — a regex that will not compile, a column that does not exist, a binary not on `path` — sitting inside a distributed system and wearing its costume. you can catch those on a laptop in seconds. spend the expensive end-to-end runs on the two or three links that are genuinely remote. **skip this** for a change confined to one process with no network in it. ceremony on work that does not need it teaches people to skip the ceremony when it matters. ## steps ### step:cut cut the system at every boundary ### step:atomic test every yes link, before touching the remote system ### step:reproduce reproduce the remote condition locally ### step:assert assert shape and behaviour, never mere success ### step:attribute distinguish "different" from "wrong" ### step:budget spend the expensive runs deliberately ### step:record write down what the tests caught, and what they got wrong

entries.name: the-algorithm
entries.describe: First-principles + deletion-first engineering audit. Runs the full three-tool stack against a target system, service, feature, page, table, agent tool, architecture, or process — decompose to constituents and rebuild (first principles), find the gap between truth and price (Idiot Index), then run Musk's five steps IN ORDER (question the requirement, delete the part, simplify what survives, accelerate the cycle, automate last). Enforces the existence test, the 10% add-back calibration, and the architecture split triggers. Use BEFORE optimizing, refactoring, splitting a service, or automating anything.

order (question the requirement, delete the part, simplify what survives, accelerate the cycle, automate last). enforces the existence test, the 10% add-back calibration, and the architecture split triggers. use before optimizing, refactoring, splitting a service, or automating anything. version: 2 args: target: type: string required: true description: what to audit — a path, service, table, component, config file, agent tool, page, architecture diagram, or a named process ("the deploy checklist", "the tool registry", "splitting billing into its own service"). domain: type: string required: false default: auto enum: [auto, architecture, code, process, product] description: which reference layer to weight. architecture = distributed-systems physics and the split triggers; code = modules, config, dead paths; process = checklists, approvals, meetings, reports; product = features, screens, flows. auto = infer from the target. action: type: string required: false default: audit enum: [audit, restore-check] description: audit = run the full pass. restore-check = score a completed deletion pass against the 10% rule. model: type: string required: false default: iris/glm-5.3-flash description: model for the reasoning steps. on-error: continue timeout: 420 --- # the algorithm — decide what's real, then delete before you optimize > "the most common error of a smart engineer is to optimize a thing that should not exist." > "the best part is no part. the best process is no process. it weighs nothing, costs nothing, > can't go wrong." ## the three stacked tools most teams invert this stack — they automate an analogical process that first principles would have deleted. | # | tool | the question it answers | |---|------|------------------------| | 1 | **first principles** | what is actually true, and what is the *function*? | | 2 | **idiot index / cost-of-atoms** | where is the gap between truth and price? | | 3 | **the algorithm** | delete, then simplify, then speed, then automate | **first principles is how you decide what is real. the algorithm is how you operate.** the one-line operating system: > treat physics as law, named requirements as claims, and everything else as optional. rebuild the > function from constituents. if a part is not required by that rebuild, it should not exist. only > then is it worth optimizing. --- ## tool 1 — first principles > "boil things down to the most fundamental truths and then reason up from there, as opposed to > reasoning by analogy." — musk two jobs in one sentence: **strip inherited stories**, then **rebuild from what physics (or the actual problem) will still allow**. aristotle called a first principle an *archē*: the starting point from which a thing is known, not deduced from something prior. the modern test: p is first-principle ⟺ p cannot be reduced further without leaving the domain of the problem **usually are first principles:** conservation of energy · mass, geometry, material properties · a customer must get from a to b · a battery stores charge by moving ions through an electrolyte · software must transform state without losing required information. **usually are not:** "rockets cost $x because that's what aerospace charges" · "batteries will stay at $600/kwh because they always have" · "we need this approval step because legal said so" · "microservices are how serious companies build backends" · "a car needs a folding key." that last group are **analogies wearing a lab coat**. they sound like knowledge. they are compressed history. ### the real opponent: reasoning by analogy analogy: new situation ≈ old situation ⟹ reuse old solution analogy is cheap and mostly correct — it is how you drive, cook, hire, and write code. the problem is that **analogy cannot invent**. copy only "what people like us do" and you get a faster horse, a slightly cheaper expendable rocket, a nicer $600 pack. | | analogy | first principles | |---|---|---| | starting point | precedent, industry, best practice | what must be true | | question | "how is this usually done?" | "what are we sure is true?" | | output | incremental variant | possible rebuild | | cost | low mental energy | high | | failure mode | invisible ceilings | wrong axioms, overbuild | | best use | known games, local optimization | new games, cost/physics ceilings | **when analogy is rational:** use it when the context delta is small and the cost of being wrong is low. you do not first-principles your grocery list. you first-principles the thing everyone swears is impossible. ### the five moves 1. **name the goal as a function, not a form.** not "build a cheaper aerospace rocket" — "move mass to orbit and, if possible, reuse the vehicle." 2. **separate facts from folklore.** write every constraint down and label each one: *physics* · *named human requirement* · *industry custom* · *fear / just-in-case*. only the first is sacred. the second is negotiable. the third and fourth are deletion candidates. 3. **decompose to constituents.** what is it *made of* — materials, forces, information, incentives? 4. **price or bound the constituents.** this is where it becomes quantitative (see tool 2). 5. **rebuild upward.** given these constituents and these true constraints, what is the simplest machine that produces the function? **the rebuild is where deletion happens.** ### why it is hard it takes more mental energy — analogy is pattern-matching, first principles is reconstruction. institutions prefer analogy because it is socially safe: you can always point at "how it's done." and school trains you to answer the assigned question, never to reject its hidden assumptions. so people **fake** it: they say "from first principles…" and then list three industry benchmarks. that is analogy with better branding. **a real pass feels slightly illegal** — you are saying out loud that a respected constraint might be folklore. --- ## tool 2 — the idiot index idiot index = price of finished part / cost of raw materials high ratio (often cited > 10 for production hardware) means over-machining, inherited process, certification theater, or a part that should not exist. musk's rocket check: raw materials were ~2% of typical rocket price, a ~50× markup over atoms. battery check in 2012: pack ~$600/kwh against materials ~$80/kwh. **a high index does not prove you can close the gap. it proves the ceiling is not physics.** ported to software: cost = c_essential + c_process + c_interfaces + c_failure_modes + c_overhead every added part pays all five terms. **deleting a part zeros all five. optimizing it shrinks one.** that is the whole argument for "the best part is no part." headroom = c_market − c_min, where c_min ≈ c_materials + c_energy + c_information large headroom means the opportunity is process and architecture — not "try harder at the current design." --- ## tool 3 — the algorithm the five steps, **in this order**. the order is the whole method. | # | step | the question | what it costs to skip | |---|------|--------------|----------------------| | 1 | question every requirement | who named this, and is it forced by physics/law/a live customer? | you build the wrong thing perfectly | | 2 | delete the part or process | does the intended function still happen without it? | you polish waste | | 3 | simplify and optimize | make what survived elegant | you optimize ghosts | | 4 | accelerate cycle time | same work, shorter loop | you go faster at the wrong work | | 5 | automate | only now hand it to a machine | you scale a mistake | musk ran it backwards himself at fremont — automate, accelerate, simplify, *then* discover the step never needed to exist — and called the resulting over-automation his own mistake ("excessive automation was a mistake… humans are underrated," 2018). **this playbook exists to force the order.** ### why smart people optimize things that shouldn't exist the diagnosis is psychological, not technical. school rewards answering the question you were given; you get no points for saying the question is dumb. so engineers inherit a straitjacket: given a part, make it faster, lighter, cheaper — never ask whether it should exist. two traps: - **smart-person requirements are the most dangerous.** people hesitate to challenge them, so a requirement from "legal," "safety," or a brilliant colleague survives with no owner. - **"just in case" bias.** you can invent a reason to keep almost anything. the rule: a requirement needs a **named human**, not a department. if no living person will defend it today, it is a deletion candidate. ### the three tests this playbook enforces **existence test.** for a part `p` and the intended function `f`: v(p) = f(with p) − f(without p) if `v(p) ≈ 0` on the *actual* function, delete `p`. not "make it cheaper" — delete it. keep p ⟺ the system without p fails the intended function if the car is still quiet, still fire-safe, still manufacturable without the pad, the pad was never a part. it was a superstition with a bom line. **the 10% add-back calibration.** delete aggressively enough that some deletions fail and come back: aggressiveness = items_restored / items_deleted target ≈ 0.10 `0` = timid, you left junk in. `≫0.10` = you deleted function, not waste. this is the honest answer to chesterton's fence: you don't refuse to remove the fence, you remove it and **pay** for the ones you were wrong about. **complexity tax and reliability.** parts cost themselves *and* their pairwise interfaces: tax(n) ∝ n + c(n,2) · c_interface r_system ≈ ∏ rᵢ two hundred parts at 99.5% each is a 37% system. deleting fifty beats improving any one of them. deletion is **superlinear** in value. ### why deletion makes the system better, not just cheaper a part is not only mass and dollars. it is a failure mode, a supplier, an inspection, a fixture, a robot cell, a tolerance stack, a training item, a warranty claim, and a coordination meeting. lean calls the compounding *muda*. systems people call it **gall's law**: a complex system that works evolved from a simple system that worked. you cannot optimize your way from the bloated version to the simple one — you have to delete back to it. ### the canonical examples - **tesla nvh/fire pad.** safety said noise required it; noise said safety required it; nobody owned the requirement. they pulled it, measured both, saw no difference, deleted it — and bypassed a ~$2m robot cell that existed only to install it. - **giga casting.** two mega-castings replaced ~70–171 stamped parts and ~1,600 welds. deletion at the architecture level, not a cheaper bracket. - **raptor 3.** external plumbing, wiring, and the engine-bay heat shield deleted or folded into the primary structure. delete the shield and a small leak dumps into plasma that is already on fire — the leak stops being a failure mode. "undesign" as the design win. - **grid fins that don't fold.** a folding mechanism is a whole extra system. add the hinge later if physics demands it; do not pre-install "in case." - **the anti-example: fremont automation.** the algorithm is partly a scar. --- ## architecture from first principles *(the reference layer for `--domain architecture`)* software architecture is **not** "microservices," "hexagonal," "event-driven," or "an agent mesh." those are forms. the function is simpler: > **turn inputs into correct, durable outputs, under change, failure, and finite resources — at a > cost a team can still understand.** everything else is a part. if you can delete it and that function still holds, the architecture got better. architecture = state + computation + boundaries - **state** — facts that must survive a request, a crash, or a deploy - **computation** — the transformations that make those facts useful - **boundaries** — where you cut so humans and machines can change one piece without detonating the rest brooks's split holds: **essential complexity** is the domain (billing rules, permissions, a workflow that must not double-charge); **accidental complexity** is everything added because of tools, fashion, or fear. architecture's job is to pay the essential cost and refuse the rest. a 40-service diagram drawn before the first user is analogical theater. the first-principles question is never "what stack should we use?" it is: > what state must exist, what transformations are required, and which cuts are **forced** — by > physics, consistency, scale, or independently changing teams — rather than by blog posts? ### the real first principles (these are close to physics) - **computation is local and cheap. coordination is remote and expensive.** an in-process call is nanoseconds and nearly certain; a network call is milliseconds, lossy, and has a different failure model. treating rpc as a local call is the original sin. deutsch's fallacies exist because every team rediscovers this. - **you cannot hide distribution.** split state across two computers and you inherit cap/pacelc: during a partition, consistency or availability; even healthy, consistency or latency. not a framework preference — a constraint. - **serial reliability multiplies downward.** `r_request ≈ ∏ rᵢ`. ten services at 99.9% in a synchronous chain is ~99.0%. you bought an order of magnitude more downtime by drawing boxes. - **latency adds; tail latency multiplies.** `t ≈ σtᵢ + t_queue + t_retry`. a 25 ms monolith query becomes 200+ ms as a chatty graph, and under partial slowness retries turn one slow dependency into a load amplifier. that is how "well-architected" systems melt. - **interfaces dominate cost.** bugs and outages live at seams. `cost ∝ n + c·c(n,2)_coupled` — **coupling, not box count, is the mass.** - **change is the long-run cost function.** after v1 the money goes to modification. a cut that does not match a real change boundary is a part that should not exist. - **human working memory is a hard limit.** a design nobody can hold in their head will be changed incorrectly. cognitive load is an operational constraint, same as ram. - **correctness needs a single writer per invariant.** spreading "an order cannot be paid twice" across four services does not distribute the rule — it **deletes** the rule and hopes a saga puts it back. ### what is almost never a first principle | folklore | what it pretends | what is actually true | |---|---|---| | start with microservices | scale and team independence are free | you paid the microservice premium on day one: deploys, tracing, eventual consistency, on-call. worth it only when a monolith is already too expensive to change. | | one service = one db = purity | data isolation is architecture | split data only when the *write invariant* can live in one place. shared-db "services" are a distributed monolith with extra latency. | | event-driven = decoupled | async deletes coupling | it defers coupling into payload schemas, ordering, and "who owns the truth." | | kubernetes from request one | production-grade | orchestration is a process for many processes. zero processes do not need a cluster. | | hexagonal / clean / cqrs / ddd everywhere | professionalism | patterns are compression for specific pains. used early they are second-system jewelry. | | gateway + mesh + queue + workflow engine + flags + cdp | completeness | each is a part. most products need two of those, not six. | | multi-agent graph as default | intelligence | an agent is a loop over tools and state. extra agents are extra parts with extra coordination. | | "we'll need it at scale" | prudence | yagni plus gall: you do not know your real boundaries until the domain hurts. | fowler's observation is empirical, not aesthetic: successful microservice systems usually *grew out of* a monolith; greenfield microservice systems often get into serious trouble. ### the architecture idiot index i_arch = (runtime components + control planes) / owned invariants if the diagram has twenty boxes and the constituent list still has five items, you are looking at process, not physics. high `i_arch` means you are optimizing a factory that builds parts the product does not need. **constituents, for reference.** *the user needs:* a state change · an identity · a durable record · a way to see status · a way to change the rules later. *the machine needs:* bytes on disk · a cpu · a clock · a network **only** when two failure domains must be separate · observability. *the team needs:* a boundary they can change in one pr · a test that encodes the invariant · a deploy that cannot strand half the invariant on another team's release train. ### delete candidates that usually survive deletion - a service whose only job is to crud one table - a synchronous hop that could be an in-process function - a second database for a second service that always joins the first - an orchestration engine wrapping a 4-step script - a workflow engine plus an agent runtime plus a rules engine doing the same job - dual writes "for now" - an api layer that only translates json to json - a cache in front of a database that is already fast - a message queue between two modules that deploy together and fail together - a redesign of auth when a signed session already works if checkout still charges once, shows status, and survives a crash without `p`, `p` was not architecture. it was furniture. ### the first-principles default shape not because monoliths are morally better — because this matches the constituents. that system **already has architecture**: module boundaries + owned invariants + explicit async for slow/retryable work. ### the four split triggers — the only reasons for a second deployable 1. **independent scale axis** — transcode saturates cpu; the api does not. 2. **independent failure domain** — a blast radius you cannot accept in-process. 3. **independent change cadence / team** — two groups on incompatible clocks, with a stable contract. 4. **a hard consistency island** — payments, ledger, or tool-calls that must serialize. until one is true **and named**, a new process is a part. and when you do split, **split along the invariant, not along nouns.** "userservice / notificationservice" recreates the er diagram on the network — that is analogy to a database schema, not design. ### worked rebuilds **checkout.** function: reserve stock, take money at most once, emit a receipt. *first-principles cut:* one component owns the order row and the payment idempotency key; inventory decrement is in the same transaction or an explicit reservation record; email is a queue; loyalty points are off the critical path. *analogical cut:* order → inventory → pricing → tax → payment → notification. you turned one acid transaction into a saga so you could draw boxes, then spent a year making the saga correct. **crm / outreach / agent os.** function: a durable record of people and conversations, plus a runner that can take the next allowed action. constituents: contacts, threads, permissions, a job queue, tool adapters, an audit log. you do not need a lead microservice, an agent orchestration cluster, a memory vector db, and a workflow engine on day one. you need one store for source-of-truth records, one runner for tool calls with idempotency, and prompts/policies as data. extra agents and buses are heat shields around a function that is still "update row, call api, write result." **read-heavy product.** forced: a cache or a read replica. not forced: five cqrs services and a kafka backbone before you have a slow query. **multi-tenant saas.** forced: tenant isolation in the data model, authz on every query, noisy-neighbor limits. not forced: a cluster per tenant at ten customers. ### formulas for a design review split ⟺ ∃ a scale, failure, team, or invariant axis that a module cannot absorb t_p99 ≈ n · l_net + σ t_svc + t_retry_amplification — if n hops exist only to preserve diagram cleanliness, delete hops one writer ≫ many writers + coordinator — every extra writer on an invariant requires consensus or a saga; consensus is a part good cut ⟺ (prs inside one module) / (prs touching ≥2 modules) is high for the changes you ship — if most real work crosses the cut, the cut is wrong; merge the services (that is the 10%) c_total = c_domain + c_distribution + c_platform + c_ceremony — quality is how small you make the last three without growing the first --- ## what counts as a "part" a part is anything with an interface, a failure mode, and an owner: a service · a queue · a feature flag · a config entry · a db column · a migration · a middleware · an approval step · a cron job · a registry entry · a component prop · a wrapper around a wrapper · a cli flag · a checklist item · a recurring meeting · a status report nobody reads shapes that are almost always a finding — calibration for what one looks like: - **a registry, menu, or api surface that has grown far past what its consumers can hold.** when the list is three times longer than a comparable one that works, the count and the bugs are one problem, not two. - **a capability that needs n places wired before it does anything**, and fails silently if any one is missed. a high wiring count is `i_arch` screaming. - **a stale duplicate of something that lives elsewhere.** not merely unnecessary — actively misleading, because people read it and believe it. - **declared-vs-actual drift** (props, schemas, contracts, config) that quietly disables a feature. those are deletion candidates, not documentation candidates. ## steps ### step:inventory gather the evidence — do not speculate ### step:principles tool 1 — decompose to constituents and rebuild you are running first principles on: ${{args.target}} (domain: ${{args.domain}}) repository evidence: ${{steps.inventory.output}} do not propose changes yet. establish what is true. run the five moves: 1. name the goal as a function, not a form. one sentence a stranger could test. not "a workflow engine" — "runs n ordered steps, survives a crash mid-run, and never runs a step twice." 2. separate facts from folklore. every constraint this thing currently satisfies, one per row, labeled exactly one of: physics (or a hard technical/consistency constraint) · named-human · industry-custom · fear. only physics is sacred. named-human is negotiable. the last two are deletion candidates. a department is not a name. watch for analogy wearing a lab coat — "this is how serious teams do it" is industry-custom, never physics. 3. decompose to constituents. what is this actually made of — state, transformations, boundaries, identities, records, incentives? for architecture, list the owned invariants by name (the rules that must never be violated) and say which single component owns each. 4. bound it. estimate the irreducible cost of the function versus what it currently costs (components, layers, hops, config entries, deploys, meetings). give the idiot index: i = (runtime components + control planes) / owned invariants, or the closest honest analogue. a high index does not prove you can close the gap — it proves the ceiling is not physics. 5. rebuild upward. given only the physics constraints and the constituents, describe the simplest machine that produces the function. ignore what exists today. this rebuild is the reference the deletion pass will measure against. be blunt. if a real pass here does not feel slightly illegal — if you have not named at least one respected constraint as folklore — you ran analogy with better branding. go again. no preamble. ### step:requirements step 1 — make the requirements less dumb step 1 of the algorithm on: ${{args.target}} the rebuild: ${{steps.principles.output}} a requirement is valid only if forced by one of: (a) physics / a hard technical or consistency constraint, (b) law, regulation, or a signed contract, (c) the customer's actual job-to-be-done, (d) a named living person who would defend it today. "legal said so", "safety requires it", "the platform team owns it" are not owners. a department is not a person. requirements from smart or senior people are the most dangerous, because nobody challenges them — hold those to a higher bar, not a lower one. now walk the delta between what exists and the rebuild. for every requirement the current thing satisfies that the rebuild does not, output one row: | requirement | claimed owner | real owner (named person / "none") | forced by | verdict | verdict: valid · unowned · folklore · just-in-case. anything not valid is a deletion candidate in step 2. for architecture targets, apply the split test to every existing boundary: split ⟺ ∃ a scale, failure, team, or invariant axis a module cannot absorb. name which of the four triggers justifies each boundary, or mark it unjustified. "team independence" counts only if two groups genuinely cannot share a deploy. ### step:delete step 2 — delete the part step 2. target: ${{args.target}} rebuild: ${{steps.principles.output}} requirement audit: ${{steps.requirements.output}} apply the existence test to every part: v(p) = f(with p) − f(without p). if the intended function survives without p, p goes. you may add it back later — you are supposed to add back about 10%. if your list is so safe that nothing would ever need restoring, you have not deleted enough; go again and get more aggressive. for architecture targets, weight these known-survivors: a service that only cruds one table · a synchronous hop that could be an in-process function · a second db that always joins the first · an orchestration engine wrapping a 4-step script · overlapping workflow/agent/rules engines · dual writes "for now" · a json-to-json api layer · a cache in front of an already-fast db · a queue between two modules that deploy and fail together · an auth redesign when a signed session works. output exactly two lists. delete — ordered by (value freed × confidence). for each: what it is · what breaks if you are wrong · how you'd verify in one command or one browser check · and what it takes with it (the interfaces, contracts, tests, config entries, monitors, docs, deploys, and meetings that existed only to serve it). deletion is superlinear — count the interfaces, not just the box. keep — with the specific function or owned invariant that dies without it, one line each. if you cannot name it in one line, it belongs in delete. then state the predicted add-back: which ~1-in-10 of your delete list you expect to restore, and what signal would tell you. chesterton check: for any deletion where nobody can say what the part was for, say so explicitly. that is a finding, not a license — the add-back budget is how you pay for being wrong. ### step:simplify step 3 — simplify what survived step 3. only now do you touch what remains. target: ${{args.target}} survivors: ${{steps.delete.output}} for the keep list only — never for anything on delete — propose simplifications, ranked by idiot index (total cost of the unit ÷ the irreducible work it actually does). prefer, in order: merge two parts into one · collapse a layer · replace a configurable with a constant · replace a wrapper with the thing it wraps · delete a code path for a case that cannot occur. for architecture, the patterns are now allowed and only now: a modular monolith with hard module boundaries (packages, compile-time isolation, separate schemas inside one deploy) · explicit module apis that could become network apis later · one write model per invariant · an outbox if you later need events, never "events first" · idempotency keys on anything retryable · timeouts and limits on every remaining remote call. flag any proposal that is really a step-2 deletion in disguise — promote it back to step 2 rather than implementing it here. ### step:accelerate step 4 — cycle time on the remaining work step 4. target: ${{args.target}} ${{steps.simplify.output}} only for work that survived steps 1–3, shorten the loop. name the current cycle time from "change made" to "change verified", the bottleneck, and the shortest honest path to feedback. architecture that cannot ship in a day is lying about its quality. the cycle is: change module → test invariant → deploy. if a two-line pricing fix needs four repos, a contract pr, and a coordinated rollout, you accelerated the wrong graph — say so and send it back to step 2. speeding a doomed step only burns cash faster. if you find yourself accelerating something on the delete list, stop and name it. call out any verification step that cannot distinguish "not deployed" from "deployed and broken". those are worse than slow — they are false signals, and they belong in step 2. ### step:automate step 5 — automate last, and only what is real step 5. target: ${{args.target}} ${{steps.accelerate.output}} automate only work that survived all four previous steps. ci, orchestrators, meshes, auto-scalers, agent schedulers: last. automating a bad topology produces a faster distributed monolith. for each candidate: what is automated, what stays human and why, and the trigger that would tell you the automation itself became a part worth deleting. then write the final verdict as a report with these sections and nothing else: ## the algorithm — ${{args.target}} ### the function (one testable sentence) ### constituents and owned invariants — who owns each ### folklore found (constraints that failed the truth filter) ### idiot index — before → after ### deleted (with what each one takes with it) ### kept, and the function or invariant that justifies it ### simplified ### cycle time: before → after ### automated (and what stayed human) ### predicted add-back (the 10%) ### verification — the exact command or browser check that proves the function still holds end with one line: **the intended function this system exists to perform**, stated so plainly that a stranger could test it. ### step:calibrate the 10% check — did you actually reach the edge score a completed deletion pass on ${{args.target}}. aggressiveness = items_restored / items_deleted - 0.00 — you did not reach the edge. name the three parts you were afraid to touch, and why. - ~0.10 — correct. you probed the limit and paid for it honestly. - >0.25 — you deleted function, not waste. which deletions were architecture, not clutter? for architecture: a restored split (two services merged back) is the healthiest possible add-back — it means the cut did not match a real change boundary and you found out cheaply. say which of the four triggers you thought applied and which one actually did not. output the ratio, the verdict, and the next deletion pass if the ratio was 0. ## how this fails know these before you trust a result. **first-principles failure modes** - **wrong layer of "fundamental."** commodity metal prices are not physics; they are a market snapshot. "http + json + postgres" is a good local minimum, not a law. treating either as sacred is also analogy. - **true axioms, incomplete set.** you can reason cleanly and still miss regulation, an offline mobile client, a compliance rule, or a partner who only speaks sftp. the proof is valid; the model is too small. add the constraint — do not add a mesh "in case." - **reductionism that kills the whole.** a system is not only its parts. delete a "useless" joint and you may have deleted the thing that damped vibration. that is what the 10% add-back is for. - **overcomplicating in the name of purity.** first principles can produce baroque inventions (rain-sensing via full vision instead of a $3 sensor) when a boring analogical part was fine. - **confusing "possible in physics" with "possible this year."** not breaking physics is necessary, not sufficient. yield, capital, talent, and cycle time still exist. **architecture-specific failure modes** - **deletion that deletes the invariant.** merging billing into growth experiments because "it's one app" recreates the ball of mud. the test is function, not repo count. a modular monolith with a sealed `billing` module is deletion of *distribution*, not of *structure*. - **conway denial.** if two teams genuinely cannot share a deploy, the org is a distributed system. ignoring that is not first principles either. split as far as the org and the invariant demand — then stop. - **purity after product-market fit.** rewriting a working monolith into "proper" services because the architecture is embarrassing is optimizing a thing that should not exist: the rewrite. ## when not to run this - **on safety-critical behavior you have not measured.** the battery pad was deleted *after* testing noise and fire risk and finding no difference — not instead of testing. this attacks un-owned safety theater, never the measurement itself. - **before you know why the fence was built.** if nobody can say what a part is for, that is a finding, not a license. - **as an excuse to ship less function.** if deleting the part breaks the intended function, it comes back. that is the 10% rule working, not the method failing. - **it is not anti-automation.** automation is step 5, after the work is real. ## related - **lean / toyota / muda** — same instinct, higher deletion temperature. - **occam's razor** — do not multiply entities beyond necessity. - **yagni** — the software-native form of step 2. - **gall's law** — a working complex system evolved from a working simple one. - **chesterton's fence** — the honest counterweight, priced at 10%. - **brooks** — essential vs accidental complexity. -
