entries.name: agent-browser
entries.describe: Browser Automation with agent-browser
entries.haystack: agent-browser browser automation with agent-browser <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: agent-browser description: browser automation cli for ai agents. use when the user needs to interact with websites, including navigating pages, filling forms, clicking buttons, taking screenshots, extracting data, testing web apps, or automating any browser task. triggers include requests to "open a website", "fill out a form", "click a button", "take a screenshot", "scrape data from a page", "test this web app", "login to a site", "automate browser actions", or any task requiring programmatic web interaction. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run agent-browser ` # browser automation with agent-browser ## core workflow every browser automation follows this pattern: 1. **navigate**: `agent-browser open <url>` 2. **snapshot**: `agent-browser snapshot -i` (get element refs like `@e1`, `@e2`) 3. **interact**: use refs to click, fill, select 4. **re-snapshot**: after navigation or dom changes, get fresh refs ## command chaining commands can be chained with `&&` in a single shell invocation. the browser persists between commands via a background daemon, so chaining is safe and more efficient than separate calls. **when to chain:** use `&&` when you don't need to read the output of an intermediate command before proceeding (e.g., open + wait + screenshot). run commands separately when you need to parse the output first (e.g., snapshot to discover refs, then interact using those refs). ## essential commands ## common patterns ### form submission ### authentication with auth vault (recommended) ### authentication with state persistence ### session persistence ### data extraction ### parallel sessions ### connect to existing chrome ### color scheme (dark mode) ### visual browser (debugging) ### local files (pdfs, html) ### ios simulator (mobile safari) **requirements:** macos with xcode, appium (`npm install -g appium && appium driver install xcuitest`) **real devices:** works with physical ios devices if pre-configured. use `--device "<udid>"` where udid is from `xcrun xctrace list devices`. ## security all security features are opt-in. by default, agent-browser imposes no restrictions on navigation, actions, or output. ### content boundaries (recommended for ai agents) enable `--content-boundaries` to wrap page-sourced output in markers that help llms distinguish tool output from untrusted page content: ### domain allowlist restrict navigation to trusted domains. wildcards like `*.example.com` also match the bare domain `example.com`. sub-resource requests, websocket, and eventsource connections to non-allowed domains are also blocked. include cdn domains your target pages depend on: ### action policy use a policy file to gate destructive actions: example `policy.json`: auth vault operations (`auth login`, etc.) bypass action policy but domain allowlist still applies. ### output limits prevent context flooding from large pages: ## diffing (verifying changes) use `diff snapshot` after performing an action to verify it had the intended effect. this compares the current accessibility tree against the last snapshot taken in the session. for visual regression testing or monitoring: `diff snapshot` output uses `+` for additions and `-` for removals, similar to git diff. `diff screenshot` produces a diff image with changed pixels highlighted in red, plus a mismatch percentage. ## timeouts and slow pages the default playwright timeout is 25 seconds for local browsers. this can be overridden with the `agent_browser_default_timeout` environment variable (value in milliseconds). for slow websites or large pages, use explicit waits instead of relying on the default timeout: when dealing with consistently slow websites, use `wait --load networkidle` after `open` to ensure the page is fully loaded before taking a snapshot. if a specific element is slow to render, wait for it directly with `wait <selector>` or `wait @ref`. ## session management and cleanup when running multiple agents or automations concurrently, always use named sessions to avoid conflicts: always close your browser session when done to avoid leaked processes: if a previous session was not closed properly, the daemon may still be running. use `agent-browser close` to clean it up before starting new work. ## ref lifecycle (important) refs (`@e1`, `@e2`, etc.) are invalidated when the page changes. always re-snapshot after: - clicking links or buttons that navigate - form submissions - dynamic content loading (dropdowns, modals) ## annotated screenshots (vision mode) use `--annotate` to take a screenshot with numbered labels overlaid on interactive elements. each label `[n]` maps to ref `@en`. this also caches refs, so you can interact with elements immediately without a separate snapshot. use annotated screenshots when: - the page has unlabeled icon buttons or visual-only elements - you need to verify visual layout or styling - canvas or chart elements are present (invisible to text snapshots) - you need spatial reasoning about element positions ## semantic locators (alternative to refs) when refs are unavailable or unreliable, use semantic locators: ## javascript evaluation (eval) use `eval` to run javascript in the browser context. **shell quoting can corrupt complex expressions** -- use `--stdin` or `-b` to avoid issues. **why this matters:** when the shell processes your command, inner double quotes, `!` characters (history expansion), backticks, and `$()` can all corrupt the javascript before it reaches agent-browser. the `--stdin` and `-b` flags bypass shell interpretation entirely. **rules of thumb:** - single-line, no nested quotes -> regular `eval 'expression'` with single quotes is fine - nested quotes, arrow functions, template literals, or multiline -> use `eval --stdin <<'evaleof'` - programmatic/generated scripts -> use `eval -b` with base64 ## configuration file create `agent-browser.json` in the project root for persistent settings: priority (lowest to highest): `~/.agent-browser/config.json` < `./agent-browser.json` < env vars < cli flags. use `--config <path>` or `agent_browser_config` env var for a custom config file (exits with error if missing/invalid). all cli options map to camelcase keys (e.g., `--executable-path` -> `"executablepath"`). boolean flags accept `true`/`false` values (e.g., `--headed false` overrides config). extensions from user and project configs are merged, not replaced. ## deep-dive documentation | reference | when to use | |-----------|-------------| | [references/commands.md](references/commands.md) | full command reference with all options | | [references/snapshot-refs.md](references/snapshot-refs.md) | ref lifecycle, invalidation rules, troubleshooting | | [references/session-management.md](references/session-management.md) | parallel sessions, state persistence, concurrent scraping | | [references/authentication.md](references/authentication.md) | login flows, oauth, 2fa handling, state reuse | | [references/video-recording.md](references/video-recording.md) | recording workflows for debugging and documentation | | [references/profiling.md](references/profiling.md) | chrome devtools profiling for performance analysis | | [references/proxy-support.md](references/proxy-support.md) | proxy configuration, geo-testing, rotating proxies | ## ready-to-use templates | template | description | |----------|-------------| | [templates/form-automation.sh](templates/form-automation.sh) | form filling with validation | | [templates/authenticated-session.sh](templates/authenticated-session.sh) | login once, reuse state | | [templates/capture-workflow.sh](templates/capture-workflow.sh) | content extraction with screenshots |

entries.name: agentic-loop
entries.describe: Agentic Loop (loop engineering)
entries.haystack: agentic-loop agentic loop (loop engineering) <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: agentic-loop description: stop babysitting a long multi-step task by hand. point this at a goal and it plans the work, fans it out to specialists, checks its own output against what you actually asked for, and remembers what it learned for next time — optionally repeating itself on a weekly schedule with nobody there to kick it off. the same engine behind the builder, scout, and growth demos, generalized to any goal you give it. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run agentic-loop ` > steps: plan → build → scout → growth → verify → synthesize → write-memory → schedule → summary # agentic loop (loop engineering) a runnable reference for the "set the goal once, the agents prompt themselves" pattern: each specialist below is a `prompt` step you can later swap for a real agent fanned out across the hive — `iris hive run <node> "iris agents chat <specialistid> '…' --bloq <mem>"` — for true parallel execution. see `iris how-to view agentic-loops`. all ai steps use **gpt-4.1-nano** (cheap, closed-loop economics). memory persists to a local next-steps file (the video's "memory outside the conversation") and, if `--bloq` is given, is ingested into that knowledge base for recall next cycle. ## before you schedule this unattended this loop is built to run with nobody watching — that's the point of `--action schedule`. unattended is exactly the condition where a subtle failure survives longest, so before you wire the weekly cadence, know what real benchmarking of models on loop-shaped tasks (planning, drafting, self-verification) actually found. none of this is theoretical — it changes how you should read this loop's own output: - **confident and true are different axes.** the most fluent, best-written answer in one benchmark was also the least accurate one — it read best precisely because it was the most invented, while the honest answers scored lower on style for saying less. nothing in this loop currently checks scout's or growth's output against a real source. treat their output as a claim, not a fact, until something — you, or an added grounding step — checks it. - **a refusal is a correct answer, not a failed one.** if a specialist step comes back saying it doesn't have enough to work with instead of inventing something plausible, that is the loop working, not the loop failing. don't tune a prompt to eliminate refusals — that trains fabrication instead, and it's how a confident wrong answer replaces an honest uncertain one. - **the verify step is only as good as its own reliability.** a checker that always reports success is indistinguishable from having no checker at all, and that failure mode is invisible until you deliberately feed it something that should fail. before trusting `step:verify` on a real goal, run the loop once on an obviously incomplete cycle and confirm it actually returns `verdict: iterate` — don't assume it discriminates just because it's there. - **a memory step that writes but is never read back is not memory.** confirm the round trip, not just the write: run two cycles and check that cycle 2's plan actually references something from cycle 1's next-steps, not just that `next-steps.md` exists on disk. - **cheap can be the right choice, not just the affordable one.** this loop defaults to gpt-4.1-nano throughout — in the same kind of benchmarking, small/cheap models have out-scored notably larger ones on cost per *correct* answer, precisely because reliability and honest brevity beat confident length. don't assume upgrading every step to a bigger model makes the loop better; measure it on your own goal before you pay for it. ## steps --- """ with open(mem, "a") as f: f.write(entry) print(f"memory appended -> {mem}") py bloq="${{args.bloq}}" if [ -n "$bloq" ] && [ "$bloq" != "0" ] && [ "$bloq" != "null" ]; then echo "ingesting memory into bloq $bloq for rag recall next cycle…" iris bloqs ingest "$bloq" "$mem" && echo "ingested into bloq $bloq" || echo "(bloq ingest skipped — check the bloq id)" else echo "no --bloq given; memory is the local file only. pass --bloq <id> to make it rag-recallable." fi ```

entries.name: architecture-review
entries.describe: Architecture Review — Pre-Implementation Analysis Skill
entries.haystack: architecture-review architecture review — pre-implementation analysis skill <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: architecture-review description: catch the design flaw that would have cost you a rewrite, before you write a single line of code. seven proven review lenses — from security holes to scaling limits to what happens when this needs to change later — run against your proposed change so the expensive mistake gets caught on paper. pass the proposed change as argument. allowed-tools: - read - grep - glob - bash - agent - task --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run architecture-review ` # architecture review — pre-implementation analysis skill run a structured architectural analysis on a proposed technical change **before** writing any code. the goal is to catch design flaws, security holes, scaling limits, and migration gaps upfront. ## arguments `$arguments` — description of the proposed change, feature, or design decision to analyse. examples: - `/architecture-review add marketplace skill execution to v6toolregistry` - `/architecture-review migrate queue backend from database to redis streams` - `/architecture-review add multi-tenant secret isolation for installed workflows` - `/architecture-review refactor reactloopservice checkpointing to be async` --- ## how this skill works when invoked, run **all 7 frameworks** against the proposed change. for each framework, read the relevant source files to ground the analysis in actual code — never speculate about implementation details without reading them first. output a single structured report with all 7 sections, then a final **go / no-go / conditional go** recommendation. --- ## framework 1: swot analysis — strategic viability evaluate the proposed change from a strategic perspective. | category | what to assess | |----------|---------------| | **strengths** | what existing code/patterns does this leverage? how much reuse vs new code? what safety mechanisms does it inherit? | | **weaknesses** | what's brittle, hardcoded, or fragile in the approach? what coupling does it introduce? | | **opportunities** | what future capabilities does this unlock? revenue, scale, or ecosystem benefits? | | **threats** | what could go wrong in production? data leaks, race conditions, sync drift, breaking changes? | **source check**: read the files that will be modified. identify the exact functions/classes affected. --- ## framework 2: gap analysis — transition planning map the journey from current state to target state. 1. **current state**: what exists today? read the actual code. what does it do, what doesn't it do? 2. **target state**: what should exist after this change? be specific about behaviour, not just structure. 3. **the gap**: what's missing? list each discrete piece of work. 4. **bridge (action plan)**: ordered steps to close the gap. flag any steps that require migrations, env var changes, or cross-service coordination. **source check**: read the current implementation files. identify what already exists vs what needs building. --- ## framework 3: search — system traits assessment evaluate 6 non-functional requirements. rate each as low / medium / high / exceptional with a one-line justification. | trait | question | |-------|----------| | **s — scalability** | does this change scale horizontally? what's the bottleneck (db writes, memory, api calls)? | | **e — extensibility** | can future developers extend this without modifying the core? is it pluggable? | | **a — availability** | what happens when a dependency fails? is there a fallback? graceful degradation? | | **r — reliability** | can this produce incorrect results silently? what invariants could be violated? | | **c — consistency** | in concurrent/async scenarios, can state become inconsistent? race conditions? | | **h — health / observability** | can we tell if this is working? logs, metrics, health checks, alerts? | --- ## framework 4: stride — threat modelling for each stride category, assess whether the proposed change introduces or mitigates the threat. only flag categories that are **actually relevant** — skip categories with no meaningful exposure. | threat | definition | assessment approach | |--------|-----------|-------------------| | **spoofing** | faking identity | can an unauthorized actor trigger this? are auth checks in place? | | **tampering** | modifying data | can inputs/state be manipulated to produce unintended behaviour? | | **repudiation** | denying actions | is there an audit trail? can we prove what happened? | | **information disclosure** | data leaks | could secrets, pii, or internal state leak across tenant boundaries? | | **denial of service** | resource exhaustion | can this be abused to exhaust cpu, memory, db connections, api quotas? | | **elevation of privilege** | gaining access | could this bypass permission checks or escalate user capabilities? | **source check**: read auth middleware, secret management, and permission checks in the affected code paths. --- ## framework 5: atam — architecture tradeoff analysis identify the **top 3 architectural decisions** in the proposed change. for each: 1. **decision**: what architectural choice is being made? 2. **optimises for**: which quality attribute does this favour? (performance, reliability, extensibility, etc.) 3. **trades off**: which quality attribute suffers? be specific about the cost. 4. **sensitivity point**: under what conditions does this tradeoff become painful? 5. **mitigation**: what could reduce the downside without losing the upside? --- ## framework 6: c4 model — structural impact zoom through 4 levels to show where this change fits architecturally. only go as deep as needed — skip levels that aren't affected. - **level 1 — context**: how does this change affect system boundaries? new external dependencies? changed data flows between systems? - **level 2 — containers**: which services/containers are affected? (iris-api, fl-api, fl-elon-web-ui, n8n, daemon, etc.) - **level 3 — components**: which modules/services/controllers within those containers are modified? - **level 4 — code**: which specific classes, methods, or functions change? what's the call chain? present as a concise list, not a diagram. reference actual file paths. --- ## framework 7: adr — architecture decision record write a draft adr for the most significant decision in this change. --- ## final verdict after all 7 frameworks, deliver a clear recommendation: ### recommendation: **[go / no-go / conditional go]** **if go**: list the implementation order (what to build first, what to defer). **if conditional go**: list the specific conditions that must be met before proceeding (e.g., "add migration for x first", "verify y doesn't break z"). **if no-go**: explain why and propose an alternative approach. ### critical risks (if any) - numbered list of risks that could cause production incidents if ignored. ### suggested implementation order 1. step 1 — [what + why first] 2. step 2 — [what + why second] 3. ... --- ## research protocol before writing the analysis, you must: 1. **read the affected files** — use glob/grep/read to find and examine the actual code that will change. 2. **check for existing patterns** — search for how similar problems are already solved in the codebase. 3. **verify assumptions** — if the proposal mentions a table, class, or config, confirm it exists and check its current state. 4. **check recent git history** — look at recent commits to the affected files to understand momentum and context. do not speculate about code you haven't read. if you can't find a file or class mentioned in the proposal, flag it explicitly.

entries.name: atlas-shareable-context
entries.describe: Building Shareable Context Items with IRIS Atlas
entries.haystack: atlas-shareable-context building shareable context items with iris atlas <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: atlas-shareable-context description: share a markdown doc as a public, linkable atlas context item without guessing at the cli — author it, publish past the phi guard with the right force flag, grab the url, and land it in the right project bloq. pass a topic such as publish, guard, bloq, or verify. allowed-tools: - read - write - edit - bash - glob - grep - skill --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run atlas-shareable-context ` # building shareable context items with iris atlas a shareable context item is a **markdown file turned into a public url** you can drop into a chat, a bloq, or a client portal. atlas hosts it, gives it a stable `public_url`, and tracks the source file so re-running syncs edits. this is the fastest way to hand someone a living document — a plan, an epic, a spec — without pasting walls of text or losing version history. ## arguments `$arguments` — a topic: - `/atlas-shareable-context publish` — turn a markdown file into a public item and get the url. - `/atlas-shareable-context guard` — the phi / public safety gate and how to pass it deliberately. - `/atlas-shareable-context bloq` — land the item inside a project bloq (and the permissions trap). - `/atlas-shareable-context verify` — confirm it is actually public and the body is there. - `/atlas-shareable-context gotchas` — the defaults that bite everyone once. --- ## 1. publish — file to public url write your markdown first (any path; keep it out of the main repo if it is scratch — `.iris/` is fine). `--public` marks the intent; `--force-public` is the deliberate override of the safety gate (see §2). re-running `publish` on the same file **syncs** edits into the same item instead of duplicating — as long as the file carries the `iris_item_id` the first run stamped into it. ### verbs | command | what it does | |---|---| | `atlas:item publish <file..>` | markdown → atlas item (private by default; `--public` + `--force-public` for a url) | | `atlas:item make-public <id>` | widen an existing item to public (`--force` past the gate) | | `atlas:item make-private <id>` | revoke public sharing | | `atlas:item unpublish <file>` | make private again; `--delete` removes it | | `atlas:item list` | your published items + urls | --- ## 2. the guard — and why it is not a nag atlas **refuses to make an item public without an explicit terminal/force confirmation**. the message is blunt because it is serious: > refusing to widen note "…" to public without a terminal. this puts the note on the open > internet — anyone at all, including crawlers. once fetched it can be cached, indexed and > forwarded. making it private later does not un-send it. this fires when: - the item is in (or associated with) a **`contains_phi`** bloq, or - the cli cannot get an interactive confirmation. passing `--force-public` (on `publish`) or `--force` (on `make-public`) is you accepting that. **only do it for content with no real patient, client, or internal data** — architecture, plans, specs. if the doc sits in a phi project board, stop and ask which data is actually in it before forcing. --- ## 3. landing it in a project bloq an atlas item is not automatically in the bloq you care about. two paths: **a) publish defaulted to the wrong bloq.** `atlas:item publish` takes a **file, not a target bloq**, and has **no flag to choose the destination board**. it silently lands in your **account default bloq** (e.g. published docs). there is no cli flag to redirect it — this is a known gap (logged as iris cli bug #182488). workarounds: - move it after the fact with `blobs update-item <id> --to-bloq <bloq-id>`, or - paste the `public_url` into a new item on the correct bloq via `atlas add-item <bloq> <list> --title … --text …`. **b) write permission trap.** adding or moving an item into a bloq you are only a **shared (read-only) member** of fails with *"bloq not found or unauthorized"* — even though you can read it. `contains_phi` bloqs are especially strict. if the move is blocked: - do it in the web app where you have owner write, or - have the session granted write to that bloq, then retry. --- ## 4. verify — a 200 is not proof after publishing, confirm the item is genuinely public and carries the body: do not conclude from a green "published" message alone — check the url renders the body. --- ## 5. gotchas (learned the hard way today) - **publish has no destination-bloq flag.** it lands in your default bloq every time. decide up front whether that is where you want it, or plan to move it. (bug #182488.) - **phi guard needs `--force`.** a doc in a phi-context bloq will not go public on `--public` alone. - **re-run syncs, doesn't duplicate** — but only once the file holds its `iris_item_id`. the first run that hit the guard may have *created the item privately* before refusing; check `atlas:item list` before assuming nothing happened. - **shared bloqs are read-only from the cli.** reading works; writing/moving does not, regardless of `--user-id`. - **public is irreversible in practice.** crawlers cache. if unsure, publish private first, review, then `make-public`. --- ## reference - item verbs: `iris atlas:item --help` - bloq item move: `iris bloqs update-item <id> --to-bloq <bloq-id>` - bloq item create: `iris atlas add-item <bloq-id> <list-id> --title … --text …` - design standard (for anything client-facing):

entries.name: bespoke
entries.describe: Bespoke — custom-HTML Genesis pages
entries.haystack:
bespoke bespoke — custom-html genesis pages --- name: bespoke description: ship a bespoke (custom-html) genesis /p/ page — a hand-designed html+css document published through the composable page builder. two lanes — the customhtml component (raw html inside a composable page) and the standalone html template (full document via public-html blade). handles the whole pipeline — write scoped html, build the page json, batch-publish, and verify the live /p/ render. pass a subject brief or a slug as argument. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run bespoke ` # bespoke — custom-html genesis pages > ## stop — read the design standard before writing any html > `iris how-to view genesis-design-standard` · > > score the page against the **10-point audit** before publishing (9–10 ship · 6–8 revise · 0–5 redesign). > **check 01 predicts the rest:** could this design be moved onto a different subject unchanged? > if yes it is a template — restart from the subject, local fixes will not save it. > > three that silently break a genesis page: > 1. switch themes on **`html.dark`**, never `@media (prefers-color-scheme)` — the host owns the > theme, and a block that follows the os renders dark inside a light page. > 2. a customhtml block must **not paint its own `background`** — it becomes a floating slab. > 3. **namespace every selector** — `v-html` gives no isolation; bare `body`/`section`/`table` leak. > > and point 10: **render-verify in a browser.** grepping the served html is not verification. publish a hand-designed html page (audit report, one-pager, animated landing, spec sheet) as a live genesis page at ` use this when the composable component catalog can't express the design and you want full html+css freedom. ## arguments `$arguments` — a subject/brief (`"bug-bounty payout audit"`) or an existing slug to update. ## two lanes — pick one | lane | what | when | how it renders | |------|------|------|----------------| | **customhtml component** | a raw-html block *inside* an otherwise-composable page (`components:[{type:customhtml,props:{html}}]`) | you want one bespoke section, or a full doc, but keep it in the normal page pipeline (tailwind loaded, theme toggle works) | iris-api renders the page; `customhtml.vue` injects your html via `v-html` **inline, no isolation** | | **standalone `html` template** | a *full* html document (`render_mode=html`, `iris pages create --template=html`) served by `public-html.blade.php` | a truly standalone page — arbitrary ``, no framework, your own everything | the blade outputs your html with only a minimal baseline reset injected before your css | default to the **customhtml component** lane — it's what `pages:batch` supports cleanly and it inherits the page shell + theme. reach for the standalone lane only when you need a bare document. ## the recipe (customhtml lane) — proven ### 1. write the html — scope every selector under a wrapper class `customhtml` injects via `v-html` **with no shadow dom / iframe**, so unscoped rules collide with the genesis page shell in *both* directions. common class names (`.card`, `.tag`, `.status`, `.step`, `.meta`) and bare element selectors (`body`, `*`, `h1`, `table`) will clash. - wrap all content in one class: `
…
`. - prefix **every** selector: `.xx .card{…}`, `.xx h2{…}`, `.xx *{box-sizing:border-box}`. - put css variables + base font/color on the wrapper: `.xx{--bg:…;background:var(--bg);…}` — **not** `:root`/`body`. - theme both modes at the wrapper: `@media (prefers-color-scheme:dark){.xx{--bg:…}}` **plus** `:root[data-theme="dark"] .xx{…}` / `:root[data-theme="light"] .xx{…}` (the viewer toggle stamps `data-theme` on the root). - fonts: **csp blocks font cdns** — use system stacks (`ui-monospace,…` / `-apple-system,…`), never a webfont ``. use `font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums` for any column of figures. - design both light + dark; give headings `text-wrap:balance`; keep wide tables in an `overflow-x:auto` wrapper. ### 2. build the page json — do not use `iris pages create` `iris pages create` scaffolds from a template that auto-adds a `sitefooter` requiring a `copyright` field → **`component validation failed`**. hand-build the json and publish with `pages:batch` instead. build it with a small script so the html is json-escaped correctly: ### 3. publish via batch result: ` to **update** later: `iris pages pull `, edit `json_content.components[0].props.html`, `iris pages push ` (auto-drafts), then `iris pages publish `. (`iris pages set json_content...` also works for small edits.) ### 4. verify the live render — don't trust the publish genesis has render gotchas (a `codeblock` renders blank; an `imageblock` needs `imageurl`). always screenshot the live page: check: the wrapper's css applied (no collisions with the shell), both themes legible, tables scroll, no white gap. if it's an otp-gated page, drive the real cookie flow — not `?atlas_token=` — to verify. ## standalone `html` lane (when you need a bare document) then `pages pull` → put your **full** `…` in the html field → `pages push` → `pages publish`. `public-html.blade.php` injects a minimal reset (`box-sizing`, `html,body{margin:0}`, responsive media) *before* your css, so you can override it. no tailwind, no theme toggle — you own the whole document. ## gotchas banked - **scope or die** — customhtml is inline `v-html`; unscoped css wrecks the page shell (and vice-versa). - **`create` adds a footer** that fails validation — use `pages:batch` with hand-built json. - **fonts** — system stacks only (csp blocks cdns). - **trust gate** — raw html / `customhtml` from untrusted owners is rejected 403; owner must be trusted. - **two repos for new *components*** (not needed for bespoke html): a real component needs `customhtml.vue` + `.schema.json` + `usecomponentmap.ts` in iris-api and the fl-api `genesis-component-schemas.php` allowlist. bespoke html needs none of that — that's the point. - **verify by screenshot**, every time. ## reference - live example: ` (this playbook shipped it). - prior art: `daily-diary/2026-06-15-two-lane-genesis-bespoke-pages.md`, `daily-diary/2026-06-21-bespoke-page-body-reset.md`. - related skills: `pages` (composable cli), `import-preline-to-genesis-ui` (building real components). custom html hand-designed page artifact branded page one-pager landing page report page custom css

entries.name: beta-test-operator
entries.describe: Beta-Test Operator
entries.haystack: beta-test-operator beta-test operator <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: beta-test-operator description: beta-test a real use case end-to-end against the iris cli (or any tool), find bugs / gaps / ux issues, and file them via `iris bug report` — operator mode, report don't patch. pass the use case as argument (e.g., "download an x livestream → transcribe → cut clips → folder", "enroll a lead and send the welcome sequence", "publish a page and verify the live url"). allowed-tools: - bash - read - grep - glob - websearch - agent --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run beta-test-operator ` # beta-test operator exercise a real use case against the iris cli like a client would, surface every bug / gap / ux rough edge, and **file them** so the platform team and other agents can fix them. you are a tester and reporter, **not** an implementer. ## arguments `$arguments` — the use case to beta-test, end-to-end. examples: - `/beta-test-operator download an x livestream → transcribe → cut clips → folder` - `/beta-test-operator enroll a lead, gate payment, and send the welcome outreach` - `/beta-test-operator create a page from json, publish it, and verify the live url + qr` --- ## prime directive — operator mode: report, don't patch when something is missing or broken, **log it via `iris bug report`**. never hand-build the missing code to work around it — a workaround hides the gap from the platform and defeats the test. the deliverable is **filed bugs + a synthesis**, never patched product code. (the one thing you *may* build is a small, clearly-labeled **reference/spec** that *proves the correct pattern* and gets attached to a bug — never a shipped fix.) --- ## method 1. **define** the use case in one sentence. then keep refining it as reality emerges — the real asset is often not what it first looked like (a "video post" turns out to be a 6-hour broadcast; a "lead" turns out to be a teammate). re-scope out loud. 2. **enumerate edge cases before running.** write the matrix: happy path, boundaries (tiny / huge / long-form), malformed input, missing media, auth / rate-limit, tracking params, legacy domains/aliases, live-vs-finished, idempotency, output-dir issues, permissions. 3. **run it for real.** do not infer behavior from `--help`. execute with real inputs and confirm with the actual artifact: file on disk, **exit code**, duration, row count. `--help` lies; runtime tells the truth. 4. **stay safe while probing.** never trigger destructive / expensive / outward-facing actions to test (publishing, mass-send, multi-gb pulls, enabling live channels). probe safely first: metadata-only, `--dry-run`, smallest format, list-formats, `--text-only`, background + monitor. when in doubt, confirm with the user before any irreversible action. 5. **on a failure, get ground truth.** capture the exact command, full output, **exit code**, and tool versions. separate the iris wrapper bug from the upstream tool — re-run the underlying tool directly (yt-dlp, ffmpeg, curl, artisan) to see the real error the wrapper swallowed. 6. **apply the architecture lens.** ask whether each step's logic and output **generalize across many use cases** — is the primitive's input/output contract right, and does it scale to long-form / high-volume? if a pattern is broken, **prove the correct pattern** with a quick, measured demo and capture the numbers. 7. **check for duplicates** before filing: `iris bug list` (and `iris bug list --json | grep`). 8. **file each finding** with a tight, actionable card: - **avoid shell metacharacters** (`;` `|` `&` `<` `>` `(` `)` `` ` ``) inside the arg values — the bug-report guard rejects them. write "then" / "and" / commas instead. - severity guide: data loss / silent failure / blocks the use case = **high**; misleading ux or missing flag = **medium**; polish = **low**; security or prod incident = **critical**. 9. **think distribution.** when a fix is really a platform feature, don't stop at one card: file a coordinating **epic**, link the child bug cards, and add a **rollout intent** card — "one build → every cli user via `iris update` + every web user via deploy, no per-client rebuild" (land in the canonical `iris-daemon` repo, not a stale fork). --- ## output deliver a synthesis (do not just dump command logs): - the **refined use case** + the **edge-case matrix** you tested. - a **findings table**: each row = symptom, severity, and the **filed bug id**. - an **architecture recommendation** — and if you found a broken pattern, the proven correct one with measured numbers. - confirm you stayed in operator mode (reported, didn't hand-build a workaround). --- ## worked reference (the standard to match) the x-broadcast→clip beta test (2026-06-15, iris 1.3.88): refined "download an x video" into a **6-hour broadcast**; found `iris download` silently exits 0 on aborted pulls and swallows yt-dlp errors even at debug, has no `--quality`/time-range (forces ~6 gb), and the clip cutter is youtube/cdn-only. proved the correct **segment-addressable** pattern — `yt-dlp -g` → `ffmpeg -ss` time-range cut — pulling a 30s clip from the 2-hour mark in **7.2 s, none of the 6 gb**. filed #137379, #137380, #137384, #137385, #137386 (architecture), #137392 (spec + runnable reference), #137397 (feature epic), #137398 (rollout intent). that is the bar: real run → root cause → proven pattern → filed, distributable cards.

entries.haystack: bloq-chat-assistant bloqchatassistant — readiness atlas & development playbook <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: bloq-chat-assistant description: atlas and readiness tracker for the bloqchatassistant system across all surfaces (ui, cli, api, tui). audits feature parity, identifies gaps, maps the 17k-line component, and enforces readiness standards. pass a mode as argument (e.g., "audit", "gaps", "standards", "component-map", "design-system"). allowed-tools: - read - grep - glob - bash - agent --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run bloq-chat-assistant ` # bloqchatassistant — readiness atlas & development playbook manage, audit, and develop the bloqchatassistant across all 4 surfaces: **ui**, **cli**, **api**, **tui**. ## arguments `$arguments` — mode to run. one of: `audit`, `gaps`, `standards`, `component-map`, `design-system` examples: - `/bloq-chat-assistant audit` — cross-surface readiness matrix - `/bloq-chat-assistant gaps` — feature gap analysis with priorities - `/bloq-chat-assistant standards` — print readiness tier definitions - `/bloq-chat-assistant component-map` — index bloqchatassistant.vue sections - `/bloq-chat-assistant design-system` — theme/responsive/token audit --- ## readiness standards every feature across every surface is scored on this 4-tier scale: | tier | label | criteria | |------|-------|----------| | **t0** | prototype | code exists, untested, may crash. internal use only. | | **t1** | internal ready | works for dev/admin users. basic error handling. no public exposure. | | **t2** | ui ready | responsive, themed, accessible. mobile + desktop. eslint clean. | | **t3** | production ready | e2e tested, health-checked, deployed, monitored. documented. | **promotion rules:** - t0 -> t1: must handle errors gracefully, no console.error spam in production - t1 -> t2: must be responsive (mobile/desktop), follow theme system, pass eslint - t2 -> t3: must have e2e test coverage, be deployed, have health monitoring --- ## key files | file | surface | purpose | |------|---------|---------| | `fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui/components/dashboard/bloq/bloqchatassistant.vue` | ui | main chat component (17k lines) | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui/components/dashboard/bloq/bloqsidebar.vue` | ui | workspace left rail (1.4k lines): workflows, a2a, tools, machines, schedules (+ hive\|calendar toggle), files, leads, activity | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui/components/dashboard/bloq/bloqchatsettings.vue` | ui | chat settings modal | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui/components/dashboard/bloq/assistantpromptinput.vue` | ui | message input with voice/file upload | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui/mixins/usemodels.js` | ui | model loading/caching mixin | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-elon-web-ui/utils/mixins/messages.js` | ui | toast messages (use this, not this.$toast) | | `iris-code/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/platform-chat.ts` | cli | `iris chat` command | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/app/http/controllers/v6/chatstreamcontroller.php` | api | v6 chat execute/stream | | `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/app/http/controllers/chatcontroller.php` | api | v5 chat start/resume | | `iris-code/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/tui/app.tsx` | tui | terminal ui framework | --- ## surface inventory ### ui (bloqchatassistant.vue) — t3 production ready **chat modes:** - standard agent chat - multi-agent chat (council/discuss) - model-only chat (iris ai default: `iris/deepseek-v4`) - a2a sessions (agent-to-agent coding sessions) - echo mode (voice + imessage integration) **agent/model selection:** - combined project + agent selector (responsive: stacked mobile, inline desktop) - featured models list (iris ai first, then gpt/gemini/grok) - ollama local models (when bridge connected) - team agents (personal, per-project) - workflow agents + standalone workflows **features:** - file upload (images, pdfs, documents) - rag/knowledge base integration - text-to-speech with voice selection - typing effect (configurable speed) - artifacts (generated files from workflows) - cloud files (persistent reports) - conversation memory (configurable depth) - real-time workflow tracking (pusher/echo) **workspace sidebar (`bloqsidebar.vue`):** - collapsible accordion sections: workflows/campaigns, a2a sessions, tools & integrations, machines, schedules, files, leads, activity - **schedules section** has a `hive | calendar` toggle — calendar lazy-loads the connected google calendar agenda from `/api/v1/calendar/events` (read-only, source-labeled). see the `project_calendar_display` system + `iris calendar`. **settings:** - response mode (creative/balanced/precise) - context window size - communication style - integrations toggle - echo mode config (wake words, silence delay) ### cli (`iris chat`) — t2 ui ready **capabilities:** - `iris chat "message"` — send message to agent - `--agent <id>` / `-a` — select agent (interactive picker if omitted) - `--bloq <id>` / `-b` — knowledge base for rag - `--no-rag` — disable knowledge base - `--json` — json output - `--timeout <seconds>` — max wait (default 300s) - `--continue <workflow-id>` — resume workflow - `iris chat approve <id>` — approve paused workflow **missing vs ui:** - no model override (`--model` flag) - no multi-agent mode - no streaming output - no file upload - no voice/echo mode - no conversation memory/history ### api (iris-api) — t3 production ready **v5 (legacy):** - `post /api/chat/start` — start chat - `post /api/chat/resume` — resume paused workflow - `post /api/chat/summarize` — summarize conversation **v6 (modern):** - `post /api/v6/chat/execute` — execute with polling/pusher - `post /api/v6/chat/stream` — streaming execution - `post /api/v6/chat/classify-intent` — intent classification debug - `get /api/v6/chat/{workflowid}/result` — async result fetch **workflow status:** - `get /api/workflows/{workflowid}` — get status - `get /api/users/{userid}/workflows` — list workflows - `get /api/users/{userid}/workflows/stats` — workflow stats ### tui — t0 prototype **what exists:** - solidjs terminal rendering framework (`app.tsx`, 22k lines) - agent picker dialog - session list dialog - mcp server connection ui - command palette, keybindings, themes **what's missing:** - no dedicated chat view/route - no message display - no agent response rendering - uses cli command instead of native tui chat --- ## mode: `audit` --- ## mode: `gaps` --- ## mode: `standards` --- ## mode: `component-map` --- ## mode: `design-system`

entries.name: bounty-os
entries.describe: Bounty OS
entries.haystack: bounty-os bounty os <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: bounty-os description: make sure reported work actually earns. filing without credit fails silently — the item saves fine, the reporter just never gets paid — so this covers attributing a bug or feature at the moment you file it, proving the credit landed, and checking what a hunter is owed before you quote them a number. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run bounty-os ` > steps: file-bug → file-feature → verify-attribution → standing → my-standing → pay # bounty os filing work so it earns, and checking the money afterwards. two boards can earn, and only two — bugs on **#297** and feature requests on **#652**. that list is `config('bounty.credited_bloq_ids')`, and it is short on purpose: every id on it becomes payable in a sweep. **bloq 503 is deliberately absent** — it holds 914 items, and adding it would make all of them payable at once. ## the one rule that costs money when it is broken **attribution goes on at filing time.** `--reporter-lead` is what makes work earn; without it the item is credited to whoever ran the command, and nothing anywhere surfaces the mistake. `bug update --reporter-lead` exists to repair a ticket already filed, but it only works on the bug board — an item filed anywhere else cannot be repaired after the fact. **never pass `--reporter-name`.** it is a per-bug snapshot, and using it to correct an attribution once renamed a hunter across all 108 of their bugs. the display name resolves from the lead. passing only `--reporter-lead` is both correct and safe. ## steps

entries.name: brand-name-clearance
entries.describe: Brand name clearance
entries.haystack: brand-name-clearance brand name clearance <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: brand-name-clearance description: screen a product or sub-brand name before it reaches a domain, a repository, an app store or a customer. catches the three ways a name becomes expensive — a living estate that enforces, a mark already registered in your class, and a name nobody actually verified the spelling of. a pre-screen that decides whether to pay a lawyer, never a substitute for one. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run brand-name-clearance <name> <what>` > steps: spell → identity → internal → domain → marks → verdict → record # brand name clearance **the one idea:** a name is nearly free to change before it ships and very expensive after. the cost is not the rename — it is the domain, the app store listing, the printed material, the ad account, the customer who knows you by it, and the letter. **this is a pre-screen, not legal advice.** its only job is to sort a name into *proceed*, *get a lawyer to look*, or *drop it now*. a clean run here does not clear anything; it means the obvious problems are absent and paying for a real search is worth it. ## the case this came from on 2026-09-02 a meeting chose **khalo** for an ai-augmented design system, explicitly inspired by **frida kahlo**. three things were true at once and only one had been noticed: - the **frida kahlo corporation** holds and actively enforces the mark, including against products that merely evoke her. - our own meeting notes name her as the inspiration, which **documents intent** — the thing a defence would most want absent. - the transcript's other candidates were **speech-to-text garbled**: oshun came through as "ocean", itzamná as "it's amna", sankofa as both "suncopa" and "wisconsin". screening from that list would have searched names nobody proposed. the name was chosen anyway, which is a legitimate call for the person who owns the brand. what this playbook exists to prevent is that call being made *without the exposure on the table*, or the name reaching a domain before anyone checked. ## the three failure modes, in the order they bite 1. **a living estate.** artists, musicians, athletes and their foundations enforce aggressively, and sound-alike spellings do not help — they can worsen it, because changing one letter looks like evasion rather than coincidence. 2. **a registered mark in your class.** trademarks are per goods/services class. "halo" in software is crowded; "halo" in shampoo is irrelevant to you. **screen your class, not the word.** 3. **a name nobody verified.** transcripts, voice notes and memory all corrupt names. screening the wrong spelling returns a clean result that means nothing. ## steps

entries.name: bridge-doctor
entries.describe: Bridge Doctor — Local Compute Debugging Skill
entries.haystack: bridge-doctor bridge doctor — local compute debugging skill <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: bridge-doctor description: diagnose, fix, and manage the iris bridge/daemon system — the local compute layer that executes hive tasks (som, code_generation, etc.). use when the bridge won't start, daemon shows "stopped", tasks aren't executing, port conflicts, key mismatches, or docker container collisions. pass an action as argument (e.g., "status", "diagnose", "fix", "restart", "sync-key"). allowed-tools: - read - bash - grep - glob - edit - task --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run bridge-doctor ` # bridge doctor — local compute debugging skill diagnose and fix issues with the iris bridge + embedded daemon system. ## arguments `$arguments` — action to perform. examples: - `/bridge-doctor status` — quick health check of bridge, daemon, and node - `/bridge-doctor diagnose` — full diagnostic (port, keys, docker, config, daemon) - `/bridge-doctor fix` — auto-fix all safe issues (stop conflicting containers, sync keys) - `/bridge-doctor restart` — kill and restart bridge in local mode - `/bridge-doctor sync-key` — push current db key to ~/.iris/config.json via bridge api - `/bridge-doctor logs` — show recent bridge/daemon output - `/bridge-doctor tasks` — list pending/running tasks on this node - `/bridge-doctor port` — check what's on port 3200 --- ## architecture quick reference ### components | component | role | location | |-----------|------|----------| | **bridge** (`index.js`) | express server on port 3200. handles cli sessions (claude, ollama, opencode), file system access, messaging bots (telegram, discord, imessage) | `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/index.js` | | **embedded daemon** | authenticates with iris-api cloud, subscribes to pusher, executes dispatched tasks. runs inside the bridge process | `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/index.js` | | **schedule registry** | local cron scheduling via `node-cron`. persists to `schedules.json`, fires scripts, reports results to cloud with offline fallback | `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/schedule-registry.js` | | **config** | api keys, pusher config, pause state | `~/.iris/config.json` | | **doctor** | diagnostic script that checks all the above | `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/doctor.js` | ### startup flow ### key files - **bridge main**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/index.js` - **daemon class**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/index.js` - **cloud client**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/cloud-client.js` - **task executor**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/task-executor.js` - **pusher client**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/daemon/pusher-client.js` - **doctor script**: `fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/doctor.js` - **config file**: `~/.iris/config.json` - **bridge .env**: `~/.iris/bridge/.env` ### npm commands ### common failure modes #### 1. "bridge already running — attaching as monitor" + daemon=stopped **root cause**: docker container `fl-coding-agent-bridge` is occupying port 3200. the bridge process can't bind, falls back to monitor mode against the docker container (which has no daemon). **diagnosis**: **fix**: `docker stop fl-coding-agent-bridge && npm run bridge:local` **auto-fix**: in iris_local=1 mode, index.js now auto-stops the docker container on eaddrinuse. #### 2. "http 401: invalid api key" on daemon startup **root cause**: key in `~/.iris/config.json` doesn't match any node in the iris-api database. usually happens when key was regenerated via ui but config file wasn't updated. **diagnosis**: **fix**: update `~/.iris/config.json` with the correct key from the db, or use ui "connect" modal → "sync to bridge". #### 3. daemon starts but tasks never execute **check**: is the node status `busy` with old tasks? are tasks stuck in `dispatched` status? #### 4. "no node_api_key found — bridge-only mode" **root cause**: no key in env var `node_api_key` and no `~/.iris/config.json` with `node_api_key` or `local_api_key`. **fix**: register a node via the hive ui, then either: - click "connect" → "sync to bridge" in the ui - or manually add key to `~/.iris/config.json` ### config file format - `node_api_key`: used when `iris_local` is not set (production mode) - `local_api_key`: used when `iris_local=1` (local development mode) - both connect to the same daemon code, just different api targets ### bridge api endpoints (for programmatic access) ### apple mail — send emails with attachments & cc the bridge can send emails via mail.app using applescript. supports file attachments and cc recipients. **parameters:** | field | type | required | description | |-------|------|----------|-------------| | `to_email` | string | yes | recipient email address | | `to_name` | string | no | recipient display name (defaults to email) | | `cc_email` | string or string[] | no | cc recipient(s) | | `subject` | string | yes | email subject line | | `body_text` | string | yes | plain-text email body | | `attachments` | string[] | no | array of absolute file paths to attach | **laravel (bridgeservice):** **requirements:** macos with mail.app configured. bridge must be running (`npm run bridge:local`). ### backend (iris-api) endpoints | endpoint | method | auth | purpose | |----------|--------|------|---------| | `/api/v6/nodes` | get | bearer | list user's nodes (now includes `api_key`) | | `/api/v6/nodes` | post | bearer | register new node (returns key once) | | `/api/v6/nodes/{id}/regenerate-key` | post | bearer | generate new key (invalidates old) | | `/api/v6/nodes/heartbeat` | post | x-node-key | daemon heartbeat (auth by node key) | | `/api/v6/nodes/tasks` | get/post | bearer | list/create tasks | ### frontend component - **hivenoderegistry**: `fl-elon-web-ui/components/hive/hivenoderegistry.vue` - connect modal shows key directly from node data (`api_key` field) - "sync to bridge" button pushes key to local bridge via `post /api/config/key` - "regenerate key" auto-syncs to bridge after generating - **vuex store**: `fl-elon-web-ui/store/nodes.js` --- ## action implementations ### status run `npm run bridge:doctor` and summarize the output. if bridge is healthy, confirm. if issues, explain each one. ### diagnose full investigation: 1. `lsof -i :3200` — who owns the port? 2. `curl — is bridge responding? 3. `cat ~/.iris/config.json` — are keys present? 4. `docker ps --filter "publish=3200"` — docker conflict? 5. check iris-api db for node + key match 6. check daemon logs for auth errors ### fix run `npm run bridge:doctor -- --fix` for automated fixes. for key mismatches, query the db and update config. ### restart ### sync-key 1. query iris-api for the node's current `api_key` 2. push to bridge via `post 3. verify with `get ### logs ### tasks

entries.haystack: capture-sops-and-process-maps capture sops and process maps <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: capture-sops-and-process-maps description: capture sops as screen recordings instead of written docs, turn them into process maps, and separate out the rules that aren't procedures at all. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run capture-sops-and-process-maps ` > steps: step-1 → step-2 → step-3 → step-4 → step-5 → step-6 → step-7 # capture sops and process maps capture a process by recording your screen while you do it, turn that into a formal process map — and catch the parts that are actually rules, not procedures, before they get miscaptured as steps. > written from two experience art / x-art team calls: the sop-capture decision on > 2026-08-24 (bloq #570, board #182224) and the rules-gap discussion on 2026-08-21 > (board #181754/#181753). read every step before running it. ## why this exists — two capture problems, not one this team hit two distinct problems while building their "company brain," and conflating them is the failure mode this playbook exists to prevent: 1. **written sops are slow and drift from reality.** the fix: record the screen while doing the work, narrate the reasoning out loud, and let an agent turn that into the formal document — instead of someone writing it up after the fact from memory. 2. **not everything that feels like an sop is a procedure.** some of what people were trying to capture had no steps, no owner running it weekly, no maturity level — it was a **rule**: a scope (where it applies), a direction (do / never), and a reason someone will otherwise argue with. filing a rule as if it were a process step loses the part that actually matters. ## the worked example that makes the distinction concrete a company description existed in two versions, ~140 words each. one mentioned a specific brand touchstone; the other didn't. - version a (with the touchstone) → fine for journalists, fine for sales and clients - version a → **never** website-facing or public-facing that's not a process — there's no sequence of steps. it's a rule: **scope** (which channel), **direction** (use it / never use it here), **reason** (context journalists and sales conversations have that a cold website visitor doesn't). a second example from the same session: a coined phrase the team wants press to use but would never put on their own website, because nobody searches a phrase they invented — same shape, different rule. **where rules like this go:** not as loose bullet points beside the main content, but as their own linked pools — e.g. a "press language" skill linking out to approved pr keywords and the pr copy folder, separate from a "marketing language" skill with its own (different, sometimes contradictory) rules. rather than writing independent rules scattered across documents, group each audience/context into its own skill, and have each skill link to its proper pool of source data. that cross-referencing structure is the point — it's what keeps rule a ("always" for sales) from silently contradicting rule b ("never" for the public site) when they're read out of context. **rule of thumb for when to split:** keep a topic in one document until it gets too big; fork a section into its own skill only when it becomes a real, distinct business component that needs its own context — not preemptively. ## the capture pipeline itself manually-written sops are slow to produce and drift from what people actually do. the team's decision: the screen recording (with narration) is the source document. a written version is an *output* generated from it afterward, not a separate authoring step someone has to remember to do. a validated real-world signal this works: one team member ran a similar context-extraction pass over their own ai chat history and email, looking for codified rules rather than routine processes — and it surfaced roughly **47 distinct rule/inconsistency findings** (small corrections made repeatedly, like avoiding overuse of a specific word) that had never been written down anywhere as an explicit rule. the value wasn't in the prose responses — it was specifically in the corrections: the small moments where a person had to fix an ai's output for a domain-specific reason. that correction *is* the rule, and it's usually invisible until someone goes looking for it. ## steps --- ## why these steps are instructions, not commands this was authored from two live meeting discussions, not a single recorded walkthrough of one process. each step is an instruction a person or agent carries out and can check first — not a black-box automation. promote a step to `mode: shell` yourself once you know the exact command for your own transcription/ingest tooling.
