list-connected`, show health per integration | | `connect <type>` | run `iris connect <type>`, walk user through oauth flow | | `setup <type>` | run `iris integrations setup <type>` with api key flags | | `exec <type> <fn>` | run `iris integrations exec <type> <function> [params]` | | `functions <type>` | list available functions for a specific integration type | | `test <type>` | execute a minimal function call to verify connectivity | | `test all` | loop through connected integrations, test each one | | `debug` | check logs, env vars, token expiry, cross-service auth | | `add <type>` | guide through adding a new integration service class | ### when listing integrations 1. run `iris integrations list-integrations` 2. cross-reference with connected status if available 3. group by category (oauth, api-key, platform-internal) 4. show which ones are connected vs available ### when connecting an oauth integration 1. run `iris connect <type>` — this generates an oauth url 2. tell the user to complete the browser auth flow 3. verify connection: `iris integrations exec <type> <simple_function>` 4. report success or troubleshoot ### when executing a function 1. validate the integration type exists in the registry 2. run `iris integrations exec <type> <function> [key=value ...]` 3. parse and display the json response 4. if error, check: (a) is integration connected? (b) are params correct? (c) is token expired? ### when debugging 1. check `iris list-connected` for connection status 2. check iris-api logs: `tail -f storage/logs/laravel.log | grep integration` 3. verify env vars in production: ssh + `php artisan tinker` 4. test with minimal function call 5. if oauth issue, re-connect: `iris connect <type>` 6. if cross-service issue, check `fl_raichu_api_token` ### when adding a new integration 1. create service class in `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/app/services/integrations/<name>integrationservice.php` 2. register in `integrationregistry.php` (both iris-api and fl-api if needed) 3. add routes in `routes/api.php` if custom endpoints needed 4. add oauth config to `config/services.php` if oauth-based 5. create migration for any custom tables 6. add to this skill's registry table above 7. test: `iris integrations exec <new-type> <function>` --- ## notes - **test emails always go to alex@freelabel.net** — never send test emails to real clients - **ai models**: when testing integrations that use ai (intent routing, servis-ai analysis), only use gpt-5-nano, gpt-4.1-nano, or gpt-4o-mini - **iris-api vs fl-api**: both have integration registries. iris-api is the primary for cli execution. fl-api has its own for backend workflows - **composio**: some integrations were originally built on composio but migrated to native. if composio is mentioned in code, prefer the native implementation - **rate limits**: google apis have per-user quotas. mercury has strict rate limits. buffer has posting limits per plan - **credential storage**: all credentials encrypted at rest in the `integrations` table. never log or expose raw tokens

entries.name: iris-khalo
entries.describe: IRIS Khalo
entries.haystack: iris-khalo iris khalo <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: iris-khalo description: produce a finished design artefact from the iris khalo component system — pick an existing layout instead of inventing one, render it, and catch the four defects that have shipped from this system before. every check here is one that reached a live page or a paid ad. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run iris-khalo <subject>` > steps: inventory → literals → render → thumbnail → verify → publish → card → record # iris khalo **ai-augmented design, not image generation.** khalo does not invent a picture from a prompt. it pours a subject into a layout that already exists, in a brand ink that already exists, and returns an artefact you can verify. thirty-one components sit under `remotion/src/carousel/`; two brand kits already name the inks, the type roles and what each layout is for. **so the job is choosing, not designing.** a brief written on 2026-09-01 invented hero objects and palettes for three campaigns without opening either kit. all of it already existed, named, with a rule attached. ## the four defects this system has actually shipped not hypotheticals. all four happened, all four rendered *cleanly* while being wrong. 1. **components carry copy from the subject they were born for.** five found in one day: `pingslide` printed **"■ you did nothing"** on an iris install ad; `apprenticeshipslide` printed **"no tuition"** and, on the red flip bar, **"you stop paying → you start getting paid"** on a $49/mo subscription — a false claim about money in the ad's most prominent element; `indexslide` hardcoded the corner wordmark to **iris** and the badge to the iris cube on a freelabel creative. **grep the component for string literals before you trust the render.** 2. **a layout that overflows argues against its own headline.** `indexslide` at 12 entries showed eight, under a headline reading twelve products. it rendered perfectly. nothing catches this but looking at the output. 3. **a document layout is grey mush at 110px, which is where an ad is first seen.** measured: press/document creatives ran **8,348 impressions for 2 clicks at $1.29 cpc**, against **$0.0043** for a poster-format ad on the same account the same week. two of four line items produced zero clicks across 3,432 impressions. 4. **flyer lines collide when adjacent lines are similar in width.** `flyerslide` sets every line at a fixed 162px with `nowrap` and `lineheight: 0.86`, so lines always overlap by design — and in light mode the offset plate uses `multiply`, printing heavy. `keep / 100% / ownership` steps short→medium→long and reads as layering. `already / earning? / keep 100%` is three long lines and reads as mush. **it is not a character limit** — an earlier version of this file said six characters and that was wrong; `ownership` is nine and reads fine. ## choosing the form from the brand kits, and it is a mapping, not a preference: announcing something -> masthead a dateline and a band read as news listing n capabilities -> index numbering makes a list finite one line that is the product -> flyer give the sentence the whole canvas comparing tiers or specs -> ledger label -> value rows on hairlines one number that carries it -> stat the figure is the hero a threshold someone crosses -> apprentice a rule, with the ink reversing across it what runs while you are away -> night sheet the industry's own paperwork for absence one move, n destinations -> patch list a patch bay is a handover who keeps what -> settlement the middle column is the argument **if the form does not carry the argument, the copy is doing work the layout should do.** two angles changed form mid-build on 2026-09-01 for exactly this reason and both got better. ## steps

entries.name: iris-lexicon
entries.describe: IRIS Lexicon
entries.haystack: iris-lexicon iris lexicon <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: iris-lexicon description: run a legal matter end to end through lexicon's five doors — intake, conflicts, engagement, chronology, demand — in the order a matter actually moves, with the one gate nothing in the tooling enforces called out where it belongs. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run iris-lexicon ` > steps: intake → open → conflicts → engage → chronology → demand → close # iris lexicon **what it is:** the front door onto five legal playbooks that already existed — `legal-matter-intake`, `legal-conflict-check`, `legal-engagement-letter`, `legal-matter-chronology`, `legal-demand-letter` — given a name a firm can type. `iris lexicon demand 123` and `iris playbook run legal-demand-letter 123` are the same rails. **what it is not: a matter management system.** no tables, no routes, no service class. it stores nothing — not which matters are open, which conflicts are cleared, which letters went out — and it has no send command. **what it is not: a lawyer.** every artefact below is a **draft for a qualified person to review**: the sweep surfaces conflict candidates and does not clear a conflict, the letter is a drafting aid rather than approved terms, the demand says `attorney review required` and means it. **this is not a sixth implementation.** it is the order of operations — what the five playbooks cannot know, because none knows what ran before it. ## the order a matter moves — and the gate nothing enforces enquiry ──intake──> matter record ──conflicts──> clearance ──engagement──> engaged ▲ │ an attorney, not a command │ demand <──readiness── chronology <─────────────────────┘ - **conflicts must precede the engagement letter.** `legal-matter-intake` says so in prose; its brief ends `next: run legal-conflict-check on the conflict_names before engaging.` - **nothing enforces it.** verified: `legal-engagement-letter` contains no reference to a conflict check — no gate, no precondition — and neither does the demand or the chronology. `iris lexicon engagement 123` runs happily on a matter never swept. the order is a discipline this playbook carries; it is not a rail. - **chronology before demand is a dependency, not etiquette.** the demand's readiness step reads the log the chronology assembles; off an empty log, `ready with gaps` means *we could not look*. ## the state everyone misreads **there is no matter state.** the lead's crm status is the only durable field and its taxonomy is a sales one — `new, prospected, qualified, proposal, in negotiation, active, won, lost`. none means *conflicts cleared* or *engaged*, and nothing in lexicon writes it. "has this been swept?" is answerable only from the bloq, or from a person. - **`--bloq` without `--list` silently does not file.** all five playbooks print `no --list given; printing instead of filing` and exit 0 — a successful-looking run that wrote nothing. get the list id from `iris bloqs get <bloq>`. - **intake and everything after it speak different languages.** `intake` takes an enquiry *string*; the other four take a numeric *lead id*. the bridge is `--open yes` → `iris leads create`, called **without `--json`**, so the new id is printed in prose and read off the output by eye. - **args are positional, in declaration order** (`enquiry party lead bloq`) — enter mid-lifecycle by passing empty strings for the earlier ones: `iris playbook run iris-lexicon "" "jane roe" 29092 570`. an empty optional interpolates to an empty string, so every step tests and skips rather than run on nothing. ## steps

entries.name: iris-memory
entries.describe: IRIS Agent Memory — Unified Memory Management
entries.haystack: iris-memory iris agent memory — unified memory management <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: iris-memory description: give your agents a memory that survives between conversations instead of starting over every session. store what matters, ask for it back in plain language later, and see how a lead, task, or invoice connects to everything else around it. pass an action and arguments. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run iris-memory ` # iris agent memory — unified memory management store, search, and manage persistent agent memory through the iris cli. the memory namespace provides both **unstructured working memory** (facts, insights, context, documents) and **structured crm entity access** (leads, tasks, invoices, outreach steps) through a single unified interface. ## arguments `$arguments` — action and parameters. examples: - `/iris-memory store 11 "client prefers morning meetings"` — store a fact - `/iris-memory store 11 document "contract: john doe hired as dj..."` — store a document - `/iris-memory search 11 "meeting preferences"` — search memories - `/iris-memory list 11` — list all memories for agent - `/iris-memory entities 11` — list leads in agent's workspace - `/iris-memory entities 11 tasks` — list tasks across all leads - `/iris-memory graph 11` — full entity relationship map - `/iris-memory delete <uuid>` — delete a memory --- ## important: always use production api **all memory and diary commands must hit the production iris-api**, not local docker containers. the local environment often lacks agent data and will return "agent not found" errors. **production base url**: ` (railway production url — replaces old do endpoint) ### primary method: direct curl to production ### fallback method: sdk cli (for local debugging only) the sdk `.env` at `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/.env` has `iris_env=production`, but agent resolution can still fail if the agent id doesn't exist as a `bloqagent` in the production fl_api db. when using the diary endpoint, prefer `bloq_id=217` over `agent_id=11`. ### agent/bloq id reference | agent | bloq | name | |-------|------|------| | 11 | 217 | iris platform growth - q1 2026 | | 407 | (default) | production general agent | for diary entries, always use `bloq_id` (more reliable than `agent_id`). --- ## memory types | type | purpose | dedup | |------|---------|-------| | `fact` | learned information ("client budget is $50k") | yes | | `insight` | discovered patterns ("open rates peak tuesdays") | yes | | `context` | project/workflow status ("phase 3 of 5 complete") | yes | | `preference` | user preferences ("prefers formal tone") | yes | | `relationship` | info about other agents | yes | | `document` | contracts, agreements, reference docs | **no** (dedup skipped) | **dedup behavior:** for all types except `document`, the system checks the first 200 chars for >80% similarity via `similar_text()`. if a match is found, the existing memory is updated instead of creating a duplicate. documents skip this entirely because contracts with the same event/date prefix would incorrectly merge. --- ## commands reference ### store memory ### search memory ### list memories ### delete memory ### entity memory (structured crm proxy) these commands resolve the **agent -> bloq -> leads** chain automatically. --- ## architecture ### three-tier memory ### url routing the sdk routes memory requests to **iris-api** (`heyiris.io`), not fl-api: - memory endpoints: ` - routing rule in `sdk/php/src/http/client.php:buildurl()` matches `/v6/memory` - entity endpoints query fl_api db via iris-api's `fl_api` database connection ### key files | file | purpose | |------|---------| | `fl-iris-api/app/http/controllers/api/agentmemorycontroller.php` | rest api (crud + entities + graph) | | `fl-iris-api/app/neuron/tools/agentmemorytool.php` | agent tool path (used by ai agents during workflows) | | `fl-iris-api/app/models/agentsurfacememory.php` | memory model (uuid, soft-delete, chromadb embeddings) | | `fl-iris-api/app/models/flapi/lead.php` | lead model with tasks/invoices/outreach relationships | | `fl-iris-api/app/models/flapi/leadtask.php` | task model for entity proxy | | `fl-iris-api/app/models/flapi/customrequest.php` | invoice/deal model for entity proxy | | `fl-iris-api/app/models/flapi/leadoutreachstep.php` | outreach step model for entity proxy | | `fl-iris-api/routes/api.php` | routes under `v6/memory` prefix | | `sdk/php/src/resources/memory/memoryresource.php` | sdk resource class (cli auto-proxy) | | `sdk/php/src/http/client.php` | url routing (`/v6/memory` -> irisurl) | ### entity chain resolution --- ## daily diary the diary provides a **unified timeline** that merges two data sources: 1. **diary entries** (bloqitems) — structured markdown entries from heartbeats and manual cli input 2. **heartbeat memories** (agentsurfacememory) — auto-stored summaries from the heartbeat system diary lives at the **bloq level** — each bloq has a "daily diary" list. agents resolve to their bloq automatically. ### diary commands ### diary architecture --- ## common workflows ### daily standup ### store contracts ### sales agent context load --- ## troubleshooting ### "the selected memory type is invalid" the `memory_type` enum in the database doesn't include the type you're trying to use. run the migration: ### 404 on memory endpoints the sdk might be routing to fl-api instead of iris-api. check `sdk/php/src/http/client.php:buildurl()` — memory endpoints must contain `/v6/memory` to route to `irisurl` (heyiris.io). ### documents getting merged/overwritten the dedup check in `agentmemorycontroller.php` and `agentmemorytool.php` must skip `type=document`. look for: ### "agent has no associated bloq" on entities the agent doesn't have a `bloq_id` set. entities require the agent -> bloq -> leads chain. check: --- ## steps ### 1. parse the argument | argument pattern | action | |-----------------|--------| | `store <agent_id> "<content>"` | store as fact (default) | | `store <agent_id> <type> "<content>"` | store with specific type | | `search <agent_id> "<query>"` | search memories | | `list <agent_id>` | list memories (optionally with filters) | | `delete <uuid>` | delete a memory | | `entities <agent_id>` | list leads | | `entities <agent_id> <type>` | list tasks/invoices/outreach | | `graph <agent_id>` | full relationship graph | ### 2. run the command via production api always use direct curl to the production iris-api do url: for diary entries, use `bloq_id=217` instead of `agent_id=11` (more reliable). only fall back to the sdk cli (`cd fl-docker-dev/sdk/php && php bin/iris ...`) when explicitly debugging local development. ### 3. display results format the json response for readability. for `graph` responses, consider displaying the tree structure visually.

entries.name: iris-pulse
entries.describe: IRIS Pulse
entries.haystack: iris-pulse iris pulse <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: iris-pulse description: score health for a subject that has a row and for work that does not — read your own account readiness, one account's deal health, or sweep the trail a topic left across commits, diary, files, agent sessions and mail. then arm an alert so the score comes to you instead of you going to it. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run iris-pulse ` > steps: score → read → lead → trail → file → alerts → arm → agency # iris pulse **what it is:** a scoring engine with its own subjects, history and alarms. `scoperegistry` declares seven subjects — `lead`, `user`, `heartbeat_lead`, `heartbeat_user`, `creator`, `project`, `topic` — each scored across ~20 signals (setup, agent liveness, comms, billing, integrations, outreach, tasks, content, knowledge, meetings, response time, referrals, deliverables, opportunities). `pulse:tick` snapshots those scores into `readiness_runs`, `pulse_alert_rules` fire against consecutive snapshots, `readiness_remediation_tasks` hold what to do about it. **what it is not: a view over your crm.** that is the obvious guess and it is wrong. three scopes — `creator`, `project`, `topic` — score subjects that **have no crm row at all**. that is the point of `pulse check`: *"creator os" has no id, no owner and no record — only a trail*, across commits, diary, agent transcripts, files, messages and mail. pulse walks that trail and files the result as a scored entity in the **signal corpus** (`signal_entities`, `signal_observations`, `signal_entity_vectors`), so the second time you ask there is history to diff instead of a fresh grep. leads cannot represent that subject, so this cannot be a view over them. ## three subjects, one word iris pulse → you how healthy is my own account? iris leads pulse <id> → one account how healthy is this deal? iris pulse --admin → every client agency scorecard (other people's data) iris pulse check "<kw>" → a trail is this thread warm enough to continue? **confusing these is the most common pulse mistake.** a bad number on the wrong subject sends you to fix the wrong thing. ## the state everyone misreads **a low signal usually means "not measured," not "unhealthy."** setup scoring 10/100 because `iris init` never ran looks identical to setup scoring 10/100 because setup is broken. the score cannot distinguish *we looked and it is bad* from *we could not look*. confirm the input exists before acting on a red — otherwise you are optimising a measurement gap. three more, each of which has cost someone an afternoon: - **`--for n` counts `pulse:tick` snapshots, not your cli runs.** the tick is `everytwohours()`, so `--for 3` is roughly six hours of sustained badness. (the comment above it still says "every 15 min" — stale. trust the code.) - **momentum `null` is not "flat."** null means no prior observation to diff against. a first sweep is always null. - **the corpus scheduler is off unless `corpus_scheduler_enabled` is set.** `corpus:tick` and `corpus:sweep` spend quota and send discord, so a deploy is deliberately not allowed to start them. if nobody enabled it, corpus scores are as fresh as the last manual sweep. ## steps

entries.name: iris-reachr
entries.describe: IRIS Reachr
entries.haystack: iris-reachr iris reachr <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: iris-reachr description: turn "we should follow up with these people" into a sequence that survives the week — audit the offer you are carrying, build an outreach strategy once, apply it to a lead, work the steps through the comms router so every touch lands in the ledger, and issue the licence when someone says yes. reachr owns the whole arc — what you sell, how it reaches people, and what a yes produces. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run iris-reachr <bloq>` > steps: offer → existing → design → create → apply → work → review # iris reachr **what it is:** the revenue chain. reachr's end state is a **collected payment** you can trace back through fulfilment → licence → payment → package → opportunity → buyer → organization. if you cannot walk that chain, a relationship is missing. offers what you are selling iris reachr offers audit strategies how it reaches somebody iris reachr list / apply <- the steps below send the touch actually going out iris outreach-send send licence what a yes produces iris reachr licence issue **the crm models relationships, not contacts.** a person belongs to several organizations, may influence one deal while somebody else pays, may refer, may administer a licence. an organization has locations, brands, subscriptions, licences and several live opportunities. every connection is stored with a **role** — buyer · decision maker · champion · billing contact · user · referral source · partner · licence administrator. five atlas datasets hold this: reachr-organization the account reachr-relationship person <-> org <-> opportunity, with a role reachr-opportunity one primary package, expected value, next action, owner reachr-payment the closing event, linked to everything around it reachr-fulfilment what was delivered, checkpoints, renewal, churn risk, expansion **the four questions.** for every active relationship the system must answer: what is the highest-value outcome available · what package fits it · what evidence or action moves it forward · who owns the next action. **no package, no next action, no owner, or no expected value means it is not a deal — it is an unqualified contact**, and it does not belong in a forecast. **the progression.** captured → qualified → scoped → package selected → checkout sent → payment pending → paid → activated → fulfilled → retained → expanded → referred. the point is not more stages; it is that every stage creates a **measurable position relative to payment**. **rank by expected collected revenue, not activity.** package value × likelihood × urgency × relationship strength × decision-maker access, decayed by time since the last real touch — and **subtract** for no next step, no identified buyer, no package selected, stale follow-up. the output is one answer to "what do i do today": move the highest-value, most-likely-to-pay opportunity one step closer to checkout. **payment does not end it.** payment creates entitlement, entitlement defines access, and access belongs to a person *or an organization*. on payment: assign the package, issue the licence, start fulfilment, schedule checkpoints, watch renewal, surface expansion. a *strategy* is a sequence of steps — what to say, in what order, how long to wait. you write it once, apply it to any lead, and reachr tracks where each person is in it. **the middle part is only as good as the first.** a sequence carries an offer; if the offer has no stack, no price anchor and no guarantee, more follow-ups will not fix it — they will just reach more people with the same reason to say no. that is why this playbook starts by auditing the offer rather than by writing copy. **what it is not: a single send button — yet.** `outreach-send send`, `vary` and `personalize` report **"not yet available"**. that is a **missing wire, not a missing capability**: this platform sends every day, through paths that already log to the comms ledger. iris mail send <to> email, via the comms router — lands in the log iris imessage send <handle> sms/imessage, logged to the comms ledger those two are the only commands that call the router (`routersend` in comms-send.ts). `iris som` is campaign machinery against /api/v1/som/campaigns — it has its own server-side ledger, but it is not the same code path and should not be reached for when you mean "send this one person their next step". **and the missing wire is 40 lines, not a feature.** the server door is already built: `post /api/v1/atlas/comms/send` (`routes/api.php:2789`) carries the comment *"every non-php surface (cli `reachr send`, agent tools, dashboard) sends through here so the ledger write cannot be skipped"*. `commsrouter` enforces caps and suppression, writes `lead_comms`, and `outreachprogress::oncommlogged()` **completes the step automatically** from `step_id`. the cli's `sendcmd` is a stub that says *"not implemented on the server"* — which is no longer true. **so the loop is real, it is just not one command.** reachr says who is owed what; you send through `mail`, `imessage` or a som campaign; the comms ledger records it; you mark the step complete. the gap between "reachr told me to send this" and "the send happened" is currently a human, and closing it is wiring `outreach-send send` to the router that `mail` and `imessage` already use — not building a sender. **know which one you are in.** som is for *campaigns* — many leads, one script, with a ledger and retry. reachr is for *sequences* — one lead, several steps, over time. using som for a sequence gives you no memory of where each person is; using reachr for a campaign means sending by hand a hundred times. ## the shape offer what the sequence is carrying │ iris reachr offers audit ▼ strategy (lives on a board, reusable) step 1 ─┐ step 2 │ apply to a lead step 3 ─┘ │ ▼ lead's own step list ── you send it ──> mark complete ──> yes ──> licence └─ cannot contact ─> mark invalid iris reachr licence issue **a strategy belongs to a board, not to a person.** that is why every command takes a `<bloq-id>` — and it is what makes the strategy reusable instead of something one person keeps in their notes. ## what lands in the ledger, and what silently does not **send through reachr, or log it after. never neither.** a touch that is not on the lead record did not happen, as far as anyone else is concerned — no follow-up fires, no one covering for you knows it went out, and "we never heard from you" becomes unarguable. the trap is inverted, which is why it keeps catching people: **the flags that make a message more deliberate are the ones that drop it out of the record.** a specific sender identity, a cc, an attachment — each one silently switches to a direct bridge send. it prints `not logged to comms` and exits 0, so nothing looks wrong. sending from a client address, the most careful thing you can do, is exactly what loses the trace. tracked as **#183515**. same for anything sent by hand — gmail in a browser, mail.app, a phone. it is not in the ledger until you put it there. ### log a touch that went out any other way `--channel` takes any of the ten real channels — `gmail · imessage · apple_mail · whatsapp · instagram · linkedin · sms · phone · in_person · other`. the help used to list four of them and validate none, so people concluded email could not be logged and skipped it. fixed in **#183514**; if your cli still shows four, upgrade. then confirm it actually landed — the write succeeding is not the same as the row being there: ### do not reach for `comms ingest` to backfill `ingest` sweeps a channel and attaches what it finds. its lead matching has been wrong in production: `--channel all` on a client lead once pulled **22 messages from an unrelated private conversation** onto that client's record, because phone matching used a substring comparison. fixed in **#183513**, but the lesson survives the fix — **ingest writes to a named client record without asking.** prefer `comms log` for one known touch. if you do ingest, name one channel, never `all`, and read `comms list` immediately after. if something wrong does land: it refuses to run unnarrowed, shows you what matches, and asks before deleting. ## before you start you need a **board id** and, to get past planning, at least one **lead id** on it. if you have neither, this is the wrong playbook — you need leads first. ## steps

entries.name: launch-event-concept
entries.describe: Launch an Event Concept
entries.haystack: launch-event-concept launch an event concept <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: launch-event-concept description: stand up a new recurring event concept end to end — pick an under-used brand, make calendar room, define and hire the hosts who run it, create the events, and publish them. use when asked to "launch a new event series", "spread our concepts", "diversify the event slate", "hire stream hosts", or "make room on the calendar". pass a brand key, concept name, or "audit" as argument (e.g. "audit", "beatbox", "song wars atx", "hire hosts"). allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - bash - glob - grep --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run launch-event-concept ` # launch an event concept the motion is always the same: **find an idle brand → make room → staff it → ship it.** skipping the middle two is why series die after three weeks. ## arguments `$arguments` — `audit` (coverage report, launch nothing), a brand key (`beatbox`, `discover`, `capital_collective`, `vanguard`, `emc_radio`), a concept name, or `hire hosts`. --- ## step 1 — audit coverage before inventing anything nearly every "new" concept already exists as a brand with a tagline or a bloq with no events attached. look there first. a brand with a tagline and **no event** is the candidate. cross-reference against a bloq — if one exists, the concept is already scoped and you are scheduling, not inventing. score a candidate on what it *diversifies*, not on whether it sounds good: | axis | ask | |---|---| | audience | does this reach someone the current slate does not? | | format | competition / workshop / showcase / roundtable — or another meetup? | | daypart | everything is evenings. is this daytime or weekend? | | revenue | community-shaped or revenue-shaped? | | geography | austin again, or somewhere else? | if it only scores on "sounds good," it is a content idea, not an event. ## step 2 — make room first **a new series added on top of a full calendar fails.** cut before you add. reduction levers, cheapest first: 1. **weekly → biweekly** on the heaviest series. a weekly dj night is 4 events a month of production load; biweekly halves it and rarely costs attendance. 2. **drop the thinnest instances**, not whole series — keep the cadence legible. 3. **merge** two low-turnout concepts into one night with two segments. 4. **keep cheap formats.** a 1-hour recurring call costs almost nothing; cut the ones that need a venue, staff, and a load-in. delete from the platform (`iris events delete <id>`) rather than leaving ghosts — and if it is already on posh, cancel it there too (settings → cancel event), which closes rsvps and notifies attendees. never silently orphan a published event. ## step 3 — define the roles before you source a concept without a named owner is a concept that does not happen. for a host-driven series, write the seat down before recruiting: - **show** it runs, and the cadence - **run-of-show length** — pre-roll, main, outro - **live or recorded**, and on which channels - **commitment** — shows per month - **trial gate** — what they must produce to pass six seats covering a slate typically look like: one host per concept, plus one **floater** who covers illness, travel, and overflow. without the floater every absence cancels a show. ## step 4 — source from the warm list, not the famous list ⚠️ **the discover streamer roster is not a candidate pool.** `iris discover streamers list` returns ~49 names, but they are national creators featured *as content* — ishowspeed, pokimane, tpain, hasanabi. only a handful are yours (`freelabelnet`, `hourdemayo`, `miasiax`, `ninadaddyisback`). recruiting against that list wastes a cycle. the genuinely warm pools are people who have already worked with you: | bloq | what it holds | |---|---| | **#529 live stream guests** | ~50 contacts — prior guests, the best pool | | **#255 sophdagoat — ig influencers** | ~50 contacts | | **#282 sxsw artist interviews** | on-camera talent you have already filmed | | **#364 artists + creator management** | roster you already manage | | **#287 job outreach & recruiting** | the pipeline board itself | ## step 5 — run the pipeline on a board use bloq **#287 job outreach & recruiting pipeline**. stage the seats as items and move them as candidates advance: stage gates that actually filter: 1. **sourced** — identified, not contacted 2. **contacted** — outreach sent 3. **screened** — 15-min call; can they hold a room without a script? 4. **trial** — *they run one real segment on air.* this is the only gate that predicts performance. never skip it. 5. **offer** 6. **onboarded** — has run-of-show, channel access, and a first booked date track one item per **seat**, not per candidate, so an empty seat stays visible when a candidate drops. ## step 5b — post the seats publicly a board tracks candidates you already know. an **opportunity** is how new people find you, and it is what surfaces on discover. `--roles-file` takes an array of `{key, title, count, description}`, so **one listing can carry many seats** — crew and every host seat belong on a single posting, not seven. ⚠️ **check for an existing listing before creating one.** opportunities accumulate and overlap badly. a real example: a new dj listing was created alongside **#670 "nights with noys — dj slots"**, which already existed *with real rates* (headliner $150, opener $75, rolling weekly). the new one was strictly worse and had to be deleted. also watch for **stale** listings pinned to a past event — #674 targeted "sat jul 25" and #671 targeted "thu jul 23" long after both had passed. retire those rather than letting them sit on the marketplace. ⚠️ **use `--preview` when rates are not decided.** preview mode shows the banner but disables applications. never invent compensation on a public listing — publish in preview, set the rates, then flip it live. ## step 6 — create the events conventions the rest of the tooling depends on: - **recurring series carry a `#nnn` counter** in the platform title. keep it — the posh skill strips it and date-qualifies instead. - set `start_time`/`end_time` in **local wall-clock**. a night ending after midnight gets its end date rolled forward automatically. - attach a video with `metadata.video` (a watch url). do **not** use `source_url` — that runs yt-dlp and rehosts the file. ## step 7 — flyer and publish then run the **`posh-events`** playbook to publish. it handles the field order, the required flyer, the ledger that prevents duplicate publishing, and `--audit` for keeping posh in sync when the platform record changes. ## step 8 — decide the cadence *after* the first run launch new concepts **monthly or as one-offs**. promote to weekly only once one has sold out or filled twice. committing a weekly slot to an unproven concept is how the calendar gets full of series nobody attends. --- ## timing a launch work backwards from the launch date. a host-driven series needs **8–9 weeks**: | weeks | work | |---|---| | 1–2 | define seats, open the pipeline, source from the warm bloqs | | 3–5 | screen, then **trial segments on air** — the long pole | | 6–7 | offers, onboarding, run-of-show, channel access | | 8–9 | first shows, hosts in place | compressing weeks 3–5 is the classic mistake: it produces hosts who have never been on air before their first booked show. ## anti-patterns - adding a series without cutting one — the calendar fills, quality drops. - recruiting from the featured/discover roster instead of prior collaborators. - hiring n hosts for n shows with no floater. - hiring on a screening call alone, with no trial segment. - publishing to posh before a host is named — the listing goes up, the show does not.

entries.name: lead-health-sweep
entries.describe: Lead Health Sweep
entries.haystack: lead-health-sweep lead health sweep <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: lead-health-sweep description: sweep all active leads, identify the weakest pulse scores, generate ai follow-up recommendations, and optionally send outreach. run daily or on-demand to keep deals from going cold. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run lead-health-sweep ` > steps: fetch-and-filter → report → draft-followups → send-outreach → summary # lead health sweep automated deal health maintenance. finds leads with low pulse scores, analyzes why they're stalling, and generates (or sends) follow-up actions. ## steps

entries.name: legal-conflict-check
entries.describe: Legal — Conflict Check
entries.haystack: legal-conflict-check legal — conflict check <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: legal-conflict-check description: sweep the firm's own records — leads, profiles, and a matter board — for a prospective party, and assemble a candidate sheet for an attorney to clear. surfaces candidates; it does not clear the conflict. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run legal-conflict-check <party>` > steps: sweep → assess → file # legal — conflict check sweeps the firm's own records for a prospective party and assembles a candidate sheet. **read this before using it.** there is no conflicts database behind this playbook, and iris has no cross-matter item search — so this covers leads, profiles, and one named matter board, and nothing else. a clean result means *"nothing surfaced in these sources"*, which is **not** the same as *"no conflict exists"*. **an attorney clears the conflict.** this only makes sure they are looking at what the firm can see. ## steps

entries.name: legal-demand-letter
entries.describe: Legal — Demand Letter
entries.haystack: legal-demand-letter legal — demand letter <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: legal-demand-letter description: check a matter is ready to demand, then draft the demand from the record — liability, damages, and the number, argued rather than guessed. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run legal-demand-letter <lead>` > steps: record → readiness → draft → file # legal — demand letter readiness check first, then the draft. the readiness step exists because the expensive failure is not a weak letter — it is a demand sent before the evidence supports it. **the number is the attorney's.** this playbook will not invent one; if `--demand` is absent it drafts with the figure left open. ## steps --- ${{steps.draft.output}}" 2>&1 | tail -5 ```

entries.name: legal-engagement-letter
entries.describe: Legal — Engagement Letter
entries.haystack: legal-engagement-letter legal — engagement letter <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: legal-engagement-letter description: draft an engagement letter from the matter record, and check an existing one for the defects that surface at resolution — missing signature, wrong scope, party mismatch. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run legal-engagement-letter <lead>` > steps: matter → draft → review → file # legal — engagement letter draft or review the instrument that lets you act. a defective engagement is not discovered when it is signed — it is discovered at resolution, when it is far too late. this is a drafting and checking aid: **an attorney approves the letter and its fee terms**, and the fee arrangement must comply with your jurisdiction's rules, which this does not check. ## steps

entries.name: legal-matter-chronology
entries.describe: Legal — Matter Chronology
entries.haystack: legal-matter-chronology legal — matter chronology <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: legal-matter-chronology description: assemble every logged communication on a matter into a dated chronology with a work summary — the thing you reach for when a client disputes what was done. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run legal-matter-chronology <lead>` > steps: gather → chronology → value → file # legal — matter chronology pulls the unified communications log and the matter notes, and assembles a dated chronology of what the firm actually did. this is the use case that pays for itself: reconstructing a matter history by hand is hours of work, and it is what you need when a client asks what they are paying for. **estimates are estimates.** any time or value figure below is derived from logged communications, not from a timekeeping system. it is a starting point for a bill review, never a substitute for one. ## steps

entries.name: legal-matter-intake
entries.describe: Legal — Matter Intake
entries.haystack: legal-matter-intake legal — matter intake <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: legal-matter-intake description: turn a free-text enquiry (call note, web form, email) into a structured matter intake — parties, posture, dates that bite, and a routing recommendation — then open it as a lead. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run legal-matter-intake <enquiry>` > steps: extract → brief → open # legal — matter intake structured capture from an unstructured enquiry. extracts the fields a matter record needs, flags what is missing, and recommends where it should go. **this does not qualify or engage anyone.** whether a licensed attorney must speak to a prospective client before engagement is a rule of your jurisdiction, not a setting here. run `legal-conflict-check` before any engagement. ## steps

entries.name: licensing
entries.describe: Licensing — from "we agreed" to "they are working"
entries.haystack: licensing licensing — from "we agreed" to "they are working" <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: licensing description: put a client on iris with a licence key instead of a discount code — issue it, send it, confirm they can actually use it, and price it while the deal is still being negotiated. covers the whole path from "we agreed to work together" to "they are working", including the checks that catch a client seeing an empty workspace before they do. allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run licensing ` # licensing — from "we agreed" to "they are working" every command below runs against production via `railway ssh -s fl-api -- php artisan ...`. each one has worked examples in `--help`; this playbook is the order, which `--help` cannot show. ## the shape of the thing a licence **exists before anyone owns it** — that is what makes it sendable. claiming sets the owner and the first seat. seats are rows rather than a counter, so you can always see *which* people. nothing is deleted: released seats and removed products stay for the audit trail. three commercial states are **derived, never stored**: there is no `--state` flag. a stored state would be a copy that can disagree with the fields it came from, and the disagreement is silent. see `/p/epic-licence-pricing`. ## steps ### 1 · issue the licence `--trial-days` ends the **free part**. `--days` sets an expiry, which ends **access**. they are different and you almost always want the first — otherwise a 45-day trial is implemented by threatening to switch someone off on day 46. seats should match their headcount, not their first user. a key that runs out on person four is a support conversation you scheduled for yourself. ### 2 · provision the workspace before sending anything this is the step that gets skipped, and it is the one a client notices. signing up creates a user and nothing else. without a workspace row they sign in perfectly and see an **empty product**, which reads as broken rather than unfinished. check the bloq name before you use its id. if it says *"not client-visible"*, it means it. ### 3 · confirm their workspace actually answers the rag suite proves the *pipeline* works against its own fixtures. this proves **their** workspace answers from **their** material — a different question, and the only one they care about. retrieval and generation are reported separately: a generic answer is either "nothing retrieved" or "plenty retrieved and ignored", and one number cannot tell those apart. do not send the email until every query retrieves something. ### 4 · send the key client onboarding and partner copy are **different commands on purpose**. sending client onboarding to the partner who set the deal up explains their own product back to them. never print a multi-seat key on a public page. a promo code with a use cap can live in public; a licence key **is** the access, and the first n strangers to find it take the seats. ### 5 · price it while they use it price is a **sum over products × seats**, never a number typed on the licence. `--price` is per seat per month in **cents**. `--agreed` records what was actually settled, which may be less than the quote — both are kept, so "why is this $600 when the products say $750" is answerable next year. agreeing a price during a trial does **not** end the trial. that is the point: you negotiate while they are using it. ### 6 · answer "is this person licensed?" one call covers both levels — their own licence, or a seat on someone else's team licence. it exits non-zero when they are not, so it drops straight into a script. ## traps - **credits are not licences.** `--credits` touches the marketplace balance. it does **not** change what a desktop client may spend — that is a dollar cap in `fl-iris-api`. granting credits to fix "they cannot use the app" changes nothing at all. - **a licence key typed into the sign-in window works.** it is recognised by shape (`iris-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx`) in the same field that takes promo codes. if someone reports it rejected, check the shape before checking the licence. - **`license:manage list` shows revoked keys too.** revoking keeps seats and history — that is deliberate, and it means the list is not a list of live licences. - **releasing a seat removes access immediately**, and the row stays. "who had access in march" is a question that gets asked. ## related - `/p/epic-licence-pricing` — why the state enum was deleted, and what is still knowingly wrong - `/p/epic-billing-unification` — why credits and desktop spend are two different meters

entries.name: live-meeting-to-build-pipeline
entries.describe: Live meeting → build pipeline
entries.haystack: live-meeting-to-build-pipeline live meeting → build pipeline <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: live-meeting-to-build-pipeline description: turn a live client meeting into a shared atlas item, an open-questions list, a scoped epic, landed data and a shipped ui — then onboard, collect feedback, and run it again. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run live-meeting-to-build-pipeline ` > steps: step-1 → step-2 → step-3 → step-4 → step-5 → step-6 → step-7 → step-8 → step-9 → step-10 → step-11 → step-12 # live meeting → build pipeline capture a live team/client meeting as it happens, synthesize it into a single living atlas item the room can watch update in real time, surface the open questions instead of burying them, turn decisions into a scoped epic with child tickets, and carry that through to shipped sops, landed data, a genesis ui, and any automation the meeting called for. it is a loop, not a line. the last step onboards the people who will use what shipped and collects their feedback — which is a live meeting, which is step one again. the second lap captures better than the first, because people critique a real thing far more precisely than they describe a hypothetical one. ## steps ### a — the human sop draft it from the transcript or from a written summary: iris playbook sop <transcript-or-audio> # same walkthrough, human form iris sop draft <transcript-or-audio> # equivalent entry point do not hand-write this from memory when a transcript exists. the whole point of capturing the meeting was to avoid a second-hand retelling. the raw meeting atlas item from step 3 is not the sop. it is the source material — chronological, full of asides, organised around when things were said rather than around what someone has to do. the sop is derived from it: ordered steps, decision points, inputs and outputs, and the role that owns each one. keep the atlas item; it is the evidence the sop is faithful. pull the rules out separately while you are here. some of what sounds like a step is really a rule — a scope, a direction ("never / always"), and a reason someone will otherwise argue with — with no sequence and no owner running it weekly. filing a rule as a step loses the part that matters. (the `capture-sops-and-process-maps` playbook covers this split in depth; use it rather than repeating its work here.) ### b — the playbook write the runnable version at .iris/playbooks/<name>/playbook.md, verify it parses, and publish it. frontmatter `version` must be exactly 2 or the steps silently fail to register and you get a playbook with zero steps that still reports success — check with the platform's doctor command if a step count ever comes back 0. ### then bind them — a playbook is a container, not just a step list this is the part that gets skipped, and it is the part that makes the two deliverables one thing instead of two orphans. a playbook holds procedures and skills: iris playbook items add <playbook> --label "intake approval sop" \ --bloq-item <atlas-item-id> # the human sop, by reference iris playbook items add <playbook> --label "score a case" --skill <id> iris playbook items list <playbook> iris playbook roles add <playbook> --title "intake coordinator" `--bloq-item` takes the atlas item id holding the procedure text, so the sop lives in one place and the playbook points at it. nothing is copied, so nothing goes stale. `--skill` attaches a runnable capability. `--role` says who owns it, and `roles` builds the org chart around the work. the end state this is walking toward: a playbook that carries the human sops and the collection of skills for a job, rendered and managed the same way by both the ui and the cli — so "here is how we do this" and "here is the thing that does it" stop being two systems a team has to keep in sync by hand. note on provisioning a library from templates: if you are standing up a new team's sop library rather than adding one procedure, check what exists before writing anything — fork an existing playbook's structure rather than starting empty. verify the command name in `iris playbook --help` at the time you run it; this surface is newer than most and the verb has moved. ### surface — composed component, or one hand-written block a genesis page is either composed from components or a single authored html block. this is a real fork, and picking wrong costs a rewrite. reach for a component when the surface is data-driven over records the page already has: an operational queue, a client dashboard, an intake form, a filterable list with a status somebody moves. you get server-side query, paging and tenant scoping for free, and the same component points at another customer by changing an address on the page rather than the code. reach for a hand-written block when the page is an argument rather than a table — a pitch, a report, a one-off narrative layout. know the structural reason this is still common for polished pages: a composable page has no container primitive. the component host renders with `display: contents`, so it has no box, and edge-to-edge is the default outcome of a correctly written component. there is no way to say "centre these in a column with gutters." that is a limit of the page layer, not of the format, and it is why most production pages that need real layout are one block. ### data — bind by address, and pick the right store a page binds an address; where rows live sits behind it. four addresses: item:181094 a card's carried table — the card is a container of rows list:2115 the cards in a list are the rows bloq:620 the cards in a workspace are the rows dataset:sessions typed records the dividing line is not storage. it is who reads a row: · a board list — a human reads every item. tens to hundreds. curated, prose-bearing, dragged and assigned. todos, sops, bug reports. · an atlas dataset — nothing reads them individually. hundreds to hundreds of thousands. uniform, generated, queried and aggregated. ledger rows, sessions, bids, analytics. 560 generated rows should not be 560 draggable cards; a curated todo list should not need a schema migration. getting this wrong is the expensive mistake on this step, because it is the one that is painful to undo later. one more trap worth knowing before you plan capacity: a card's carried table is a json array inside a single row, so there is nothing to query — that provider runs mode_materialised and declares a maxrows(). past the cap the read is refused, not truncated, deliberately: a silently short answer is indistinguishable from a correct one. ### authoring — inside the closed world a component is `export default { … }` and nothing else in the script. no imports. every capability arrives on `this`: this.$dataset rows, meta, loading, query(opts), create(fields) this.$datasets the several named feeds the page bound this.$page slug, title, theme, brand, viewer (viewer is null when signed out — that is how you express an auth gate) this.$toast · this.$format · this.$emit · this.$props there is no window, document, fetch or localstorage, and no route to one. a component cannot name its own data source, which is exactly what makes pointing it at the wrong tenant something an author is unable to do. do not fight a refusal. every rule has an error code, a line number and a sentence saying what to do instead — read it and correct the component. the common ones: no `obj[variable]` (use `.find()`), no `v-html`, no bound `:href`/`:src`, no `v-bind="obj"`, `data()` returns literals only, every `$emit` name declared in `emits`, `<style>` must be scoped. the compiler is the specification. where this playbook and the compiler disagree, the compiler is right. ### score — the ten-point audit, before publishing one point each. 9-10 ship · 6-8 revise · 0-5 redesign. 01 subject-derived the design could not be swapped onto another subject 02 neutrals chosen grays hue-biased; no #f5f5f5, no #000 03 semantic ≠ accent every color can be named and its job stated 04 three type roles display/body/data distinct; numbers monospace and tabular; body near 65ch 05 structure is true shuffling the sections would actually break something 06 figures argue deleting a figure loses meaning, not just height 07 copy is clean no bloq, board, provider, raw ids or http codes reach the reader 08 both themes tokens redefined; dark was designed, not inverted 09 motion used once, with a reason 10 render verified checked in a real browser check 01 is the predictor. the falsifying question: could this design be moved onto a completely different subject without changing? if yes it is a template, it will rarely score above four, and no amount of local fixing rescues it — restart from the subject rather than the stylesheet. check 07 catches this pipeline specifically. everything upstream — the atlas item, the epic, the tickets — is written in internal vocabulary, and it is very easy to carry "bloq", "board item" or a raw id straight onto a screen a client reads. order the work by what a failure costs: pages a prospect sees before they trust you, then pages a client sees every day (scanned not read — state encoded in form as well as number, summary before detail), then documents. ### render traps — learned, not guessable · theme comes from the host, not the os. inside a genesis page switch on `html.dark` — never `@media (prefers-color-scheme)`. a block that follows the os renders dark inside a light page. (standalone artifacts are the opposite: they own their document and do use prefers-color-scheme.) · a customhtml block must not paint its own `background` — it becomes a slab floating on the page ground. · namespace every selector. customhtml injects via v-html with no isolation, so a bare `body`/`section`/`table` rule leaks into the host. · no webfont cdns. the csp blocks them and it silently falls back to arial. build stacks from faces that ship on macos and windows, or inline a data uri. (components are stricter still: a remote `url()` in css is refused at compile time, because the request alone leaks that the page was viewed.) ### verify — in a real browser, then close the loop grepping strings out of the served html is not verification. check 10 exists because that failed in production. open the page. if a screenshot looks broken but the source looks right, inspect the dom before concluding the page is broken — see step 5 for why (a correctly rendered block screenshotted as solid black across multiple attempts). then build whatever hive tools, scripts and automations the tickets called for — notification wiring, scoring calculations, assignment logic — and update the epic and its child tickets to reflect what actually shipped, noting anything that shipped differently than scoped, with why. an epic whose tickets still describe the plan rather than the outcome is how the next person inherits a wrong map. ``` --- ## why these steps are instructions, not commands several of these were drafted from a live working session, not a single clean recorded walkthrough. each step is an instruction a person or agent carries out and can verify — not a black-box automation. promote a step to `mode: shell` once you know the exact command for your own atlas/bloq/lead tooling; this playbook deliberately stays tool-agnostic on flag names since those are known to drift (see the linked platform bug reports for two real examples hit while building this).

entries.haystack: local-devops local devops — docker development environment manager <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: local-devops description: manage the local docker development environment — start/stop services, switch profiles (minimal/workers/n8n/full), check status, view logs, reset containers, run migrations. use when docker isn't starting, services are down, you need workers, want to add n8n, or need to troubleshoot the local stack. pass an action as argument (e.g., "status", "up", "up workers", "up n8n", "down", "logs api", "reset iris-api", "diagnose"). allowed-tools: - read - bash - grep - glob - edit - askuserquestion --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run local-devops ` # local devops — docker development environment manager manage the freelabel docker compose development stack with profile-based service tiers. ## arguments `$arguments` — action to perform. examples: - `/local-devops status` — show running containers, ports, health, resource usage - `/local-devops up` — start minimal dev stack (7 services) - `/local-devops up workers` — start with queue workers + scheduler + iris-worker - `/local-devops up n8n` — start with n8n workflow automation stack - `/local-devops up full` — start everything (20 services) - `/local-devops down` — stop all services - `/local-devops restart [service]` — restart one or all services - `/local-devops logs <service>` — tail logs for a service (api, iris-api, elon-frontend, etc.) - `/local-devops reset <service>` — rebuild and restart a single container - `/local-devops diagnose` — full diagnostic (docker running, ports, disk, health, envs) - `/local-devops mysql` — open mysql console - `/local-devops tinker` — open laravel tinker in fl-api - `/local-devops migrate` — run migrations on fl-api - `/local-devops shell <service>` — shell into a container --- ## architecture the docker compose stack uses **profiles** to control which services start: ### default (7 services) — `docker compose up -d` | service | container | port | purpose | |---------|-----------|------|---------| | database | fl-database | 3306 | mysql 8 | | redis | fl-redis | 6379 | cache, sessions, queues | | api | fl-api | 9000 (fpm) | laravel backend | | api-nginx | fl-api-nginx | 8000 | nginx → api reverse proxy | | api-worker | fl-api-worker | — | queue worker (default, agent-jobs, workflows, background, video-processing) | | iris-api | fl-iris-api | 7201 | iris api (v6 workflows, pages, agents) | | elon-frontend | fl-elon-frontend | 9300 | nuxt 2 frontend | ### `--profile workers` (adds 3 services) | service | container | purpose | |---------|-----------|---------| | api-scheduler | fl-api-scheduler | laravel scheduler (runs every minute — heavy cpu) | | fl-api-workflows-worker | fl-api-workflows-worker | dedicated workflow queue worker | | iris-worker | fl-iris-worker | iris api queue worker | ### `--profile n8n` (adds 3 services) | service | container | port | purpose | |---------|-----------|------|---------| | postgres-n8n | fl-n8n-postgres | 5433 | postgresql for n8n | | n8n | fl-n8n | 5678 | n8n workflow automation ui | | n8n-worker | fl-n8n-worker | — | n8n queue worker | ### `--profile full` (adds everything above + extras) additional: typesense, langraph-api, elizabeth, coding-agent-bridge, proxy (80/443) ### `--profile hive` (specialized) | service | container | purpose | |---------|-----------|---------| | hive-daemon | fl-hive-daemon | local hive compute node | ### `--profile hive-test` (specialized) | service | container | purpose | |---------|-----------|---------| | hive-node-alpha | fl-hive-node-alpha | test hive node a | | hive-node-beta | fl-hive-node-beta | test hive node b | ## key directories ## common operations ### starting services ### checking status ### viewing logs ### running commands inside containers ### rebuilding ### common issues | symptom | cause | fix | |---------|-------|-----| | "cannot connect to docker daemon" | orbstack/docker not running | open orbstack app or `open -a orbstack` | | port 3306 in use | mysql already running on host | `brew services stop mysql` or change port in compose | | port 9300 in use | another nuxt instance | `lsof -ti:9300 \| xargs kill` | | api container exits | missing .env or composer deps | `docker compose exec api composer install` | | iris-api crashes | missing chromium / memory | check dockerfile.dev has chromium, increase docker memory | | elon-frontend slow | node_modules volume stale | `docker compose down -v elon_node_modules && docker compose up -d elon-frontend` | | "table not found" | migrations not run | `docker compose exec api php artisan migrate` | | queue jobs not processing | api-worker not started | it's in default profile now — check `docker compose ps` | | elon 401s on every fl-api call | dead `fl_raichu_api_token` (reseed wiped the user/token the jwt points to) | `./fix-elon-token.sh` (see below) | | elon 401→**500** after reseed | corrupted/incomplete db schema (missing tables) | `docker compose exec api php artisan migrate --force` then `./fix-elon-token.sh` | | `.env` change ignored after `restart` | `restart` reuses existing env; env_file only read at **create** | `docker compose up -d --no-build --force-recreate <service>` (not restart, not rebuild) | ### environment files - `fl-api/.env` — laravel backend config (db, redis, api keys) - `fl-iris-api/.env` — iris api config (same pattern) - `fl-elon-web-ui/.env` — frontend config (api urls, pusher) > **⚠️ editing a `.env` does not take effect on `docker compose restart`.** `restart` reuses the > container's *existing* environment — `env_file` is only read when a container is **created**. to > pick up a new `.env` value you must **recreate** the container: > `docker compose up -d --no-build --force-recreate <service>`. you almost never need an image > **rebuild** for env changes (nuxt dev / laravel read env at runtime). restart = stale, > recreate = fresh, rebuild = unnecessary. ### elon → fl-api 401 / 500 (the `fl_raichu_api_token` nuance) elon (`fl-elon-frontend`) authenticates **every** fl-api call with `bearer $fl_raichu_api_token` (set in `fl-elon-web-ui/.env`). that token is a passport jwt tied to a specific user + an `oauth_access_tokens` row. a `migrate:fresh`/reseed wipes them → passport rejects the token → the whole frontend 401s ("auth broken"). **one-command fix:** it mints a fresh token (`php artisan elon:mint-token --quiet-token`), writes it into `fl-elon-web-ui/.env` (backup first), `--force-recreate`s the elon container, and curl-verifies `/api/v1/profile`. **manual equivalent:** use `elon:mint-token` (real passport `->accesstoken` jwt) — not `api:generate-token`, which makes a sanctum random string elon can't authenticate with. **if a fresh token still 401s, or flips to 500 — the local db schema is incomplete.** symptom: `select count(*) from users` errors / table missing, or 500 like `table 'fl_api.jobs' doesn't exist`. diagnose + repair: fl-api migrations are guarded (`schema::hastable`/`hascolumn`) so re-running skips existing objects and creates only what's missing. gotchas: pure **data-backfill** migrations (no `schema::` ops) can stall/fail when run out-of-order (they boot eloquent models) — their data is usually already in the seed, so mark them run: `insert into migrations (migration,batch) values ('<name>',<maxbatch+1>)`. alters on big tables (`user_profiles` ≈ 518k rows) take ~20s each — run `migrate` in the background, it's not stuck. > **test against a real authed route — not `/api/v1/user` (that 404s).** use `/api/v1/profile` or > `/api/v1/user/onboarding-status`: 401 = dead token, 500 = token ok but schema broken, 200 = good. ### service urls | service | url | |---------|-----| | frontend | | | api | | | iris api | | | n8n (if started) | | | mysql | localhost:3306 (fl_user/secret) | | redis | localhost:6379 | ## diagnostic checklist when running `/local-devops diagnose`: 1. **docker daemon running?** — `docker info` should work 2. **disk space?** — `docker system df` (docker can eat 50gb+) 3. **all containers healthy?** — `docker compose ps` 4. **ports free?** — check 3306, 6379, 7201, 8000, 9300 5. **env files exist?** — fl-api/.env, fl-iris-api/.env, fl-elon-web-ui/.env 6. **mysql accepting connections?** — `docker compose exec database mysqladmin ping` 7. **redis accepting connections?** — `docker compose exec redis redis-cli ping` 8. **api responding?** — `curl -s 9. **frontend responding?** — `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" 10. **volume mounts working?** — check file changes reflect in container

entries.haystack: marketing-pipeline marketing pipeline — full lifecycle skill <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: marketing-pipeline description: run, debug, test, and maintain the full marketing pipeline: youtube feed scrape → n8n workflow (ai analysis + buffer publish) → som outreach. pass an action as argument (e.g., 'run', 'status', 'debug', 'test', 'architecture', 'gaps', 'logs'). allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - agent - task --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run marketing-pipeline ` # marketing pipeline — full lifecycle skill manages the complete content marketing pipeline from youtube ingestion through social publishing to outreach. ## arguments `$arguments` — action to perform. examples: - `/marketing-pipeline run` — run the full pipeline (yt:feed → n8n → chain som:all) - `/marketing-pipeline run dry` — dry run (scrape only, no n8n) - `/marketing-pipeline run limit=10` — run with 10 videos - `/marketing-pipeline run source=watchlater` — scrape watch later playlist - `/marketing-pipeline status` — check pipeline health (n8n, daemon, sessions, buffer) - `/marketing-pipeline debug` — diagnose why the pipeline broke - `/marketing-pipeline debug chain` — specifically debug the discover → som:all chain - `/marketing-pipeline test` — run test suite for the pipeline - `/marketing-pipeline test chain` — test the chain logic only - `/marketing-pipeline architecture` — show the full pipeline architecture - `/marketing-pipeline gaps` — analyze gaps, risks, and missing coverage - `/marketing-pipeline logs` — tail pipeline logs (daemon + n8n + discord) - `/marketing-pipeline logs n8n` — n8n execution history only - `/marketing-pipeline sessions` — check all browser session health (youtube, instagram) - `/marketing-pipeline n8n` — n8n workflow health and execution status --- ## pipeline architecture ### chain logic (task-executor.js) **critical**: chainable tasks (`discover`, `enrich_batch`, `som_batch`, `som`, `inbox_scan`) always resolve regardless of exit code. this means: - you close the browser → chain fires - ctrl+c → chain fires - daemon timeout → chain discover:yt-save-session` | | n8n chat input not found | playwright can't find textarea | data not sent to n8n | check n8n is running, workflow active | | n8n not running | `curl localhost:5678` fails | no processing | `npm run docker:up` | | instagram session expired | login redirect detected | som campaign fails | `npm run som:save-session:{campaign}` | | buffer api error | http 4xx/5xx from
