entries.describe: Merging a checkout other people are working in
entries.haystack: shared-checkout-merge merging a checkout other people are working in <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: shared-checkout-merge description: merge and push a repo that other sessions are working in, without destroying their uncommitted work. untracked files do not merge — they get clobbered, and git tells you only that they are "in the way". --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run shared-checkout-merge ` > steps: classify → preserve → merge → resolve → verify # merging a checkout other people are working in the dangerous moment is not the conflict. conflicts are visible and git makes you resolve them. the dangerous moment is the file git *refuses* to merge, because the suggested fix — move it, delete it, stash it — is where work disappears silently. measured on one evening across four repos: 72 files stood in front of one merge. 43 were byte-identical to upstream, 16 were regenerable build output, 12 were untracked copies of already-pushed files, and **exactly one** was real uncommitted work. clearing all 72 on the suggestion in git's error message would have destroyed that one and nothing else — which is precisely why it would not have been noticed. ## steps

entries.name: social-health
entries.describe: Social publishing health sweep
entries.haystack: social-health social publishing health sweep <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: social-health description: health sweep for the social publishing layer — plan capacity, expired logins, and the drift between what config/uploadpost.php claims and what upload-post actually holds. catches the silent failure where the resolver authorizes a publish and upload-post then drops it. read-only by default; --action=fix reconciles. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run social-health ` > steps: capacity → connections → expired → drift → reconcile # social publishing health sweep three things go wrong in this layer and **all three look like success**. nothing throws, the resolver returns a profile, the publish call succeeds — and no post appears. 1. **plan capacity.** profiles are what upload-post bills and caps. run out and the next tenant brand cannot be connected at all. 2. **expired logins.** `reauth_required` makes upload-post silently drop every post to that account. this is how clips stopped reaching @thediscoverpage_ for days. 3. **config-vs-upstream drift.** `config/uploadpost.php` is aspirational. it has claimed profiles that do not exist (`@capital.collective`), profile names that are wrong (`@heyiris.io` is really `heyirisio`), and platforms nobody ever linked (tiktok, on every profile). each false row makes the resolver say *yes* to a publish that then goes nowhere. drift is the dangerous one, because it is the only failure with **no error anywhere** — not in our logs, not in upload-post's response. ## why this reads the vendor and the database separately the whole point is to compare two sources that are each individually plausible. reading only our `integrations` rows tells you what we *think* is connected. reading only upload-post tells you what *is* connected but not what we would route to it. the gap between them is the bug. ## steps

entries.name: social-onboard-brand
entries.describe: Onboard a brand onto social publishing
entries.haystack: social-onboard-brand onboard a brand onto social publishing <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: social-onboard-brand description: onboard a tenant brand onto the social publishing layer — check plan capacity, mint the branded connect link where they attach their own instagram/tiktok/x, then sync what they linked into ownership rows and verify the resolver can route it. the connect step needs a human; this playbook is the two halves either side of it. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run social-onboard-brand <brand>` > steps: capacity → connect → sync → verify # onboard a brand onto social publishing run this in **two passes** with a human in between. `--stage=connect` mints the link; the tenant opens it and attaches their own accounts; `--stage=finish` writes what they attached into ownership rows. ## why the second pass is not optional `socialaccountresolver` reads ownership from `integrations` rows. upload-post knows the tenant linked their instagram; **we do not**, until sync runs. skip `finish` and you get an account that publishes perfectly upstream and is invisible everywhere authorization is decided — connected to everyone except the code that decides who may post. ## capacity is a hard wall, not a warning profiles are the billed and capped unit: 2 on free, 5 on basic, 25 on professional, 75 on advanced, 225 on business. if the plan is full the connect step returns a 409 and there is no way around it except upgrading. check first so you find out before the tenant does. ## steps

entries.name: som-outreach
entries.describe: SOM Outreach — Sales Outreach Machine Campaign Manager
entries.haystack: som-outreach som outreach — sales outreach machine campaign manager <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: som-outreach description: manage som outreach campaigns — view all campaigns at a glance, edit scripts, update strategies, manage leads, run batches, and monitor performance. pass an action as argument (e.g., "overview", "edit creators", "update-script", "leads", "run", "status"). allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - task --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run som-outreach ` # som outreach — sales outreach machine campaign manager manage the som outreach campaigns that power automated instagram dm outreach. view strategies, edit scripts, manage leads, run batches, and monitor results — all from the cli. ## arguments `$arguments` — action and parameters. examples: - `/som-outreach overview` — show all campaigns at a glance - `/som-outreach overview -s` — with full script text - `/som-outreach edit creators` — edit creator outreach scripts inline - `/som-outreach update-script creators "new script text here"` — update step 1 script directly - `/som-outreach leads creators` — show lead stats for creators board - `/som-outreach run` — trigger a full som batch (all active campaigns) - `/som-outreach run creators` — run just creators campaign - `/som-outreach status` — check latest batch results - `/som-outreach strategies` — list all strategy templates across boards --- ## campaign registry the live registry is resolved by `tests/e2e/som-config.js` via **three-tier resolution**: (1) the disk cache `.som-campaigns-cache.json` next to the config (written by `npm run som:sync` from `/api/v1/som/campaigns`), else (2) the inline baked-in defaults. **the cache wins when present** — the bridge daemon copy (`fl-docker-dev/coding-agent-bridge/som/`) has its own cache, so the daemon and a local `tests/e2e/` run can resolve differently. when in doubt, read the cache file, not the inline table. `getresolutionsource()` tells you which one is live. current campaigns (from the live cache): | campaign | board | ig account | strategy | audience | |----------|-------|------------|----------|----------| | creators | 80 | @thediscoverpage_ | creator outreach \| v1 (id:18) | artists, creators, hip-hop culture | | courses | 38 | @heyiris.io | ai course \| v3 | ai builders, tech founders | | beatbox | 224 | @thebeatbox__ | dj outreach \| v2 | djs, producers, beatmakers | | mayo | 176 | @hourdemayo | mayo outreach \| v2 | — | | freelabelnet | 80 | @freelabelnet | creator outreach \| v1 | creators (freelabelnet-branded) | | venues | 292 | @freelabelnet | venue partnership \| v1 | cafes, venues, event spaces | | atxbeauty | 283 | @atxbeautylab.lisa | beauty & wellness outreach \| v1 | beauty/wellness | | gooddeals | 302 | (linkedin) | linkedin founder outreach \| v1 | founders | | saddlepass | 337 | (linkedin) | equestrian bdr \| v1 | equestrian | > **ffat live-event invite** (first friday art trail, @freelabelnet): strategy `artist outreach | > ffat v1` — the canonical record is **strategy 35 on board 355**, with a same-named copy (**id 47**) > on **board 80** so it can be sent to the creators audience. step-1 dm names the event + date > in-body; bump the date here when the event changes. board 355's leads are exhausted — send to > board 80. ### ⚠️ strategies are matched by name, scoped to the target board `batch-with-login.spec.ts` fetches `/bloqs/{board_id}/outreach-strategy-templates` and picks the template whose `.name === strategy_name`. a strategy template only exists on the board it was created on — running `strategy="x"` against a board that has no template named exactly `x` silently won't match. to reuse a script across boards (e.g. the ffat invite on creators board 80), **create a copy on that board**, don't just reference the original. ### force all sends from one instagram account (`ig=` override) to make every campaign in a batch send from a single account (e.g. consolidate to @freelabelnet): `som.js` aliases `ig=` → `ig_account`; `som-all.js` passes it through to every campaign. this is a **runtime override** — it does not change `som-config.js`. for a durable change, edit `igaccount` in both `som-config.js` inline defaults **and** the cache json (both the `tests/e2e/` and bridge copies), since the cache wins. the sending account needs a valid session file `instagram-auth-<account>.json` in `tests/e2e/` (the bridge copies are stubs) — stale sessions force a re-login. ## cli commands ### php cli (from `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/`) ### typescript cli (iris binary — works from anywhere) --- ## how outreach scripts work each campaign has a **strategy template** with **steps**. the som batch (`npm run som:all`) applies the strategy to each lead and executes step by step: ### script flow 1. **apply strategy** → creates steps on the lead (step 1: ig dm, step 2: follow-up, etc.) 2. **generate message** → uses the step's `instructions` as the base script 3. **ai variation** → the `ai_prompt` field tells the ai how to personalize per lead (reference their bio, genre, etc.) 4. **send dm** → opens their instagram profile, pastes the varied message, sends ### script fields - **`instructions`** — the base dm/email text. merge fields: `{first_name}`, `{name}`, `{company}`, `{email}`, `{instagram}` - **`ai_prompt`** — instructions for the ai to personalize the script per lead. should specify: what to reference from their profile, tone, length limit, what not to include (urls, income claims) - **`delay_hours`** — hours to wait before this step (0 = immediate, 48 = follow-up after 2 days) - **`type`** — channel: `instagram`, `email`, `sms`, `phone`, `linkedin` ### script best practices (from swot analysis) - **no urls in step 1** — triggers instagram spam filters. save links for step 3+ - **no income claims** — "$100k monthly" triggers skepticism and spam detection - **lead with monetization** — what they get paid for, not what your tech stack is - **single audience** — don't list "founders, creators, brands, entrepreneurs" — pick one per campaign - **soft cta** — "what are you working on?" or "want an invite?" — not "sign up now" - **under 4 sentences** — mobile dms are small. get to the point - **ai prompt does the heavy lifting** — the script is the template, the ai personalizes per lead --- ## managing campaigns (toggle on/off) campaigns are toggled via `som-config.js`. use the iris cli: the `active` flag in `som-config.js` controls which campaigns run during `som:all`. turning a campaign off means it won't be included in batch runs. changes take effect on the next `som:all` run. ### current campaign state (live cache, jun 2026) > the inline fallback in `som-config.js` differs from the cache (e.g. inline marks venues/atxbeauty > off and maps `freelabelnet` to board 355). the **cache is authoritative** — verify with > `getresolutionsource()` or by reading `.som-campaigns-cache.json`. --- ## strategy templates & ai prompts ### viewing strategies or via api: ### active strategies (referenced in som-config.js) | campaign | strategy name | board | steps | |----------|--------------|-------|-------| | courses | ai course \| v3 (id: 17) | 38 | 4 | | creators | creator outreach \| v1 (id: 18) | 80 | 4 | | beatbox | dj outreach \| v2 | 224 | varies | | mayo | mayo outreach \| v1 | 176 | varies | ### understanding `instructions` vs `ai_prompt` each strategy step has two text fields that control the dm: - **`instructions`** — the base message template. this is what gets sent if there's no ai variation. should be a complete, ready-to-send message. - **`ai_prompt`** — instructions for the ai to rewrite/personalize the message per lead. when present, the "vary it" button rewrites the entire message using this prompt. when `null`, "vary it" does minor word swaps on the original `instructions` instead. **when to use `ai_prompt`:** - you want the ai to reference the lead's bio, genre, niche, or recent posts - you want significantly different messages per lead (not just word swaps) - you're ok with the ai sometimes changing the tone or structure **when to leave `ai_prompt` null:** - you want consistent messaging across all leads - the script is already personalized enough with merge fields - you want "vary it" to only do minor word substitutions (synonym swaps, sentence reordering) **as of apr 21, 2026:** `ai_prompt` was cleared from all steps on ai course v3 and creator outreach v1 because the ai rewrites were too aggressive — changing tone, adding claims, losing the original voice. now "vary it" does lightweight variation on the original script. ### updating a strategy step **via iris cli (recommended):** the `edit` command shows the current script + ai_prompt, lets you pick what to edit (script, ai prompt, both, or title), and pushes the update to the api. **via sql (for bulk operations like clearing ai_prompt):** ### creating a new strategy version when you want to test a new approach without losing the old one: 1. duplicate the existing strategy in the ui or api 2. edit the copy's steps 3. update `som-config.js` to point to the new strategy name 4. the old strategy stays intact for rollback ### step completion after sending a dm, the outreach step should be marked as completed so the lead doesn't get the same message again on the next run. two mechanisms: 1. **api-based** (reliable): `put /leads/{id}/outreach-steps/{stepid}` with `{is_completed: true}` 2. **ui-based** (fragile fallback): click the checkbox in the heyiris step card the batch script (`batch-with-login.spec.ts`) uses api-based completion after each dm send. --- ## updating scripts via api (direct) when the cli isn't available, update scripts directly via the api: **important:** the put endpoint **replaces all steps**. always send the complete step list, not just the one you're changing. fetch current steps first, modify the one you need, then send them all back. --- ## running som batches ### automated (via hive daemon) the daemon auto-chains: youtube feed import → som batch. runs on schedule. ### manual ### lead generation --- ## monitoring & troubleshooting ### check campaign health ### common issues - **"all leads already have outreach"** — board is exhausted, scrape fresh leads - **"no instagram handle — skipping"** — venue/business leads without ig. run enrichment or add ig-native leads - **"lead map api timed out"** — 4 parallel campaigns overwhelm the api. stagger helps but isn't perfect - **"no open instagram btn"** — lead doesn't have an ig handle in the system. the outreach step renders but can't open ig - **"no send message in menu"** — private account or ig blocked dms. marked as failed, moves to next lead - **422 on task completion** — output too large. fixed by truncating to 50kb ### key files - `tests/e2e/som.js` — campaign registry (board ids, strategies, ig accounts) - `tests/e2e/som-all.js` — batch orchestrator (enrichment, parallel campaigns, stagger) - `tests/e2e/batch-with-login.spec.ts` — playwright outreach spec (dm sending logic) - `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/src/console/commands/somoverviewcommand.php` — php som:overview - `fl-docker-dev/sdk/php/src/console/commands/someditcommand.php` — php som:edit - `iris-code/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/platform-som.ts` — typescript iris som - `iris-code/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/platform-outreach.ts` — typescript iris outreach --- ## steps ### 1. parse the argument | argument | action | |----------|--------| | `overview` / (empty) | run `php bin/iris som` or `iris som` | | `overview -s` | run with full scripts flag | | `edit <campaign>` | run `php bin/iris som:edit <campaign>` or `iris som edit <campaign>` | | `update-script <campaign> "<text>"` | update step 1 script via api call | | `leads <campaign>` | show leads for that board | | `run` / `run <campaign>` | trigger som batch via npm | | `status` | check daemon logs for latest batch results | | `strategies` | list all strategies across all boards | ### 2. when editing scripts 1. always fetch the current strategy first to avoid overwriting other steps 2. show the current script to the user before editing 3. after updating, run `php bin/iris som -c <campaign>` to verify 4. remind user about best practices: no urls in step 1, lead with monetization, under 4 sentences ### 3. when running batches 1. check if the daemon is running (`npm run bridge`) 2. verify lead supply (`php bin/iris som` — check lead counts) 3. if leads are exhausted, suggest running leadgen first 4. monitor via daemon logs for errors --- ## running a campaign against an existing list (board not in som-config) added 2026-08-22, after running it end-to-end against board 529. the sections above cover discovery and script editing; this one covers the case where the leads already exist on a board that has **no campaign entry** in `tests/e2e/som-config.js`. you do not need to add a campaign. `som:custom` takes overrides: `board=` / `bloq=` → board_id · `ig=` → ig_account · `dry=1` → dry_run · aliases live at the top of `tests/e2e/som.js`. ### the order that matters **1. find the board's real strategy name — do not guess it.** `som:custom` defaults to `strategy: 'custom campaign'`, which exists on **no** board. run it without a `strategy=` override and the dry run reports `⚠ strategy script not found — using fallback`, then composes a generic *"hey @handle! noticed you're doing some interesting work…"*. that is the failure this playbook's "matched by name" warning describes, seen from the other side: it does not error, it silently substitutes filler. **if you see `strategy script:` in the dry-run output you have the real script; if you see `using fallback` you do not.** **2. dry run, and read the preflight funnel.** preflight runs **before** chromium launches and prints the whole funnel: a percentage over 100% (`"social media outreach": 15/4 (375%)`) means a second, generic step set was applied to some leads and is polluting the funnel — usually the default 5-step dm/sms/email/phone/proposal template. clear it before running, or the counts lie. **3. confirm the message a human will actually receive.** the dry run truncates to ~50 chars. read the whole thing with `iris outreach-strategy show <board> <id>` — the text is in the step's `instructions` field, and the variation rules are in `ai_prompt`. **4. real sample of 2–3 before the batch.** drop `dry=1`, keep `limit=2`. **5. then the batch**, respecting the cap the run prints: `daily dm cap (@acct): 0/40 sent today`. ### what the dry run will not tell you - **`⚠ ai variation failed — using raw script`** means every recipient gets a byte-identical dm. the `ai_prompt` exists precisely to prevent that. two identical dms is a sample; 278 is a pattern instagram recognises, and the account is worth more than the list. **never run a batch while this warning is showing.** root-caused and fixed 2026-08-22 — worth knowing because the symptom is three layers from the cause. the spec calls `post /api/v1/ai/generate-personalized-message`; that controller asks for `gpt-4o-mini` (with a comment saying nano is too weak to paraphrase); and `openaiservice::generateresponseclean()` read `instructions` and `max_tokens` out of `$options` and **never read `model`**, hardcoding `callgrokdirect()`. so the chosen model was discarded, every call went to xai, xai was out of credit and 403'd, and the batch silently degraded to one identical message for everybody. fixed in `35b6863d` + `5bc9fa7b` (fl-api). to check it directly, without burning a 3-minute browser run: run it twice against different handles. **different text = working. identical, or `success:false` = do not batch.** - **session age is printed but not enforced** — `session age: 73d` still passed. meanwhile `ig preflight check failed: page.goto: target page… has been closed` appeared and the runner logged `continuing anyway`. a dry run that reports `fail: 1` on browser teardown is the harness, not the lead. - **the list is not the strategy.** board 529 is *live stream guests* and its strategy invites people to be featured — but 104 of the leads on it typed the single word "site" on one giveaway post. check `custom_fields.comment` and `source_post_url` before assuming intent: ### verified run, 2026-08-22 | | | |---|---| | command | `npm run som:custom -- board=529 ig=thediscoverpage_ "strategy=guest feature \| v1" limit=2 dry=1` | | preflight | 278 never contacted · 308 pending across 3 steps | | wrong strategy | `fail: 1`, fallback filler message | | correct strategy | `would send: 2 · skip: 0 · fail: 0`, real script loaded | | runtime | ~3.4-3.6 min for 2 leads (chromium, api-direct engine) | | after the variation fix | two distinct openings — *"we're in the process of selecting…"* / *"we're excited to feature…"* — `fail: 0` | **chromium is flaky and it is not your code.** one run in three died on `page.goto: target page, context or browser has been closed` with no orphaned processes and 53% memory free; the identical command passed on retry. `session age: 73d` is printed but never enforced, and the inbox scan fails in most runs with `continuing to outreach`. retry once before diagnosing anything.

entries.name: stress-test
entries.describe: Stress Test — Break It Before Clients Do
entries.haystack: stress-test stress test — break it before clients do <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: stress-test description: break features on purpose — generate and run edge case batteries against cli commands, api endpoints, and db writes. auto-discovers what changed, builds attack vectors (xss, injection, boundary values, type confusion, auth bypass, race conditions), runs them against production, reports pass/fail, and cleans up test artifacts. use after shipping a feature or before a client-ready check. pass a feature name, cli command, or api endpoint as argument (e.g., "iris content", "/api/v1/my/profiles", "upload flow"). allowed-tools: - read - bash - grep - glob - edit - write - agent --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run stress-test ` # stress test — break it before clients do generate and execute edge case batteries against cli commands, api endpoints, and database writes. the goal is to find bugs through adversarial input, boundary conditions, and unexpected usage patterns — the same things real users will do accidentally. ## arguments `$arguments` — what to test. examples: - `/stress-test iris content` — test all `iris content` subcommands - `/stress-test /api/v1/my/profiles` — test a specific api endpoint - `/stress-test upload flow` — test the upload workflow end-to-end - `/stress-test <feature>` — auto-discover commands and endpoints from recent commits ## how it works ### phase 1: discovery identify what to test by examining: 1. **recent commits** — `git log --oneline -5` + `git diff --name-only head~3` 2. **cli commands** — grep for `cmd({` patterns, extract command names and positional args 3. **api endpoints** — grep for `irisfetch`, `route::get/post`, extract url patterns 4. **db writes** — grep for `::create`, `->update`, `->delete`, `post /api`, `put /api`, `delete /api` ### phase 2: attack vector generation for each discovered target, generate test cases from these categories: #### category 1: input boundary testing | vector | what it tests | example | |--------|--------------|---------| | empty string | null/empty handling | `iris content get ""` | | zero | off-by-one, division | `--profile 0`, `--limit 0` | | negative numbers | unsigned assumptions | `iris content get -1` | | very large numbers | integer overflow | `iris content get 999999999999` | | max length strings | buffer/truncation | `--title "$(python3 -c "print('a'*10000)")"` | | unicode/emoji | encoding issues | `--search "日本語🔥"` | | null bytes | c-string termination | `--title $'\x00hidden'` | | whitespace only | trim failures | `--search " "` | | special url chars | encoding issues | `--search "a&b=c?d#e"` | #### category 2: security testing | vector | what it tests | example | |--------|--------------|---------| | xss in text fields | html injection | `--title '<script>alert(1)</script>'` | | sql injection | parameterized queries | `--search "'; drop table users;--"` | | path traversal | file access | `--profile "../../etc/passwd"` | | command injection | shell escaping | `--title "$(whoami)"`, `` --title "`id`" `` | | auth bypass | token handling | call endpoint without auth header | | idor | object ownership | access another user's content by id | | rate limiting | abuse prevention | 20 rapid sequential calls | #### category 3: type confusion | vector | what it tests | example | |--------|--------------|---------| | string where number expected | type coercion | `iris content get "abc"` | | number where string expected | type coercion | `--search 12345` | | boolean-ish strings | truthy/falsy | `--profile "false"`, `--profile "null"` | | array-like input | parser confusion | `--type "video,article"` | | json in string field | injection | `--title '{"key":"value"}'` | #### category 4: state & concurrency | vector | what it tests | example | |--------|--------------|---------| | duplicate create | idempotency | upload same url twice | | delete then access | ghost references | delete video, then `get` it | | modify then diff | consistency | push changes, immediately diff | | rapid sequential ops | race conditions | 5 uploads in parallel | | stale local file | sync conflicts | modify local json, api changes independently | #### category 5: ux flow testing | vector | what it tests | example | |--------|--------------|---------| | first-run experience | empty state | run command with no data | | ctrl+c mid-operation | cleanup | interrupt during upload | | --json piping | machine-readable output | `cmd --json 2>/dev/null \| python3 -c "import json,sys;json.load(sys.stdin)"` | | --help completeness | self-documentation | every subcommand has --help | | error message quality | user guidance | error says what to do next | | non-interactive mode | ci/cd compat | pipe input, no tty | #### category 6: user journey paths (the important one) this is the category that catches "it works in isolation but the workflow is broken." walk through the paths a real client takes — in order, with real data, checking that each step's output feeds correctly into the next. **how to build journey tests**: for each feature, map the 3-5 most common user workflows. each journey is a sequence of commands where the output of step n informs the input of step n+1. if any step fails or produces output that can't feed the next step, the journey fails. ##### journey templates **journey a: discovery → first use → daily use** **journey b: create → verify → modify → delete (full lifecycle)** **journey c: error recovery** **journey d: power user multi-step** **journey e: onboarding (brand new user)** ##### journey test execution pattern ##### persona-based journey matrix every feature must be tested from **5 personas**. each persona has different context, expectations, and failure modes: **persona 1: new user (day 1)** - just ran `iris init`, has auth but no content/profiles - expectation: guided experience, no jargon, clear next steps - common failures: empty state crashes, "no data" with no guidance, assumes config exists **persona 2: existing user (daily driver)** - has profiles, content, active workflows - expectation: fast, reliable, remembers context - common failures: slow queries on large datasets, stale cache, pagination breaks **persona 3: admin/operator (managing for clients)** - managing content across multiple profiles/brands - expectation: bulk operations, cross-profile access, --json for scripting - common failures: user scoping blocks admin access, no bulk operations, id confusion between profiles **persona 4: ci/automation (non-interactive)** - running in a script, cron job, or hive task - expectation: no prompts, predictable exit codes, parseable output - common failures: interactive prompts block execution, ansi codes in piped output, non-zero exit on success **persona 5: adversarial user (pentester/abuse)** - trying to break things, access other users' data, inject payloads - expectation: every input sanitized, auth enforced, no 500s - common failures: xss stored, idor, sql injection, command injection, path traversal ##### what makes a good journey test | good | bad | |------|-----| | tests a sequence of 3-5 related commands | tests isolated commands (that's category 1-5) | | output of step n feeds step n+1 | steps are independent | | uses real production data | uses mocked/fake data | | tests the path a client would take | tests the path a developer would take | | includes at least one error/recovery step | only tests the happy path | | verifies cleanup (no orphans) | leaves test data behind | ### phase 3: execution run each test case and collect results: ### phase 4: cleanup after all tests: 1. delete any test records created (videos, profiles, etc.) 2. restore any modified records (push original json back) 3. verify no test artifacts remain in production 4. report any artifacts that couldn't be cleaned ### phase 5: report output format: ## pre-built test suites ### cli command suite for any `iris <command>`: ### sensitive data leak detection when checking for leaked secrets in source code, use **precise patterns** that match actual credential variables — not display-only words like "tokens" (token counts) or "secret_count". **why this matters:** broad patterns like `console.log.*token` flag every line that displays token *counts* (e.g., `${tokens}` showing "12.5k tokens"), password *requirements* text, or secret *status* messages. these false positives erode trust in the test suite — teams start ignoring failures. use assignment/interpolation context to distinguish "logging a credential value" from "displaying a word that contains 'token'". ### api endpoint suite for any `get/post/put/delete /api/v1/<path>`: ### upload/write suite for any feature that creates db records: ## integration with production deploy the stress-test skill can be invoked from `/production-deploy client-ready` as part of gate 2: to invoke programmatically: ## severity levels | level | criteria | action | |-------|----------|--------| | **critical** | 500 error, data loss, auth bypass, command injection | block ship. fix immediately. | | **high** | xss stored, idor, rate limit bypass | fix before client-ready. | | **medium** | poor error message, missing validation, slow response (>5s) | fix in follow-up. ship with known issue. | | **low** | cosmetic (emoji in output, truncation off-by-one) | note it. fix when convenient. | ## quick start examples

entries.describe: Test something distributed, atomically
entries.haystack: test-distributed-atomically test something distributed, atomically <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: test-distributed-atomically description: test a feature that spans several machines without using production as your debugger. cut the system at its boundaries, test every part that is not genuinely remote with no network at all, reproduce the remote condition locally instead of borrowing the remote system, assert shape rather than success, and make distributed answers attributable rather than identical. use when a change touches a queue, a daemon, a webhook, a device, a worker, or anything else where "just deploy and see" is the tempting move. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run test-distributed-atomically <feature>` > steps: cut → atomic → reproduce → assert → attribute → budget → record # test something distributed, atomically **the trap.** a feature spans five hosts. you cannot put that under a debugger, so you test it end to end, it fails, you guess, you deploy, you wait, you test again. each lap costs a build. three laps in you have learned almost nothing, because an end-to-end failure tells you *that* it broke, never *where*. **the claim.** most bugs in a distributed feature are not distributed bugs. they are ordinary bugs — a regex that will not compile, a column that does not exist, a binary not on `path` — sitting inside a distributed system and wearing its costume. you can catch those on a laptop in seconds. spend the expensive end-to-end runs on the two or three links that are genuinely remote. **skip this** for a change confined to one process with no network in it. ceremony on work that does not need it teaches people to skip the ceremony when it matters. ## steps

entries.name: the-algorithm
entries.describe: The Algorithm — decide what's real, then delete before you optimize
entries.haystack: the-algorithm the algorithm — decide what's real, then delete before you optimize <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: the-algorithm description: first-principles + deletion-first engineering audit. runs the full three-tool stack against a target system, service, feature, page, table, agent tool, architecture, or process — decompose to constituents and rebuild (first principles), find the gap between truth and price (idiot index), then run musk's five steps in order (question the requirement, delete the part, simplify what survives, accelerate the cycle, automate last). enforces the existence test, the 10% add-back calibration, and the architecture split triggers. use before optimizing, refactoring, splitting a service, or automating anything. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run the-algorithm <target>` > steps: inventory → principles → requirements → delete → simplify → accelerate → automate → calibrate # the algorithm — decide what's real, then delete before you optimize > "the most common error of a smart engineer is to optimize a thing that should not exist." > "the best part is no part. the best process is no process. it weighs nothing, costs nothing, > can't go wrong." ## the three stacked tools most teams invert this stack — they automate an analogical process that first principles would have deleted. | # | tool | the question it answers | |---|------|------------------------| | 1 | **first principles** | what is actually true, and what is the *function*? | | 2 | **idiot index / cost-of-atoms** | where is the gap between truth and price? | | 3 | **the algorithm** | delete, then simplify, then speed, then automate | **first principles is how you decide what is real. the algorithm is how you operate.** the one-line operating system: > treat physics as law, named requirements as claims, and everything else as optional. rebuild the > function from constituents. if a part is not required by that rebuild, it should not exist. only > then is it worth optimizing. --- ## tool 1 — first principles > "boil things down to the most fundamental truths and then reason up from there, as opposed to > reasoning by analogy." — musk two jobs in one sentence: **strip inherited stories**, then **rebuild from what physics (or the actual problem) will still allow**. aristotle called a first principle an *archē*: the starting point from which a thing is known, not deduced from something prior. the modern test: p is first-principle ⟺ p cannot be reduced further without leaving the domain of the problem **usually are first principles:** conservation of energy · mass, geometry, material properties · a customer must get from a to b · a battery stores charge by moving ions through an electrolyte · software must transform state without losing required information. **usually are not:** "rockets cost $x because that's what aerospace charges" · "batteries will stay at $600/kwh because they always have" · "we need this approval step because legal said so" · "microservices are how serious companies build backends" · "a car needs a folding key." that last group are **analogies wearing a lab coat**. they sound like knowledge. they are compressed history. ### the real opponent: reasoning by analogy analogy: new situation ≈ old situation ⟹ reuse old solution analogy is cheap and mostly correct — it is how you drive, cook, hire, and write code. the problem is that **analogy cannot invent**. copy only "what people like us do" and you get a faster horse, a slightly cheaper expendable rocket, a nicer $600 pack. | | analogy | first principles | |---|---|---| | starting point | precedent, industry, best practice | what must be true | | question | "how is this usually done?" | "what are we sure is true?" | | output | incremental variant | possible rebuild | | cost | low mental energy | high | | failure mode | invisible ceilings | wrong axioms, overbuild | | best use | known games, local optimization | new games, cost/physics ceilings | **when analogy is rational:** use it when the context delta is small and the cost of being wrong is low. you do not first-principles your grocery list. you first-principles the thing everyone swears is impossible. ### the five moves 1. **name the goal as a function, not a form.** not "build a cheaper aerospace rocket" — "move mass to orbit and, if possible, reuse the vehicle." 2. **separate facts from folklore.** write every constraint down and label each one: *physics* · *named human requirement* · *industry custom* · *fear / just-in-case*. only the first is sacred. the second is negotiable. the third and fourth are deletion candidates. 3. **decompose to constituents.** what is it *made of* — materials, forces, information, incentives? 4. **price or bound the constituents.** this is where it becomes quantitative (see tool 2). 5. **rebuild upward.** given these constituents and these true constraints, what is the simplest machine that produces the function? **the rebuild is where deletion happens.** ### why it is hard it takes more mental energy — analogy is pattern-matching, first principles is reconstruction. institutions prefer analogy because it is socially safe: you can always point at "how it's done." and school trains you to answer the assigned question, never to reject its hidden assumptions. so people **fake** it: they say "from first principles…" and then list three industry benchmarks. that is analogy with better branding. **a real pass feels slightly illegal** — you are saying out loud that a respected constraint might be folklore. --- ## tool 2 — the idiot index idiot index = price of finished part / cost of raw materials high ratio (often cited > 10 for production hardware) means over-machining, inherited process, certification theater, or a part that should not exist. musk's rocket check: raw materials were ~2% of typical rocket price, a ~50× markup over atoms. battery check in 2012: pack ~$600/kwh against materials ~$80/kwh. **a high index does not prove you can close the gap. it proves the ceiling is not physics.** ported to software: cost = c_essential + c_process + c_interfaces + c_failure_modes + c_overhead every added part pays all five terms. **deleting a part zeros all five. optimizing it shrinks one.** that is the whole argument for "the best part is no part." headroom = c_market − c_min, where c_min ≈ c_materials + c_energy + c_information large headroom means the opportunity is process and architecture — not "try harder at the current design." --- ## tool 3 — the algorithm the five steps, **in this order**. the order is the whole method. | # | step | the question | what it costs to skip | |---|------|--------------|----------------------| | 1 | question every requirement | who named this, and is it forced by physics/law/a live customer? | you build the wrong thing perfectly | | 2 | delete the part or process | does the intended function still happen without it? | you polish waste | | 3 | simplify and optimize | make what survived elegant | you optimize ghosts | | 4 | accelerate cycle time | same work, shorter loop | you go faster at the wrong work | | 5 | automate | only now hand it to a machine | you scale a mistake | musk ran it backwards himself at fremont — automate, accelerate, simplify, *then* discover the step never needed to exist — and called the resulting over-automation his own mistake ("excessive automation was a mistake… humans are underrated," 2018). **this playbook exists to force the order.** ### why smart people optimize things that shouldn't exist the diagnosis is psychological, not technical. school rewards answering the question you were given; you get no points for saying the question is dumb. so engineers inherit a straitjacket: given a part, make it faster, lighter, cheaper — never ask whether it should exist. two traps: - **smart-person requirements are the most dangerous.** people hesitate to challenge them, so a requirement from "legal," "safety," or a brilliant colleague survives with no owner. - **"just in case" bias.** you can invent a reason to keep almost anything. the rule: a requirement needs a **named human**, not a department. if no living person will defend it today, it is a deletion candidate. ### the three tests this playbook enforces **existence test.** for a part `p` and the intended function `f`: v(p) = f(with p) − f(without p) if `v(p) ≈ 0` on the *actual* function, delete `p`. not "make it cheaper" — delete it. keep p ⟺ the system without p fails the intended function if the car is still quiet, still fire-safe, still manufacturable without the pad, the pad was never a part. it was a superstition with a bom line. **the 10% add-back calibration.** delete aggressively enough that some deletions fail and come back: aggressiveness = items_restored / items_deleted target ≈ 0.10 `0` = timid, you left junk in. `≫0.10` = you deleted function, not waste. this is the honest answer to chesterton's fence: you don't refuse to remove the fence, you remove it and **pay** for the ones you were wrong about. **complexity tax and reliability.** parts cost themselves *and* their pairwise interfaces: tax(n) ∝ n + c(n,2) · c_interface r_system ≈ ∏ rᵢ two hundred parts at 99.5% each is a 37% system. deleting fifty beats improving any one of them. deletion is **superlinear** in value. ### why deletion makes the system better, not just cheaper a part is not only mass and dollars. it is a failure mode, a supplier, an inspection, a fixture, a robot cell, a tolerance stack, a training item, a warranty claim, and a coordination meeting. lean calls the compounding *muda*. systems people call it **gall's law**: a complex system that works evolved from a simple system that worked. you cannot optimize your way from the bloated version to the simple one — you have to delete back to it. ### the canonical examples - **tesla nvh/fire pad.** safety said noise required it; noise said safety required it; nobody owned the requirement. they pulled it, measured both, saw no difference, deleted it — and bypassed a ~$2m robot cell that existed only to install it. - **giga casting.** two mega-castings replaced ~70–171 stamped parts and ~1,600 welds. deletion at the architecture level, not a cheaper bracket. - **raptor 3.** external plumbing, wiring, and the engine-bay heat shield deleted or folded into the primary structure. delete the shield and a small leak dumps into plasma that is already on fire — the leak stops being a failure mode. "undesign" as the design win. - **grid fins that don't fold.** a folding mechanism is a whole extra system. add the hinge later if physics demands it; do not pre-install "in case." - **the anti-example: fremont automation.** the algorithm is partly a scar. --- ## architecture from first principles *(the reference layer for `--domain architecture`)* software architecture is **not** "microservices," "hexagonal," "event-driven," or "an agent mesh." those are forms. the function is simpler: > **turn inputs into correct, durable outputs, under change, failure, and finite resources — at a > cost a team can still understand.** everything else is a part. if you can delete it and that function still holds, the architecture got better. architecture = state + computation + boundaries - **state** — facts that must survive a request, a crash, or a deploy - **computation** — the transformations that make those facts useful - **boundaries** — where you cut so humans and machines can change one piece without detonating the rest brooks's split holds: **essential complexity** is the domain (billing rules, permissions, a workflow that must not double-charge); **accidental complexity** is everything added because of tools, fashion, or fear. architecture's job is to pay the essential cost and refuse the rest. a 40-service diagram drawn before the first user is analogical theater. the first-principles question is never "what stack should we use?" it is: > what state must exist, what transformations are required, and which cuts are **forced** — by > physics, consistency, scale, or independently changing teams — rather than by blog posts? ### the real first principles (these are close to physics) - **computation is local and cheap. coordination is remote and expensive.** an in-process call is nanoseconds and nearly certain; a network call is milliseconds, lossy, and has a different failure model. treating rpc as a local call is the original sin. deutsch's fallacies exist because every team rediscovers this. - **you cannot hide distribution.** split state across two computers and you inherit cap/pacelc: during a partition, consistency or availability; even healthy, consistency or latency. not a framework preference — a constraint. - **serial reliability multiplies downward.** `r_request ≈ ∏ rᵢ`. ten services at 99.9% in a synchronous chain is ~99.0%. you bought an order of magnitude more downtime by drawing boxes. - **latency adds; tail latency multiplies.** `t ≈ σtᵢ + t_queue + t_retry`. a 25 ms monolith query becomes 200+ ms as a chatty graph, and under partial slowness retries turn one slow dependency into a load amplifier. that is how "well-architected" systems melt. - **interfaces dominate cost.** bugs and outages live at seams. `cost ∝ n + c·c(n,2)_coupled` — **coupling, not box count, is the mass.** - **change is the long-run cost function.** after v1 the money goes to modification. a cut that does not match a real change boundary is a part that should not exist. - **human working memory is a hard limit.** a design nobody can hold in their head will be changed incorrectly. cognitive load is an operational constraint, same as ram. - **correctness needs a single writer per invariant.** spreading "an order cannot be paid twice" across four services does not distribute the rule — it **deletes** the rule and hopes a saga puts it back. ### what is almost never a first principle | folklore | what it pretends | what is actually true | |---|---|---| | start with microservices | scale and team independence are free | you paid the microservice premium on day one: deploys, tracing, eventual consistency, on-call. worth it only when a monolith is already too expensive to change. | | one service = one db = purity | data isolation is architecture | split data only when the *write invariant* can live in one place. shared-db "services" are a distributed monolith with extra latency. | | event-driven = decoupled | async deletes coupling | it defers coupling into payload schemas, ordering, and "who owns the truth." | | kubernetes from request one | production-grade | orchestration is a process for many processes. zero processes do not need a cluster. | | hexagonal / clean / cqrs / ddd everywhere | professionalism | patterns are compression for specific pains. used early they are second-system jewelry. | | gateway + mesh + queue + workflow engine + flags + cdp | completeness | each is a part. most products need two of those, not six. | | multi-agent graph as default | intelligence | an agent is a loop over tools and state. extra agents are extra parts with extra coordination. | | "we'll need it at scale" | prudence | yagni plus gall: you do not know your real boundaries until the domain hurts. | fowler's observation is empirical, not aesthetic: successful microservice systems usually *grew out of* a monolith; greenfield microservice systems often get into serious trouble. ### the architecture idiot index i_arch = (runtime components + control planes) / owned invariants if the diagram has twenty boxes and the constituent list still has five items, you are looking at process, not physics. high `i_arch` means you are optimizing a factory that builds parts the product does not need. **constituents, for reference.** *the user needs:* a state change · an identity · a durable record · a way to see status · a way to change the rules later. *the machine needs:* bytes on disk · a cpu · a clock · a network **only** when two failure domains must be separate · observability. *the team needs:* a boundary they can change in one pr · a test that encodes the invariant · a deploy that cannot strand half the invariant on another team's release train. ### delete candidates that usually survive deletion - a service whose only job is to crud one table - a synchronous hop that could be an in-process function - a second database for a second service that always joins the first - an orchestration engine wrapping a 4-step script - a workflow engine plus an agent runtime plus a rules engine doing the same job - dual writes "for now" - an api layer that only translates json to json - a cache in front of a database that is already fast - a message queue between two modules that deploy together and fail together - a redesign of auth when a signed session already works if checkout still charges once, shows status, and survives a crash without `p`, `p` was not architecture. it was furniture. ### the first-principles default shape not because monoliths are morally better — because this matches the constituents. that system **already has architecture**: module boundaries + owned invariants + explicit async for slow/retryable work. ### the four split triggers — the only reasons for a second deployable 1. **independent scale axis** — transcode saturates cpu; the api does not. 2. **independent failure domain** — a blast radius you cannot accept in-process. 3. **independent change cadence / team** — two groups on incompatible clocks, with a stable contract. 4. **a hard consistency island** — payments, ledger, or tool-calls that must serialize. until one is true **and named**, a new process is a part. and when you do split, **split along the invariant, not along nouns.** "userservice / notificationservice" recreates the er diagram on the network — that is analogy to a database schema, not design. ### worked rebuilds **checkout.** function: reserve stock, take money at most once, emit a receipt. *first-principles cut:* one component owns the order row and the payment idempotency key; inventory decrement is in the same transaction or an explicit reservation record; email is a queue; loyalty points are off the critical path. *analogical cut:* order → inventory → pricing → tax → payment → notification. you turned one acid transaction into a saga so you could draw boxes, then spent a year making the saga correct. **crm / outreach / agent os.** function: a durable record of people and conversations, plus a runner that can take the next allowed action. constituents: contacts, threads, permissions, a job queue, tool adapters, an audit log. you do not need a lead microservice, an agent orchestration cluster, a memory vector db, and a workflow engine on day one. you need one store for source-of-truth records, one runner for tool calls with idempotency, and prompts/policies as data. extra agents and buses are heat shields around a function that is still "update row, call api, write result." **read-heavy product.** forced: a cache or a read replica. not forced: five cqrs services and a kafka backbone before you have a slow query. **multi-tenant saas.** forced: tenant isolation in the data model, authz on every query, noisy-neighbor limits. not forced: a cluster per tenant at ten customers. ### formulas for a design review split ⟺ ∃ a scale, failure, team, or invariant axis that a module cannot absorb t_p99 ≈ n · l_net + σ t_svc + t_retry_amplification — if n hops exist only to preserve diagram cleanliness, delete hops one writer ≫ many writers + coordinator — every extra writer on an invariant requires consensus or a saga; consensus is a part good cut ⟺ (prs inside one module) / (prs touching ≥2 modules) is high for the changes you ship — if most real work crosses the cut, the cut is wrong; merge the services (that is the 10%) c_total = c_domain + c_distribution + c_platform + c_ceremony — quality is how small you make the last three without growing the first --- ## what counts as a "part" a part is anything with an interface, a failure mode, and an owner: a service · a queue · a feature flag · a config entry · a db column · a migration · a middleware · an approval step · a cron job · a registry entry · a component prop · a wrapper around a wrapper · a cli flag · a checklist item · a recurring meeting · a status report nobody reads shapes that are almost always a finding — calibration for what one looks like: - **a registry, menu, or api surface that has grown far past what its consumers can hold.** when the list is three times longer than a comparable one that works, the count and the bugs are one problem, not two. - **a capability that needs n places wired before it does anything**, and fails silently if any one is missed. a high wiring count is `i_arch` screaming. - **a stale duplicate of something that lives elsewhere.** not merely unnecessary — actively misleading, because people read it and believe it. - **declared-vs-actual drift** (props, schemas, contracts, config) that quietly disables a feature. those are deletion candidates, not documentation candidates. ## steps ### the function (one testable sentence) ### constituents and owned invariants — who owns each ### folklore found (constraints that failed the truth filter) ### idiot index — before → after ### deleted (with what each one takes with it) ### kept, and the function or invariant that justifies it ### simplified ### cycle time: before → after ### automated (and what stayed human) ### predicted add-back (the 10%) ### verification — the exact command or browser check that proves the function still holds end with one line: **the intended function this system exists to perform**, stated so plainly that a stranger could test it. --- name the job. list the invariants. put each invariant next to one owner. keep those owners in one process until a named axis forces a second. treat every new box as a rocket part: it has mass, failure modes, and an idiot index. question the requirement, delete the box, simplify the module that remains, then speed up the loop, then automate. **the best service is no service. the best queue is a function that returns. the best orchestration layer is a for-loop you can read.** when those stop working — measured, not imagined — you add a part. function first · existence second · elegance third · speed fourth · robots last. if you can delete it and the thing still does the job, you did not lose architecture. you found it.

entries.describe: V6 Agent Tools — The Five-Layer Wiring Skill
entries.haystack: v6-tools v6 agent tools — the five-layer wiring skill <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: v6-tools description: add, debug, or audit a v6 agent tool in the iris platform (fl-iris-api). a v6 tool needs all five layers wired or it silently no-ops ("tool unavailable"). use this when an agent should be able to call a new capability in conversation (slack/chat), when a tool exists but the agent says it's unavailable, or when auditing tool wiring. pass the tool intent as argument (e.g. "add get_settlement_status backed by the cases dataset", "debug why get_credentialing_alerts says unavailable"). allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - grep - glob - bash - agent - task --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run v6-tools ` > run this playbook: `iris playbook run v6-tools ` # v6 agent tools — the five-layer wiring skill a **v6 agent tool** is a capability an agent can call mid-conversation (slack, chat, channel) — distinct from an `iris` **cli verb** a human types. the two are separate surfaces: shipping a cli command does not make a tool callable by an agent, and vice versa. this skill is for the **agent-tool** surface. the engine is **fl-iris-api** (`fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api`, laravel) — not fl-api. the path is `reactlooprequest::chat()/::channel()` → `v6toolregistry::gettoolsforagent()` → `execute()`. ## arguments `$arguments` — the tool intent or the failing tool. examples: - `/v6-tools add get_settlement_status backed by the cases dataset` - `/v6-tools debug why get_credentialing_alerts says "tool unavailable"` - `/v6-tools audit the pathways agent's tool wiring` --- ## ⚠️ the core law **a v6 agent tool needs all five layers wired or it silently no-ops.** a missing layer never throws a loud error — it gets laundered into a generic *"that tool is unavailable"* and the agent moves on. most "the tool doesn't work" reports are one missing layer. mirror a known-good sibling (`get_denial_risk`, `get_overdue_followups`, `get_credentialing_alerts`) across all five. `gpt-4.1-nano` is too weak to route to niche tools; `gpt-4o-mini` is better — but the **yaml registry matters more than the model**. (per global rule: only ever use the nano/mini models — gpt-5-nano, gpt-4.1-nano, gpt-4o-mini.) --- ## the five layers all file paths are under `fl-docker-dev/fl-iris-api/`. always **read the canonical sibling first** and copy its shape — do not invent structure. ### layer 1 — registry: definition + executor **`app/services/v6/v6toolregistry.php`** in `gettoolsforagent()` (~line 440), a tool is pushed to the list and its executor closure is registered. mirror the sibling: then add your `getxxxtooldefinition()` (openai function schema) and `executexxx()` method. the `executexxx()` typically delegates to `appdataservice::getcollectiondata($slug, '<collection>', $filters)` and formats the result into a human-readable message + structured `data`. ### layer 2 — `config/system-tools.yaml` (the single source of truth for discoverability) without a yaml entry, weak models never route to the tool — a hardcoded `$tools[]` is **not** enough. copy a complete sibling entry: the `functions.<name>` key is the function name the model emits. the `description` is your routing signal — write it with the phrases a user would actually say. ### layer 3 — collection dispatch (the data behind the tool) **`app/services/appdataservice.php`** two flavors — pick the one the sibling uses: - **non-atlas computed collection:** add the name to the `$virtualcollections` array in `getcollectiondata()` (~line 117) and a `case` in its `match()`: - **atlas-backed collection (reads `atlas_records`):** add a `getatlasmappings()` entry (~line 980) mapping `{slug}/{collection}` → `{schema}:{subtype}`, then a `case` in the `switch ($subtype)` inside `getatlasvirtualcollection()` (~line 1393): **missing the `getatlasmappings()` entry is the #1 silent failure** → the router returns `"atlas mapping not found"` → agent says "unavailable." ### layer 4 — the rule method (the actual logic) **`app/services/appdataservice.php`** — write `buildxxx(array $rows): array` returning the canonical shape: mirror `buildatlasdenialrisk()` (~line 1599) for scoring/threshold/terminal-stage-filtering patterns. ### layer 5 — agent allowlist + the execute() health gate - **allowlist:** add the function name to the agent's `config['tools']` (a bloq_agent json keep-set, e.g. patty #420). `filtertoolsbyagentallowlist()` (~line 719): an empty/null allowlist = full set; a present allowlist filters to listed names + `core_tool_names`. if the agent has an allowlist and your name isn't in it, the tool is invisible to that agent. - **health gate:** `execute()` (~line 1717) calls `istoolhealthy()` before running. it resolves the tool by the **function name the model calls** via `findtoolbyfunction()` (~line 208), which scans `functions[].name` in the yaml. if it can't resolve (yaml missing/typo'd, or `requires_api_key` points at an unconfigured service), the tool is marked unhealthy → `execute()` blocks it → laundered into "unavailable." internal tools with no `requires_api_key` are always healthy. --- ## canonical end-to-end trace — `get_denial_risk` | layer | file | symbol | |------|------|--------| | 1 registry | `v6/v6toolregistry.php:573` | `getdenialrisktooldefinition()` + `$executors['get_denial_risk']` | | 2 yaml | `config/system-tools.yaml:529` | `getdenialrisk:` → `functions.get_denial_risk` | | 3 dispatch | `appdataservice.php:1206/1393` | `getatlasmappings()['pathways-dashboard/denial-risk'] = 'cases:denial-risk'` → `switch` case | | 4 rule | `appdataservice.php:1599` | `buildatlasdenialrisk()` | | 5a allowlist | `v6/v6toolregistry.php:719` | `filtertoolsbyagentallowlist()` ← `$agent->config['tools']` | | 5b health gate | `v6/v6toolregistry.php:1717/208` | `execute()` → `istoolhealthy()` → `findtoolbyfunction()` | | exec | `v6/v6toolregistry.php:3006` | `executegetdenialrisk()` → `appdataservice::getcollectiondata($slug,'denial-risk',[])` | to add a tool: read each row's symbol, copy its shape, swap the names. parity tests `v6toolregistryyamldriventest.php` + `chatpathtoolparitytest.php` keep the layers honest. --- ## verification — what lies and what's trustworthy verification of v6 tools is full of false signals. trust only the ✅ paths: - ❌ `iris agents chat` / `iris chat` — historically an **unfaithful** harness (#137387). don't trust it for tool routing. - ❌ `integrations exec` — 422s on internal tools. - ❌ public http to `/api/v1/app-data/...` for **pathways** collections — phi-gated, returns 404/empty when unscoped. a gated 404 does not mean "no data." - ✅ **compute in-container** — run the rule via an artisan command or `appdataservice` directly through `railway ssh`. bypasses the http gate; proves deploy + data at once. - ✅ **a real slack message** to the agent — the only faithful end-to-end channel test. > `railway ssh -- <cmd>` re-shells the flattened argv, so parens/quotes/pipes break. for anything needing php logic, **write a real artisan command, deploy it, run it** — clean argv, reusable. see `fl-docker-dev/production_debugging_guide.md`. --- ## "agent says a tool is unavailable" — debug order walk the five layers; the failure is almost always #2, #3-mapping, or #5b: 1. **yaml (layer 2)** — is there a `functions.<name>` entry matching the exact name the model calls? missing/typo'd → unhealthy. 2. **atlas mapping (layer 3)** — for atlas tools, is there a `getatlasmappings()` entry? missing → "atlas mapping not found." 3. **health gate (layer 5b)** — does `findtoolbyfunction()` resolve it? does `requires_api_key` point at a configured service? 4. **allowlist (layer 5a)** — is the function name in the agent's `config['tools']`? 5. **deploy/branch-sync** — is the new code actually live, and are api + worker on the same commit? confirm the fix with a **real slack message**, never `iris agents chat`. --- ## research protocol before adding or editing a tool, you must: 1. **read the canonical sibling** end-to-end (`get_denial_risk` / `get_overdue_followups`) across all five files. copy its shape. 2. **grep for the function name** to confirm it isn't already half-wired. 3. **confirm the data source** exists (atlas schema/collection or computed rows) before writing the rule. 4. after deploy: grep the new symbol in-container, check api/worker commit parity, then test via slack. do not speculate about code you haven't read. if a layer's file/method has moved, re-trace from the sibling rather than trusting these line numbers.

entries.haystack: v6-workflows build, debug, test, and extend the v6.5 unified workflow system — the core execution engine powering agentic/steps/code modes, quality loops, reflection, eval suites, and callable workflows. pass an action as argument (e.g., \"debug\", \"add-tool\", \"eval\", \"test\", \"deploy\", \"status\", \"architecture\"). --- description: "build, debug, test, and extend the v6.5 unified workflow system — the core execution engine powering agentic/steps/code modes, quality loops, reflection, eval suites, and callable workflows. pass an action as argument (e.g., \"debug\", \"add-tool\", \"eval\", \"test\", \"deploy\", \"status\", \"architecture\")." allowed-tools: - read - edit - write - bash - grep - glob - task - agent --- # v6.5 unified workflows — development & operations skill build on, debug, and extend the unified workflow system across frontend, backend, and cli. ## arguments `$arguments` — action to perform. examples: - `/v6-workflows status` — overview of system health, recent runs, eval scores - `/v6-workflows debug <workflow_id>` — investigate a failed workflow run - `/v6-workflows architecture` — show full system diagram and data flow - `/v6-workflows add-tool <name>` — register a new tool in the v6 registry for workflows - `/v6-workflows add-step-type <name>` — add a new step type to the steps mode - `/v6-workflows eval run <workflow_id>` — run eval suite against a workflow - `/v6-workflows eval add <workflow_id>` — add eval assertions to a workflow - `/v6-workflows test` — run full test suite (php + playwright e2e) - `/v6-workflows deploy` — push iris-api to railway, verify deployment - `/v6-workflows transpile <workflow_id>` — generate sdk script from steps - `/v6-workflows reflection` — check reflection loop config, token budgets - `/v6-workflows quality` — inspect quality evaluation settings and thresholds - `/v6-workflows bugs` — show known bugs and their fix status - `/v6-workflows extend` — guide for adding new capabilities to the system --- ## architecture overview ### three execution modes, one system **key insight**: steps and code are synced views of the same `fixed` execution mode. the db stores `execution_mode: 'agentic' | 'fixed'`. transpilation converts steps json to executable scripts (node.js/python/bash). ### execution flow ### sub-tab architecture (phase 6) ### database schema --- ## file map ### frontend (fl-elon-web-ui) | file | lines | purpose | |------|-------|---------| | `components/dashboard/bloq/cardeditorworkflowtab.vue` | 3,646 | main ui: gallery, mode toggle, sub-tabs, editor panels | | `utils/workflowexecutionservice.js` | 45 | service class for dispatching workflow api calls | ### backend (fl-iris-api) | file | lines | purpose | |------|-------|---------| | `app/http/controllers/api/v6workspacecontroller.php` | 4,499 | api endpoints: run-agentic, result, cancel, run-callable | | `app/jobs/runworkspaceagenticjob.php` | 1,344 | async job: executes workflow, quality retries, caching | | `app/services/v6/reactloopservice.php` | 4,434 | core react loop: reasoning, tool calling, doom-loop detection | | `app/services/v6/qualityevaluationservice.php` | ~530 | score output 0-100 against success criteria, pii sanitization | | `app/services/v6/erroranalysisservice.php` | 177 | categorize failures: timeout, auth, rate_limit, empty, invalid_params, internal, unknown | | `app/services/v6/executionreflectionservice.php` | 184 | select retry strategy: simplify, pivot_tool, add_context, decompose, retry_as_is | | `app/services/v6/evalsuiterunner.php` | 737 | run eval test cases, 10 assertion types, scoring, badges | | `app/services/v6/workflowtransformerservice.php` | 298 | transpile steps json to node.js/python/bash sdk scripts | | `app/services/integrations/workflowcomposer/workflowcomposerintegrationservice.php` | 1,781 | ai workflow generation, marketplace, 12 functions | | `app/neuron/tools/callworkflowtool.php` | 344 | callable workflows: workflow-calls-workflow with depth guard | | `config/integrations/workflow-composer.yml` | 387 | yaml config: 12 workflow composer integration functions | ### cli (iris-code) | file | lines | purpose | |------|-------|---------| | `packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/platform-workflows.ts` | 1,724 | 14 cli commands: list, generate, run, eval, hub, pull/push/diff | ### tests | file | purpose | |------|---------| | `fl-iris-api/tests/` (filter: quality, workspace, workflow) | php unit + feature tests (40+ quality, 36+ workspace) | | `tests/e2e/workflow-mode-toggle.spec.ts` | playwright e2e: mode toggle, sub-tabs, code editor, screenshots | --- ## self-healing reflection loop (phase 5) when a workflow execution fails, the system automatically attempts recovery: --- ## quality evaluation (phase 5.5) ### how it works after workflow completes, `qualityevaluationservice` scores output: - compares output against user-defined `successcriteria` array - sends to ai eval (gpt-4o-mini) with pii-sanitized output - returns score 0-100, per-criterion results, improvement suggestions - if score < `qualitythreshold` (default 70), re-dispatches job with feedback ### eval suite (10 assertion types) ### cli commands --- ## key api endpoints --- ## known bugs & fixes (april 2026) | bug | status | fix | |-----|--------|-----| | #69378 pii leak in quality eval | fixed (fe1d7e5) | `sanitizeforevaluation()` masks emails, phones, ssns, api keys, cards | | #69379 cache key race during retries | fixed (fe1d7e5) | versioned keys `workspace_result:{id}:attempt:{n}` | | #69377 static calldepth race condition | fixed (fe1d7e5) | laravel `context` facade instead of static property | | #69380 vuex strict mode in playwright | not a bug | dev-only; test runs against production url where strict mode is off | --- ## common operations ### adding a new tool to workflows 1. register executor in `reactloopservice` or `v6toolregistry`: 2. add tool definition to agent's available tools (frontend workspacetoolslist or agent settings) 3. if it's an integration tool, add to `config/integrations/` yaml and `integrationregistry` ### adding a new step type 1. define step schema in `workflowcomposerintegrationservice::getsteptypes()` 2. add ui rendering in `cardeditorworkflowtab.vue` step accordion 3. add transpilation support in `workflowtransformerservice::transpilestep()` 4. add execution handler in `reactloopservice` or as a tool executor ### debugging a failed workflow ### running tests ### deploying changes --- ## extension points (what to build next) ### immediate (v6.5.1) - **workflow versioning**: snapshot steps + settings on each save, rollback support - **parallel step execution**: steps with no dependencies run concurrently - **webhook triggers**: external events trigger workflow execution ### medium-term (v6.6) - **workflow marketplace**: publish/discover community workflows - **conditional branching**: if/else logic in steps mode - **multi-agent orchestration**: workflow steps assigned to different agents - **streaming results**: real-time token-by-token output to frontend ### long-term (v7) - **visual dag editor**: drag-and-drop node graph (replaces linear steps) - **workflow-as-api**: expose any workflow as a rest endpoint - **cross-workspace composition**: workflows calling workflows across bloqs --- ## architecture decisions (adrs) | decision | choice | why | |----------|--------|-----| | 2 execution modes, not 3 | `agentic` + `fixed` | steps and code are views of same data; reduces db complexity | | service object, not vue mixin | `workflowexecutionservice.js` | explicit deps, testable, no silent collision risk in vue 2 | | campaign templates = read-only | import into `bloq_workflows` | zero existing code removed; templates stay pristine | | 50k cumulative token budget | hard cap on reflection retries | prevents runaway costs from infinite retry loops | | pii sanitization in eval | regex-based masking | defense-in-depth; eval ai call is separate context from execution | | request-scoped call depth | laravel `context` facade | prevents cross-request state bleed in long-lived php processes | | versioned cache keys | `workspace_result:{id}:attempt:{n}` | prevents stale reads during quality retry race conditions | --- ## steps (for the skill runner) ### 1. parse the argument | argument | action | |----------|--------| | `status` | show recent workflow runs, eval scores, error rates | | `debug <id>` | investigate specific workflow failure (logs, cache, retries) | | `architecture` | display full system diagram from this document | | `add-tool <name>` | guide through registering a new tool | | `add-step-type <name>` | guide through adding a new step type | | `eval run <id>` | execute eval suite via cli | | `eval add <id>` | add eval assertions interactively | | `test` | run php + playwright test suites | | `deploy` | push to railway, verify health | | `transpile <id>` | generate sdk script from workflow steps | | `reflection` | inspect reflection loop config and token budgets | | `quality` | inspect quality eval settings and recent scores | | `bugs` | show known bugs table from this document | | `extend` | show extension points and how to add capabilities | | (empty) | show this help summary | ### 2. execute the action read the relevant files listed in the file map above. use the architecture diagrams and code paths to guide investigation or implementation. ### 3. after making changes - always run `npm run fix-file <path>` after editing vue files - run relevant php tests: `docker compose exec -t iris-api php artisan test --filter="<area>"` - run playwright tests if ui changed: `npx playwright test tests/e2e/workflow-mode-toggle.spec.ts` - never use `this.$toast` — use `messagesutility` mixin - never use gpt-3.5-turbo — only gpt-5-nano, gpt-4.1-nano, or gpt-4o-mini
