entries.haystack: work-the-epic work the epic <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: work-the-epic description: start a piece of work the way it should be started — an epic written before the work, published so the user can watch it without asking for status, existing bugs attached instead of duplicated, and a diary entry at the end that records what you got wrong. work that isn't written down gets re-derived; a user who can't see what you're doing can't redirect you. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run work-the-epic <goal>` > steps: search → draft → publish → verify → graph → fanout → work → diary # work the epic the loop this project actually runs on: plan in public, attach don't duplicate, draw it when words are doing badly, and write down the wrong turns at the end. **skip this for a typo, a one-line answer, or a question.** ceremony on trivial work trains people to ignore the ceremony, and then it isn't there when it matters. ## steps --- # writing it well nine techniques taken from epics in this workspace that actually did their job. they are about wording, because wording is where these documents fail — not structure. ## 1. state the goal so it can be scored, not just read > `## the vision, stated so it can be scored against` quote the goal, then immediately say what would count as done. a goal nobody can score becomes "in progress" forever, because there is no sentence that would end it. ## 2. give every component a verdict, not a status not "in progress". real verdicts from a real epic: 1 · format ✅ solid 2 · data ✅ solid 3 · composition this is the gap, and it is the only one left 4 · execution built, and not connected "built, and not connected" tells you what to do next. "in progress" does not. notice the third one also says what it is not: *untouched, not half-done*. ## 3. record the decision, and the mistake it prevents ## adr-01 · s2.1 is deferred. there is no shared server node. **status: accepted, 2026-08-28.** ### the mistake this record exists to prevent decisions get re-litigated when only the conclusion was written down. write the confusion it resolved — that adr existed because one word, "server node", had silently covered two different products, and the epic had been planning both at once. ## 4. say why not the alternatives > `## why this, and not something new` the strongest part of a plan is usually the option it rejected. without it, the first person to think of that option re-opens the whole question. ## 5. sequence the work, and then argue against your own sequence > `## sequencing` … then `### against the sequencing` steelman the objection in the document. if it survives, the plan is stronger; if it does not, you have changed the plan before building the wrong thing. ## 6. date the status line > `## where this stands — 2026-08-27` an undated status is worse than none, because it is trusted after it stops being true. ## 7. name the method before the findings > `## the method: build one, and count what breaks` state how you are going to find out. it lets the reader judge whether the answer is worth anything, and it stops you quietly changing the method when the answer is inconvenient. ## 8. give each bug an aphoristic title real ones: - **a name is not an identity** - **present-but-empty is not present** - **a node that reports healthy while dying** - **the mode that worked only in the case with no purpose** - **a suggestion that cannot explain itself cannot be approved** - **it was broken, and broken in the shape that hides** a title that states the general lesson makes the bug findable and transferable. "fixed node lookup" teaches nobody anything. ## 9. draw the bug, not just the fix > `## the bugs, drawn` two layers side by side, with the data flowing down each and the point where they diverge: orchestration layer transport layer ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │ node: macbookpro │ │ node: macbookpro │ └────────┬─────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘ │ passed through as uuid │ matched by name ▼ ▼ 500 server error no match — dead end ship both an ascii version and an `svg` block when it will be read on the web: ascii survives a terminal and a diff, svg scales on the page. ## 10. verify on the real workload, not an easier one the most expensive false green is not a check that fails to run. it is a check that runs, passes, and was pointed at something smaller than the thing you are shipping. on 2026-08-28 i qualified a model with **6/6 successful completions** and made it the default for every playbook. the prompt was one line. on a real playbook-sized prompt: same model, same day, opposite verdict. and i had *just written*, in the file i was editing, "membership is earned by real completions, never by the docs" — then earned it with completions that were not the workload. the same shape, three times in one session: - recommended `iris gmail inbox` to a client after testing it **on my own account**, where it works because my connection sits in the store that command reads. hers did not. - reported a fix live from `grep -c ... || echo 0`, which appends a second `0` on no-match, so `"0\n0" != "0"` was true. my verification had the bug i had spent the day fixing. - called a release deployed because the tag existed, while its assets were still uploading. **the questions that catch it:** - is my test input the size and shape of production input, or a convenient miniature? - am i running as the user who has the problem, or as myself with different state? - does my check distinguish *absent* from *equal*? (`"" != ""` is false. so is `0 == 0` when both sides failed to populate.) - if the thing i am testing were completely broken, would this check say so? **and the corollary, which is the real cost:** when someone reports a problem you have already measured as fine, the disagreement is almost never about the measurement. it is about **what got measured**. a client said a download was wrong seven times; each time the url resolved, returned 200, and served a working application — the wrong one. seven repetitions is a very loud instrument to read as noise. ## the one rule under all ten **write the thing that stops the next person repeating your dead end.** findings age. "ruled out, and here is how" does not.

entries.describe: X Ads — paid campaign, built paused
entries.haystack: x-ads x ads — paid campaign, built paused <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: x-ads description: launch a paid x ads campaign without the risk of a runaway bill. it checks your funding, confirms no one else is already spending, builds the whole thing paused, and waits for you to personally say go before a single dollar moves — with every campaign and its cost logged automatically so you always know what ran. --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run x-ads <objective> <daily_budget> <total_budget>` > steps: preflight-funding → armed-check → registry-state → budget-math → create → review → activate → record # x ads — paid campaign, built paused paid placement on x, with the guardrails that came out of a real near-miss. ## ⚠️ what this playbook can and cannot execute today the x ads surface is an **mcp server** (` playbook steps are `shell`, `prompt` or `human` — **none of them can call an mcp tool.** so every step that touches x is `mode: human`: it prints the exact tool call and stops for a person or an agent holding the mcp connection to run it. that is deliberate. a shell step that silently could not reach x would report success and do nothing, which is the exact defect class this playbook exists to prevent. **this becomes fully automated when `iris ads` ships** (epic — native x ads in iris). at that point every `mode: human` step below becomes `mode: shell` calling `iris ads …`, and the procedure does not change. ## why every money step stops on 2026-08-23 a campaign called `2026 sxsw season` was found `entity_status: active`, `effective_status: running`, `servable: true` — and had spent **$0.00**. it was not paused. it was **starved**: the funding instrument was dead. ads manager called it *"funding paused"*, a state that appears in neither api field. **billing being broken was the only thing standing between a stale campaign and $150.** the moment a working card was added, it was armed to spend $10/day with 2024 creative. hence `armed-check` below. no other ads tool has that step, and it is the reason this playbook exists rather than a checklist. ## two traps that cost real time, encoded here so nobody rediscovers them 1. **`credit_remaining_local_micro: 0` does not mean out of money.** on a `credit_card` instrument it reads 0 on a perfectly healthy card — verified against ads manager showing 0% of a $200 limit used. **trust `able_to_fund` + `reasons_not_able_to_fund` only.** 2. **activating a campaign alone does nothing.** the line item is where delivery happens. activate one without the other and it silently does not run — or, worse, you conclude the campaign failed when it never started. ## eight more, found running this for real (2026-08-23 · 2026-08-27) the steps above were checklist-accurate but untested against the live api until this run (objective: recruit to paid bounties, campaign `p5ib7`, line item `xhd4m`). it surfaced things no amount of reading the tool descriptions would have caught: 3. **`create_ad_post` does not truncate — `"truncated": true` in its response is a lie.** *(corrected 2026-08-24. the first version of this entry claimed a ~140-char limit that ate your url. that was wrong, and the wrong version shipped — read on.)* the create response returns the x api **v1.1 compatibility `text` field**, which always shows a 140-char legacy view ending in a `t.co` link to the tweet's own permalink, with `"truncated": true` beside it. it looks exactly like your copy was cut off and the landing url deleted. **it wasn't.** read the post back with `list_account_posts(tweet_ids=...)`: `full_text` is complete, `truncated: false`, and the url is present as a normal `t.co` link (that shortening is just how x stores links). verified on post `2091645697636417939`, and consistent with the 2026-02 `[mk-08]` ads, which are 204–279 characters and perfectly intact. **so: long ad copy is fine.** do not shorten to work around a limit that does not exist. bare-url-at-the-end copy is still a good *choice* — x expands it into a rich twitter card pulled live from the page — but it is a preference, not a constraint. 4. **skip `media_upload` for images entirely if a landing-page card will do.** the tool requires the full file **base64-encoded inline in the tool call** — an 80kb png is ~108,000 base64 characters, which cost over 100k tokens to push through an agent's context (and got truncated mid-file even just reading it back). for a promoted post whose real job is driving clicks to a url, let `create_ad_post`'s auto twitter card do the visual work instead of uploading creative. reach for `media_upload` only when the image itself is the message and there's no reasonable landing page to card-ify. 5. **`create_line_item` requires `bid_amount_local_micro` in practice**, even though the tool description says `bid_strategy: auto` (the default) needs no bid amount. the live api rejects an auto/no-bid call with `missing_parameter`. use `bid_strategy="max"` with an explicit `bid_amount_local_micro` (e.g. `1500000` = $1.50) until/unless auto is confirmed working again. 6. **there is no `list_promotable_users` tool.** `create_ad_post` needs `as_user_id`, the numeric x user id to post as. get it from `list_account_posts(account_id=..., tweet_type="published", count=1)` → `data[0].user.id` — any existing post on the account carries the right id. 7. **ads cannot contain hashtags.** `create_ad_post` accepts them, `promote_post` returns `approval_status: accepted`, and then the ad is silently rejected ~30 seconds later — the campaign stays `running`/`servable: true` while serving nothing. the exact string, which appears in **no api response**, is: *"ads cannot include hashtags in the ad text. please choose a different post to promote."* strip every `#tag` from promoted copy. (an organic post with the same caption is fine — this rule is specific to paid.) 8. **a conversion event cannot be attached to a `website_clicks` campaign.** `primary_web_event_tag` reads `null` on such a line item and there is no way to set it: `update_line_item` does not expose the field, and ads manager does not render the control on a click-objective ad group — the field only exists on a campaign built with a conversion objective. so "add conversion tracking to the campaign already running" is **not a task**; it is a new campaign. budget for that before promising anyone a cost per signup. (found 2026-08-27 on `p5ib7`/`xhd4m`, after the tracking itself was working.) 9. **the pixel being installed is not the same as the conversion page being instrumented.** `theme.analytics.xpixel` is set **per genesis page**. on 2026-08-27 `/p/freelabel` carried the pixel and `/p/freelabel-start` — the intake the ads were paying to reach, where the conversion actually happens — had **no analytics config at all**. events manager looked healthy the whole time (two auto-created events recording daily), so nothing anywhere said "the money page is dark". **check the page that completes the action, not the page that starts it.** 10. **an event that has never fired reads as a zero, not as a gap.** the account's `purchase` event had status `inactive` and `last recorded: —` since creation, and the dashboard rendered that as `purchases 0`. a number that means "never wired" is indistinguishable from a number that means "nobody bought". in events manager, read the **last recorded** column before believing any conversion count. ## the one that made all the others irrelevant (2026-09-01) campaign `p6ykz` / line item `xj75r`, the bug-bounty poster b04. **the best-performing ad this account has ever run, and it converted nothing, because nobody was eligible to convert.** 11. **check who is eligible before you check anything else.** b04 bought 354,060 impressions and 1,319 link clicks at **$0.0057 each — 63× cheaper than the $0.359 recruit-side baseline** — plus 136 likes, 7 reposts and a reply, which is the first real organic pickup any campaign here has had. submissions: **0**. not a low rate. the apply endpoint gates on confirmed program membership (`opportunitycontroller::apply`, #166095), every funded bounty carries a `program_id`, and every one of those programs had **`member_count: 0`**. the set of people permitted to apply was empty, so the intersection with 1,319 clickers was empty too. **no spend level changes an intersection with an empty set.** three real defects were found and fixed first, and each would independently have suppressed conversion: the landing page rendered `available to pay out $0` on a bounty that had already paid out $150; the bug-bounty apply form asked for a dj mix, a portfolio reel and the applicant's availability; and twelve entry points across two brands did not resolve. fixing all three and *still* seeing zero is what exposed the fourth — and only the fourth made the outcome impossible rather than merely unlikely. **before spending on a campaign that asks anyone to apply, sign up or submit, get a number for "how many people are currently allowed to complete this action."** it is one query. if the answer is zero, no creative, budget, targeting or landing-page work can matter. full write-up: `/p/epic-bounty-gate`. 12. **the ad platform will not tell you the funnel is dead — every metric it owns looked excellent.** cpc, ctr, impressions, engagement and spend pacing were all outstanding *because they measure the half of the journey x controls*. every number on the dashboard was real, and every one of them was about a click that could never become anything. when ad metrics are strong and outcomes are zero, stop reading the ad platform: the fault is always past the click, and the ad platform cannot see past the click. 13. **a targeting id longer than 15 digits silently becomes a different audience.** `search_targeting_interests` returns 19-digit values (e.g. technology / software development = `1925953040130953216`). passing that to `add_targeting_criterion` — whose schema types the field as a **string** — sent `23005` and applied **"computer certification"**, a completely different interest. the call returned `200` with a success body. nineteen digits exceeds javascript's safe integer range (2^53), so the value is coerced somewhere in transit and lands on whatever the truncated number happens to mean. **always `list_targeting_criteria` after adding, and compare the `name` you got to the one you asked for.** the add response itself already showed the wrong name — it just looked like a success. **prefer `broad_keyword` over `interest` where the offer allows it.** a keyword is text with no id to mangle: `"bug bounty"` arrives as `"bug bounty"`. it is also better targeting for a specific offer — someone posting about penetration testing is a far stronger signal than membership of a broad technology bucket. 14. **a line item created through the api has no targeting at all, and that is not an error.** both bug-bounty line items ran with zero criteria — no country, no interest, no keyword, worldwide, everybody. the create-flow ui shows "united states" as a default, but a line item built by `create_line_item` inherits none of it, and nothing warns you. broad delivery is exactly the profile that produces very cheap, very low-quality clicks: 1,319 of them produced 44 landings. `list_targeting_criteria` returning `{"data":[]}` is the check. empty means worldwide. 15. **read this file before solving a media problem — trap 4 is already the answer.** on 2026-09-01 i needed four poster creatives into an ad account, measured the pngs at ~86kb (~115,000 base64 characters), tested jpeg (worse: 156kb — these are flat-colour posters with sharp type, which png compresses far better), and hunted for a media-library upload url. all of it rediscovering **trap 4 above**, in a file i had appended two entries to earlier the same day. trap 4's condition — "if a landing-page card will do" — had just become true, because the five bounty landing pages had been given correct server-rendered `og:title`, `og:description` and `og:image`. `create_ad_post` with a bare url and no `media_keys` produced four correctly-branded ads in four calls and zero uploads. **ads pointed at a url rarely need uploaded creative.** give the landing page real og tags and let x build the card. reach for `media_upload` only when the image is the message. 16. **a client-side title is invisible to the ad.** `document.title = ...` fixes the browser tab and nothing else: x builds the link-card headline from the **served html**, and never runs the page's javascript. a bug-bounty ad ran previewing as "open bounty — iris bounty os" while the tab said "bug bounty — iris platform", because the fix had been verified by looking at the tab. before pointing an ad at any url, run `iris playbook run page-seo-audit "<the exact url including query string>" -y`. it fetches with curl, which is what a link card does. a page can also have every og tag present and still be wrong — inheriting the site-wide default is how `/downloads` previewed as "iris - business operations system" to everyone who clicked a signup link. ## before any creative: the order is templates → kit → ad (2026-09-01) 17. **the layouts already exist. choosing one is the job; designing one is not.** twenty-five slide components sit under `remotion/src/carousel/` — mastheadslide, indexslide, flyerslide, splitsheetslide, pingslide, tallyslide, fineprintslide and more — and both brand kits (`/p/iris-brand-kit`, `/p/freelabel-brand-kit`) already name the inks, the type roles and what each layout is for. the `editorial-ad` playbook maps copy shape to form: announcing something -> masthead a dateline and a band read as news listing n capabilities -> index numbering makes a list finite one line that is the product-> quote give the sentence the whole canvas comparing specs or tiers -> ledger label -> value rows on hairlines one number that carries it -> stat the figure is the hero a brief written on 2026-09-01 invented hero objects and palettes for three campaigns without opening either kit. all of it already existed, named, with a rule attached. **read the kit first; the ad is copy poured into a chosen form.** 18. **the 110px rule disqualifies document layouts for paid social.** from the freelabel kit, on flyer: *"the only layout that survives the profile grid — at 110px a document is grey mush and this reads clean."* an ad is seen at that size in a feed. measured cost of ignoring it: the press campaign ran split sheet, run sheet and patch list — all document-dense — as paid ads. **8,348 impressions, 2 clicks, $6.29 per click**, against $0.0057 for a poster-format bounty ad on the same account in the same week. two of the four line items produced zero clicks across 3,432 impressions. render full size, then look at it at 110px before approving. if it is mush, use flyer and carry the argument as three lines. 19. **the landing page's `og:image` is part of the creative.** a text-only ad's "creative" is the link card, built from the destination's og tags. on 2026-09-01 an iris ad reached **6,500 views showing a grey placeholder** because `/downloads` had no `og:image` — and `app.blade.php` picks the card format from whether an image exists, so the missing image also silently downgraded `twitter:card` from `summary_large_image` to the small `summary`. one missing field cost both the artwork and the format. **run `iris playbook run page-seo-audit "<exact destination incl. query string>" -y` before promoting anything.** it fetches with curl, which is what a link card does. a poster in the post and a placeholder in the card is still a broken ad. 20. **`page-seo-audit` reports "7 passed" and prints none of the values it checked.** run on 2026-09-02 against all four ad destinations, it returned seven green ticks in 1.9s — title, og, generic, match, canonical, image, verdict — and not one actual tag. a pass you cannot see the evidence for is the same instrument this file keeps warning about: it cannot distinguish "the tag is correct" from "the check did not really look". **read the tags yourself before promoting.** and read them with something that survives quoting — the first attempt here used a shell loop with nested quotes inside `grep -oe`, which reported **`og:title: ** missing **`, `og:image: ** missing **` on all four pages**. every one of them was present and correct. the script had failed to run, and printed the same word it would have printed if the pages were genuinely broken. a working reader, which is what a link card does: **also check the image ratio, which the audit does not.** `summary_large_image` wants ~1.91:1. `fllogo.png` is **2000x2000** and was serving as the og:image for two different campaigns at once — x crops a square, and two campaigns shipping one cropped logo is two ads with the same weak creative. fixed by rendering `flyerslidewide` (1200x675, ratio 1.78) per destination, so each card shows its own poster. 21. **a stale link card cannot be busted with a query string — the canonical collapses them. re-scrape it with the card validator, which a browser agent can drive.** on 2026-09-02, four destination pages had their titles, descriptions and og:images corrected. every ad post created afterwards still carried the old card: creator os previewed as *"free rung forever, you keep 100% of your rights"* — the exact copy that had just been removed — with the superseded long title and the old logo. `curl` on the live page returned the new tags. **x was serving a cached card, and the ad would have shipped the retired copy to paid impressions.** the obvious fix fails. appending `?utm_source=x&utm_medium=paid&utm_campaign=…` produced a byte-identical stale card, because the page carries `<link rel="canonical" href=" and **x keys its card cache on the canonical**, so every query-string variant resolves to one entry. verified: two `create_ad_post` calls, different urls, same cached `card_img` id. **what works: ` (redirects to `cards-dev.x.com`), driven through the browser agent.** it forces a re-crawl. the log is the confirmation — `page fetched successfully` / `n metatags were found` / `twitter:card = … tag found` / `card loaded successfully`. the very next `create_ad_post` returned the corrected title, description and image. note the page says *"card preview has moved to tweet composer"*: the preview pane is gone, but **the re-scrape still happens** and the log still prints. driving it — react-controlled input, so set the value through the native setter or the field reverts on submit: loop it over every destination before promoting. **unverified:** this ran in a browser already signed in as the ads account, so whether the validator re-scrapes for a logged-out visitor was not tested — assume login is needed until someone checks. **the general rule: after changing any og tag, the page is fixed and the card is not.** `page-seo-audit` and `curl` read the page; a link card reads x's cache of the page. those are different instruments answering different questions, and only the second one is what the ad displays. ## `approval_status: accepted` is not an approval — re-read it `promote_post` returns `accepted` at attach time for **every** post, including ones that are rejected seconds later. on 2026-08-23 the hashtag rejection landed 30s after a green-looking attach. nothing in `get_campaign` or `list_line_items` reflects it: campaign `running`, line item `active`, `servable: true`, `reasons_not_servable: []` — all healthy, zero impressions. `list_promoted_posts(account_id=..., line_item_ids="<id>")` → `approval_status` is the closest the api gets. **`rejected` there is trustworthy. `accepted` there is not.** *(sharpened 2026-08-24, second pass. the first version of this section said this was "the only api surface that shows it" and to re-read at ~60s — implying `accepted` after the wait meant approved. it does not.)* promoting the five `[mk-08]` posts produced, after seven minutes of polling: | ad | api `approval_status` | `updated_at` moved? | ads manager | |---|---|---|---| | all those jobs | **accepted** | no | **halted — adult content** | | more than talent | rejected | yes | halted — adult content | | teams of 50 / while you sleep / minimal hype | accepted | no / no / yes | active | **the mechanism, pinned down the next morning: `list_promoted_posts` serves stale cached reads.** it is not that review is slow. re-reading the same records ~9 hours later returned: | ad | status then (03:26) | status now | its `updated_at` | |---|---|---|---| | all those jobs | accepted, `updated_at` unmoved | **rejected** | **03:21:54** | | teams of 50 | accepted, unmoved | accepted | 03:21:29 | | while you sleep | accepted, unmoved | accepted | 03:22:05 | those `updated_at` values are all *earlier* than the 03:26 poll that reported them unmoved. the records had already been decided; the api handed back a stale copy — including a stale `updated_at` — for minutes afterward. so "`updated_at` hasn't moved" proves nothing at all: it is not evidence of pending review, it can simply be the cached row. **the ads manager ads tab (`?tab=ads`) is the authoritative delivery status**, and it was right in real time while the api was wrong. use the api to catch a fast `rejected`; use the ui to confirm anything is actually serving. never conclude "still in review" from an unmoved timestamp. **rejection reasons seen so far:** *"ads cannot include hashtags in the ad text"* and **"adult content"** — the latter on ordinary creator-business copy ("you're an artist, not an accountant"), i.e. the classifier is noisy. a wrong-looking category is worth appealing; the ads tab shows an **appeal** button when appeal is still open, versus **appeal declined** when it is spent. **the rejection reason is not in the api at all.** ads manager → campaign row → "n suggestions" → *review in editor* prints it under "1 issue needs to be fixed before publishing". the ads tab only shows `halted` / `appeal declined`, which does not say why — and "appeal declined" can appear within a minute of creation, so it means *auto-declined*, not that a human reviewed anything. **corollary — do not diagnose a halted ad from its copy.** the first read here guessed a financial-claims policy ("get paid", "real payouts") and was wrong; the real cause was one trailing `#bounty`. read the editor string before changing anything. **confirmed working order, end to end:** `create_ad_post` (nullcast, short text, no media) → `create_campaign` (paused) → `create_line_item` (paused, `bid_strategy="max"` + `bid_amount_local_micro` set) → `search_targeting_locations` → `add_targeting_criterion` → `promote_post` (attach the ad-post tweet id) → gate → `activate_campaign` → `activate_line_item` → `get_campaign` to independently re-verify (`entity_status: active`, `effective_status` may read `scheduled` with `reasons_not_servable: ["starts_in_future"]` if `start_time` is a few minutes out — that is expected, not a failure). **the sxsw near-miss above was resolved during this same session**: `oe3y5` was independently re-read (`entity_status: active`, `effective_status: running`, `servable: true`), paused on alex's explicit instruction, and re-verified (`entity_status: paused`, `servable: false`) — the update response was not trusted alone. ## money units every budget field in the x api is `*_local_micro` = **dollars × 1,000,000**. `10000000` is $10.00. this playbook takes dollars as arguments and converts once, explicitly, at the boundary. never hand-edit a micro value. ## steps --- ## six more, from a creative test (2026-08-28 · 2026-08-29) 11. **`link_clicks: null` is not `link_clicks: 0`.** three image creatives ran 1,309 impressions reporting `link_clicks: null`, `clicks: null`, `card_engagements: null`. the control alongside them reported `link_clicks: [1]`. **`null` means the metric does not exist for that creative — there is no link to count.** an image post attached to an `engagements` line item carries no website card, and if the copy has no url either, the ad is unclickable. it still earns likes and replies, so it looks like a working ad with poor click-through. read `null` as *"no link"*, never as *"nobody clicked"*. 12. **a root redirect on the landing domain can eat the whole query string.** if the destination host answers `/` with a redirect built by string concatenation rather than by preserving the request uri, every `?utm_source=` dies at the first hop — before any analytics sees it. downstream, "which ad produced this signup?" is not answered wrongly, it is **unanswerable**, which reads exactly like a campaign that produced nothing. test it with one command before spending anything: `curl -ssi " | grep -i location` if `utm_source` is missing from the `location`, the campaign cannot be measured. 13. **there is no way to detach a promoted post via the api.** `promote_post` attaches; no tool removes. `update_line_item` cannot change `entity_status`. so a "replacement" creative does not replace anything — both serve, and delivery splits between them. if the old one is broken, half the spend stays broken. detach in ads manager, or build the replacement on a **new line item** rather than the same one. 14. **`create_card` rejects its own `components` payload** (`components: '' is not a valid seq`) whether the json is compact or spaced. website cards are not currently buildable through this surface. put the url in the post text instead — x renders it as a link and `link_clicks` tracks normally. 15. **comparing a carousel against a single image on raw engagement rate is rigged.** `carousel_swipes` count as engagements and a single image cannot earn them. in one run the carousel's headline rate was ~4× its swipe-adjusted rate, which flattered the old creative and would have killed three better ones. **subtract `carousel_swipes` from `engagements` before comparing anything to anything.** 16. **equal budget and equal bid do not produce equal delivery.** four line items at identical `$2.50/day` and identical `$1.50` bids delivered 2,353 / 587 / 409 / 313 impressions. the oldest post — with engagement history and a card format — won the auction repeatedly. **the incumbent creative starves the challengers of the very sample you are paying to collect.** cap the incumbent's daily budget, or raise the challengers' bids, or the test never resolves. --- # reusable models *generalized from running this. nothing below is specific to one advertiser — these are the patterns that transfer.* ## model 1 · the pre-flight: can this click even be counted? most wasted ad spend is not bad targeting or bad creative. it is a **broken chain** where every individual link reports healthy. walk it before spending, in this order, because each step invalidates everything after it: every one of these fails silently. a linkless ad earns engagements. a stripped utm returns a valid 302. a cta-less landing page returns 200. an unpixelled page looks identical to a pixelled one with no conversions. **a chain of green lights is not evidence the chain works** — it is evidence that nothing in it is instrumented to go red. ## model 2 · normalize before you compare creatives different ad formats earn different *free* engagements. carousels earn swipes; videos earn partial views; polls earn votes. comparing formats on the headline rate compares formats, not messages. report it per thousand impressions, alongside cost per comparable engagement. if you cannot name what the freebie is for a given format, you cannot compare that format to another one yet. ## model 3 · the control that eats the test an a/b against an incumbent has a structural bias: the incumbent has history, and ad auctions reward history. left alone it will take most of the delivery *and* most of the spend, while the challengers accumulate samples too small to decide anything. **cap the control at roughly a quarter of the challengers' budget.** you need it running for a concurrent baseline — auction conditions change day to day, so a historical baseline is worth less than a live one — but you do not need it running at parity. watch spend share, not just budget: equal budgets can still produce a 60/40 spend split. ## model 4 · where to send cold traffic — the direction rule when choosing between a **content/browse surface** and a **pitch/landing page**, do not argue about which is more on-brand. measure the *direction* between them: **send cold traffic to whichever page keeps both doors open.** usually that is the pitch, because a pitch page is designed to link outward and a feed is designed to retain. the browse surface is for people who already know who you are; ads are, by definition, for people who do not. then verify by searching the *rendered* text of the destination for the words a buyer needs — "sign up", "pricing", "get started". if none appear, the page cannot convert regardless of how good it looks. ## model 5 · reading null vs zero, generally this recurs across every ads and analytics api: | reading | means | looks like | |---|---|---| | `null` / absent | the metric does not apply — nothing is wired | a zero | | `0` | wired, measured, nobody did it | a zero | | `"last recorded: —"` | the event has never fired | a zero | | a stale cached row | already decided, you got an old copy | "still pending" | **a dashboard renders all four as `0`.** before drawing any conclusion from a zero, find the field that distinguishes "not measured" from "measured as none". if no such field exists, the number cannot support a conclusion in either direction. ## model 6 · one promise, n proofs when one advertiser sells several products, per-product ads fragment the budget and each one has to win its own audience from scratch. the alternative: find the **single claim** all the products happen to make, advertise that, and let each product be evidence for it. test for it — write each product's value in one plain sentence, then look for the word that repeats. if the products genuinely share a promise, that promise usually outperforms any individual feature claim, because it survives reaching the wrong person: a broad promise still lands on someone outside the target segment, and a feature does not. ## model 7 · frequency tells you whether you have an audience problem yet `get_campaign_reach` returns `average_frequency` alongside reach. at **~1.0**, essentially nobody has seen the ad twice — the audience is untouched and any weak result is a *creative* or *offer* signal, not fatigue. fatigue arguments only become available once frequency is meaningfully above 1. check it before concluding an audience is exhausted. ## the rule under all seven **prefer the instrument that can distinguish "broken" from "not measured".** most of the traps in this playbook are the same defect wearing different clothes: a check that returns the same value whether the thing works or was never connected. when you can only afford one verification, spend it on the step that would otherwise fail silently.

entries.haystack: xart-exhibit-deck x-art exhibit deck — pick the works, get the deck <!-- auto-generated by iris playbook sync — do not edit --> --- name: xart-exhibit-deck description: build a client-ready exhibit deck for experience art (x-art) from works in the xart-listing dataset. two lanes — a prompt handoff that keeps claude's design interface for refinement (live today), and direct generation that returns a finished .pptx with no copy-paste (v2, not built). pass an action or an event brief as argument (e.g., "prompt 2026-09-12 dallas", "works burning-man", "status", "setup-brand", "check-data"). allowed-tools: - read - write - edit - grep - glob - bash --- > run this playbook: `iris playbook run xart-exhibit-deck ` # x-art exhibit deck — pick the works, get the deck experience art pitches events by assembling a deck of specific artworks for a specific client, date and venue. the picker is live on their dashboard; this playbook is the procedure behind it, and the place the deck's rules live so the picker, the agent, and devon's portal all build the same deck. ## arguments `$arguments` — action and parameters. examples: - `/xart-exhibit-deck prompt 2026-09-12 "deep ellum, dallas"` — build the deck prompt for an event - `/xart-exhibit-deck prompt 2026-09-12 dallas --works=12,17,23` — restrict to specific listings - `/xart-exhibit-deck works` — list what is actually in `xart-listing` right now - `/xart-exhibit-deck works --category=sculpture` — filter the catalogue - `/xart-exhibit-deck check-data` — report field completeness and known defects before building - `/xart-exhibit-deck setup-brand` — the one-time brand-token extraction (currently blocking lane b) - `/xart-exhibit-deck status` — what is live, what is blocked, what is undecided ## the two lanes **lane a — prompt handoff. live today.** the picker writes the prompt, a person pastes it into claude, the deck comes back. this is what the `deckbuilder` component on the dashboard does now. **lane b — direct generation. not built, and not yet decided.** our backend calls the messages api, claude builds the file, we hand back a finished `.pptx`. do not treat lane b as strictly better. arthur made the counter-argument on 14 aug and it is a good one: claude's own interface beats anything we would build for minute tweaks — *"the logo's the wrong size, make it bigger"* — and it is usable by people on the team who do not otherwise touch ai. lane b removes the copy-paste on the first draft; it does not improve the draft, which is already ~90% right. **the recommendation is both, not a replacement**: generate the first pass automatically, and still hand back the prompt so refinement continues where refinement is good. the decision belongs to devon, who owns the product build of this tool. ## where the works come from canonical source is the **`xart-listing`** dataset — 28 works, schema v2 as of 14 aug. google drive is the upstream source; the dataset is the queryable layer the picker and this playbook read. get the live feed url from the page rather than hardcoding it (feeds are minted with a column allowlist and can be re-minted): ### fields you can rely on | field | notes | |---|---| | `title`, `artist`, `category` | populated | | `year` | 27 of 28. one genuinely has no year at source (*balloon compositions*) | | `dimensions` | object — `{length, width, height, unit}`. 25 of 28 parsed | | `dimensions_raw` | the 3 that are genuinely non-numeric (*various dimensions*, *variable footprint* ×2), preserved verbatim | | `images` | populated on all 28 | | `description_short` | **empty by design.** needs a human-written factual sentence | | `description_long` | **empty by design, and internal-only — see the hard rule below** | | `location` | **null on all 28.** known ingestion defect; the zip exists at source | ### hard rules 1. **never put `description_long` in a deck, a prompt, or anything a client sees.** arthur: the long form is the *"nice, long, complex, contemplative"* explanation and he would never want it published. it is excluded from the public feed by an explicit column allowlist, so it cannot leak through that path — do not reintroduce it by reading the dataset directly. 2. **do not invent works, dimensions, or years.** if a field is empty it is empty; say so or leave it out. there are 28 works, not more. 3. **do not render `location` from the dataset** until the mapping defect is fixed — it is null on every record and will print blank. 4. **use `dimensions_raw` when `dimensions` is absent**, rather than dropping the piece or guessing a number. "various dimensions" is the correct thing to show. ## the brand system — this is what blocks lane b the deck's whole value is that it looks like x-art. today that brand system lives **inside claude design as a project**, which is exactly why lane a works and lane b cannot: the api has no access to it. ⚠️ **verified 14 aug: there is no x-art brand in the brand system.** `iris brands list` returns 13 brands and none is theirs. so this is a real, unmet dependency — not a lookup someone forgot. the one-time setup, once arthur exports the guide: after that, `iris brands dt get xart` is the single source for palette, type and rules — and the deck procedure reads from it rather than restating brand values here. **brand values have one home; this playbook is not it.** ## lane a — build the prompt 1. resolve the works: all of `xart-listing`, or the subset passed via `--works` / `--category`. 2. compose per work: title, artist, year, dimensions (or `dimensions_raw`), and the image. 3. compose the brief: event date, venue, client. 4. emit the prompt. the shape the live picker uses: > build a client-ready pitch deck for an event on `{date}` at `{location}`, featuring the following > works: `{items}`. use the x-art brand style guide. one slide per work, with the artist and dimensions. hand it over — do not try to improve on claude's design output from here. ## lane b — direct generation (design notes, not yet implemented) for whoever builds it. there is **no "claude design api"** — claude design is the claude.ai interface. what is callable is the **messages api**, so this is a backend service in `fl-iris-api` (never call the model from the frontend — backend-centric integration rule). producing an actual `.pptx` has two viable routes: - **the `pptx` agent skill** — claude writes and runs code in a sandboxed container and returns a file id we download via the files api. closest to arthur's "spit back out a powerpoint". - **structured slides + our own renderer** — claude returns slide json, we render through x-art's real `.pptx` template. more work, but output matches their template exactly rather than claude's interpretation of it. generation is slow enough to need streaming and a progress ui — minutes, not seconds. whichever route, the brand system arrives from the design tokens above, not from a prompt string pasted into the code. ## status | piece | state | |---|---| | picker on the dashboard, reading `xart-listing` | **live** — no longer 28 hardcoded pieces | | `xart-listing` v2 (dimensions object, year, short/long) | **live**, 28 records migrated | | lane a prompt handoff | **live** | | `description_short` / `description_long` content | **empty** — needs human authoring | | `location` mapping | **broken** — null on all 28 | | x-art brand tokens | **does not exist** — blocks lane b | | lane b direct generation | **not built, not decided** — devon's call | ## related - project bloq **#570** — experience art, agentic os & company brain - dashboard: `/p/experience-art-dashboard` · architecture: `/p/experience-art-iris-architecture` - deck v2 decision is parked deliberately, not forgotten — see the pinned item on the bloq
